docs.title: 4.1.1 Deep Vein Thrombosis / Pulmonary Embolism (DVT/PE)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I82.409

Deep vein thrombosis is clot formation within the deep venous system, usually in the calf, thigh, or pelvic veins. The clot may cause a local problem at the site of formation or may dislodge and lead to thromboembolism in other parts of the body, particularly the lungs, resulting in pulmonary embolism.

Causes

  • Venous stasis, meaning slowing of blood flow
  • Increased coagulability states
  • Endothelial injury

Risk factors

  • Immobilisation, prolonged bed rest, surgery, or limb paralysis
  • Heart failure or myocardial infarction
  • Blunt trauma or venous injury, including cannulation
  • Oral contraceptive pill use
  • Pregnancy and postpartum period
  • Malignancies and some forms of chemotherapy
  • Long-distance air travel
  • Inherited thrombophilic states

Clinical features

Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism may be clinically silent in some patients.

Features of deep vein thrombosis may include:

  • Pain, swelling, and warmth of the calf, thigh, or groin

Features of pulmonary embolism may include:

  • Dyspnoea
  • Tachycardia
  • Chest pain
  • Hypotension

Half of pulmonary embolism cases may be associated with silent DVT.

Differential diagnosis

For DVT:

  • Cellulitis
  • Myositis
  • Phlebitis
  • Contusion

For pulmonary embolism:

  • Bronchopneumonia
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Other causes of dyspnoea and chest pain

Investigations

  • Compression ultrasound with or without Doppler
  • In suspected pulmonary embolism, chest CT angiogram
  • Other useful but non-specific tests:
    • Blood D-dimer
    • ECG
    • Chest X-ray
    • Echocardiogram

Management

Treatment LOC Give enoxaparin, a low molecular weight heparin, 1 mg/kg every 12 hours for at least 5 days. No routine monitoring is required. H Start warfarin 5 mg as a single evening dose on the same day as heparin. Continue overlap treatment with heparin and warfarin. Stop heparin when warfarin achieves an optimal INR of 2–3. H Continue warfarin maintenance dose as a single daily dose, adjusted according to INR. Typical maintenance dose may range from 2.5 mg to 7.5 mg daily. Some patients may require higher maintenance doses, especially where interacting medicines are present. H If enoxaparin is not available, give unfractionated heparin 5,000 units IV bolus, then 1,000 units hourly, or 17,500 units subcutaneously every 12 hours for 5 days. Adjust dose according to activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). H Alternative unfractionated heparin regimen: give 333 units/kg subcutaneously as an initial dose, followed by 250 units/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours. Use with warfarin as above. H

Alternative to warfarin and heparin combination

Rivaroxaban may be used as an alternative anticoagulant.

  • No need to initiate with heparin.
  • Give rivaroxaban 15 mg orally twice daily for 3 weeks, then 20 mg once daily for the duration of anticoagulation.
  • Patients should take the medicine at the same time every day to prevent re-thrombosis.
  • Do not use in pregnant or breastfeeding mothers.
  • It is associated with reduced bleeding risk compared with warfarin.

Apixaban may also be used as an alternative anticoagulant.

  • Give apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily for the duration of anticoagulation.
  • It is associated with reduced bleeding risk compared with warfarin.
  • Do not use in pregnant or breastfeeding mothers.

Notes

  • Monitor for bleeding complications.
  • When using apixaban, patients should be encouraged to ambulate as soon as possible.
  • See section 1.3.10 for treatment of warfarin overdose and the PGD 2015 monograph on protamine for excessive heparin dose.
  • Do not start therapy with warfarin alone because it initially increases the risk of thrombus progression.
  • Encourage early mobilisation.
  • Provide prophylaxis with enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily in acutely ill medical patients and in prolonged admission.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Infective Endocarditis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I33.0

Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart valves and the lining of the heart chambers by microorganisms. It is usually bacterial and rarely fungal.

Causes

Infective endocarditis is classified into three main types:

  • Sub-acute endocarditis: usually caused by low-virulence organisms such as Streptococcus viridans.
  • Acute endocarditis: usually caused by common pyogenic organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Post-operative endocarditis: occurs after cardiac surgery or prosthetic heart valve placement. The most common organism involved is Staphylococcus aureus.

Clinical features

The disease may present as acute or chronic depending on the microorganism involved and the patient’s condition.

Common clinical features include:

  • Fatigue and weight loss
  • Low-grade fever and chills, or acute severe septicaemia
  • Embolic phenomena affecting different organs, including the brain
  • Heart failure
  • Prominent or changing heart murmurs
  • Splenomegaly or hepatomegaly
  • Anaemia
  • Splinter haemorrhages in the nail bed or retina
  • Finger clubbing

The diagnostic triad is:

  • Persistent fever
  • Emboli
  • Changing murmur

Risk factors

  • Rheumatic heart disease
  • Congenital heart disease
  • Prosthetic valve
  • Invasive dental, diagnostic, or surgical procedures, including cardiac catheterisation
  • Immunosuppression
  • Intravenous drug use

Note

Any unexplained fever in a patient with a heart valve problem should be regarded as possible infective endocarditis.

Differential diagnosis

  • Cardiac failure with heart murmurs
  • Febrile conditions associated with anaemia

Investigations

  • Blood cultures. These are usually positive, and all efforts should be made to identify the responsible pathogen and obtain sensitivity data.
  • At least three sets of blood cultures, 8 mL each, should be obtained from separate venepuncture sites at least one hour apart.
  • Complete blood count
  • ESR
  • Urinalysis for microscopic haematuria and proteinuria
  • Echocardiography
  • ECG

Management

Treatment LOC Bed rest. H Treat complications, such as heart failure. H Start initial empirical antibiotic therapy with benzylpenicillin 5 MU IV every 6 hours for 4 weeks. H Children: benzylpenicillin 50,000 IU/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 weeks. H Add gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 2 weeks. RR If staphylococcal infection is suspected, especially with acute onset, add cloxacillin 3 g IV every 6 hours. RR Children: cloxacillin 50 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 weeks. RR If MRSA is suspected, give vancomycin 500 mg IV every 6 hours. RR Children: vancomycin 10 mg/kg IV, infused over 1 hour, every 6 hours for 6 weeks. RR Once the pathogen has been identified, amend treatment according to culture and sensitivity results. RR

Prevention

For patients at risk, such as those with valvular defects, congenital heart disease, or prosthetic valves, give prophylaxis before dental procedures and tonsillectomy.

  • Give amoxicillin 2 g as a single dose 1 hour before the procedure.
  • For children, give amoxicillin 50 mg/kg as a single dose 1 hour before the procedure.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Heart Failure
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I50

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome caused by inadequate cardiac output for the body’s needs despite adequate venous return.

For management purposes, heart failure may be classified as:

  • Congestive or acute heart failure
  • Chronic heart failure
  • Acute pulmonary oedema. See section 4.1.4.

Causes

  • Hypertension
  • Valvular heart disease, such as rheumatic heart disease
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Myocarditis
  • Prolonged rapid irregular heartbeat or arrhythmias
  • Congenital heart disease
  • Severe anaemia
  • Thyroid disease

Clinical features in infants and young children

  • Respiratory distress with rapid breathing
  • Cyanosis
  • Wheezing
  • Subcostal, intercostal, or sternal recession
  • Rapid pulse
  • Gallop rhythm
  • Excessive sweating
  • Tender hepatomegaly
  • Difficulty with feeding
  • Cardiomegaly

Clinical features in older children and adults

  • Palpitations
  • Shortness of breath
  • Exercise intolerance
  • Fatigue
  • Orthopnoea
  • Exertional dyspnoea
  • Wheezing
  • Rapid pulse
  • Gallop rhythm
  • Raised jugular venous pressure
  • Dependent oedema
  • Enlarged tender liver
  • Basal crepitations

Differential diagnosis

  • Severe anaemia
  • Severe acute malnutrition
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Cirrhosis
  • Severe pneumonia
  • Any severe illness in infants

Investigations

  • Chest X-ray
  • Haemogram, including assessment for anaemia
  • ESR
  • Urea and electrolytes
  • Echocardiogram
  • ECG

Management of acute or congestive heart failure

Treatment LOC Bed rest with the head of the bed elevated. HC4 Prop up the patient in a sitting position. HC4 Reduce salt intake and limit fluid intake to 1–1.5 L/day. HC4 Give furosemide 20–40 mg orally or IV daily or every 12 hours, increasing as required to 80–160 mg according to response. HC4 Children: furosemide 1 mg/kg orally or IV daily or every 12 hours according to response. Maximum dose: 8 mg/kg/day. HC4 Start ACE inhibitors at a low dose. Give enalapril 2.5 mg once daily and increase gradually over 2 weeks to 10–20 mg, maximum 40 mg, if tolerated. Alternatively, give lisinopril 5 mg once daily and increase gradually over 2 weeks to 40 mg. H Children: enalapril 0.1–1 mg/kg/day in 1–2 divided doses. H Alternatively, give captopril 6.25–12.5 mg every 8–12 hours and increase over 2–4 weeks to a maximum of 150 mg/day in divided doses. H Children: captopril 0.1–0.3 mg/kg every 8–12 hours. H If available, and when the patient is stable, add carvedilol 3.125 mg every 12 hours and increase gradually every 2 weeks to a maximum of 25 mg every 12 hours. Alternatively, give bisoprolol 1.25 mg once daily and increase gradually to a maximum of 10 mg once daily. H Children: carvedilol 0.05 mg/kg every 12 hours and increase gradually to a maximum of 0.35 mg/kg every 12 hours. H

Additional medicines

Treatment LOC Spironolactone 25–50 mg once daily. H Children: spironolactone initially 1.5–3 mg/kg/day in divided doses. H Digoxin 125–250 micrograms daily. HC4 Children: digoxin maintenance dose 15 micrograms/kg/day. HC4

Caution

Use ACE inhibitors and beta blockers with caution if systolic blood pressure is less than 90 mmHg. Monitor renal function.

Use digoxin with caution in elderly patients and in patients with renal disease.

Prevention

  • Manage risk factors.
  • Diagnose and treat the underlying cause early, such as hypertension.
  • Support treatment adherence.

Chronic heart failure

Patients with chronic heart failure need continuous treatment to control symptoms and prevent disease progression and complications.

Management of chronic heart failure

Treatment LOC Periodic monitoring of body weight, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation. HC2 Salt and fluid restriction. HC2 Limit alcohol intake. HC2 Regular exercise within the limits of symptoms. HC2 Continue treatment with the medicines listed above, with doses progressively increased to achieve control. HC4

docs.title: 4.1.4 Pulmonary Oedema
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I50.21

Pulmonary oedema may be:

  • Cardiogenic
  • Due to severe fluid overload, such as renal failure or iatrogenic fluid overload
  • Non-cardiogenic, such as severe pneumonia, altitude sickness, inhalation of toxic gases, or acute respiratory distress syndrome

Clinical features

  • Severe dyspnoea
  • Rapid breathing
  • Breathlessness
  • Tachycardia
  • Wheezing
  • Cough with frothy blood-stained sputum

Differential diagnosis

  • Pneumonia
  • Pleural effusion
  • Foreign body
  • Trauma, including pneumothorax or pulmonary contusion

Investigations

  • Chest X-ray
  • ECG
  • Renal function tests
  • Electrolytes
  • Echocardiography

Management

Treatment LOC Prop up the patient in a sitting position. HC4 Give high-concentration oxygen. Start with 5 L/min and aim for SpO₂ >95%. HC4 Give furosemide 40–80 mg IM or slow IV. Repeat as needed up to every 2 hours according to response. HC4 Children: give furosemide 0.5–1.5 mg/kg every 8–12 hours. Maximum dose: 6 mg/kg/day. HC4 Give glyceryl trinitrate 500 micrograms sublingually every 4–6 hours. H Give morphine 5–15 mg IM or 2–4 mg slow IV. HC4 Children: give morphine 0.1 mg/kg slow IV as a single dose. HC4 Repeat the above measures every 4–6 hours until there is improvement. HC4 Consider digoxin loading dose IV 250 micrograms, given 3–4 times in the first 24 hours, then maintenance dose of 125–250 micrograms daily. H Children: give digoxin 10 micrograms/kg per dose as above, then maintenance dose of 15 micrograms/kg/day. H

Caution

Do not give a digoxin loading dose if the patient has had digoxin within the past 14 days. Give maintenance dose only.

Prevention

  • Diagnose and treat cardiac conditions early.
  • Support compliance with treatment for chronic cardiac conditions.
  • Avoid fluid overload.

docs.title: 4.1.5 Atrial Fibrillation
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I48

Atrial fibrillation is a common cardiac arrhythmia characterised by an irregular pulse due to loss of regular atrial electrical activity. Its onset may be acute or chronic, and it may be symptomatic or asymptomatic.

Risk factors

  • Heart disease, including:
    • Heart failure
    • Valvular heart disease
    • Ischaemic heart disease
  • Thyroid disease, especially hyperthyroidism

Clinical features

  • Irregular pulse in frequency and volume
  • Heart rate may be normal or very high
  • Acute onset, often with high heart rate, may present with:
    • Palpitations
    • Dizziness
    • Fainting
    • Chest pain
    • Shortness of breath
  • Chronic atrial fibrillation with normal or near-normal heart rate may be asymptomatic and discovered during routine checks
  • May precipitate heart failure or pulmonary oedema
  • May cause embolic stroke if clots form in the heart and dislodge to the cerebral circulation

Investigations

  • ECG

Objectives of management

  • Control heart rate
  • Restore normal rhythm where possible, under specialist care
  • Prevent or treat complications
  • Treat underlying conditions

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute onset, high heart rate, or patient in congestive heart failure and/or pulmonary oedema Treat heart failure according to section 4.1.3. Use digoxin and/or carvedilol or bisoprolol to reduce heart rate. HC4 Acute onset with high heart rate but no signs of heart failure Use atenolol 50 mg to control heart rate. HC4 Chronic atrial fibrillation with normal heart rate Treat underlying conditions only. H Need for stroke prevention assessment Refer to regional level to assess indication for anticoagulation with aspirin or warfarin to prevent stroke. H

docs.title: 4.1.6 Hypertension
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I10

Hypertension is persistently high resting blood pressure, defined as blood pressure >140/90 mmHg on at least two measurements taken five minutes apart with the patient seated, and confirmed on at least 2 or 3 occasions one week apart.

Classification of blood pressure

Category SBP, mmHg DBP, mmHg Normal <120 and <80 Pre-hypertension 120–139 or 80–89 Hypertension, stage 1 140–159 or 90–99 Hypertension, stage 2 ≥160 or ≥100

SBP = systolic blood pressure. DBP = diastolic blood pressure.

Causes

In most cases, the cause is not known. This is referred to as essential hypertension.

Secondary hypertension may be associated with:

  • Kidney disease
  • Endocrine disease
  • Eclampsia or pre-eclampsia
  • Medicines, including steroids and decongestants containing caffeine or pseudoephedrine

Risk factors

  • Family history
  • Race
  • Obesity
  • Physical inactivity
  • Excessive salt intake
  • Excessive alcohol intake
  • Diabetes
  • Dyslipidaemia

Clinical features

Most patients are asymptomatic and are diagnosed during routine examination or screening.

General symptoms may include:

  • Headache
  • Palpitations
  • Dizziness

Hypertension may also present through complications affecting:

  • Brain, such as stroke
  • Heart, such as heart failure
  • Kidney, such as renal failure
  • Eyes, such as impaired vision

Differential diagnosis

  • Anxiety

Investigations

Investigations are done to identify complications and possible secondary causes of hypertension.

  • Urinalysis
  • Blood sugar
  • Plasma urea and electrolytes
  • Chest X-ray
  • ECG

Management of hypertension

Target blood pressure is below 140/90 mmHg.

For patients with high cardiovascular disease risk, such as diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke, or chronic kidney disease, the target blood pressure is <130/80 mmHg.

Hypertension, stage 1

Step Treatment LOC Step 1 Lifestyle adjustment: do not add extra salt to cooked food, increase physical activity or exercise, reduce body weight, stop smoking, and decrease alcohol intake. HC3 Step 2 If lifestyle measures fail within 3 months, initiate medicine therapy while continuing lifestyle changes. Give amlodipine 5 mg once daily. HC3 Follow-up If blood pressure is not controlled after 1 month, treat as stage 2 hypertension. HC3

Hypertension, stage 2

Step Treatment LOC Step 3 Give amlodipine 5 mg once daily plus an angiotensin II receptor blocker, such as losartan 50 mg, valsartan 80 mg, or telmisartan 40 mg once daily. Instead of an ARB, an ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril 20 mg or enalapril 5 mg once daily may be used. HC3 Step 4 If blood pressure remains ≥140/90 mmHg after 1 month, give amlodipine 10 mg once daily plus losartan 50 mg, valsartan 80 mg, or telmisartan 40 mg once daily. HC3 Step 5 If blood pressure remains ≥140/90 mmHg after 1 month, give amlodipine 10 mg once daily plus losartan 100 mg, valsartan 160 mg, or telmisartan 80 mg once daily, plus a thiazide diuretic such as hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg or bendroflumethiazide 5 mg once in the morning. HC3 Step 6 If blood pressure remains ≥140/90 mmHg after 1 month, continue amlodipine 10 mg once daily plus losartan 100 mg, valsartan 160 mg, or telmisartan 80 mg once daily, plus a thiazide diuretic such as hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg or bendroflumethiazide 5 mg once in the morning. HC3 Step 7 If blood pressure remains ≥140/90 mmHg, refer for further management at a higher level of care. HC3

Provision for specific patients

  • Assess cardiovascular disease risk in all patients with hypertension.
  • Patients with diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke, or chronic kidney disease are considered to have high cardiovascular disease risk.
  • In people with high cardiovascular disease risk, target blood pressure is <130/80 mmHg.
  • Start a statin, such as atorvastatin 20–40 mg once daily or simvastatin 20–40 mg once daily, in people at high risk.
  • Start aspirin 75 mg in people with a prior heart attack or ischaemic stroke.
  • Start a beta blocker, such as atenolol 50 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, or nebivolol 5 mg once daily, in people who had a heart attack within the past 3 years.
  • In patients with chronic kidney disease, a combination of an ACE inhibitor or ARB with a calcium channel blocker or diuretic is recommended as initial therapy.
  • For hypertension secondary to thyroid disease, consider adding propranolol 40 mg twice daily.

Caution

In pregnancy, do not use ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or diuretics. Methyldopa and calcium channel blockers are safe to use.

Do not use both an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together because of increased risk of side effects.

Choice of antihypertensive medicine

Choice of medicine may depend on concomitant risk factors or other conditions.

Risk factor / condition Suitable medicine consideration Heart failure Consider medicines appropriate for heart failure management, including ACE inhibitor or ARB, selected beta blocker, diuretic, and aldosterone antagonist where indicated. Post-myocardial infarction Consider beta blocker, ACE inhibitor or ARB, statin, and aspirin where indicated. Angina Consider beta blocker or calcium channel blocker where appropriate. Diabetes Consider ACE inhibitor or ARB, especially where kidney protection is needed. Mild or moderate kidney disease Consider ACE inhibitor or ARB, with renal function monitoring. Advanced chronic kidney disease Refer or manage with specialist input. Stroke Control blood pressure and manage cardiovascular risk according to stroke guidance. Beta blocker selection Where beta blocker use is indicated in heart failure, carvedilol or bisoprolol are preferred.

Prevention

  • Regular physical exercise
  • Reduced salt intake
  • Healthy diet
  • Smoking cessation
  • Periodic blood pressure screening

docs.title: 4.1.6.1 Hypertensive Emergencies and Urgency
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I16.2

Hypertensive emergency is blood pressure >180/110 mmHg with symptoms and acute life-threatening complications.

Complications may include:

  • Hypertensive encephalopathy, presenting with severe headache, confusion, seizures, or visual disturbances
  • Acute angina or acute myocardial infarction
  • Pulmonary oedema
  • Acute kidney failure
  • Acute aortic dissection
  • Eclampsia or pre-eclampsia. See sections 16.3.7 and 16.3.8.

Management of hypertensive emergency

Treatment LOC Admit the patient and give parenteral medicines. HC4 Aim to lower blood pressure over 24 hours. Do not lower blood pressure too rapidly unless absolutely necessary. HC4 Treat according to the presenting complication. HC4 In acute ischaemic stroke, do not lower blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg. HC4 In acute aortic dissection, lower blood pressure rapidly. HC4 In pulmonary oedema or acute myocardial infarction, treat the complication. HC4 Give IV furosemide 40–80 mg where indicated. HC4 If aggressive blood pressure lowering is needed, give IV hydralazine 5–10 mg slowly over 20 minutes. Check blood pressure regularly and repeat the dose after 20–30 minutes if necessary. HC4

Hypertensive urgency

Hypertensive urgency is blood pressure >180/110 mmHg without evidence of target organ damage, such as pulmonary oedema, cardiac ischaemia, neurological deficits, or acute renal failure.

Management of hypertensive urgency

Treatment LOC Admit the patient. HC4 Treat with a combination of oral antihypertensive therapy, such as ACE inhibitor or ARB plus calcium channel blocker, with or without a diuretic. HC4 Aim to lower blood pressure over the next 48–72 hours. HC4

docs.title: 4.1.7 Ischaemic Heart Disease (Coronary Heart Disease)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I20, I21, I25

Ischaemic heart disease is a condition in which there is insufficient blood flow through the coronary arteries of the heart, leading to ischaemia and/or infarction.

Cause

  • Deposition of fatty material, such as cholesterol plaques, and platelet aggregation inside the coronary arteries causing partial or total obstruction of blood flow

Risk factors

  • Hypertension
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Smoking
  • Obesity
  • Unhealthy diet
  • Physical inactivity
  • Hyperlipidaemia
  • Family history of heart disease

Clinical features

Acute coronary syndrome, including acute myocardial infarction, may present with:

  • Prolonged chest pain, which may be localised on the left or central part of the chest
  • Pain ranging from mild to severe
  • Pain sometimes radiating to the left arm, neck, and back
  • Sweating
  • Dyspnoea
  • Vomiting
  • Anxiety
  • Low blood pressure
  • Tachycardia

Stable angina may present with:

  • Tightness in the chest or a sense of oppression
  • Worsening on exertion
  • Relief by rest
  • Pain lasting only a few minutes

Sudden cardiac death may occur, usually due to fatal arrhythmias.

Differential diagnosis

  • Indigestion
  • Hiatus hernia
  • Peptic ulcer
  • Pleurisy
  • Pericarditis
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Dissecting aneurysm

Investigations

  • Cardiac enzymes, including CPK and troponin
  • ECG, including resting ECG and stress ECG
  • Echocardiogram

Management of acute coronary syndrome

Treatment LOC Give acetylsalicylic acid 300 mg as a single dose, to be chewed. HC2 Refer immediately to hospital. HC2 Give glyceryl trinitrate 500 micrograms sublingually. Repeat after 5 minutes if there is no response. H Give oxygen therapy if SpO₂ <94%. H Give morphine 2.5–5 mg IV if pain persists. H Give simvastatin 40 mg or atorvastatin 40 mg. H Give enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours. H Treat complications accordingly, such as pulmonary oedema or arrhythmias. H

Consider adding

Treatment LOC Beta blocker if there are no contraindications, such as systolic BP <90 mmHg or heart rate <60 bpm. Examples include atenolol 25–50 mg daily. H Ensure close observation of pulse rate and circulatory status. H ACE inhibitor, such as enalapril 2.5–10 mg daily. H Refer for further management at a higher level of care if unstable. H

When the patient is stable, continue:

  • Acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg once daily
  • Atorvastatin 40 mg daily
  • Beta blocker, such as atenolol, carvedilol, or bisoprolol, and ACE inhibitor if tolerated
  • Lifestyle changes, including healthy diet, no smoking, regular exercise, and control of other risk factors

Management of stable angina

Treatment LOC Aggressive control of risk factors, including hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and obesity. HC2 Give acetylsalicylic acid 75–150 mg once daily. H Give atorvastatin 40 mg once daily. H Give beta blockers, such as atenolol 25–100 mg, if the patient is not diabetic. H Refer to a higher level of care if still uncontrolled. H

Prevention

  • Low-fat, low-cholesterol diet
  • Stop smoking
  • Effective control of hypertension and diabetes mellitus
  • Consider treatment with acetylsalicylic acid and statin in patients with multiple risk factors

docs.title: 4.1.8 Pericarditis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I30

Pericarditis is inflammation of the heart membrane, the pericardium.

It may be:

  • Acute and self-limiting
  • Subacute or chronic
  • Fibrinous
  • Serous
  • Haemorrhagic
  • Purulent

Causes

  • Idiopathic or viral causes, which are the most common causes, such as Coxsackie A and B, influenza A and B, and varicella
  • Bacterial causes, such as mycobacterium, staphylococcus, meningococcus, streptococcus, pneumococcus, gonococcus, and mycoplasma
  • Fungal causes, such as histoplasmosis
  • Severe kidney failure
  • Hypersensitivity, such as acute rheumatic fever
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Radiation
  • Trauma
  • Neoplasms

Clinical features

Pericarditis without effusion may present with:

  • Retrosternal pain radiating to the shoulder
  • Pain that worsens on deep breathing, movement, change of position, or exercise
  • Pericardial rub, which is a diagnostic sign

Pericardial effusion may present with:

  • Reduced cardiac impulses
  • Muffled heart sounds
  • Cardiomegaly

Cardiac tamponade may occur in cases of massive effusion or constrictive pericarditis and may present with:

  • Dyspnoea
  • Restlessness
  • Rising pulmonary and systemic venous pressure
  • Rapid heart rate
  • Pulsus paradoxus
  • Low blood pressure
  • Low-output cardiac failure

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of chest pain
  • Other causes of heart failure

Investigations

  • ECG
  • Chest X-ray
  • Echocardiography

Management

Treatment LOC If viral or idiopathic, advise rest. H Give ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours. H If there is fluid, perform pericardial tapping. H If there are other causes, treat accordingly. H

Prevention

  • Early detection and treatment of potential treatable causes

docs.title: 4.1.9 Rheumatic Fever
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I00, I01

Rheumatic fever is a systemic connective tissue disease that follows a streptococcal upper respiratory tract infection. It may involve the heart, joints, skin, subcutaneous tissue, and central nervous system.

The first attack usually occurs between 3 and 15 years of age.

Cause

  • Hypersensitivity reaction to group A streptococcal throat infection

Clinical features

  • Arthritis, typically migrating asymmetric polyarthritis
  • Acute rheumatic carditis, with signs of cardiac failure, murmurs, and pericarditis
  • Subcutaneous nodules
  • Chorea, presenting as involuntary movements of the limbs
  • Skin rash
  • Other minor signs and symptoms, including fever, arthralgia, and abnormal laboratory findings

Differential diagnosis

  • Any form of arthralgia or arthritis, including sickle cell disease and haemophilia
  • Pyrexia with cardiac failure

Investigations

  • Haemogram, including assessment for raised ESR
  • Chest X-ray
  • ECG
  • Echocardiography
  • Antistreptolysin O titre (ASOT)

Diagnostic criteria: revised Jones criteria

Diagnosis requires evidence of recent streptococcal infection, such as:

  • Elevated ASO titre or other streptococcal antibody titres
  • Positive throat swab for group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus

Plus either:

  • Two major manifestations, or
  • One major manifestation and two minor manifestations
Major manifestations Minor manifestations Polyarthritis Polyarthralgia Carditis Fever Erythema marginatum Acute phase reactants, such as increased ESR or CRP Subcutaneous nodules ECG showing prolonged PR interval Sydenham’s chorea

Management

Treatment LOC Bed rest. HC4 To eradicate streptococci, give phenoxymethylpenicillin (Pen V) 250 mg every 6 hours for 10 days. HC4 Children: phenoxymethylpenicillin 125 mg per dose. HC4 Alternatively, give benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 MU IM stat. HC4 Children <30 kg: benzathine benzylpenicillin 0.6 MU IM stat. HC4 Children >30 kg: benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 MU IM stat. HC4 To treat inflammation, give acetylsalicylic acid 4–8 g/day until signs of inflammation subside, usually after 4–8 weeks. HC4 Children: acetylsalicylic acid 80–100 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses. HC4 Add magnesium trisilicate compound 2–4 tablets every 8 hours, taken 30 minutes after acetylsalicylic acid. HC4 If allergic to aspirin, give low-dose steroid. HC4 If there are carditis or heart failure symptoms, treat according to heart failure guidance. See section 4.1.3. H Consider high-dose steroids for carditis or heart failure symptoms. Specialist guidance is required. H If chorea is present, give valproate 10–20 mg/kg/day. H

Prophylaxis

To prevent further episodes:

Treatment LOC Give phenoxymethylpenicillin (Pen V) 500 mg every 12 hours. HC3 Children: phenoxymethylpenicillin 125–250 mg every 12 hours. HC3 Alternatively, give benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 MU IM every 4 weeks. HC3 Children <30 kg: benzathine benzylpenicillin 0.6 MU IM every 4 weeks. HC3 If allergic to penicillin, give erythromycin 250 mg every 12 hours. HC3 Children: erythromycin 10 mg/kg twice daily. HC3

Duration of prophylaxis

Duration depends on disease severity:

  • Rheumatic fever without carditis: for 5 years or until age 18 to 21 years
  • Carditis without residual heart disease: for 10 years or until age 25 years
  • Carditis with residual heart disease: until age 40 to 45 years or for life

Prevention

  • Early diagnosis and treatment of group A streptococcal throat infection
  • Avoid overcrowding
  • Improve housing conditions
  • Promote good nutrition

docs.title: 4.1.10 Rheumatic Heart Disease
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I05–I09

Rheumatic heart disease is disease of the heart valves following an episode of rheumatic fever.

The valves commonly involved are:

  • Mitral valve, leading to stenosis, incompetence, or both
  • Aortic valve, leading to stenosis, incompetence, or both

Clinical features

  • Heart failure
  • Arrhythmias and palpitations
  • Thromboembolic complications, such as stroke
  • Heart murmurs depending on the valve affected and the nature of the lesion
  • Asymptomatic disease, where the valvular lesion is discovered incidentally
  • Congestive cardiac failure triggered by increased cardiac demand, such as in pregnancy or anaemia

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of cardiac failure

Investigations

  • Chest X-ray
  • ECG, where available
  • Echocardiography

Management

Treatment LOC Treat heart failure if present. HC4 Provide prophylaxis for life as described under rheumatic fever. NR Consider cardiac surgery if necessary. This is available only at national referral hospital level. NR

Prevention

  • Prevent recurrent rheumatic fever through continuous prophylaxis.
  • Diagnose and treat streptococcal throat infection early.
  • Strengthen adherence to long-term prophylaxis in patients with previous rheumatic fever.

docs.title: 4.1.11 Stroke
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: I63

Stroke is a cerebral neurological dysfunction caused by a problem in blood circulation to the brain. It may result from a clot, causing ischaemic stroke, or bleeding, causing haemorrhagic stroke.

Causes

  • Clot, either a thrombus in a brain vessel or an embolus from a clot elsewhere. This is the most common cause.
  • Haemorrhage, either spontaneous or due to trauma.

Clinical features

  • Focal neurological deficits, such as one-sided weakness of the face, arm, or leg
  • Hemiparesis or hemiplegia
  • Difficulty in speaking
  • Difficulty in swallowing
  • Severe headache, especially in haemorrhagic stroke
  • Altered level of consciousness
  • Convulsions

Investigations

  • CT scan of the brain

In the absence of neuroimaging, the following clinical features may help distinguish stroke subtypes:

Type Clinical course Risk factors Other clues Intracerebral haemorrhage Gradual progression over minutes or hours Hypertension, trauma, bleeding disorders, illicit drug use Patients may have reduced alertness and severe headache. Subarachnoid haemorrhage Abrupt onset of very severe headache. Focal symptoms are less common. Smoking, hypertension, illicit drug use, or sometimes no clear risk factor due to rupture of congenital aneurysms Patients may have reduced alertness. It may occur in young people. Ischaemic stroke, thrombotic Gradual development of focal deficits over hours or days Age, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidaemia Symptoms may improve and worsen in the following days. Ischaemic stroke, embolic Sudden onset of focal deficits Age, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, valvular heart disease, and arrhythmias Often improves slowly.

Management

General care

Treatment LOC Ensure airway and respiration if the patient is unconscious. H Do not give anything by mouth before assessing swallowing ability, to avoid aspiration. H Provide IV fluids or nasogastric tube feeding for hydration and nutrition if the patient is unable to swallow. H Control blood sugar with insulin if the patient is diabetic. H

Management of ischaemic stroke

Treatment LOC Give aspirin 150–300 mg every 24 hours. H In the acute phase, treat hypertension only if it is extreme, above 220/120 mmHg, or if there are other complications such as pulmonary oedema or angina. H If there are no acute complications, restart antihypertensive treatment 24 hours after the event and reduce blood pressure slowly. H Consider DVT prophylaxis with enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily. H

Management of clinically haemorrhagic stroke

Treatment LOC Provide supportive care as above. H Refer for CT scan and neurosurgical evaluation. H

Chronic care of ischaemic stroke

Treatment LOC Start early mobilisation and physiotherapy. H Give aspirin 75–100 mg once daily for life. H Give atorvastatin 40 mg once daily for life. H Control risk factors. H

docs.title: Chapter 4: Cardiovascular Diseases
docs.text:
Cardiovascular Diseases

Thrombosis/Pulmonary Embolism (DVT/PE) ICD10 CODE: I82.409

Clot formation within the deep venous system, usually of the calf, thigh, or pelvic veins. The clot can cause a local problem at site of formation or dislodge, leading to thromboembolism in various parts of the body, particularly the lungs (pulmonary embolism). Causes

Venous stasis (slowing of blood flow)

Increased coagulability states

Endothelial injury

Risk factors

Immobilisation, prolonged bed rest, surgery, limb paralysis

Heart failure, myocardial infarction

Blunt trauma, venous injury including cannulation

Oral contraceptive pills, pregnancy and postpartum

Malignancies and some forms of chemotherapy

Long distance airtravel

Inherited thrombophilic states

For PE: any other cause of dyspnoea and chest pain e.g. bronchopneumonia and myocardial infarction

50% of cases may be clinically silent

Pain, swelling and warmth of the calf, thigh, and groin

Dislodgement of the thrombus may lead to pulmonary embolism characterised by dyspnoea, tachycardia, chest pain, hypotension

Half of the cases of PE are associated with silent DVT

Clinical features

Differential diagnosis  Cellulitis, myositis, phlebitis, contusion  For PE: any other cause of dyspnoea and chest pain

Investigations » In case of pulmonary embolism: chest CT angiogram » Other useful tests (not specific): blood D-dimer, ECG, Chest X ray, echo cardiogram Management TREATMENT

LOC

Enoxaparin (Low molecular weight heparin- LMWH) 1 mg/ kg every 12 hours for at least 5 days

  • No monitoring is required Plus warfarin 5 mg single dose given in the evening, commencing on the same day as the heparin

  • Maintenance dose: 2.5-7.5 mg single dose daily,

  • adjusted according to the INR 2 -3

H

CHAPTER 4: Cardiovascular Diseases

Compression ultrasound +/- doppler

H

If enoxaparin not available

  • Unfractionated heparin given as: 5000 units IV

bolus and then 1000 units hourly or 17500 units subcutaneuosly 12 hourly for 5 days. Adjust dose according to activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)

H

Management TREATMENT

LOC

  • Or 333 units/kg SC as an initial dose followed by

H

250 units/kg SC every 12 hours

  • Plus warfarin as above Alternative to warfarin and heparin combination:

CHAPTER 4: Cardiovascular Diseases

Rivaroxiban

  • No need to initiate with heparin

  • Dose: 15mg orally twice a day for 3 weeks then 20mg daily for the duration of anticoagulation.

  • Patients must take the drug at the same time every day to prevent re-thrombosis.

  • Not to be used in pregnant or breast feeding mothers

  • Associated with reduced bleeding risk compared to warfarin Apixaban

  • Dose: 10mg twice a day for 7 days then 5mg twice a day for the duration of the anticoagulation

  • Associated with a reduced bleeding risk than warfarin

  • Not to be used in pregnant or breast-feeding mothers Notes  Monitor for bleeding complications  When using Apixaban, patients should be asked to ambulate as soon as possible  See section 1.3.10. for treatment of warfarin overdose and PGD 2015 monograph on protamine for excessive heparin dose  Do not start therapy with warfarin alone because it initially increases risk of thrombus progression

 Early mobilisation  Prophylaxis with enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily in any acutely ill medical patient and in prolonged admission

docs.title: 4.1.2 Infective Endocarditis
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I33.0

An infection of the heart valves and lining of the heart chambers by microorganisms, usually bacterial, rarely fungal.

Management

TREATMENT LOC  Low molecular weight heparin-- (LMWH) e.g., Enoxaparin given as 1 mg/kg- every 12 hours or 1.5mg/kg once a day, for at least 5 days Plus warfarin 5 mg single dose given in the evening, commencing on the same day as the heparin. Overlap treatment of warfarin and heparin. Heparin is stopped when the warfarin dose leads to an optimal INR of 2-3. HH  Maintenance dose: single dose daily, that need a higher maintenance dose than others especially when there are drugs that may interact with warfarin. Typical dose may range between 2.5 – 10mg daily. adjusted according to the INR 2 -3 H

Causes It is classified into 3 types:

 Sub-acute endocarditis: caused by low virulence organisms such as Streptococcus viridans  Acute endocarditis: caused by common pyogenic organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus

 Post-operative endocarditis: following cardiac surgery and prosthetic heart valve placement. The most common organism involved is Staphylococcus aureus

Clinical features

 Disease may present as acute or chronic depending on the

microorganism involved and patient’s condition  Fatigue, weight loss  Low grade fever and chills or acute severe septicaemia  Embolic phenomena affecting various body organs (e.g. brain)  Heart failure, prominent and changing heart murmurs  Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly  Anaemia  Splinter haemorrhages (nail bed and retina)  Finger clubbing  Diagnostic triad: persistent fever, emboli, changing murmur

Risk factors

 Rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease  Prosthetic valve  Invasive dental/diagnostic/surgical procedures (including cardiac

catheterization)  Immunosuppression  IV drug use/abuse

Note: Any unexplained fever in a patient with a heart valve problem should be regarded as endocarditis

Differential diagnosis

 Cardiac failure with heart murmurs  Febrile conditions associated with anaemia

Investigations

 Blood cultures: These are usually positive and all efforts should be made to identify the responsible pathogen and obtain sensitivity data

 At least 3 sets of blood cultures (8 ml) each should be obtained

(each from a separate venipucture) at least one hour apart  Blood: Complete blood count, ESR  Urinalysis for microscopic haematuria, proteinuria  Echocardiography  ECG

TREATMENT LOC Bed restTreat complications e.g. heart failure Initial empirical antibiotic therapyBenzylpenicillin 5 MU IV every 6 hours for 4 weeks H Child: Benzylpenicillin 50,000 IU/kg every 6 hours for 4 weeksPlus gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 2 weeks If staphylococcus suspected, (acute onset) add:Cloxacillin IV 3 g every 6 hours Child: 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 weeks If MRSA (Multi-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus)Vancomycin 500 mg IV every 6 hoursChild: 10 mg/kg (infused over 1 hour) 6 hourly for 6 weeks Once a pathogen has been identifiedAmend treatment to correspond with the sensitivity results RR

Prevention

 Prophylaxis in case of dental procedures and tonsillectomy in patients at risk (valvular defects, congenital heart disease, prosthetic valve). Give amoxicillin 2 g (50 mg/kg for children) as a single dose, 1 hour before the procedure.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Heart Failure
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I50

Clinical syndrome caused by inadequate cardiac output for the body’s needs, despite adequate venous return.

For management purposes, it can be classified into:

  • Congestive/acute heart failure

    • Chronic heart failure
    • Acute pulmonary oedema (see section 4.1.4) Causes

 Hypertension  Valvular heart disease, e.g. rheumatic heart disease  Myocardial infarction  Myocarditis  Prolonged rapid irregular heartbeat (arrhythmias)  Congenital heart disease  Severe anaemia, thyroid disease

Clinical features Infants and young children

 Respiratory distress with rapid respiration, cyanosis, wheezing,

subcostal, intercostal, and sternal recession  Rapid pulse, gallop rhythm, excessive sweating  Tender hepatomegaly  Difficulty with feeding  Cardiomegaly

Older children and adults

 Palpitations, shortness of breath, exercise intolerance  Fatigue, orthopnea, exertional dyspnoea, wheezing  Rapid pulse, gallop rhythm  Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP)  Dependent oedema, enlarged tender liver  Basal crepitations

Differential diagnosis

 Severe anaemia, severe acute malnutrition  Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis  Severe pneumonia  Any severe sickness in infants

Investigations

 Chest X-ray  Blood: Haemogram (for ESR, anaemia)  Urea and electrolytes  Echocardiogram, ECG

TREATMENT LOC Bed rest with head of bed elevatedProp up patient in sitting positionReduce salt intake and limit fluid intake (1-1.5 L/ day) Furosemide 20-40 mg oral or IV daily for every 12hours increasing as required to 80-160 mg according to response Child: 1 mg/kg oral or IV daily or every 12 hours according to response (max: 8 mg/kg daily)ACE inhibitors: start with low dose Enalapril 2.5 mg once daily, increase gradually over 2 weeks to 1020 mg (max 40 mg) if tolerated (or Lisinopril 5mg increase gradually over 2 weeks to 40mg)Child: Enalapril 0.1-1 mg/kg daily in 1-2 doses OrCaptopril 6.25-12.5 mg 8 -12 hourly, increase over 2-4 weeks to max 150 mg daily in divided dosesChild: Captopril 0.1-0.3 mg/kg daily every 8-12 hours If available and when patient stable add:Adults: Carvedilol 3.125 mg every 12 hours, increase gradually every 2 weeks to max 25 mg 12 hourly (or Bisoprolol 1.25mg once daily increase gradually to max 10mg)Child: Carvedilol 0.05 mg/kg every 12 hours, increase gradually to max 0.35 mg/kg every 12 hours HC4HC4HC4HH TREATMENT LOC Additional medicines (second/third line) Spironolactone 25-50 mg once a dayChild: Initially 1.5-3 mg/kg daily in divided dosesDigoxin 125-250 micrograms/daily Child maintenance dose: 15 micrograms/kg daily HHC4 CautionUse ACE inhibitors and beta blockers with caution if systolic BP is less than 90 mmHg: monitor renal functionUse digoxin with caution in elderly and renal disease CautionUse ACE inhibitors and beta blockers with caution if systolic BP is less than 90 mmHg: monitor renal functionUse digoxin with caution in elderly and renal disease

Prevention

 Management of risk factors  Early diagnosis and treatment of the cause (e.g. hypertension)  Treatment adherence

Chronic heart failure

Patients with chronic heart failure need continuous treatment to control symptoms and prevent disease progression and complications

Management

TREATMENT LOC Periodic monitoring of body weight, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturationSalt and fluid restrictionLimit alcohol intakeRegular exercise within limits of symptomsContinued treatment with the medicines listed above, with doses progressively increased to achieve control HC2HC4

docs.title: 4.1.4 Pulmonary Oedema
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I50.21

 Cardiogenic  Severe fluid overload e.g. in renal failure or iatrogenic  Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: severe pneumonia, altitude

sickness, inhalation of toxic gases, acute respiratory distress syndrome

Clinical features

 Severe dyspnoea, rapid breathing, breathlessness  Tachycardia, wheezing  Cough with frothy blood stained sputum

Differential diagnosis

 Pneumonia, pleural effusion  Foreign body  Trauma (pneumothorax, pulmonary contusion)

Investigations  Chest X-ray  ECG  Renal function, electrolytes  Echocardiography

Management

docs.title: 4.1.5 Atrial Fibrillation
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I48

Common cardiac arrhythmia characterised by irregular pulse due to the loss of the regular atrial electrical activity. Its onset can be acute or chronic, and it can be symptomatic or asymptomatic.

Risk factors

 Heart disease (heart failure, valvular heart diseases, ischaemic heart disease)

 Thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism) Clinical features

 Irregular pulse (frequency and volume), heart rate can be either normal or very high  Acute onset (often with high heart rate): palpitations, dizziness, fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath  Chronic (with normal or almost normal heart rate): often

asymptomatic, discovered at routine checks  It can precipitate heart failure or pulmonary oedema  It can cause embolic stroke if clots form in the heart and are then

dislodged to the brain circulation Investigations

 ECG

Objectives

 Control heart rate  Restore normal rhythm if possible (specialist only)  Prevent or treat complications  Treat underlying conditions

Management

TREATMENT LOC If acute onset, high heart rate or patient in congestive heart failure and/ or pulmonary oedema:Treat heart failure as per guidelines (section 4.1.3), use digoxin and or Carvedilol (or Bisoprolol) to reduce heart rate If acute onset and high heart rate but no signs of heart failure:Use atenolol 50 mg to control heart rate HC4HC4

Management

TREATMENT LOC If chronic but normal heart rate: Only treat underlying conditionsRefer to regional level to assess indication for anticoagulation with aspirin or warfarin to prevent stroke H

ICD10 CODE: I16.2

BP >180/110 mmHg with symptoms and acute life threatening complications:

docs.title: 4.1.6 Hypertension
docs.text:
ICD10 code: I10

Persistently high resting blood pressure (>140/90 mmHg for at least two measurements five minutes apart with patient seated) on at least 2 or 3 occasions 1 week apart.

Classification of blood pressure (BP)

Category Sbp Mmhg Dbp Mmhg Normal <120 and <80 Pre-hypertension 120-139 or 80-89 Hypertension, stage 1 140-159 or 90-99 Hypertension, stage 2 >160 or >100 SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure

Causes

 In the majority of cases, the cause is not known (essential hypertension)

Secondary hypertension is associated with:

 Kidney diseases  Endocrine diseases  Eclampsia/pre-eclampsia  Medicines (steroids and decongestants containing caffeine and

pseudoephedrine) Risk factors

 Family history, race  Obesity, physical inactivity  Excessive intake of salt and alcohol  Diabetes and dyslipidaemia

Clinical features

The majority of cases are symptomless and are only discovered on routine examination or screening.

General symptoms include:

 Headache  Palpitations, dizziness

Hypertension may present as a complication affecting:

 Brain (stroke)  Heart (heart failure)  Kidney (renal failure)  Eyes (impairment of vision)

Differential diagnosis

 Anxiety Investigations To identify complications and possible cases of secondary hypertension: » Urine analysis » Blood sugar » Plasma urea and electrolytes

 Chest X-ray  ECG

Management of hypertension Target: blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg

Step7If BP is ≥ 140/90mmHg, refer for further management to a higher level of care. --- Provision for specific patients Assess the cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in all patients with hypertension. Patients with diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke or chronic kidney disease are considered having a high CVD risk. The target BP is <130/80 mmHg in people with high CVD risk. --- --- --- --- Start statin (atorvastatin 20-40 mg once daily or simvastatin 20-40 mg once daily) and aspirin 75mg in people with prior heart attack or ischemic stroke. Consider statin in people at high risk. --- Start beta blocker (Atenolol 50mg or Bisoprolol 5mg or Nebivolol 5mg once daily) in people with heart attack in past 3 years. --- A combination of ACEI or ARB and a CCB or a diuretic is recommended as initial therapy in patients with chronic kidney disease. --- For hypertension secondary to thyroid disease consider adding Propranolol 40mg twice daily --- Provision for specific patients Assess the cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in all patients with hypertension. The target BP is <130/80 mmHg in people with high CVD risk. --- --- --- --- Start statin (atorvastatin 20-40 mg once daily or simvastatin 20-40 mg once daily) and aspirin 75mg in people with prior heart attack or ischemic stroke. Methyldopa and calcium channel blockers are safe to useDon’t use both an ACEI and ARB due to increased risk of side effects

Choice of antihypertensive medicine

Choice of medicine may depend on concomitant risk factors/ other conditions: the table below indicates the suitable medicines for such patients.

docs.title: 4.1.11 Stroke
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I63

A cerebral neurological dysfunction due to a problem in blood circulation: a clot (ischaemic stroke) or bleeding (haemorrhagic stroke).

Causes

  • Clot (a thrombus in a brain vessel or an embolus from a clot

sowhere else) – most common

  • Haemorrhage (from trauma or spontaneous) Clinical features

  • Focal neurological deficits as one-sided weakness (face,

arm, leg. Note that eyes are not affected) – hemiparesis or hemiplegia

  • Difficulty in speaking/swallowing

  • Severe headache (especially in haemorrhage)

  • Alteration of consciousness

  • Convulsions Investigations  CT scan of the brain In the absence of neuroimaging, the following clinical features may help to distinguish the stroke subtypes:

Type Clinical Course Risk Factors Other Clues Intracerebral haemorrhage Gradual progression over minutes/ hours Hypertension, trauma, bleeding disorders, illicit drugs Patients may have reduced alertness and severe headache Subarachnoid haemorrhage Abrupt onset of very severe headache, focal symptomsless common Smoking, hypertension, illicit drugs, but at times none (due to rupture of congenital aneurysms) Patients may have reduced alertnessIt may happen in young people Ischaemic (thrombotic) Gradual development of focal deficits over hours or days Age, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia Symptoms can improve and worsenin the following days Ischaemic (embolic) Sudden onset of focal deficits As above plus valvular heart disease and arrhythmias Often improves slowly

Management of stable angina

TREATMENT LOC General care  Ensure airways and respiration if unconscious  Do not give anything by mouth before assessing theability to swallow, to avoid risk of inhalation  IV or NGT for hydration and nutrition if unable to swallow  Control blood sugar with insulin if diabetic H TREATMENT LOC If ischaemic stroke  Aspirin 150-300 mg every 24 hours In the acute phase, treat hypertension only if extreme (more than 220/120) or if there are other complications (pulmonary oedema, angina, etc), otherwise re-start antihypertensive 24 hours after the event and reduce blood pressure slowly Consider DVT prophylaxis with enoxaparin 40 mgSC daily If stroke clinically haemorrhagic  Supportive care as above  Refer for CT scan and neurosurgical evaluation Chronic care of ischaemic stroke  Early mobilization and physiotherapy f Aspirin 75-100mg once daily for life f Atorvastatin 40 mg daily for life  Control of risk factors H

Cardiovascular Diseases

Thrombosis/Pulmonary Embolism (DVT/PE) ICD10 CODE: I82.409

Clot formation within the deep venous system, usually of the calf, thigh, or pelvic veins. The clot can cause a local problem at site of formation or dislodge, leading to thromboembolism in various parts of the body, particularly the lungs (pulmonary embolism). Causes

Venous stasis (slowing of blood flow)

Increased coagulability states

Endothelial injury

Risk factors

Immobilisation, prolonged bed rest, surgery, limb paralysis

Heart failure, myocardial infarction

Blunt trauma, venous injury including cannulation

Oral contraceptive pills, pregnancy and postpartum

Malignancies and some forms of chemotherapy

Long distance airtravel

Inherited thrombophilic states

For PE: any other cause of dyspnoea and chest pain e.g. bronchopneumonia and myocardial infarction

50% of cases may be clinically silent

Pain, swelling and warmth of the calf, thigh, and groin

Dislodgement of the thrombus may lead to pulmonary embolism characterised by dyspnoea, tachycardia, chest pain, hypotension

Half of the cases of PE are associated with silent DVT

Clinical features

Differential diagnosis  Cellulitis, myositis, phlebitis, contusion  For PE: any other cause of dyspnoea and chest pain

docs.title: 4.1.2 Infective Endocarditis
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I33.0

An infection of the heart valves and lining of the heart chambers by microorganisms, usually bacterial, rarely fungal.

Management

TREATMENT LOC  Low molecular weight heparin-- (LMWH) e.g., Enoxaparin given as 1 mg/kg- every 12 hours or 1.5mg/kg once a day, for at least 5 days Plus warfarin 5 mg single dose given in the evening, commencing on the same day as the heparin. Overlap treatment of warfarin and heparin. Heparin is stopped when the warfarin dose leads to an optimal INR of 2-3. HH  Maintenance dose: single dose daily, that need a higher maintenance dose than others especially when there are drugs that may interact with warfarin. Typical dose may range between 2.5 – 10mg daily. adjusted according to the INR 2 -3 H

Causes It is classified into 3 types:

 Sub-acute endocarditis: caused by low virulence organisms such as Streptococcus viridans  Acute endocarditis: caused by common pyogenic organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus

 Post-operative endocarditis: following cardiac surgery and prosthetic heart valve placement. The most common organism involved is Staphylococcus aureus

Clinical features

 Disease may present as acute or chronic depending on the

microorganism involved and patient’s condition  Fatigue, weight loss  Low grade fever and chills or acute severe septicaemia  Embolic phenomena affecting various body organs (e.g. brain)  Heart failure, prominent and changing heart murmurs  Splenomegaly, hepatomegaly  Anaemia  Splinter haemorrhages (nail bed and retina)  Finger clubbing  Diagnostic triad: persistent fever, emboli, changing murmur

Risk factors

 Rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease  Prosthetic valve  Invasive dental/diagnostic/surgical procedures (including cardiac

catheterization)  Immunosuppression  IV drug use/abuse

Note: Any unexplained fever in a patient with a heart valve problem should be regarded as endocarditis

Differential diagnosis

 Cardiac failure with heart murmurs  Febrile conditions associated with anaemia

Investigations

 Blood cultures: These are usually positive and all efforts should be made to identify the responsible pathogen and obtain sensitivity data

 At least 3 sets of blood cultures (8 ml) each should be obtained

(each from a separate venipucture) at least one hour apart  Blood: Complete blood count, ESR  Urinalysis for microscopic haematuria, proteinuria  Echocardiography  ECG

TREATMENT LOC Bed restTreat complications e.g. heart failure Initial empirical antibiotic therapyBenzylpenicillin 5 MU IV every 6 hours for 4 weeks H Child: Benzylpenicillin 50,000 IU/kg every 6 hours for 4 weeksPlus gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 2 weeks If staphylococcus suspected, (acute onset) add:Cloxacillin IV 3 g every 6 hours Child: 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 weeks If MRSA (Multi-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus)Vancomycin 500 mg IV every 6 hoursChild: 10 mg/kg (infused over 1 hour) 6 hourly for 6 weeks Once a pathogen has been identifiedAmend treatment to correspond with the sensitivity results RR

Prevention

 Prophylaxis in case of dental procedures and tonsillectomy in patients at risk (valvular defects, congenital heart disease, prosthetic valve). Give amoxicillin 2 g (50 mg/kg for children) as a single dose, 1 hour before the procedure.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Heart Failure
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I50

Clinical syndrome caused by inadequate cardiac output for the body’s needs, despite adequate venous return.

For management purposes, it can be classified into:

  • Congestive/acute heart failure

    • Chronic heart failure
    • Acute pulmonary oedema (see section 4.1.4) Causes

 Hypertension  Valvular heart disease, e.g. rheumatic heart disease  Myocardial infarction  Myocarditis  Prolonged rapid irregular heartbeat (arrhythmias)  Congenital heart disease  Severe anaemia, thyroid disease

Clinical features Infants and young children

 Respiratory distress with rapid respiration, cyanosis, wheezing,

subcostal, intercostal, and sternal recession  Rapid pulse, gallop rhythm, excessive sweating  Tender hepatomegaly  Difficulty with feeding  Cardiomegaly

Older children and adults

 Palpitations, shortness of breath, exercise intolerance  Fatigue, orthopnea, exertional dyspnoea, wheezing  Rapid pulse, gallop rhythm  Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP)  Dependent oedema, enlarged tender liver  Basal crepitations

Differential diagnosis

 Severe anaemia, severe acute malnutrition  Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis  Severe pneumonia  Any severe sickness in infants

Investigations

 Chest X-ray  Blood: Haemogram (for ESR, anaemia)  Urea and electrolytes  Echocardiogram, ECG

TREATMENT LOC Bed rest with head of bed elevatedProp up patient in sitting positionReduce salt intake and limit fluid intake (1-1.5 L/ day) Furosemide 20-40 mg oral or IV daily for every 12hours increasing as required to 80-160 mg according to response Child: 1 mg/kg oral or IV daily or every 12 hours according to response (max: 8 mg/kg daily)ACE inhibitors: start with low dose Enalapril 2.5 mg once daily, increase gradually over 2 weeks to 1020 mg (max 40 mg) if tolerated (or Lisinopril 5mg increase gradually over 2 weeks to 40mg)Child: Enalapril 0.1-1 mg/kg daily in 1-2 doses OrCaptopril 6.25-12.5 mg 8 -12 hourly, increase over 2-4 weeks to max 150 mg daily in divided dosesChild: Captopril 0.1-0.3 mg/kg daily every 8-12 hours If available and when patient stable add:Adults: Carvedilol 3.125 mg every 12 hours, increase gradually every 2 weeks to max 25 mg 12 hourly (or Bisoprolol 1.25mg once daily increase gradually to max 10mg)Child: Carvedilol 0.05 mg/kg every 12 hours, increase gradually to max 0.35 mg/kg every 12 hours HC4HC4HC4HH TREATMENT LOC Additional medicines (second/third line) Spironolactone 25-50 mg once a dayChild: Initially 1.5-3 mg/kg daily in divided dosesDigoxin 125-250 micrograms/daily Child maintenance dose: 15 micrograms/kg daily HHC4 CautionUse ACE inhibitors and beta blockers with caution if systolic BP is less than 90 mmHg: monitor renal functionUse digoxin with caution in elderly and renal disease CautionUse ACE inhibitors and beta blockers with caution if systolic BP is less than 90 mmHg: monitor renal functionUse digoxin with caution in elderly and renal disease

Prevention

 Management of risk factors  Early diagnosis and treatment of the cause (e.g. hypertension)  Treatment adherence

Chronic heart failure

Patients with chronic heart failure need continuous treatment to control symptoms and prevent disease progression and complications

Management

TREATMENT LOC Periodic monitoring of body weight, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturationSalt and fluid restrictionLimit alcohol intakeRegular exercise within limits of symptomsContinued treatment with the medicines listed above, with doses progressively increased to achieve control HC2HC4

docs.title: 4.1.5 Atrial Fibrillation
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I48

Common cardiac arrhythmia characterised by irregular pulse due to the loss of the regular atrial electrical activity. Its onset can be acute or chronic, and it can be symptomatic or asymptomatic.

Risk factors

 Heart disease (heart failure, valvular heart diseases, ischaemic heart disease)

 Thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism) Clinical features

 Irregular pulse (frequency and volume), heart rate can be either normal or very high  Acute onset (often with high heart rate): palpitations, dizziness, fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath  Chronic (with normal or almost normal heart rate): often

asymptomatic, discovered at routine checks  It can precipitate heart failure or pulmonary oedema  It can cause embolic stroke if clots form in the heart and are then

dislodged to the brain circulation Investigations

 ECG

Objectives

 Control heart rate  Restore normal rhythm if possible (specialist only)  Prevent or treat complications  Treat underlying conditions

Management

docs.title: 4.1.6 Hypertension
docs.text:
ICD10 code: I10

Persistently high resting blood pressure (>140/90 mmHg for at least two measurements five minutes apart with patient seated) on at least 2 or 3 occasions 1 week apart.

Classification of blood pressure (BP)

Category Sbp Mmhg Dbp Mmhg Normal <120 and <80 Pre-hypertension 120-139 or 80-89 Hypertension, stage 1 140-159 or 90-99 Hypertension, stage 2 >160 or >100 SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure SBP=systolic blood pressure; DBP=diastolic blood pressure

Causes

 In the majority of cases, the cause is not known (essential hypertension)

Secondary hypertension is associated with:

 Kidney diseases  Endocrine diseases  Eclampsia/pre-eclampsia  Medicines (steroids and decongestants containing caffeine and

pseudoephedrine) Risk factors

 Family history, race  Obesity, physical inactivity  Excessive intake of salt and alcohol  Diabetes and dyslipidaemia

Clinical features

The majority of cases are symptomless and are only discovered on routine examination or screening.

General symptoms include:

 Headache  Palpitations, dizziness

Hypertension may present as a complication affecting:

 Brain (stroke)  Heart (heart failure)  Kidney (renal failure)  Eyes (impairment of vision)

Differential diagnosis

docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: I16.2

seizures, visual disturbances)  Acute angina or acute myocardial infarction (AMI)  Pulmonary oedema  Acute kidney failure  Acute aortic dissection  Eclampsia or pre-eclampsia (section 16.3.7 and 16.3.8)

ICD10 CODE: I63
