If jaundiced, suspect liver failure, stop drugs (see below)2. If no jaundice, suspect Isoniazid, increase dose of pyridoxine Side-Effects Drug(S) Likely To Cause Management Visual impairment (other causesexcluded) Ethambutol Stop Ethambutol. Use streptomycin

Hypersensitivity reaction Most anti-TB drugs can cause hypersensitisation between week 3 and week 8 of treatment in order of frequency: ethambutol, pyrazinamide, rifampicin and isoniazid. If mild (simple itchy rash), give antihistamine (e.g. chlorpheniramine) and moisturizer and continue treatment. Severe reactions are characterised by

    • Fever, headache, vomiting
    • Macular dark erythematous rash which can progress to a Steven Johnson-Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis syndrome

Adjunctive treatment

TREATMENT LOC  Stop all drugs immediately  Manage supportively  Refer for specialised management H RR

Drug-induced hepatitis

Severe hepatic damage, presenting with jaundice, vomiting, severe malaise. In order of frequency, the implicated drugs are Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Rifampicin and Ethambutol.

Adjunctive treatment

TREATMENT LOC  Stop all drugs immediately  Manage supportively  When jaundice has resolved, re-introduce single drugs at3-7 days interval, starting from the least likely involved H RR

Adjunctive treatment

TREATMENT LOC  If reaction very severe, do not try to restart pyrazinamide. If RH tolerated, do not try pyrazinamide Use alternative regimen avoiding the causative drug H RR

docs.title: 5.3.2.2 Prevention and Infection Control of TB
docs.text:
• Early detection of cases and initiation of appropriate TB treatment

  • Treatment under directly observed treatment (DOT) and fol-

low up to ensure adherence and cure Contact tracing

  • Tracing of contacts of TB patients

  • Routine screening of health workers for latent & active TB High Priority Patients For Contact Tracing

  • Bacteriologically confirmed PTB (Smear positive or Xpert

positive or Culture positive)

  • Cavitation of chest x-ray

  • Age < 5 years

  • MDR TB • PLHIV Other preventive measures

  • BCG vaccination at birth to prevent severe forms of TB

  • TB Preventive Treatment for categories at risk General hygiene

  • Avoidance of overcrowding

  • Avoid drinking unboiled milk

  • Cough hygiene (cover cough with pieces of cloth, washing

hands with soap, proper disposal of sputum)

  • Good nutrition

  • Promote good ventilation in housing & transport

• Open ventilators, windows & doors that allow air exchange

docs.title: 5.3.2.3 Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment
docs.text:
Tuberculosis preventive treatment is recommended to prevent the development of active TB disease in an individual who has latent TB infection (LTBI).

Uganda guidelines for programmatic management of Latent TB infection recommend TB preventive treatment (TPT ) in the following categories of people:

    • Persons living with HIV
    • Child & adult contacts of pulmonary TB patients

General principles

  • The country has adopted patient centered care. It is recommended that all TB medicines are taken under direct observation by a treatment supporter (DOT). Digital Adherence Technologies (DAT) have been introduced to support treatment adherence.

  • Anti-TB drugs are given in fixed dose combination (FDC) regimens according to the patient’s TB classification

• Treatment is divided into two phases: an initial (intensive) phase of 2 months and a continuation phase of 4 months (longer in severe forms of TB particularly TB meningitis and osteoarticular TB)TB treatment regimens are expressed in a standard format, e.g. 2RHZE/4RH where:

    • Letters represent abbreviated drug names
    • Numbers show the duration in months
    • shows the division between treatment phases

  • Other shorter term (4-months) treatment regimen recently adopted

  • • 2 HRE(Z)/2RH for children 2 months to 16 years

  • • 2 HPMZ/2HPM for adults

  • Anti-TB drugs have side effects and they should be man-

aged appropriately (see section 5.3.2.1)

  • TB treatment monitoring should be done by clinical, sputum and where possible radiological

  • A conclusion of “treatment outcome” status should be done for every patient treated for TB.

First line anti-TB medication

Important: The choice of regimen now depends on rifampicin sensitivity and not on the previous history of treatment: All patients without rifampicin resistance (either new or re-treatments) are treated with 1st line regimen. Patients with rifampicin resistance (either new or re- treatments) are treated with second line medication in a designated MDR-TB treatment facility.

Susceptible TB: 1st line treatment regimens

For patients without rifampicin resistance to Gene Xpert MTB/Rif (both new and re-treatment cases).

New cases not belonging to priority (risk) groups and in which diagnosis was done by sputum examination will also be treated with this regimen.

Type Of TB Disease Regimen For Susceptible TB Regimen For Susceptible TB LOC Type Of TB Disease Intensive Phase Continuation Phase LOC All forms of TB in adults and children of all ages but excluding TB meningitis and Bone TB) 2RHZE 4RH HC3 TB meningitis Bone (Osteoarticular) TB 2RHZE 10RH HC4and above Alternative 1st-line treatment regimen All forms of TB in children (2 months to 16 years) with non-severe disease 2 HRE(Z) 2RH General Hospital and above All forms of TB in adults above 12 years, weight >40 Kgs, if HIV positive CD4>100 cells/L 2 HPMZ 2HPM

Drug -resistant TB

Patients with drug-resistant TB should undergo culture and Drug Sensitivity testing, and be treated with second line regimens according to national guidelines.

Notify the relevant TB focal persons and organize referral to MDR-TB treatment initiation center for appropriate management.

Type Of TB Disease Regimen For Drug Resistant TB LOC INH mono-resistance 6(H)REZ–levofloxacin) DTUS RR/MDR TB Treatment at designated MDR TB treatment initiation centers as per the national guidelines Hospital and above Pre XDR, XDR Treatment at designated MDR TB treatment initiation centers as per the national guidelines Hospital and above in consultation with national panel

Adjunctive treatment

TREATMENT LOC  Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): 25 mg per day; given concomitantly with isoniazid for the duration of therapy, to prevent peripheral neuropathy Prednisolone in TB patients in whom complications of fibrosis are anticipated because of severe inflammation such as TB meningitis.- Prednisolone is given in a dose of 1-2 mg/kg body weight (not more than 60 mg/day) as a single dose for 4 weeks, and then tapered off over 2 weeks HC3H Laboratory Monitoring (For Pulmonary Tb) At the end of the initial 2 months:- Sputum smear-negative; start continuation phase- Sputum smear-positive; do GeneXpert to rule out rifampicin resistance, start continuation phase and Xpert MTB/XDR where accessible, to rule out resistance to other drugs- If Rifampicin-resistant, refer for MDR-TB treatment and- If Rifampicin-sensitive, continue with first-line- treatment, explore adherence issues but repeat smear at At the beginning of 5 months:- Sputum smear-negative, continue with continuation treatment- Sputum smear-positive, diagnose Treatment Failure- Take sputum for GeneXpert to rule out Rifampicin Resistance and Xpert MTB/XDR where accessible, to rule out resistance to other drugs- If Rifampicin Resistant, refer for DR treatment- If INH resistant manage as INH mono-resistant TB as above- If TB detected but not Rifampicin Resistant, restart first line regimen but explore adherence issues

Monitoring of susceptible TB

During the 6th month:- Sputum smear-negative, complete treatment and declare cured or treatment completed- Sputum smear-positive, diagnose treatment failure- Take sputum for GeneXpert to rule out rifampicin resistance and Xpert MTB/XDR where accessible, to rule out resistance to other drugs- If Rifampicin-resistant, refer for MDR-TB treatment- If Rifampicin-sensitive, restart first-line treatment, explore adherence issues Clinical Monitoring (For All Tb Cases) - Monitor wellbeing and weight gain- Assess and reinforce treatment adherence- Assess and manage side effects Note Radiological monitoring– this method should not be used as the sole monitoring tool.

Management of treatment interruptions Refer to NTLP manual Treatment outcomes

A conclusion should be made regarding treatment outcome of EVERY TB patient who has been started on anti-TB treatment.

OUTCOME DESCRIPTION Cure A pulmonary TB patient with bacteriologically confirmed TB at the beginning of treatment who was smear- or culture-negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion Treatment completed A TB patient who completed treatment without evidence of failure BUT with no record to show that sputum smear or culture results in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion were negative, either because tests were not done or because results are unavailable Lost to follow-up A TB patient who did not start treatment, or completed more than one month of treatment and whosetreatment was interrupted for two or more consecutive months OUTCOME DESCRIPTION Died A TB patient who dies for any reason before starting or during the course of treatment Treatment failure A TB patient whose sputum smear or culture is positive at month five or later during treatment Not evaluated A patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned. This includes cases “transferred out” to another treatment unit as well as cases for whom the treatment outcome is unknown to the reporting unit Treatment success The sum of cured and treatment completed

docs.title: 5.3 TUBERCULOSIS (TB)
docs.text:
A chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. It commonly affects lungs but can affect any organ (lymph nodes, bones, meninges, abdomen, kidney).

For more information on the management of TB see:  Manual of the National TB/Leprosy Programme (NTLP) inUganda 4th Edition, 2022  NTLP desk guide  Latent TB guidelines  National drug resistant TB guidelines

Causes

  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (e.g. M. tuberculosis,

  • M. bovis, M. avium, M. africanum and M. Microti)

  • M. tuberculosis is the commonest cause of tuberculosis

  • Transmission by droplet inhalation (cough from a patient

with open pulmonary TB); can also be through drinking unpasteurised milk, especially M.bovis

Clinical features General symptoms

  • Fevers especially in the evening,

  • excessive night sweats

  • Weight loss and loss of appetite Pulmonary TB

  • Chronic cough of >2 weeks (however, in HIV settings,

cough of any duration)

  • Chest pain, purulent sputum occasionally blood-stained, shortness of breath

Extrapulmonary TB

  • Lymphnode TB: Localized enlargement of lymph nodes de-

pending on the site affected (commonly neck)

  • Pleural or pericardial effusion

  • Abdominal TB: ascites and abdominal pain

  • TB meningitis: subacute meningitis (headache, alteration of

consciousness)

  • Bone or joint TB: swelling and deformity Complications

  • Massive haemoptysis - coughing up >250 mL blood per

episode

  • Spontaneous pneumothorax and pleural effusion

  • TB pericarditis, TB meningitis, TB peritonitis

  • Bone TB: can be TB spine with gibbus, TB joints with

deformity)

  • Respiratory failure

TB Case Definitions

CASE DEFINITION DESCRIPTION Presumptive TB patient Any patient who presents with symptoms and signs suggestive of TB or found to have chest X-ray suggestive of active TB disease Bacteriologically confirmed TB patient Patient in whom biological specimen is positive by smear microscopy, culture or molecular WHO Recommended Diagnostic (mWRD) test like GeneXpert Truenat or TB LAMP. All such cases should be notified (registered in the unit TB register) Clinically diagnosed TB patient Patient who does not fulfil the criteria for bacteriological confirmation but has been diagnosed with active TB by a clinician on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms supported by relevant investigations

Classification of TB Disease

CASE DEFINITION DESCRIPTION Site of the disease Pulmonary TB: bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case, affecting lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree. Site of the disease Extrapulmonary TB: Any other case of TB. Isolated TB pleural effusion and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without lung tissue involvement is considered extrapulmonary TB If the patient has pulmonary and extrapulmonary involvement, he/ she will be classified as pulmonary TB History of treatment New: no previous TB treatment (or treatment less < 1 month) History of treatment Relapse: patient who completed a previous course of treatment, was declared cured or treatmentcompleted, and is now diagnosed with a recurrent episode of TB History of treatment Treatment after failure: those who have previously been treated for TB and whose treatment failed at the end of their most recent course of treatment History of treatment Treatment after loss to follow-up: Patient has been previously treated for TB and were declared lost to follow-up at the end of their most recent course of treatment. CASE DEFINITION DESCRIPTION Treatment history unknown: Those who have previously been treated for TB but whose Outcome after their most recent course of treatment is unknown or undocumented Drug susceptibility status (based on drug susceptibility Tests) Drug Sensitive TB (DS-TB): These are sensitive to 1st line anti-TB drugsDrug resistant TB (DR-TB): Resistant to any anti-TB drug. Can be classified as follows.Rifampicin resistant: any case ofrifampicin resistance (isolated or in combination with other resistance) (RR-TB) Drug susceptibility status (based on drug susceptibility Tests) Monoresistant: resistant to only one first line anti-TB drug Drug susceptibility status (based on drug susceptibility Tests) Poly drug resistant: resistant to more than one first line anti TB other than both rifampicin and isoniazid Multi drug resistant: resistant to rifampicin and isoniazid (MDR –TB) Extensive drug resistance (XDRTB): resistant to rifampicin, isoniazid (MDR TB) and any fluoroquinolone and at least one of either bedaquiline or Linezolid ) HIV status Positive: patients who tested HIV-positive at time of diagnosis or already enrolled in HIV care CASE DEFINITION DESCRIPTION HIV status Negative: patients who tested negative at the moment of diagnosisUnknown: If testing is then performed at any moment during treatment, patient should be re classified

Differential diagnosis

  • Histoplasma pneumonia, trypanosomiasis, brucellosis

  • Pneumonia

  • COVID-19

  • HIV/AIDS

  • Malignancy

  • COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis, emphysema etc.

  • Post TB lung disease

  • Fungal infection of the lungs e.g. Aspergillosis Screening and diagnosis of TB disease TB screening: is defined as the systematic identification of people at risk for TB disease, in a predetermined target group, by assessing using tests, examinations or other procedures that can be applied rapidly TB screening approaches:

  • • Symptom screening or CXR

  • • All individuals seeking health care should be screened for TB at each visit

Investigations for TB

Obtain sputum sample or other relevant samples from presumptive TB patients for diagnosis

• Xpert MTB/RIF is the recommended diagnostic test for TB diagnosis

• Where Xpert MTB/RIF test is not available, do Sputum smear microscopy for AAFBs (ZN stain) but send the sample

for Xpert MTB/RIF test.

GeneXpert MTB/Rif: automated DNA test on body samples (sputum, lymphonodes tissue, pleural fluid, CSF etc) which can diagnose pulmonary TB and determine susceptibility to Rifampicin. It is superior to microscopy. Other investigations

 X- ray, abdominal ultrasound, biopsies etc. can be used for sputum and GeneXpert negative patients or in case of extrapulmonary TB according to clinical judgement

 TST can be used as a supportive test to guide decision to treat for TB in children

 putum culture and Drug susceptibility test: is a confirmatory test for TB and also provides resistance pattern to TB medicines. Do this test for:

 Patients with Rifampicin resistance reported with GeneXpert  Also patients on first-line treatment who remain positive at 2 months

and are reported Rifampicin sensitive on GeneXpert  Patients suspected to be failing on first-line treatment

Note: All presumed and diagnosed TB patients should be offered an HIV test

5.3.1.1Tuberculosis in Children and adolescents

TB may present at any age in children though the risk is highest below the age of two years. When compared to adults, children are more prone to TB infection, TB disease, and severe forms of TB disease.

Risk factors

  • Contact with infectious (pulmonary) case of TB

  • Age < 5 years

  • Immunosuppression (HIV, malnutrition, diabetes, etc).

  • Age < 1 year and lack of BCG vaccination are risk factors

for severe disease Clinical features

  • Suspect TB in all children with

    • Fever > 2 weeks
    • Cough >2 weeks
    • Poor weight gain for one month
    • Close (home) contact of pulmonary TB case.
    • In young children, reduced playfulness, poor feeding, decreased activity
    • Other signs include swollen lymph nodes in the neck, groin region etc.

Investigations  Bacteriological confirmation of TB is more difficult in children.

The diagnosis of TB in children is dependent on conducting a detailed clinical assessment combined with available tests

 Whenever possible, geneXpert should be performed Management

The principles and objectives of TB treatment are similar to those of adults. In addition, effective treatment of TB in children promotes growth and development.

docs.title: 5.1.1 Asthma
docs.text:
Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that leads to bronchial muscle spasm, mucus plugging, and oedema. It causes recurrent wheezing, cough, breathlessness, and chest tightness.

Severe asthma may present with inability to complete sentences, darkening of the lips, oral mucosa, or extremities due to cyanosis.

Differential diagnosis

  • Heart failure
  • Other causes of chronic cough
  • Bronchiolitis
  • Bronchiectasis

Investigations

Diagnosis is mainly clinical.

Specialised investigations may include:

  • Peak flow rate, where peak flow improves after administration of a bronchodilator
  • Spirometry, showing an increase in forced expiratory volume (FEV) of >12% after bronchodilation
  • Sputum examination for eosinophilia
  • Chest X-ray, if there is evidence of bacterial infection
  • Complete blood count, if there is evidence of bacterial infection

General principles of asthma management

The four essential components of asthma management are:

  • Patient education
  • Control of asthma triggers
  • Monitoring for changes in symptoms or lung function
  • Pharmacologic therapy

The inhalation route is preferred because it delivers medicines directly to the airways, requires smaller doses, and reduces systemic side effects.

Examples include nebuliser solutions for acute severe asthma, usually given over 5 to 10 minutes and driven by oxygen in hospital.

In children with acute asthma attacks, use spacers to administer inhaler puffs.

The oral route may be used if inhalation is not possible, but systemic side effects occur more frequently, onset of action is slower, and higher doses are required.

The parenteral route should be used only in very severe cases when nebulisation is not adequate.

docs.title: 5.1.1.1 Acute Asthma
docs.text:
An asthma attack is a substantial worsening of asthma symptoms. The severity and duration of attacks are variable and unpredictable. Most attacks are triggered by viral infections.

Assess severity using the table below.

Assessment of severity

Severity Children below 12 years Adults and children >12 years Mild to moderate Able to talk in sentences.Peak flow is >50% of predicted or personal best.Pulse:- Child >5 years: <125 beats/minute- Child <5 years: <140 beats/minuteRespiratory rate:- Child >5 years: <30 breaths/minute- Child <5 years: <40 breaths/minuteSpO₂ ≥92%. Able to talk.Pulse <110 beats/minute.Respiratory rate <25 breaths/minute.Peak flow >50% of predicted or personal best.SpO₂ ≥92%. Severe Cannot complete sentences in one breath, or is too breathless to talk or feed.Peak flow <50% of predicted or personal best.Pulse:- Child >5 years: >125 beats/minute- Child <5 years: >140 beats/minuteRespiratory rate:- Child >5 years: >30 breaths/minute- Child <5 years: >40 breaths/minuteUse of accessory muscles for breathing, especially in young children.SpO₂ <92%. Cannot complete sentences in one breath.Pulse ≥110 beats/minute.Respiratory rate >25 breaths/minute.Peak flow <50% of predicted or personal best.SpO₂ <92%. Life-threatening Silent chest, feeble respiratory effort, cyanosis, hypotension, bradycardia or exhaustion, agitation, reduced level of consciousness, peak flow <33% of predicted or personal best, or arterial oxygen saturation <92%. Silent chest, feeble respiratory effort, cyanosis, hypotension, bradycardia or exhaustion, agitation, reduced level of consciousness, peak flow <33% of predicted or personal best, or arterial oxygen saturation <92%.

Note

Not all features may be present. If the patient says they feel very unwell, listen to them.

Management of asthma attacks

Severity Treatment LOC Mild to moderate Treat as an outpatient.Reassure the patient and place them in a half-sitting position.Give salbutamol:- Inhaler 2 to 10 puffs via a large volume spacer, or- Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg, or 2.5 mg in children.Repeat every 20 to 30 minutes if necessary.Give prednisolone 50 mg, or 1 mg/kg in children.Monitor response for 30 to 60 minutes. If not improving, or if relapse occurs within 3 to 4 hours, refer to a higher level of care. HC3 Mild to moderate, improving Send home with prednisolone 50 mg once daily, or 1 mg/kg in children.Duration:- Adults: 5 days- Children: 3 daysInstitute or step up chronic treatment. See section 5.1.1.2.Follow up after 1 to 2 weeks.Instruct the patient on self-treatment and when to return.Review in 48 hours.Do not give routine antibiotics unless there are clear signs of bacterial infection. HC3 Severe asthma Patients with severe asthma need referral to HC4 or hospital after initial treatment.Admit the patient and place them in a half-sitting position.Give high-flow oxygen continuously, at least 5 L/minute, to maintain SpO₂ ≥94% if available.Give salbutamol:- Inhaler 2 to 10 puffs via a large volume spacer, or- Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg, or 2.5 mg in children.Repeat every 20 to 30 minutes if necessary during the first hour.Give prednisolone 50 mg, or 1 mg/kg in children.Alternatively, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 hours until the patient can take oral prednisolone. In children, give hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg IV every 6 hours, maximum 100 mg per dose.Monitor response after nebulisation. HC4 Severe asthma with poor response Give ipratropium bromide nebuliser 500 micrograms, or 250 micrograms in children below 12 years, every 20 to 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then every 4 to 6 hours.Alternatively, give aminophylline 250 mg slow IV bolus, or 5 mg/kg in children, if the patient is not taking oral theophylline. HC4 Severe asthma, improving If symptoms have improved, respiration and pulse are settling, and peak flow is >50%, step up the usual treatment.Continue prednisolone to complete 5 days of treatment.Review within 24 hours.Monitor symptoms and peak flow.Arrange a self-management plan. HC4 Life-threatening asthma Arrange immediate hospital referral and admission.Admit the patient and place them in a half-sitting position.Give high-flow oxygen continuously, at least 5 L/minute, to maintain SpO₂ ≥94% if available.Give salbutamol:- Inhaler 2 to 10 puffs via a large volume spacer, or- Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg, or 2.5 mg in children.Repeat every 20 minutes for 1 hour.Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, or 4 mg/kg IV in children, maximum 100 mg.Alternatively, give prednisolone 50 mg, or 1 mg/kg in children.Give ipratropium bromide nebuliser 500 micrograms, or 250 micrograms in children below 12 years, every 20 to 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then every 4 to 6 hours.Monitor response for 15 to 30 minutes. HC4 Life-threatening asthma with poor response Give aminophylline 250 mg slow IV bolus, or 5 mg/kg in children, if the patient is not taking oral theophylline. HC4

Caution

The use of aminophylline and theophylline in the management of asthma exacerbations is discouraged because of their poor efficacy and poor safety profile.

Acute asthma management flow

General principles of long-term asthma management

Follow a stepped approach.

Before initiating a new medicine:

  • Check that the diagnosis is correct.
  • Check treatment adherence.
  • Check inhaler technique.
  • Eliminate trigger factors for acute exacerbations.

Start at the step most appropriate to the initial severity.

Rescue course

Give a 3 to 5 day rescue course of prednisolone at any step and at any time as required to control acute exacerbations of asthma.

Recommended prednisolone doses:

Age group Dose Child <1 year 1 to 2 mg/kg daily Child 1 to 5 years Up to 20 mg daily Child 5 to 15 years Up to 40 mg daily Adult 40 to 60 mg daily for up to 3 to 5 days

Stepping down

Review treatment every 3 to 6 months.

If control is achieved, stepwise reduction may be possible.

If treatment was started recently at Step 4, or included corticosteroid tablets, reduction may take place after a short interval. In other patients, 1 to 3 months or longer of stability may be needed before stepwise reduction can be done.

5.1.1.2 Chronic Asthma

Chronic asthma management follows a stepwise approach based on symptom frequency, night-time symptoms, activity limitation, and need for reliever medicines.

Step Clinical pattern Treatment LOC Step 1: Intermittent asthma Intermittent symptoms, less than once per week.Night-time symptoms less than twice per month.Normal physical activity. Give occasional relief bronchodilator therapy.Use an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist, such as salbutamol inhaler 1 to 2 puffs, equivalent to 100 to 200 micrograms.Use with a spacer in children.Move to Step 2 if salbutamol is needed more than twice a week or if night-time symptoms occur at least once a week. HC3 Step 2: Mild persistent asthma Symptoms more than once per week but less than once per day.Night-time symptoms more than twice per month.Symptoms may affect activity. Give regular inhaled preventer therapy.Use salbutamol inhaler 1 to 2 puffs as needed.Add regular standard-dose inhaled corticosteroid, such as beclomethasone 100 to 400 micrograms every 12 hours.Children: beclomethasone 100 to 200 micrograms every 12 hours.Assess after 1 month and adjust the dose as needed.A higher dose may be needed initially to gain control.Doubling the regular dose may be useful to cover exacerbations. HC3 / HC4 Step 3: Moderate persistent asthma Daily symptoms.Symptoms affect activity.Night-time symptoms more than once per week.Daily use of salbutamol. Children below 5 years should be referred to a specialist.Give regular high-dose inhaled corticosteroids.Use salbutamol inhaler 1 to 2 puffs as needed, up to every 2 to 3 hours. Usual use is every 4 to 12 hours.Add beclomethasone inhaler 400 to 1,000 micrograms every 12 hours.Children 5 to 12 years: beclomethasone 100 to 400 micrograms every 12 hours.In adults, also consider a 6-week trial of aminophylline 200 mg every 12 hours. HC4 Step 4: Severe persistent asthma Daily symptoms.Frequent night-time symptoms.Daily use of salbutamol. Refer to a specialist clinic, especially for children below 12 years.Give regular high-dose beclomethasone as in Step 3.Add regular prednisolone 10 to 20 mg daily after breakfast. RR

Note

If an inhaler is not available, consider salbutamol tablets.

Adult dose: salbutamol 4 mg every 8 hours.

Child below 2 years: salbutamol 100 micrograms/kg per dose.

Child 2 to 5 years: salbutamol 1 to 2 mg per dose.

Caution

Do not give medicines such as morphine, propranolol, or other beta-blockers to patients with asthma because they may worsen respiratory problems.

Do not give sedatives to children with asthma, even if they are restless.

Prevention

Avoid precipitating factors, including:

  • Cigarette smoking
  • Acetylsalicylic acid
  • Known allergens such as dust, pollen, and animal skins
  • Exposure to cold air

Exercise can precipitate asthma in children. Advise children to keep an inhaler nearby during sports and play.

Effectively treat respiratory infections.

5.1.2 Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)

ICD-10 CODE: J42–J44

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a chronic respiratory condition characterised by persistent airflow limitation. It is commonly associated with chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or both.

Content for this section should be reviewed from the source text before finalisation if the COPD section is required here.

docs.title: 5.2 Infectious Respiratory Diseases
docs.text:
Infectious respiratory diseases include conditions such as bronchiolitis, acute bronchitis, coryza, acute epiglottitis, laryngitis, pneumonia, lung abscess, and other respiratory infections.

5.2.1 Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis is an acute lower respiratory tract infection, usually affecting young children. It is mainly viral and is often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Mycoplasma may also be involved.

Causes

  • Mainly viral infection, often respiratory syncytial virus
  • Mycoplasma

Clinical features

In the first 24 to 72 hours, the child may present with rhinopharyngitis and dry cough.

Later features may include:

  • Tachypnoea
  • Difficulty in breathing
  • Wheezing, often poorly responsive to bronchodilators
  • Profuse, frothy, obstructive cough secretions
  • Mucoid nasal discharge
  • Moderate fever or no fever

Features suggesting severe bronchiolitis include:

  • Age below 3 months
  • Worsening general condition
  • Pallor
  • Cyanosis
  • Respiratory distress
  • Anxiety
  • Respiratory rate above 60 breaths per minute
  • Difficulty feeding
  • SpO₂ below 92%

Differential diagnosis

  • Asthma
  • Pneumonia
  • Whooping cough
  • Foreign body inhalation
  • Heart failure

Investigations

  • Clinical diagnosis
  • Chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia
  • Haemogram

Management

Severity Treatment LOC Mild to moderate bronchiolitis Features include wheezing, respiratory rate 50 to 60 breaths per minute, no cyanosis, and ability to drink or feed.Treat symptoms, possibly as an outpatient.Provide nasal irrigation with normal saline.Give small, frequent feeds.Increase fluids and nutrition.Treat fever with paracetamol. HC2 / HC3 Severe bronchiolitis Features include wheezing, fast breathing above 60 breaths per minute, or cyanosis.Admit and give supportive treatment.Give humidified nasal oxygen at 1 to 2 L/minute.Give salbutamol inhaler 100 micrograms per puff: 2 puffs with spacer every 30 minutes, or nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg in 4 mL normal saline.If symptoms improve, continue salbutamol every 6 hours.If symptoms do not respond, stop salbutamol.Nebulise adrenaline 1:1000, 1 mL diluted in 2 to 4 mL normal saline every 2 to 4 hours.Give as much oral fluid as the child can take, such as ORS.Use a nasogastric tube or IV line if the child cannot take fluids orally.Give basic total fluid requirement of 150 mL/kg in 24 hours, plus extra fluid to cover increased losses due to illness. HC3 / HC4

Note

Antibiotics are usually not needed for bronchiolitis because it is commonly viral.

Steroids are not recommended.

Prevention

  • Avoid exposure to cold and viral infections.
  • Ensure proper handwashing after contact with patients.

docs.title: 5.3 Tuberculosis (TB)
docs.text:
Tuberculosis is a chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. It commonly affects the lungs but can affect any organ, including lymph nodes, bones, meninges, abdomen, and kidneys.

Reference documents

For more information on the management of TB, refer to:

  • Manual of the National TB/Leprosy Programme (NTLP) in Uganda, 4th Edition, 2022
  • NTLP Desk Guide
  • Latent TB guidelines
  • National Drug-Resistant TB Guidelines

Causes

Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, including:

  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis
  • Mycobacterium bovis
  • Mycobacterium avium
  • Mycobacterium africanum
  • Mycobacterium microti

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the commonest cause of tuberculosis.

Transmission usually occurs through inhalation of droplets from a patient with open pulmonary TB. Transmission may also occur through drinking unpasteurised milk, especially with M. bovis.

Clinical features

General symptoms include:

  • Fever, especially in the evening
  • Excessive night sweats
  • Weight loss
  • Loss of appetite

Pulmonary TB

Pulmonary TB may present with:

  • Chronic cough for more than 2 weeks
  • In HIV settings, cough of any duration
  • Chest pain
  • Purulent sputum, occasionally blood-stained
  • Shortness of breath

Extrapulmonary TB

Extrapulmonary TB may present with:

  • Localised lymph node enlargement, commonly in the neck
  • Pleural or pericardial effusion
  • Abdominal TB with ascites and abdominal pain
  • TB meningitis with subacute meningitis, headache, and altered consciousness
  • Bone or joint TB with swelling and deformity

Complications

Complications of TB include:

  • Massive haemoptysis, defined as coughing up more than 250 mL of blood per episode
  • Spontaneous pneumothorax
  • Pleural effusion
  • TB pericarditis
  • TB meningitis
  • TB peritonitis
  • Bone TB, including TB spine with gibbus and TB joints with deformity
  • Respiratory failure

TB case definitions

Case definition Description Presumptive TB patient Any patient who presents with symptoms and signs suggestive of TB, or who is found to have a chest X-ray suggestive of active TB disease. Bacteriologically confirmed TB patient A patient whose biological specimen is positive by smear microscopy, culture, or molecular WHO-recommended diagnostic test, such as GeneXpert, Truenat, or TB-LAMP. All such cases should be notified and registered in the unit TB register. Clinically diagnosed TB patient A patient who does not fulfil the criteria for bacteriological confirmation but has been diagnosed with active TB by a clinician on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms, supported by relevant investigations.

Classification of TB disease

Classification area Definition Pulmonary TB A bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case affecting the lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree. Extrapulmonary TB Any other case of TB. Isolated TB pleural effusion and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without lung tissue involvement are considered extrapulmonary TB. If the patient has both pulmonary and extrapulmonary involvement, the patient is classified as pulmonary TB. New TB patient A patient with no previous TB treatment, or previous treatment for less than 1 month. Relapse A patient who completed a previous course of treatment, was declared cured or treatment completed, and is now diagnosed with a recurrent episode of TB. Treatment after failure A patient who was previously treated for TB and whose treatment failed at the end of the most recent course of treatment. Treatment after loss to follow-up A patient who was previously treated for TB and was declared lost to follow-up at the end of the most recent course of treatment. Treatment history unknown A patient who was previously treated for TB, but whose outcome after the most recent course of treatment is unknown or undocumented.

Classification by drug susceptibility status

Drug susceptibility status Description Drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB) TB that is sensitive to first-line anti-TB medicines. Drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) TB that is resistant to any anti-TB medicine. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) Any case of rifampicin resistance, whether isolated or in combination with other resistance. Monoresistant TB Resistance to only one first-line anti-TB medicine. Polydrug-resistant TB Resistance to more than one first-line anti-TB medicine, other than both rifampicin and isoniazid. Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) Resistance to both rifampicin and isoniazid. Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) MDR-TB with resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one of either bedaquiline or linezolid.

Classification by HIV status

HIV status Description Positive Patient tested HIV-positive at the time of TB diagnosis or was already enrolled in HIV care. Negative Patient tested HIV-negative at the time of TB diagnosis. Unknown HIV status is unknown. If testing is later performed during treatment, the patient should be reclassified accordingly.

Differential diagnosis

  • Histoplasma pneumonia
  • Trypanosomiasis
  • Brucellosis
  • Pneumonia
  • COVID-19
  • HIV/AIDS
  • Malignancy
  • COPD
  • Asthma
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Emphysema
  • Post-TB lung disease
  • Fungal infection of the lungs, such as aspergillosis

Screening and diagnosis of TB disease

TB screening is the systematic identification of people at risk for TB disease in a predetermined target group, using tests, examinations, or other procedures that can be applied rapidly.

TB screening approaches include:

  • Symptom screening
  • Chest X-ray

All individuals seeking healthcare should be screened for TB at each visit.

Investigations for TB

Obtain sputum or other relevant samples from presumptive TB patients for diagnosis.

  • Xpert MTB/RIF is the recommended diagnostic test for TB diagnosis.
  • Where Xpert MTB/RIF is not available, do sputum smear microscopy for AAFBs using Ziehl-Neelsen stain, but also send a sample for Xpert MTB/RIF testing.

GeneXpert MTB/RIF is an automated DNA test performed on body samples such as sputum, lymph node tissue, pleural fluid, or CSF. It can diagnose pulmonary TB and determine susceptibility to rifampicin. It is superior to microscopy.

Other investigations include:

  • Chest X-ray
  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Biopsy where clinically indicated
  • Tuberculin skin test as a supportive test to guide the decision to treat TB in children

Sputum culture and drug susceptibility testing are confirmatory tests for TB and also provide the resistance pattern to TB medicines.

Do sputum culture and drug susceptibility testing for:

  • Patients with rifampicin resistance reported on GeneXpert
  • Patients on first-line treatment who remain positive at 2 months and are reported rifampicin-sensitive on GeneXpert
  • Patients suspected to be failing first-line treatment

Note

All presumed and diagnosed TB patients should be offered an HIV test.

docs.title: 5.3.1.1 Tuberculosis in Children and Adolescents
docs.text:
TB may present at any age in children, although the risk is highest below 2 years of age. Compared with adults, children are more prone to TB infection, TB disease, and severe forms of TB disease.

Risk factors

  • Contact with an infectious pulmonary TB case
  • Age below 5 years
  • Immunosuppression, including HIV, malnutrition, and diabetes
  • Age below 1 year
  • Lack of BCG vaccination, especially as a risk factor for severe disease

Clinical features

Suspect TB in children with:

  • Fever for more than 2 weeks
  • Cough for more than 2 weeks
  • Poor weight gain for 1 month
  • Close household contact with a pulmonary TB case
  • Reduced playfulness in young children
  • Poor feeding
  • Decreased activity
  • Swollen lymph nodes, especially in the neck or groin region

Investigations

Bacteriological confirmation of TB is more difficult in children. Diagnosis depends on a detailed clinical assessment combined with available tests.

Wherever possible, GeneXpert should be performed.

Management

The principles and objectives of TB treatment in children are similar to those in adults. Effective TB treatment in children also promotes growth and development.

docs.title: 6.1.1 Appendicitis (Acute)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K35–K37

Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix.

Causes

  • Blockage of the appendix duct with stool or particles, followed by infection by intestinal bacteria

Clinical features

  • Constipation, commonly
  • Pain situated around the umbilicus
  • Crampy pain that keeps increasing in severity
  • After some hours, the pain localises in the right iliac fossa and becomes continuous
  • Nausea and vomiting may occur
  • Fever, usually low-grade in the initial stages
  • Tenderness and rigidity, also called guarding, in the right iliac fossa
  • Generalised abdominal pain and signs of peritonitis may follow rupture when the contents are poured into the abdominal cavity

Differential diagnosis

  • Salpingitis in females
  • Ovarian cyst
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Pyelonephritis
  • Ureteritis
  • Intestinal obstruction
  • Peptic or duodenal ulcers

Investigations

  • No special investigations are required if there is a good history and physical examination.
  • Complete blood count to look for leucocytosis
  • Transabdominal ultrasound
  • Abdominal X-ray to assess for perforation and intestinal occlusion

Management

Treatment LOC Emergency surgery. H If surgery is delayed, start antibiotic treatment while referring. H Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily. H Children: ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg IV once daily. H Plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. H Children: metronidazole 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. H Start antibiotic prophylaxis before surgery and continue for a duration depending on the findings. Use less than 24 hours for an unperforated appendix and at least 5 days for a perforated appendix. H

docs.title: 6.1.2 Acute Pancreatitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K85

Acute pancreatitis is acute inflammation of the pancreas.

Causes

  • Excessive alcohol intake
  • Gallstones or biliary tract disease, including obstructive cancer or anatomical abnormalities
  • Infections, such as mumps, HIV, hepatitis A, and ascariasis
  • Medicines or toxic substances, such as sulphonamides, furosemide, lamivudine, analgesics, and organophosphate poisoning
  • Peptic or duodenal ulcers

Clinical features

  • Acute abdominal pain, usually in the epigastrium, radiating to the back
  • Pain worsened by eating or lying down and relieved by sitting up or leaning forward
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Abdominal distension
  • Fever
  • Tachycardia
  • Dehydration
  • Severe illness with shock may occur
  • Very tender abdomen, but in the absence of peritonitis there is no rigidity or rebound tenderness

Complications

  • Pseudocysts
  • Necrotising pancreatitis with infection
  • Peritonitis

Differential diagnosis

  • Perforated peptic ulcer
  • Peritonitis
  • Acute cholecystitis or inflammation of the biliary tract
  • Sickle-cell anaemia crisis

Investigations

  • Serum amylase
  • Complete blood count
  • Random blood sugar
  • Pancreatic amylase and lipase raised more than 3 times normal
  • Ultrasound to assess for gallstones, pancreatic oedema, and abdominal fluid
  • Liver function tests, which may show raised liver enzymes

Management of mild acute pancreatitis

Mild acute pancreatitis is pancreatitis with no organ failure, no local or systemic complications, no signs of peritonitis, normal serum creatinine, and normal haematocrit.

Treatment LOC Start early aggressive fluid resuscitation and correct acid-base balance. HC4 Prevent volume depletion using adequate fluids with Ringer’s lactate. Give 5 to 10 mL/kg/hour, or 250 to 500 mL of isotonic crystalloids in the first 12 to 24 hours, aiming for urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour. HC4 Give IV fluids to correct metabolic and electrolyte disturbances and prevent hypovolaemia and hypotension. HC4 Monitor electrolytes. HC4 Aim to decrease haematocrit and blood urea nitrogen within 48 hours. Evaluate every 4 to 6 hours. HC4

Pain control

Treatment LOC Give analgesia using opioids, paracetamol, or epidural anaesthesia. Avoid NSAIDs. HC4 Give rectal or IV paracetamol 500 mg every 6 to 8 hours. HC4 Alternatively, give pethidine 25 to 100 mg SC or IM, or 25 to 50 mg slow IV. Repeat as needed every 4 to 6 hours. HC4 Alternatively, give IV morphine 1 to 3 mg every 4 hours. HC4 Monitor for complications of opioids, including constipation, dysphagia, respiratory depression, and confusion. HC4

Management of vomiting and ileus

Treatment LOC Give anti-emetics as appropriate. HC4 Give metoclopramide 10 mg IV or IM every 8 hours. HC4 Pass a nasogastric tube for suction when persistent vomiting or ileus occurs. HC4

Feeding and nutrition

Treatment LOC Do not give feeds by mouth until signs and symptoms of acute inflammation subside, including cessation of abdominal tenderness and pain, return of hunger, and general well-being. HC4 Provide energy with dextrose 50%, 300 to 500 mL per day. Add 50 mL to 500 mL normal saline to prevent muscle wasting. HC4 Start early oral re-feeding on demand within 48 to 72 hours, as soon as the patient is able and can tolerate feeds. HC4 Start with clear liquids, then low-fat semi-solid feeds, then a normal diet according to tolerance. HC4 Monitor vital signs, fluid intake, urinary output, and gastrointestinal symptoms daily. HC4 If oral feeding is not possible, consider peripheral or central parenteral nutrition. HC4

Glycaemic control

Treatment LOC Hyperglycaemia is common. Keep serum blood sugar between 6 and 9 mmol/L. HC4 Avoid hypoglycaemia. HC4

Antibiotics

Treatment LOC Avoid inappropriate antibiotic use and other unnecessary medicines, including prophylactic antibiotics. HC4 If there is a specific infection, such as biliary sepsis, pulmonary infection, or UTI, treat vigorously with appropriate antibiotic therapy. HC4

Other measures

Treatment LOC Address the underlying cause as appropriate. HC4 Stop alcohol or causative medicines. HC4 Mobilise the patient when clinically appropriate. HC4 Evaluate for gallstones using ultrasound scan. HC4 Manage complications, such as acute peri-pancreatic fluid collections, acute necrosis, and pseudocyst. HC4

Moderately acute pancreatitis

Moderately acute pancreatitis includes:

  • Transient organ failure lasting less than 48 hours
  • Local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure
Treatment LOC Treat as above and refer or consult a specialist at a higher level of care. RR

Severe acute pancreatitis

Severe acute pancreatitis includes:

  • Persistent organ failure lasting more than 48 hours
  • Single or multiple organ failure
Treatment LOC Treat as above and refer or consult a specialist at a higher level of care. RR Admit to HDU or ICU for monitoring and nursing care where available. RR Continue volume resuscitation. RR Provide pain management. RR Provide nutrition and re-feeding support. RR Maintain glycaemic control. RR Insert a nasogastric tube where indicated. RR Give oxygen or mechanical ventilation where indicated. RR Provide renal replacement therapy where indicated. RR Address the cause where possible. RR Manage complications as appropriate, including acute peri-pancreatic fluid collection, acute necrosis, and pseudocyst. RR

Note

Look out for diabetes mellitus as a consequence of damage to the pancreas.

Prevention

  • Reduce alcohol intake to moderate consumption
  • Limit use of toxic medicines or substances

docs.title: 6.1.3 Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding
docs.text:
Upper gastrointestinal bleeding is bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract, including the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum. It can be a medical emergency.

Causes

  • Gastro-oesophageal varices
  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Severe gastritis
  • Cancer
  • Mallory-Weiss tear, which is a tear in the oesophageal mucosa caused by forceful retching

Clinical features

  • Vomiting of fresh blood, also called haematemesis
  • Coffee-brown vomitus, caused by degraded blood mixed with stomach contents
  • Melaena, which is passage of soft, dark red, smelly stool
  • Black stool in minor bleeding

Complications

  • Acute hypovolaemia, especially if bleeding is acute and abundant
  • Syncope
  • Hypotension
  • Tachycardia
  • Sweating
  • Chronic anaemia if blood loss is subacute or chronic

Diagnosis

  • Endoscopy

docs.title: 6.1.4 Peritonitis
docs.text:
Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum. It may result from bacterial contamination, perforation of abdominal organs, chemical irritation, or spread of infection within the abdominal cavity.

Causes

Bacterial causes include:

  • Ruptured appendix
  • Perforated peptic ulcer
  • Perforated bowel due to obstruction or injury
  • Perforation of the gall bladder containing infected bile
  • Perforation of the uterus
  • Tuberculosis
  • Abscess
  • Typhoid ulcers
  • Malignancy
  • Post-operative peritonitis

Chemical causes include leakage of the following into the peritoneal cavity:

  • Urine
  • Blood
  • Bile
  • Stomach contents
  • Pancreatic contents

Clinical features

  • Severe and continuous abdominal pain
  • Generalised pain if the whole peritoneum is affected
  • Abdominal swelling or distension
  • Fever
  • Vomiting
  • Tachycardia
  • Hypoxia
  • Hypovolaemic shock
  • Reduced urinary volume
  • Tender, rigid abdomen
  • Rebound tenderness, where pressure on the abdomen followed by sudden release causes sharper pain
  • Absent bowel sounds

Investigations

  • Abdominal X-ray
  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Complete blood count
  • Blood culture and sensitivity
  • Renal function tests
  • Electrolytes
  • Liver function tests

Management

Treatment LOC Refer to hospital. H Start initial treatment before referral. H Monitor temperature. H Monitor blood pressure, pulse, SpO₂, and urine output. H Put up an IV drip with normal saline, Ringer’s lactate, or any other crystalloid. Give 1 L every 1 to 2 hours until blood pressure is normal, then 1 L every 4 to 6 hours when blood pressure is normal. H Keep the patient nil by mouth. H Pass a nasogastric tube and start suction. H Ask the patient to lie on their side in a comfortable position. H Give oxygen if the patient is hypoxic. H Give pain control. Avoid NSAIDs. H Give pethidine 50 mg IM or IV. H Children: give pethidine 0.5 to 2 mg/kg. H Alternatively, give morphine 5 to 15 mg IV, IM, or SC. H Children: give morphine 2.5 to 5 mg IM, IV, or SC. H Refer the patient to hospital for further management, including possible exploratory laparotomy. H

Management when bacterial infection and fever are suspected

Give a minimum 7-day antibiotic course.

Treatment LOC Give ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV once daily. H Children: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg per dose. H Plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV daily in divided doses. H Children: gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg every 8 hours. H Plus metronidazole 500 mg by IV infusion every 8 hours. Change to metronidazole 400 mg orally every 8 hours when possible. H Children: metronidazole 12.5 mg/kg IV per dose. Change to oral route when possible. H Identify and control the source of infection. H Prevent and control complications through proper nutrition, early ambulation, and rehabilitation. H

docs.title: 6.1.5 Diarrhoea
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: Depending on the cause

Diarrhoea is defined as three or more loose, watery stools within 24 hours.

Dysentery is diarrhoea with visible blood and mucus.

Persistent diarrhoea refers to diarrhoea lasting more than 14 days.

Causes

  • Viruses, including rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus, measles virus, hepatitis A virus, hepatitis E virus, and Ebola virus
  • Bacteria, including Vibrio cholerae, E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter
  • Protozoa, including giardiasis, malaria, and cryptosporidiosis
  • Helminths, including strongyloidiasis and schistosomiasis
  • Infectious diseases, such as measles, malaria, and other fever-causing conditions
  • Malnutrition, such as kwashiorkor
  • Medicines, such as prolonged use of purgatives and broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Unhygienic feeding methods
  • Malabsorption syndrome
  • Lactose intolerance
  • HIV-associated diarrhoea
  • Irritable bowel syndrome
  • Metabolic conditions, including diabetes and thyroid disease
  • Travellers’ diarrhoea
  • Inflammatory bowel disease, where persistent diarrhoea is usually bloody

Clinical features

  • Loose watery stools
  • Abdominal cramps
  • Dehydration, presenting with thirst, sunken eyes, loss of skin elasticity, and low urine output
  • Signs of malnutrition if diarrhoea persists for more than 14 days
  • Blood in stool in dysentery

Investigations

  • Stool microscopy
  • Stool culture and sensitivity
  • Other investigations according to history and physical examination

Red flags

  • Fever
  • Extremes of age
  • History of travel from a known endemic area
  • Dysentery
  • Shock
  • Failure to feed
  • Mental confusion

Management

Treatment LOC Prevent or correct dehydration with ORS or IV fluids according to treatment Plans A, B, or C. See section 1.1.3. HC2 / HC4 Find and treat the cause if indicated. HC2 / HC4 Avoid inappropriate use of antibiotics, such as metronidazole and ciprofloxacin. HC2 / HC4 Routinely use zinc supplementation in children older than 6 months: 20 mg daily for 10 to 14 days. HC2 Prevent or treat undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies. HC2 / HC4

Persistent or chronic diarrhoea

Treatment LOC Adults only: manage as above and add codeine phosphate 30 mg every 8 to 12 hours as required. HC4 Children: give vitamin A. HC4 Children 6 to 11 months: vitamin A 100,000 IU. HC4 Children 1 to 6 years: vitamin A 200,000 IU. HC4

Prevention

  • Vaccination against measles, rotavirus, polio, and hepatitis A virus
  • Notify suspected epidemics, such as cholera, hepatitis A or E virus infection, and Ebola
  • Encourage handwashing
  • Promote use of clean drinking water
  • Promote proper waste disposal

docs.title: 6.2.1 Amoebiasis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: A06

Amoebiasis is a common parasitic infection of the gastrointestinal system acquired through faeco-oral transmission.

Cause

  • Entamoeba histolytica

Clinical features

Amoebiasis may present as amoebic dysentery or amoebic abscess.

Amoebic dysentery may present with:

  • Persistent mucoid or bloody diarrhoea
  • Abdominal pain
  • Tenesmus
  • Chronic carrier state, which may be asymptomatic

Amoebic abscess may occur following spread through the bloodstream and may present as:

  • Liver abscess, with swelling or pain in the right subcostal area, fever, chills, sweating, and weight loss
  • Brain involvement, presenting as a space-occupying lesion
  • Lung involvement, presenting with cough and blood-stained sputum
  • Amoeboma, presenting as a swelling anywhere in the abdomen, especially in the ascending colon
  • Anal ulceration, which may occur by direct extension from intestinal infection

Differential diagnosis

  • Bacillary dysentery
  • Any other cause of bloody diarrhoea
  • Cancer of the liver
  • Other causes of liver swelling
  • Carcinoma of the colon

Investigations

  • Stool microscopy for cysts and motile organisms
  • Ultrasound

Management

Treatment LOC Correct any dehydration. See section 1.1.3. HC2 Give metronidazole 800 mg every 8 hours for 10 days. HC2 / H Children: metronidazole 10 mg/kg per dose. HC2 / H Alternatively, give tinidazole 2 g daily for 5 days. HC2 / H Children: tinidazole 50 mg/kg per dose. HC2 / H

Caution

Do not use metronidazole or tinidazole in the first trimester of pregnancy.

Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours after completing treatment.

Metronidazole should be taken after food.

Prevention

  • Educate the public on personal and food hygiene, including handwashing before eating
  • Promote proper faecal disposal
  • Ensure proper management of carriers and patients
  • Promote use of clean drinking water

docs.title: 6.2.2 Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: A03.9

Bacillary dysentery is an acute bacterial disease involving the large and small intestine. It is characterised by bloody mucoid diarrhoea.

Bacillary dysentery is a notifiable disease.

Cause

  • Shigella dysenteriae
  • Shigella flexneri
  • Shigella sonnei

These organisms are spread by the faeco-oral route.

Clinical features

  • Mucoid bloody diarrhoea
  • Fever
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Abdominal cramps
  • Tenesmus, which is the sensation of desire to defecate without production of significant amounts of faeces
  • Toxaemia in some cases

S. flexneri infection may be complicated by Reiter’s syndrome, which presents with:

  • Urethritis
  • Conjunctivitis
  • Arthritis

Differential diagnosis

  • Amoebic dysentery
  • Other causes of bloody diarrhoea

Investigations

  • Stool culture and sensitivity
  • Stool microscopy

Management

Treatment LOC Correct dehydration using ORS or IV fluids according to the degree of dehydration. See section 1.1.3. HC2 / HC3 Give appropriate antibiotic treatment according to local sensitivity patterns. HC2 / HC3 Provide supportive care, including continued feeding and fluid replacement. HC2 / HC3 Notify and report cases according to national disease surveillance requirements. HC2 / HC3

Prevention

Educate the patient and the public on:

  • Rehydration with plenty of fluids
  • Continuing breastfeeding or weaning feeds
  • Personal and food hygiene
  • Washing hands before preparing or eating food
  • Washing hands after using the toilet
  • Using and drinking clean safe water
  • Proper disposal of human faeces
  • Prompt isolation, treatment, and reporting of cases

docs.title: 6.2.3 Cholera
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: A00

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease characterised by profuse watery diarrhoea and rapid dehydration. It is a notifiable disease.

Cause

  • Vibrio cholerae, spread mainly through contaminated water and food

Clinical features

  • Profuse watery diarrhoea, often described as rice-water stool
  • Vomiting
  • Rapid dehydration
  • Thirst
  • Sunken eyes
  • Reduced skin turgor
  • Weak pulse
  • Hypotension
  • Shock in severe cases
  • Muscle cramps may occur

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of acute watery diarrhoea
  • Food poisoning
  • Viral gastroenteritis

Investigations

  • Stool culture and sensitivity
  • Stool microscopy
  • Identification of mobile vibrios under microscope where available

Management

Up to 90% of patients with cholera only require prompt oral rehydration. Only severely dehydrated patients need IV fluids and antimicrobials.

Treatment LOC Start rehydration with ORS at HC1 or HC2 and refer for isolation. HC2 Give oral fluids using ORS, or IV fluids using Ringer’s lactate, according to the degree of dehydration. See section 1.1.3. HC2 / HC3 Give IV glucose for hypoglycaemia. HC3 Give maintenance fluids of at least 4 to 5 litres per day in adults, adjusted according to clinical condition. HC3 Give doxycycline 300 mg as a single dose. HC3 Children: doxycycline 4 mg/kg as a single dose. HC3 Alternatively, give erythromycin 25 to 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for 3 days in children below 12 years. HC3 Alternatively, give ciprofloxacin 1 g as a single dose. HC3 Children: ciprofloxacin 20 mg/kg every 12 hours for 3 days. HC3

Caution

Ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are usually contraindicated in pregnancy and in children below 8 years.

However, a single dose in cholera should not provoke adverse effects.

Alternative treatment: erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 days.

Prevention

Educate the patient and the public on:

  • Rehydration with plenty of fluids
  • Continuing breastfeeding or weaning feeds
  • Personal and food hygiene
  • Washing hands before preparing or eating food
  • Washing hands after using the toilet
  • Using and drinking clean safe water
  • Proper disposal of human faeces
  • Prompt isolation, treatment, and reporting of cases

docs.title: 6.2.4 Giardiasis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: A07.1

Giardiasis is a protozoan infection of the upper small intestine transmitted by the faeco-oral route.

Cause

  • Giardia lamblia, a flagellated protozoan

Clinical features

  • Often asymptomatic
  • Prolonged diarrhoea
  • Steatorrhoea
  • Abdominal cramps
  • Bloating
  • Fatigue
  • Weight loss
  • Malabsorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins

Severe giardiasis may cause:

  • Reactive arthritis
  • Damage to duodenal and jejunal mucosa

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of prolonged diarrhoea
  • Other causes of malabsorption

Investigations

  • Stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites

Management

Treatment LOC Give metronidazole 2 g after food once daily for 3 days. HC2 / H Children: metronidazole 30 mg/kg per dose, maximum 1.2 g. HC2 / H Alternatively, give tinidazole 2 g as a single dose. HC2 / H Children: tinidazole 50 mg/kg as a single dose. HC2 / H

Caution

Avoid metronidazole and tinidazole in the first trimester of pregnancy.

Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours after treatment.

Metronidazole should be taken after food.

Prevention

Provide health education on:

  • Personal and food hygiene
  • Washing hands before handling or eating food
  • Washing hands after using toilets
  • Proper disposal of human faeces
  • Use of safe clean drinking water

docs.title: 6.3.1 Dysphagia
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: R13.1

Dysphagia is difficulty in swallowing. It may be oropharyngeal dysphagia or oesophageal dysphagia.

Causes

Oropharyngeal dysphagia may be caused by:

  • Neurological conditions, including stroke, Parkinson’s disease, dementia, multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia, cerebral palsy, tardive dyskinesia, brain tumours, and trauma
  • Myopathy, including connective tissue diseases, sarcoidosis, and dermatomyositis
  • Structural causes, including Zenker’s diverticulum, webs, oropharyngeal tumours, and osteophytes
  • Infections, including syphilis, botulism, rabies, and mucositis
  • Metabolic conditions, including Cushing’s syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, and Wilson’s disease
  • Iatrogenic causes, including chemotherapy, neuroleptics, post-surgery complications, and post-radiation complications

Oesophageal dysphagia may be caused by:

  • Tumours, including cancer of the oesophagus
  • Oesophagitis, including gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, candidiasis, pill oesophagitis such as from doxycycline, and caustic soda injury
  • Extrinsic compression from tumours or lymph nodes
  • Motility disorders, including achalasia, scleroderma, and oesophageal spasms

Clinical presentation

  • Difficulty initiating a swallow
  • Repetitive swallowing
  • Nasal regurgitation
  • Coughing
  • Nasal speech
  • Drooling
  • Diminished cough reflex
  • Choking
  • Aspiration, which may occur without concurrent choking or coughing
  • Dysarthria and diplopia, which may accompany neurological conditions causing oropharyngeal dysphagia
  • Halitosis in patients with a large residue-containing Zenker’s diverticulum, advanced achalasia, or long-term obstruction with luminal accumulation of decomposing residue
  • Recurrent pneumonia
  • Other features depending on the underlying cause

Investigations

  • Medical history and physical examination
  • Timed water swallow test, complemented by a food test
  • Endoscopy, which is mandatory
  • HIV serology
  • Random blood sugar
  • Electrolytes

Management

Treatment LOC Ensure rehydration with IV fluids. HC3 Prevent malnutrition through appropriate energy replacement. HC3 Treat the cause where possible, for example fluconazole trial in suspected oral candidiasis among HIV patients. HC3 Consult and/or refer the patient. HC3

docs.title: 6.3.2 Dyspepsia
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K30

Dyspepsia is upper abdominal discomfort arising from the upper gastrointestinal tract, usually lasting more than 2 to 4 weeks.

Causes

  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
  • Functional dyspepsia
  • Gastric or oesophageal cancer
  • Oesophagitis, including drug-induced oesophagitis, candida oesophagitis, and other causes
  • Gastroparesis or gastric outlet obstruction
  • Other motility disorders

Clinical features

  • Epigastric pain or discomfort
  • Heartburn
  • Bloating
  • Early satiety
  • Fullness after meals
  • Repeated belching or regurgitation, often rumination
  • Nausea

Dyspepsia alarm features requiring endoscopy and referral

Refer for endoscopy if any of the following are present:

  • Dysphagia
  • Odynophagia among patients who are HIV negative
  • Weight loss
  • Abdominal mass
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Evidence of upper gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Iron deficiency anaemia
  • Recurrent vomiting
  • Recent dyspeptic symptoms or new dyspepsia in individuals over 40 years of age

Other indications for endoscopy

  • History of long-term smoking and alcohol misuse
  • Persistent dyspepsia despite appropriate treatment, such as proton-pump inhibitors in GERD
  • Hepatobiliary disease

docs.title: 6.3.4 Gastritis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K27

Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining. It may be acute or chronic.

Causes

Acute gastritis may be caused by:

  • Medicines such as acetylsalicylic acid, diclofenac, and ibuprofen
  • Alcohol
  • Regurgitation of bile into the stomach

Chronic gastritis may be caused by:

  • Autoimmune gastric ulceration
  • Bacterial infection, especially Helicobacter pylori

Clinical features

Gastritis may be asymptomatic or may present with:

  • Anorexia
  • Nausea
  • Epigastric pain
  • Heartburn

Differential diagnosis

  • Pancreatitis
  • Cholecystitis
  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Duodenal ulcers
  • Cancer of the stomach
  • Epigastric hernia

Investigations

  • Gastroscopy
  • Stool test for occult blood
  • Barium meal for chronic gastritis

Management

Treatment LOC Modify diet by avoiding precipitating causes and increasing milk intake. HC2 Give an antacid, such as magnesium trisilicate compound 2 tablets every 8 hours as required. HC3 If there is no response, give omeprazole 20 mg in the evening for 4 weeks. HC4 If vomiting occurs, give metoclopramide 10 mg IM, repeated when necessary up to 3 times daily. HC4 Alternatively, give chlorpromazine 25 mg deep IM or orally if tolerated, repeated as required every 4 hours. HC4

Caution

Acetylsalicylic acid and other NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with gastritis.

Prevention

  • Avoid spices
  • Avoid tobacco
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Avoid carbonated drinks
  • Encourage regular, small, and frequent meals
  • Encourage milk intake

docs.title: 6.3.5 Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
docs.text:
Peptic ulcer disease refers to ulceration in the stomach or duodenum.

Causes

  • Helicobacter pylori infection
  • Hyperacidity due to medicines such as NSAIDs, including acetylsalicylic acid, diclofenac, ibuprofen, and corticosteroids
  • Irregular meals
  • Stress
  • Alcohol
  • Smoking
  • Caffeine-containing beverages

Clinical features

General features include:

  • Epigastric pain, typically worse at night and when hungry in duodenal ulcer
  • Pain relieved by food, milk, or antacid medicine in duodenal ulcer
  • Epigastric pain that is worse with food in gastric ulcer
  • Vomiting
  • Nausea
  • Regurgitation
  • Discomfort on palpation of the upper abdomen

Bleeding ulcer may present with:

  • Haematemesis, which may be coffee-brown or red vomitus
  • Black stools, also called melaena
  • Sudden weakness and dizziness
  • Cold, clammy skin when the patient has lost a lot of blood

Perforated ulcer may present with:

  • Acute abdominal pain
  • Signs of peritonitis, such as a rigid abdomen
  • Ground coffee-brown vomitus due to blood
  • Fever
  • Shock, with weak pulse, clammy skin, and low blood pressure

Differential diagnosis

  • Pancreatitis
  • Hepatitis
  • Disease of the aorta
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Lung disease, especially haemoptysis

Investigations

  • Stool antigen test for H. pylori. This is used for diagnosis and to confirm eradication.
  • Gastroscopy
  • Biopsy of the stomach wall
  • Barium meal

Warning

The H. pylori stool antigen test may give a false negative result if the patient has taken antibiotics or omeprazole in the previous 2 weeks.

Serum antibody testing is not useful for diagnosis or follow-up.

Management

Treatment LOC Modify diet by avoiding precipitating causes and increasing milk intake. HC3 Give an antacid, such as magnesium trisilicate compound 2 tablets every 8 hours as required. HC4

Treatment for eradication of H. pylori

Treatment LOC First-line triple therapy: give amoxicillin 1 g every 12 hours plus metronidazole 400 mg every 12 hours plus omeprazole 20 mg every 12 hours for 2 weeks. HC3 Check eradication with a stool antigen test after 4 weeks. HC3

Management of bleeding or perforated ulcer

Treatment LOC Refer the patient to hospital immediately. H Give IV fluids and blood if necessary. H Give IV ranitidine 50 mg in 20 mL slowly every 8 hours. H

Note

Tinidazole 500 mg every 12 hours can be used instead of metronidazole.

Confirm eradication with a stool antigen test 1 month after completion of treatment. The test should be negative.

docs.title: 6.3.6 Chronic Pancreatitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K86.0–K86.1

Chronic pancreatitis is a disease of the pancreas in which recurrent episodes of inflammation lead to replacement of the pancreatic parenchyma with fibrotic connective tissue, formation of calculi, and loss of duct architecture. This leads to progressive loss of pancreatic function.

Causes

  • Toxic or metabolic causes, including alcohol, tobacco, hypercalcaemia, hyperlipidaemia, and chronic renal failure
  • Idiopathic causes, including tropical pancreatitis
  • Genetic or autoimmune causes
  • Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis
  • Obstructive cancer or anatomical abnormalities

Clinical features

  • Chronic pain, which is the main symptom
  • Diarrhoea
  • Loss of weight
  • Diabetes mellitus

Complications

  • Pseudocysts
  • Stenosis of the pancreatic duct
  • Duodenal stenosis
  • Vascular complications
  • Compression of the bile ducts
  • Malnutrition
  • Increased risk of cancer of the pancreas

Investigations

  • Blood tests, including serum analysis, complete blood count, and random blood sugar
  • Raised pancreatic amylase or lipase above 3 times normal
  • Ultrasound, looking for gallstones, pancreatic oedema, and abdominal fluid
  • Liver function tests, which may show raised liver enzymes

Management

Treatment LOC Refer for specialist management. RR Use the WHO pain analgesic ladder. RR Give pethidine 50–100 mg IM as required. RR Alternatively, give tramadol 50–100 mg orally or IM as required. RR Advise the patient to avoid alcohol and fatty foods. RR

docs.title: 6.4.1 Constipation
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K59.0

Constipation is a condition characterised by hardened faeces and difficulty emptying the bowels.

Causes

  • Dietary causes, including lack of roughage and inadequate fluid intake
  • Concentrated feeds in infants
  • Lack of exercise
  • Being bedridden, especially in elderly patients
  • Pregnancy
  • Certain medicines, including narcotic analgesics, antidepressants, diuretics, antipsychotics, and iron
  • Colon or anorectal disorders, including stricture, cancer, fissure, proctitis, congenital bowel abnormalities, irritable bowel syndrome, volvulus, and intussusception
  • Metabolic causes, including hypercalcaemia, diabetes, and hypothyroidism
  • Neurological disorders, including spinal cord lesions, stroke, and Parkinsonism

Clinical features

  • Abdominal discomfort
  • Small hard stools passed irregularly under strain
  • Haemorrhoids
  • Anal fissure

Alarm features

  • Symptoms and signs of intestinal obstruction or acute abdomen
  • Confusion or disorientation
  • Abnormal vital signs
  • Iron deficiency
  • Rectal bleeding, haematochezia, or rectal mass
  • Haem-positive stool
  • Age above 45 years with no previous history of colon cancer screening
  • History of colon cancer in immediate family relatives
  • Weight loss

Investigations

Physical examination may include:

  • Assessment for abdominal mass and tenderness
  • Anorectal examination for faecal impaction, stricture, rectal prolapse, or rectal mass

Other investigations may include:

  • Stool examination

For patients with alarm features, consider:

  • Abdominal series, including supine, upright, and left lateral decubitus views
  • Transabdominal ultrasound
  • Endoscopy
  • Complete blood count
  • Renal function tests
  • Serum calcium
  • Thyroid function tests
  • Blood sugar
  • Barium enema, with or without CT scan or X-ray

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC No alarm features or chronic constipation Advise high dietary fibre intake. HC2 No alarm features or chronic constipation Advise adequate fluid intake. HC2 No alarm features or chronic constipation Give bisacodyl 10 mg at night in adults. Continue until stool is passed. HC3 No alarm features or chronic constipation Children 5 to 12 years: bisacodyl 5 mg, suppository only. HC3 No alarm features or chronic constipation Bisacodyl is contraindicated in acute abdomen because it aggravates the condition. HC3 No alarm features or chronic constipation Give oral or rectal lactulose as an osmotic agent. It provides faster relief than bisacodyl. HC4 Alarm features or severe chronic constipation Refer to hospital for specialist management. HC2 / HC3

Prevention

  • Eat a diet rich in roughage, including plenty of vegetables and fruit.
  • Take plenty of oral fluids with meals.
  • Increase exercise.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Haemorrhoids (Piles) and Anal Fissures
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K64 / K60.0–K60.2

Haemorrhoids are swellings in the upper anal canal and lower rectum due to engorgement of veins. They may be internal or external.

An anal fissure is a tear in the lining of the lower rectum.

Causes

  • Constipation and straining during defecation
  • Portal hypertension from any cause
  • Compression of pelvic veins, such as from abdominal tumours or pregnancy
  • Sedentary lifestyle

Clinical features

Haemorrhoids may present with:

  • Painless rectal bleeding
  • Visible swelling at the anus or prolapse of the swelling, especially at defecation
  • Blood that is usually not mixed with stool but instead coats the surface of the stool or toilet paper
  • Mucous discharge and irritation at the anus

Anal fissure may present with:

  • Pain during passing stool
  • Bleeding during passing stool

Differential diagnosis

  • Schistosomiasis
  • Amoeboma
  • Rectal polyps
  • Prolapsed rectum
  • Anal tags
  • Harmless growths that hang off the skin around the outside of the anus
  • Tumour of the rectum
  • Anal warts

Investigations

  • Visual inspection and digital rectal examination
  • Proctoscopy
  • Sigmoidoscopy
  • Colonoscopy

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC General management Establish the cause. HC2 General management Increase fibre and fluid intake. HC2 General management Correct any constipation. HC2 General management Give a sitz bath, sitting for 10 to 15 minutes in lukewarm water with a spoon of salt, 2 or 3 times daily. HC4 General management Insert a bismuth subgallate compound rectally every 12 hours for 5 days, such as Anusol or Sediproct cream or suppositories. HC4 If signs of infection are present Give metronidazole 400 mg every 8 hours for 5 days. HC2 If signs of infection are present Give analgesics as required for pain. HC2 If there is no response Refer to hospital for surgery. HC2

Prevention

  • Maintain a high-residue, fibre-rich diet.
  • Ensure adequate fluid intake.
  • Exercise regularly.
  • Refrain from straining and reading in the toilet.

docs.title: 6.5.1 Viral Hepatitis
docs.text:
Viral hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis viruses. It may present as acute hepatitis, with or without symptoms. Hepatitis B, C, and D viruses can cause chronic hepatitis. Hepatitis B virus can also result in chronic carrier status.

Causes

  • Hepatitis A and E: oro-faecal transmission
  • Hepatitis B: sexual transmission, mother-to-child transmission, or transmission through infected body fluids or blood
  • Hepatitis C: contact with infected blood, with possible sexual and vertical transmission
  • Hepatitis D: contact with infected blood, sexual transmission, and possible vertical transmission

docs.title: 6.5.1.1 Acute Hepatitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: B15, B16, B17, B19

Clinical features

Classic acute hepatitis may present with:

  • Fever
  • Fatigue
  • Malaise
  • Right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort
  • Nausea
  • Diarrhoea
  • Anorexia
  • Jaundice
  • Dark urine
  • Pale or clay-coloured stool

Fulminant hepatitis may present as acute liver failure due to massive liver necrosis. It is often fatal. It is more common in patients with hepatitis B who have secondary infection with hepatitis D virus, and in pregnant women who get hepatitis E in the third trimester.

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of hepatitis, including drugs, herbs, tumours, and autoimmune diseases
  • Gastroenteritis
  • Relapsing fever
  • Pancreatitis
  • Malaria
  • Leptospirosis
  • Yellow fever
  • Haemorrhagic fevers, such as Marburg and Ebola

Investigations

  • Complete blood count
  • Malaria slide or rapid diagnostic test
  • Liver function tests
  • Viral antigens and antibodies, including hepatitis B and hepatitis C testing
  • HIV serology

Management

Clinical form Treatment LOC Classic form Provide supportive management. HC4 Classic form Advise rest and hydration. HC4 Classic form Give a diet high in carbohydrates, vitamins, and vegetable proteins. Avoid animal proteins. HC4 Classic form Avoid unnecessary medicines because they may aggravate symptoms. HC4 Liver failure or decompensated liver disease Refer for further management. HC4

Caution

Avoid medicines generally, especially sedatives and hepatotoxic medicines.

Ensure effective infection control measures, including barrier nursing and personal hygiene.

Patient isolation is not necessary unless there is high suspicion of viral haemorrhagic fever.

Prevention

  • Promote hygiene and sanitation.
  • Provide immunisation against hepatitis B for all children, health workers, household contacts of people with chronic hepatitis B, sex workers, and other populations at risk.
  • Promote safe transfusion practices.
  • Strengthen infection control in health facilities.
  • Screen pregnant women.
  • Promote safer sexual practices, including condom use.

docs.title: 6.5.1.2 Chronic Hepatitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: B18

Hepatitis B, C, and D viruses can cause chronic infection with low-level inflammation of the liver. This may lead to progressive liver damage and may progress to liver cirrhosis.

docs.title: 6.5.2.1 Inactive Hepatitis B Carriers
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: B18.1

A patient may be classified as an inactive hepatitis B carrier if the following are present:

  • HBsAg positive for more than 6 months
  • Persistently normal liver function, at least 3 times in 12 months
  • No evidence of viral replication, shown by negative HBeAg and/or HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL

Patients classified as inactive carriers should be monitored once a year with:

  • Complete blood count
  • Renal function tests
  • Liver function tests
  • HBsAg
  • Abdominal ultrasound

If possible, HBV DNA should be done every 3 years.

Inactive carriers are not highly infectious, but close contacts should be immunised and appropriate precautions should be followed.

docs.title: 6.5.2.2 Pregnant Mother HBsAg Positive
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: B18.1

If a pregnant mother is found to be HBsAg positive, assess HIV status.

If she is also HIV positive:

  • Start antiretroviral therapy.
  • The child should receive hepatitis B vaccine at birth.

If she is HIV negative:

  • Refer for further testing, including HBeAg and HBV DNA, to assess the risk of transmission to the baby and the possible need for antivirals.
  • The child should be immunised at birth.

Breastfeeding is safe.
