docs.title: 6.5.3 Chronic Hepatitis C Infection
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: B18.2

Clinical features

Chronic hepatitis C infection may be symptomatic or asymptomatic.

Investigations

  • Hepatitis C antibody positive at 0 and 6 months
  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Liver function tests
  • INR
  • Renal function tests
  • Blood glucose

Management

Treatment LOC Refer to a regional hospital or higher for confirmatory investigations and management. RR

docs.title: 6.5.4 Liver Cirrhosis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: K74, K70.3

Cirrhosis is a chronic disease with necrosis of liver cells followed by fibrosis and nodule formation. Decompensated cirrhosis is defined by the presence of complications such as ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, or jaundice which result from portal hypertension and liver insufficiency caused by cirrhosis.

Causes

  • Infections, such as viral hepatitis B and D, and hepatitis C
  • Intoxication with alcohol, medicines, or toxins, such as methotrexate, isoniazid, and methyldopa
  • Infiltrative disorders, such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, Wilson’s disease, and haemochromatosis
  • Iron overload, such as in over-transfused sickle cell disease patients
  • Immunological causes, including chronic autoimmune hepatitis
  • Congestion with bile, such as primary biliary cirrhosis
  • Congestion with blood, such as chronic cardiac failure and Budd-Chiari syndrome
  • Idiopathic causes

Clinical features

General symptoms may include:

  • Fatigue
  • Weight loss
  • Features of malnutrition
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Loss of appetite

Other clinical features may include:

  • Initially enlarged liver, which later decreases in size
  • Distended blood vessels on the abdomen
  • Enlarged spleen
  • Loss of libido

Cirrhosis is decompensated when the following are present:

  • Jaundice
  • Encephalopathy
  • Ascites, with or without leg oedema
  • Vomiting of blood from ruptured blood vessels in the oesophagus, or varices

Stages of cirrhosis

Stage Clinical status Death at 1 year 0 Fibrosis 1% 1 Compensated cirrhosis, with no varices and no ascites 1% 2 Varices present, with no ascites 3% 3 Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites, with or without varices 20% 4 Decompensated cirrhosis with bleeding, with or without ascites 57%

Additional complications may include:

  • Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with sepsis
  • Renal failure
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Jaundice
  • Hepatic encephalopathy

Differential diagnosis

  • Diffuse hepatic parenchymal disease
  • Metastatic or multifocal cancer in the liver
  • Hepatic vein obstruction
  • Any cause of enlarged spleen
  • Heart failure
  • Renal disease

Investigations

  • Blood haemoglobin
  • Blood film
  • White blood cell count
  • Platelet count
  • Prothrombin time or INR
  • Serology for hepatitis B, C, and D
  • HIV serology
  • Stool and urine examination
  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Liver function tests
  • Alpha-fetoprotein
  • Liver biopsy
  • APRI score greater than 2 is diagnostic
  • Endoscopy to assess for varices

Management

Refer to a regional hospital or higher for specialist attention.

Management area Treatment LOC General principles Treat the cause and prevent progression. RR General principles Stop alcohol. RR General principles Ensure appropriate nutrition. RR General principles If chronic hepatitis B is present, start antiviral treatment. RR General principles Provide specific treatment according to the cause. RR General principles Avoid herbs and self-medication. RR General principles Use medicines only after prescription from a health worker. RR General principles Manage and prevent complications. RR Complications Manage ascites. RR Complications Manage encephalopathy. RR Complications Manage bleeding varices. RR

docs.title: 6.5.4.1 Ascites
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: R18 / K70.31 / K70.11 / K71.51

Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

Clinical features

  • Ascites not infected and not associated with hepatorenal syndrome

Classification

Classification Features Grade 1 ascites (mild) Only detectable by ultrasound examination. Grade 2 ascites (moderate) Ascites causing moderate symmetrical distension of the abdomen. Grade 3 ascites (severe) Ascites causing marked abdominal distension.

Clinical diagnosis

  • Fluid thrill or fluid wave
  • Shifting dullness

Investigations

  • Abdominal ultrasound scan
  • Peritoneal tap or paracentesis
  • Analysis of ascitic fluid

Management

The main principles of management are:

  • Diet modification
  • Daily monitoring
  • Diuretics
  • Drainage
Management area Treatment LOC Diet Restrict dietary salt to a no-added-salt or low-salt diet. H Diet Avoid protein malnutrition because it is associated with higher mortality. Consume plant proteins liberally and animal proteins occasionally, titrated to symptoms and signs of hepatic encephalopathy. H Diet Restrict water if oedema and hyponatraemia are present. H Diet Abstain from alcohol, NSAIDs, and herbs. H Daily monitoring Monitor daily weight, blood pressure, pulse, stool for melaena, and encephalopathy. H Diuretics Use spironolactone 50 to 100 mg/day in the morning, aiming for weight loss of 300 to 500 g/day. If needed, increase the dose every 7 days up to a maximum of 400 mg/day. H Diuretics Furosemide may be added at a starting dose of 20 to 40 mg/day and subsequently increased to 160 mg/day if needed. It is best used if pedal oedema is present. Monitor for hypotension. H Diuretics For maintenance, titrate to the lowest effective diuretic dose. Most patients do well with spironolactone 50 mg/day if they have no ascites. H Drainage Drainage is indicated for severe ascites, Grade 3. Paracentesis is always followed by spironolactone. H Drainage Small-volume paracentesis is less than 5 L over 3 to 4 hours. Large-volume paracentesis is 5 to 10 L with infusion of a plasma expander, such as 8 g albumin per litre of ascites removed. H Drainage Monitor for hypotension or reduced urine output. H Complicated ascites Refer if the patient has or develops complicated ascites. H

docs.title: 6.5.4.2 Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K65.2

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is an acute bacterial infection of ascitic fluid. It is a common and severe complication of advanced liver cirrhosis and is associated with poor prognosis.

Clinical features

Patients must be admitted to hospital. Suspect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis when there is:

  • Increasing severity of ascites
  • Fever
  • Abdominal pain or abdominal tenderness
  • Worsening encephalopathy
  • Renal failure
  • Bleeding varices

Investigations

  • Ascitic tap
  • Ascitic fluid cell count

A neutrophil count above 250/mm³ in ascitic fluid confirms the diagnosis.

Management

Treatment LOC Treat with IV antibiotics for 5 to 10 days. H Give ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV daily. H If needed, add metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours. H Give albumin infusion 1 g/kg to prevent hepatorenal syndrome. RR Consult or refer for specialist care as soon as possible. RR

Caution

Avoid gentamicin and NSAIDs.

docs.title: 6.5.4.3 Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: K70.41 / K71.11 / K72.11 / K72.91

Hepatic encephalopathy is a syndrome of neuropsychiatric symptoms and signs, including coma, observed in patients with cirrhosis. It is probably due to accumulation of toxins in the blood.

Clinical features

Grade Clinical features Grade 0 Subclinical personality changes and construction apraxia, meaning inability or difficulty to build, assemble, or draw objects. Grade I Confusion and flap tremor. Grade II Drowsiness. Grade III Stupor. Grade IV Coma.

Hepatic encephalopathy may be aggravated by:

  • Surgery
  • Paracentesis
  • Excessive diuretics
  • Sedatives
  • Opioid analgesics

Intracranial hypertension and sepsis are the main causes of death.

Management

Management involves addressing pathophysiological mechanisms related to the brain, gut, and liver.

Treatment LOC Identify and correct precipitating factors, including renal impairment, gastrointestinal bleeding, infections, and electrolyte disturbances. H Empty the gut. H Give oral lactulose 15 to 30 mL every 8 hours until the condition resolves. Aim for 2 to 3 soft stools per day. H Lactulose may be administered through a nasogastric tube in Grade I and Grade II hepatic encephalopathy. H Lactulose may be given as an enema in acute hepatic encephalopathy Grade III and Grade IV. H Refer to a specialist. RR If referral delays, give an antibiotic with local action on the gut, such as oral metronidazole 400 to 800 mg every 8 hours for 5 days. RR Alternatively, give oral paromomycin 1000 mg every 6 hours for 5 days. RR

docs.title: 6.5.4.4 Hepatocellular Carcinoma
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: C22.0

Clinical features

  • Right upper quadrant pain
  • Hepatomegaly, with or without splenomegaly
  • Weight loss
  • Jaundice
  • Ascites
  • Lymphadenopathy

Differential diagnosis

  • Liver metastasis
  • Liver abscess
  • Hydatid cyst

Investigations

  • Abdominal ultrasound or sonogram
  • Alpha-fetoprotein
  • Liver function tests
  • Liver biopsy

Management

Treatment LOC Refer to a regional hospital or higher level of care. RR

docs.title: 6.5.5 Hepatic Schistosomiasis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: B65.1

Hepatic schistosomiasis is a common cause of liver disease among communities where Schistosoma mansoni is endemic. See section 2.

Cause

  • Inflammatory and fibrotic reaction to eggs laid by Schistosoma parasites and transported to the liver through the veins from the intestine.

Clinical features

  • Upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy
  • Splenomegaly and ruptured spleen
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Portal vein thrombosis
  • Bloody diarrhoea
  • Anaemia
  • Stunting

Investigations

  • Liver ultrasound features, including periportal fibrosis patterns and portal vein thickening as described by the World Health Organization Niamey ultrasound protocol
  • Screening for varices with endoscopy

Management

Treatment LOC Refer to a specialist. HC4 Give praziquantel 40 mg/kg as a single dose if schistosoma eggs are detected. HC4 Correct anaemia as appropriate. RR Conduct surveillance for oesophageal varices with endoscopy. RR Provide primary and secondary prevention of bleeding oesophageal varices with propranolol. See section 6.5.4.4. RR Perform endoscopic band ligation where indicated. RR Treat acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. See section 6.1.3. RR

docs.title: 6.5.6 Drug-Induced Liver Injury
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K71

Drugs are an important and common cause of liver injury. Many medicines and herbs are known to cause liver damage. Drug-induced liver injury can range from asymptomatic elevation of liver enzymes to severe hepatic failure.

Health workers must be vigilant in identifying drug-related liver injury because early detection can decrease the severity of hepatotoxicity if the drug is discontinued. Knowledge of the commonly implicated agents is essential in diagnosis.

Common causes

  • Phenytoin
  • Carbamazepine
  • Anti-tuberculosis drugs
  • Co-trimoxazole
  • Diclofenac
  • Paracetamol
  • Antiretroviral drugs
  • Ketoconazole

Clinical features

Drug-induced liver injury is a diagnosis of exclusion. Consider it in:

  • Any patient with liver enzyme elevation that cannot be attributed to infections, autoimmune disease, or malignancy
  • A patient exposed to a drug or herbal medication known to cause liver cell injury
  • A patient who presents with skin or mucosal drug reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis

Management

Treatment LOC Stop all drugs or herbs. H Give supportive care, including rehydration. H See section 1.3.5 for paracetamol poisoning. H Do not give the drug again. Do not rechallenge. H Refer to a regional hospital or higher level of care for specialist attention. H

docs.title: 6.5.7 Jaundice (Hyperbilirubinaemia)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: R17

Jaundice is yellowish discolouration of the sclera and skin due to raised levels of bilirubin in the body. Bilirubin is a by-product of red cell breakdown, processed in the liver and excreted mainly in bile. Jaundice may be benign or life-threatening.

Causes

  • Pre-hepatic causes, including haemolysis, sepsis, sickle cell disease, pregnancy-related HELLP syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and vascular causes
  • Hepatic causes, including hepatitis, drugs, tumours, alcohol, toxins, herbs, autoimmune disease, pregnancy, and cholangitis
  • Post-hepatic causes, including gall stones, strictures, tumours, surgery, pancreatitis, and biliary disease

Complications

  • Renal failure
  • Coagulopathy
  • Sepsis

Investigations

  • Liver function tests, including AST, ALT, and bilirubin
  • Coombs’ test
  • Low haptoglobin
  • LDH
  • Hepatitis A, B, and C testing
  • Malaria and sickle cell screening
  • Ultrasound to assess for dilated bile ducts and gall bladder
  • CBC
  • INR
  • RFTs
  • LDH
  • Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
  • Liver biopsy

Management

Treatment LOC Refer and/or consult as appropriate. H Treat the underlying cause. H Discontinue offending factors. H Use phototherapy with UV light for newborn babies. H Expose newborn babies to natural sun where appropriate. H

docs.title: 6.5.8 Gallstones / Biliary Colic
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K80

Gallstones are small hard masses formed in the gallbladder or biliary tree.

Risk factors

  • Age
  • Gender
  • Family history
  • Obesity
  • Diabetes
  • Use of oral contraceptives
  • Dyslipidaemia

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic and often found by chance during abdominal ultrasound
  • Biliary colic, with episodes of intense acute epigastric or right hypochondrial pain due to temporary blockage of a bile duct
  • Pain lasting from a few minutes to a few hours
  • Pain often triggered by a high-fat meal
  • Pain may occur sporadically
  • No fever or jaundice
  • Cholecystitis or cholangitis due to blockage and infection of bile
  • Pancreatitis due to blockage of the pancreatic duct

Differential diagnosis

  • Peptic ulcer disease

Investigations

  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Liver function tests

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Asymptomatic gallstones No intervention is required. HC4 Biliary colic Give diclofenac 75 mg IM and/or pethidine 50 to 100 mg IM. RR Biliary colic Advise a low-fat diet and weight management. RR Biliary colic Refer for cholecystectomy after the acute phase. RR

docs.title: 6.5.9 Acute Cholecystitis / Cholangitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: K81

Acute cholecystitis or cholangitis is inflammation of the gall bladder and/or biliary tract. It often requires surgical management.

Causes

  • Obstruction of the gall bladder duct by gall stones or calculi
  • May occur after major trauma, burns, or surgery
  • May occur in HIV-infected persons as acalculous cholecystitis

Clinical features

  • Sudden onset of pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen
  • Pain worsens on deep breathing
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Jaundice in cholangitis
  • Fever, 38–39 °C, with chills

Severity of acute cholecystitis

Grade Description Grade I, mild acute cholecystitis Associated with no organ dysfunction and limited disease in the gallbladder, making cholecystectomy a low-risk procedure. Grade II, moderate acute cholecystitis Associated with no organ dysfunction but with extensive disease in the gallbladder, resulting in difficulty safely performing cholecystectomy. Grade II features Usually characterised by elevated white blood cell count, palpable tender mass in the right upper abdominal quadrant, disease duration of more than 72 hours, and imaging studies indicating significant inflammatory changes in the gallbladder. Severe acute cholecystitis Acute cholecystitis with organ dysfunction or shock.

Differential diagnosis

  • Acute alcoholic hepatitis
  • Intestinal obstruction

Investigations

  • X-ray
  • Abdominal ultrasound, with findings such as wall thickening, stone, and pericholecystic fluid
  • Blood haemogram
  • Liver function tests
  • Pancreatitis assessment
  • Enzymes and renal function tests

Findings may include fever and elevated white blood cells.

Management

Treatment LOC Keep nil by mouth. HC4 Relieve pain with pethidine 50 to 100 mg IM every 6 hours. HC4 Rehydrate with IV fluids and electrolytes, such as Ringer’s lactate. RR Give ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g daily. RR In cholecystitis, refer to hospital within 2 to 3 days for surgery, including cholecystectomy. RR In cholangitis, if not better, refer for urgent surgical management. RR

docs.text:
TREATMENT

ICD10 CODE: DEPENDING ON THE CAUSE

3 loose, watery stools within 24 hours Dysentery: bloody diarrhoea, visible blood and mucus Persistent diarrhoea: episodes of diarrhoea lasting more than 14 days

Causes

  • Viruses: Rotavirus, Norovirus , adenovirus, measles, hepa-

titis A virus , hepatitis E virus, Ebola

  • Bacteria: Vibrio cholera, E.coli , Salmonella, shigella, cam-

pylobacter

  • Protozoa: giardiasis, malaria, cryptosporia

  • Heliminthes e.g. strongyloidiasis, schistosomiasis

  • Infectious diseases, e.g. measles, malaria, and other fever-

causing conditions

  • Malnutrition e.g. kwashiorkor

  • Drugs e.g., prolonged use of purgatives and broad-spec-

trum antibiotics

  • Unhygienic feeding methods

  • Malabsorption syndrome

  • Lactose intolerance

CHAPTER 6:Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Diseases

CHAPTER 6:Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Diseases

  • HIV associated-diarrhoea

  • Irritable bowel syndrome

  • Metabolic: diabetes, thyroid disease

  • Travellers’ diarrhoea

  • Inflammatory bowel disease (persistent diarrhoea usually

bloody) Clinical features

  • Loose watery stools

  • Abdominal cramps

  • Dehydration - thirst, sunken eyes, loss of skin elasticity, low

urine output

  • Signs of malnutrition if diarrhoea persists for > 14 days

  • Blood in stool (in dysentery) Investigations

 Stool: Microscopy, C&S  Other investigations may be necessary according to history and

physical examination Red flags

    • Fever
    • Extremes of age
    • History of travel from a known endemic area
    • Dysentery
    • Shock, failure to feed, mental confusion
TREATMENT LOC  Prevent or correct dehydration with ORS or IV fluids according to treatment plans A, B or C (see section 1.1.3) Find and treat the cause if indicated- Avoid inappropriate use of antibiotics e.g. metronidazole, ciprofloxacin HC2HC4 TREATMENT LOC  Routinely use zinc supplementation, at a dosage of 20 milligrams per day for children older than six months for 10–14 days Prevent or treat undernutrition and micronutrientdeficiencies Persistent or chronic diarrhoea:  Adults only: As above plus codeine phosphate 30 mg every 8-12 hours as required  Child: vitamin A- 6-11 months: 100,000 IU; 1-6 years: 200,000 IU HC2HC4

Prevention

  • Vaccination: measles, rotavirus, polio, hepatitis A virus

  • Notify in case of suspected epidemics e.g. cholera, hepati-

tis A or E virus infections, Ebola

  • Encourage handwashing, use of clean drinking water, and

proper waste disposal 6.2 GASTROINTESTINAL INFECTIONS 6.2.1 Amoebiasis ICD10 CODE: A06

A common parasitic infection of the gastrointestinal system acquired through oral-faecal transmission.

Causes

  • Protozoan Entamoeba histolytica

Clinical features It may present as:

CHAPTER 6:Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Diseases

CHAPTER 6:Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Diseases

Amoebic dysentery

  • Persistent mucoid/bloody diarrhoea

  • Abdominal pain, tenesmus

  • Chronic carriers are symptomless Amoebic abscess (as a result of spread via the blood stream):

  • Liver abscess: swelling/pain in the right sub-costal area,

fever, chills, sweating, weight loss

  • Brain: presenting as space-occupying lesion

  • Lungs: cough and blood stained sputum

  • Amoeboma: swelling anywhere in the abdomen, especially

ascending colon

  • Anal ulceration: may occur by direct extension from the

intestinal infection Differential diagnosis

  • Bacillary dysentery

  • Any other cause of bloody diarrhoea

  • Cancer of the liver

  • Other causes of swelling in the liver

  • Carcinoma colon Investigations

 Stool: Microscopy for cysts and motile organisms  Ultrasound

TREATMENT LOC  Correct any dehydration (section 1.1.3)  Metronidazole 800 mg every 8 hours for 10 days Child: 10 mg/kg per dose  Or tinidazole 2 g daily for 5 days Child: 50 mg/kg per dose HC2H TREATMENT LOC Caution Metronidazole/tinidazole: do not use in 1st trimester of pregnancy; avoid alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours thereafter Metronidazole: Take after food Caution Metronidazole/tinidazole: do not use in 1st trimester of pregnancy; avoid alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours thereafter Metronidazole: Take after food

Prevention

  • Educate the public on personal and food hygiene (washing

hands before eating), proper faecal disposal

  • Ensure proper management of carriers and patients

  • Promote use of clean drinking water

Dysphagia is difficulty in swallowing. It may be oropharyngeal dysphagia or oesophageal dysphagia

Causes Oropharyngeal dysphagia

  • Neurological: stroke, parkinson’s, dementia, multiple scle-

rosis, Guillianbarre, myasthenia, cerebral palsy, tardive dyskinesia, brain tumours, trauma

radiation

Oesophageal dysphagia

  • Tumours: cancer of the oesophagus

  • Oesophagiitis: gastroesophageal reflux disease, candidiasis,

pill oesophagitis (e.g. doxycycline), caustic soda injury

  • Motility: achalasia, scleroderma, oesophageal spasms Clinical presentation

  • Difficulty initiating a swallow, repetitive swallowing

  • Nasal regurgitation

  • Coughing, nasal speech, drooling

  • Diminished cough reflex

  • Choking (aspiration may occur without concurrent choking

or coughing)

  • Dysarthria and diplopia (may accompany neurologic conditions that cause oropharyngeal dysphagia)

  • Halitosis in patients with a large, residue-containing Zenker’s diverticulum or in patients with advanced achalasia or long-term obstruction with luminal accumulation of decomposing residue

  • Recurrent pneumonia

  • Other features due to causative problem Investigations

    • HBsAg positive for more than 6 months plus
    • Persistently normal liver function (at least 3 times in 12 months) and
    • No evidence of viral replication (negative HBeAg and/or

Patients classified as inactive carriers need to be monitored once a year with CBC, renal and liver tests, HBsAg, abdominal ultrasound. If possible, do HBV-DNA every 3 years.

docs.text:
SBP is an acute bacterial infection of ascitic fluid. It is a common and severe complication of advanced liver cirrhosis and it is associated with a poor prognosis.

Clinical features

Patients must be admitted to hospital and should be suspected of SBP infection when:

  • Ascites increases in severity

  • Presence of fever

  • Abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness

  • Worsening encephalopathy

  • Complications: renal failure, bleeding varices, death Investigations  Diagnosis is confirmed by an ascitic tap and cell counts. A neu-

trophil count of > 250/mm3 in ascitic fluid confirms the diagnosis Management

TREATMENT LOC  Treat with IV antibiotics for 5–10 days  IV ceftriaxone 1-2 g daily- If needed, add metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours H  Give albumin infusion 1 g/kg to prevent hepatorenal syndrome Consult or refer for specialist care as soon as possible RR Caution Avoid gentamicin and NSAIDs Caution Avoid gentamicin and NSAIDs

docs.title: 6.5.4.2 Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)
docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: K65.2

SBP is an acute bacterial infection of ascitic fluid. It is a common and severe complication of advanced liver cirrhosis and it is associated with a poor prognosis.

Clinical features

Patients must be admitted to hospital and should be suspected of SBP infection when:

  • Ascites increases in severity

  • Presence of fever

  • Abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness

  • Worsening encephalopathy

  • Complications: renal failure, bleeding varices, death Investigations  Diagnosis is confirmed by an ascitic tap and cell counts. A neu-

trophil count of > 250/mm3 in ascitic fluid confirms the diagnosis Management

TREATMENT LOC  Treat with IV antibiotics for 5–10 days  IV ceftriaxone 1-2 g daily- If needed, add metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours H  Give albumin infusion 1 g/kg to prevent hepatorenal syndrome Consult or refer for specialist care as soon as possible RR Caution Avoid gentamicin and NSAIDs Caution Avoid gentamicin and NSAIDs

CHAPTER 6:Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Diseases

docs.title: 6.5.4.3 Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE)
docs.text:
ICD10 CODES: 70.41, 71.11, 72.11, 72.91

Hepatic encephalopathy is a syndrome of neuropsychiatric symptoms and signs, including coma, observed in patients with cirrhosis. It is probably due to the accumulation of toxins in the blood.

Clinical features

  • Grade 0: Subclinical – personaity changes, construction

apraxia (inability or difficulty to build, assemble, or draw objects)

  • Grade I: Confusion, flap tremor

  • Grade II: Drowsy

  • Grade III: Stuporous

  • Grade IV: Coma

  • Encephalopathy may be aggravated by surgery, parencen-

tsis, excessive diuretics, sedatives, and opioid analgesics

  • Intracranial hypertension and sepsis are the main causes of death

Management Management involves addressing the pathophysiological mechanisms related to brain, gut and liver

Management of pneumonia

TREATMENT LOC  dentify and correct precipitating factors including renal impairment, gastrointestinal bleeding, infections, and electrolyte disturbances Empty the gut- Give oral lactulose 15-30 mL every 8 hours until the condition resolves (aim at 2-3 soft stools/ day) H

Management of pneumonia

TREATMENT LOC - Lactulose can be administered through a nasogastric tube (grade 1 and 2) or as an enema in patients with acute HE (grade 3 and 4) Refer to a specialist If referral delays  Give an antibiotic with a local action on the gut: oralmetronidazole 400–800 mg every 8 hours for 5 days  Or oral paromomycin 1000 mg every 6 hours for 5 days RR

docs.title: Chapter 6: Gastrointestinal and Hepatic Diseases
docs.text:
This chapter provides guidance on gastrointestinal emergencies, gastrointestinal infections, digestive disorders, anorectal disorders, and hepatic and biliary diseases. It includes conditions such as appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding, peritonitis, diarrhoea, amoebiasis, dysentery, dysphagia, dyspepsia, reflux disease, gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, constipation, haemorrhoids, hepatitis, cirrhosis, ascites, jaundice, gallstones, and cholecystitis.

Use this chapter to guide clinical assessment, supportive care, treatment, and referral for gastrointestinal and liver-related conditions.

Digital navigation note

This chapter landing page was added to improve navigation in the digital version of the Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023. It provides orientation only and does not replace the detailed clinical guidance in the chapter sections.

docs.title: 7.1.1 Acute Renal Failure
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N17

Acute renal failure is acute impairment of renal function.

Causes

  • Compromised renal perfusion, such as dehydration, heart failure, or shock
  • Obstructed urinary flow
  • Damage to renal tissue by infectious and inflammatory diseases, such as glomerulonephritis
  • Intoxications
  • Nephrotoxic medicines

Clinical features

  • Oliguria, defined as urine flow below 1 mL/kg/hour
  • Generalised oedema
  • Hypertension
  • Heart failure
  • Dyspnoea
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Anorexia
  • Lethargy
  • Convulsions

Differential diagnosis

  • Other renal disorders
  • Biventricular heart failure

Investigations

  • Urine analysis for blood, protein, leucocytes, and casts
  • Urea, creatinine, and electrolytes

Management

Management of acute kidney conditions can be started at hospital level, but the patient should be referred to a higher level for more appropriate management.

Treatment LOC Treat underlying conditions, such as dehydration. HC4 Monitor fluid input and output. HC4 Calculate daily fluid requirements as 10 mL/kg plus total losses through urine, vomitus, and diarrhoea. HC4 Monitor blood pressure twice daily. HC4 Weigh the patient daily. HC4 Restrict salt intake to less than 2 g daily, or about half a teaspoonful daily. HC4 Restrict potassium intake, including oranges, bananas, vegetables, meat, and fizzy drinks. HC4 Give moderate protein intake. HC4 Ensure adequate calories in the diet. HC4 Check urine and electrolytes frequently. HC4 Treat complications, such as infections, hypertension, and convulsions, adjusting medicine doses according to the clinical response where appropriate. RR If there is oliguria, give IV furosemide according to response. High doses may be necessary. RR If there is no response to the above general measures, worsening kidney function, or anuria, refer for specialist management including possible dialysis as soon as possible and before the patient’s condition becomes critical. HC4

Caution

Do not give medicines that may worsen kidney damage.

Use gentamicin with caution.

docs.title: 7.1.2 Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N18

Chronic kidney disease is chronic impairment of kidney function.

Causes and risk factors

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hypertension or cardiovascular disease
  • Age above 50 years
  • Kidney stones
  • Medicines, especially pain killers such as diclofenac, ibuprofen, and other NSAIDs
  • Family history of kidney disease
  • HIV/AIDS

Clinical features

Most patients with CKD have no symptoms until the disease is advanced.

Patients may present with:

  • Features of the predisposing risk factor
  • Anaemia
  • Lethargy
  • Easy fatigue
  • Loss of appetite
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Skin itching
  • Bone pains
  • Body swelling
  • Loin pain

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of chronic anaemia
  • Heart failure
  • Protein-energy malnutrition
  • Chronic liver disease

Investigations

  • Creatinine, urea, and electrolytes
  • Urine dipstick for protein and blood
  • Kidney ultrasound
  • Urine dipstick for protein and blood, and blood pressure measurement at least once a year in high-risk patients
  • In diabetic patients, urine microalbumin where possible, or spot urine protein:creatinine ratio at least once a year
  • If abnormalities are detected, perform serum creatinine and calculate GFR

Refer the following patients for specialist attention

  • Children
  • Persistent proteinuria or haematuria beyond 3 months
  • GFR below 60 mL/min or creatinine above 1.9 mg/dL
  • Familial kidney disease, such as polycystic kidney disease

How to screen for CKD in patients at risk

Screen high-risk patients using:

  • Blood pressure measurement
  • Urine dipstick for protein and blood
  • Serum creatinine and estimated GFR where indicated
  • Urine microalbumin or protein:creatinine ratio in diabetic patients where possible

Management

Treatment of end-stage renal disease is complex and expensive, and is available only at national referral hospital level.

Goals

  • Establish diagnosis and treat reversible disease
  • Identify co-morbid conditions and manage complications of CKD
  • Slow progression of CKD by optimising treatment
  • Plan renal replacement therapy before end-stage kidney disease is reached
Treatment LOC Preserve kidney function in patients with CKD. HC4 Encourage lifestyle modification, including weight loss, stopping smoking, exercise, healthy balanced diet, lipid control, and salt restriction. HC4 Control blood pressure. Target blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, or lower in children. HC4 Use ACE inhibitors as first-line antihypertensives for diabetic patients and patients with proteinuria, together with a low-salt diet. HC4 In diabetic patients, blood pressure control is paramount. HC4 Optimise blood sugar control. Target HbA1c is below 7%. HC4 Reduce proteinuria using ACE inhibitors and/or ARBs. Target proteinuria is below 1 g/day. RR Avoid nephrotoxic medicines, such as NSAIDs, celecoxibs, aminoglycosides, and contrast agents. HR Prevent complications. For anaemia, consider iron and folic acid supplements. Target haemoglobin is 11 to 12 g/dL. HC4 For bone mineral disease, consider adding calcium. HC4 For fluid retention or oliguria, give furosemide tablets according to response. High doses may be necessary. HC4 Refer for dialysis in end-stage cases. RR

Caution

Start ACE inhibitors at low doses and monitor renal function.

Prevention

  • Screen high-risk patients.
  • Optimise treatment of risk factors.
  • Use treatments that slow progression in the initial phases.
  • Avoid nephrotoxic medicines.

docs.title: 7.1.3 Use of Medicines in Renal Failure
docs.text:
Be very careful when prescribing any medicine in renal failure or renal impairment. Check available prescribing information, such as the Practical Guidelines for Dispensing 2015, before prescribing.

Many medicines are excreted through the kidneys and accumulate when urinary output is reduced.

Some medicines are presented as sodium or potassium salts and may contribute to accumulation of these electrolytes.

With life-threatening infections, such as meningitis, use normal or high doses of antibiotics initially, then reduce doses once the condition has responded.

Medicines usually safe in renal failure

  • Doxycycline
  • Erythromycin
  • Benzylpenicillin, maximum 6 g daily in severe impairment
  • Phenytoin
  • Rifampicin

Medicines to use with care in reduced doses

  • ACE inhibitors, such as captopril
  • Amoxicillin
  • Chloramphenicol, avoid in severe impairment
  • Ciprofloxacin
  • Cotrimoxazole
  • Diazepam
  • Digoxin
  • Insulin
  • Isoniazid-containing medicines
  • Pethidine, increase dose interval and avoid in severe impairment
  • Phenobarbital
  • Propranolol

Medicines to avoid

  • Acetylsalicylic acid and other NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen and indomethacin
  • Codeine
  • Ethambutol
  • Gentamicin
  • Metformin
  • Nalidixic acid
  • Nitrofurantoin
  • Streptomycin
  • Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)

docs.title: 7.1.4 Glomerulonephritis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N00–N01

Glomerulonephritis is inflammatory kidney disease. It commonly follows immune reactions after infection, usually 1 to 5 weeks after a streptococcal skin or throat infection.

Clinical features

  • Common in children above 3 years and adolescents
  • Haematuria, presenting as red or tea-coloured urine
  • Oedema, especially puffiness of the face or around the eyes
  • Less commonly, generalised body swelling
  • Discomfort in the kidney area, including abdominal or back pain
  • Anorexia
  • General weakness or malaise
  • High blood pressure for age
  • Headache
  • Visual disturbances
  • Vomiting
  • Occasionally pulmonary oedema with dyspnoea
  • Convulsions in hypertensive crisis
  • Oliguria as renal failure sets in
  • Evidence of primary streptococcal infection, usually acute tonsillitis with cervical adenitis
  • Less commonly, evidence of skin sepsis

Differential diagnosis

  • Kidney infections, such as TB or pyelonephritis
  • Kidney tumours
  • Heart failure
  • Malnutrition
  • Allergic reactions

Investigations

  • Urine analysis for protein
  • Urine microscopy for red blood cells, casts, and white blood cells
  • Blood urea and creatinine
  • Antistreptolysin O titre (ASOT)
  • Electrolytes
  • Kidney ultrasound

Management

Inflammatory kidney disease with oedema, hypertension, and oliguria should be referred to a regional hospital for specialised management.

Clinical situation Treatment LOC General management Monitor urine output, blood pressure, and daily weight. H General management Restrict fluid input if there is oliguria. H General management Restrict salt and regulate protein in the diet if there is oliguria. H General management Avoid, or use with caution, medicines excreted by the kidney. See section 7.1.3. H General management Treat any continuing hypertension. See section 4.1.6. H Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Treat the primary streptococcal infection with a 10-day course of phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg every 6 hours. H Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Children: phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 to 20 mg/kg per dose. H Alternative treatment Give amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours for 10 days. H Alternative treatment Children: amoxicillin 20 mg/kg per dose. H Penicillin allergy Give erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours for 10 days. H Penicillin allergy Children: erythromycin 15 mg/kg per dose. H Fluid overload or oedema Give furosemide 80 mg IV as a slow bolus. H Fluid overload or oedema Children: furosemide 1 mg/kg every 8 to 12 hours. H High blood pressure Give nifedipine 20 mg every 12 hours. H High blood pressure in children Refer to a specialist. H

Prevention

  • Treat throat and skin infections promptly and effectively.
  • Avoid overcrowding.
  • Ensure adequate ventilation in dwellings.

docs.title: 7.1.5 Nephrotic Syndrome
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N04

Nephrotic syndrome is a disorder characterised by loss of protein in the urine due to damage of the kidney. It is common in children.

Causes

  • Idiopathic or unknown cause, which accounts for the majority of cases
  • Congenital nephrotic syndrome, which is rare
  • Secondary causes, including:
    • Post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis
    • Malaria
    • Allergy
    • Urinary tract infection
    • Hepatitis B
    • HIV

Clinical features

  • Generalised oedema
  • Severe loss of protein in urine, or proteinuria
  • Low serum albumin levels, or hypoalbuminaemia
  • Hyperlipidaemia, or high blood cholesterol

Investigations

  • Investigations as for acute glomerulonephritis
  • 24-hour urine protein quantification, or albumin creatinine ratio (ACR)
  • Serum protein
  • Serum cholesterol

Differential diagnosis

  • Cardiac failure
  • Liver disease
  • Malnutrition with oedema, such as kwashiorkor
  • Malabsorption syndrome
  • Allergic states causing generalised body swelling
  • Chronic glomerulonephritis

Management

Treatment LOC Restrict salt intake to less than 2 g daily, equivalent to less than half a teaspoon per day. H Restrict water or fluid intake. H Moderate both salt and water/fluid intake until diuresis is induced and swelling is subsiding. This can take several weeks. H Give furosemide 40 to 80 mg each morning to induce diuresis. H Children: give furosemide 1 to 2 mg/kg per dose. See notes below. H Give prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily, maximum 60 mg. RR Continue prednisolone until there is no further proteinuria, usually around 6 weeks. RR Gradually reduce the prednisolone dose after the first 4 weeks, for example by 0.5 mg/kg per day each week. RR When oedema has subsided, if the patient is still hypertensive, give appropriate treatment. See section 4.1.6. RR If there are clinical signs of suspected streptococcal infection, give antibiotics as for acute glomerulonephritis. RR If the patient is from an area endemic for schistosomiasis, give praziquantel 40 mg/kg as a single dose. RR If there is no improvement after 4 weeks, or if the patient relapses, refer for further management. RR

docs.title: 7.2.1 Acute Cystitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N30

Acute cystitis is an infection or inflammation involving the bladder, which is part of the lower urinary tract. It is a common manifestation of uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI) in non-pregnant women.

Uncomplicated cystitis is less common in men and should be differentiated from prostatitis and urethritis, including sexually transmitted urethritis.

Cause

  • Bacterial infection, usually gram-negative organisms from intestinal flora, such as Escherichia coli

Clinical features

  • Dysuria, or pain and difficulty in passing urine
  • Urgency of passing urine
  • Frequent passing of small amounts of urine
  • Suprapubic pain and tenderness
  • Pyuria or haematuria, causing cloudy urine
  • Foul-smelling urine
  • Retention of urine in severe infection

Investigations

  • Midstream urine analysis for:
    • Protein
    • Blood
    • Leucocytes
    • Nitrites
    • Sediment
  • Urine culture and sensitivity if there are resistant or repeated infections

Diagnostic criteria

  • Symptoms with or without leucocytes and/or nitrites on urine analysis

Differential diagnosis

  • In women: vaginitis
  • In men:
    • Urethritis, especially in young sexually active patients
    • Prostatitis, especially in older men, which may present with fever, chills, malaise, perineal pain, or confusion

Note

Asymptomatic bacteriuria or pyuria, meaning leucocytes in urine, does not need treatment except in risk groups such as pregnant women, patients undergoing urological interventions, and post-kidney transplant patients.

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Uncomplicated UTI or cystitis in non-pregnant women Ensure high fluid intake. HC2 First-line treatment Give nitrofurantoin 100 mg every 6 hours for 5 to 7 days. Advise the patient to take it after meals. HC2 First-line treatment in children Give nitrofurantoin 3 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 6 hours for 7 days. HC2 Second-line treatment in adults Give ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 days. HC2 Second-line treatment in children Give amoxicillin 125 to 250 mg every 8 hours for 7 days. HC2 Poor response or recurrent infections Refer for urine culture and sensitivity, further investigation, and further management. HC2

Note

For urinary tract infection in pregnancy, see section 16.2.6.

Prevention

  • Improve personal and genital hygiene.
  • Pass urine after coitus.
  • Drink plenty of fluids.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Acute Pyelonephritis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N10

Acute pyelonephritis is an upper urinary tract infection involving one or both kidneys, but usually not involving the glomeruli.

Causes and risk factors

  • Bacterial infection, such as Escherichia coli, usually due to ascending infection through faecal, perineal, and urethral progression of bacteria
  • Bladder outlet obstruction
  • Malformations of the urinary tract
  • Pregnancy
  • HIV
  • Old age
  • Diabetes

Clinical features

  • Loin pain
  • Tenderness in one or both kidney areas, or renal angle tenderness
  • Fever
  • Rigors, or generalised body tremors
  • Vomiting
  • If associated with cystitis:
    • Dysuria
    • Urgency
    • Frequency
  • Diarrhoea and convulsions, especially in children
  • In infants and elderly patients, presentation may be limited to fever and poor feeding or disorientation, without other signs

Differential diagnosis

  • Appendicitis
  • Infection of the fallopian tubes, or salpingitis
  • Infection of the gall bladder, or cholecystitis

Investigations

  • Urine microscopy for pus cells and organisms
  • Midstream urine culture and sensitivity
  • Blood full count
  • Blood culture and sensitivity
  • Urea and electrolytes
  • Ultrasound of kidneys and prostate

Note

The urine specimen should reach the laboratory within 2 hours of collection, or be refrigerated at 4°C for not more than 24 hours.

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC General management Ensure adequate fluid intake, orally or IV, to irrigate the bladder and dilute bacterial concentrations. HC3 Pain and fever Give paracetamol 1 g every 6 to 8 hours. HC3 Outpatient treatment in adults only Give ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days. HC3 Severe cases, all children, or no response after 48 hours Give ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily. HC3 Severe cases in children Give ceftriaxone 50 to 80 mg/kg IV once daily. HC3 Following initial response to parenteral therapy in adults Consider changing to ciprofloxacin 750 mg every 12 hours to complete 10 days of treatment. HC3 Following initial response to parenteral therapy Alternatively, give cefixime 200 mg every 12 hours to complete 10 days of treatment. HC3 Following initial response to parenteral therapy in children Give cefixime 16 mg/kg on the first day, then 8 mg/kg to complete 10 days of treatment. HC3 Alternative regimen Give gentamicin 5 to 7 mg/kg IV as one dose or in divided doses, with or without ampicillin 2 g IV every 6 hours. HC3 Alternative regimen in children Give gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg every 8 hours, or 7.5 mg/kg once daily on outpatient basis, with or without ampicillin 25 mg/kg every 6 hours. HC3 No response after 72 hours Consider referral. HC3 Children with recurrent infections Refer to exclude urinary tract malformations. HC2

Prevention

  • Ensure perianal hygiene.
  • Ensure regular complete emptying of the bladder.
  • Encourage double voiding, meaning an additional attempt to empty the bladder after the initial urine flow ceases.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Prostatitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N41

Prostatitis is acute inflammation or infection of the prostate, a gland present in males and located below the bladder around the proximal urethra.

Cause

  • Bacterial infection, similar to urinary tract infection

Clinical features

  • Fever
  • Chills
  • Rectal pain
  • Perineal pain
  • Low back pain
  • Urinary urgency
  • Frequency
  • Dysuria
  • Acute urinary retention
  • Tender enlarged prostate on rectal examination

Caution

Avoid vigorous rectal examination.

Investigations

  • Haemogram
  • Urine analysis
  • Urine culture and sensitivity

Management

Treatment LOC Give IV fluids. HC4 Give antipyretics. HC4 Advise bed rest. HC4 Give stool softeners. HC4 Give ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 4 to 6 weeks. HC4

docs.title: 7.2.4 Renal Colic
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N23

Renal colic is acute severe pain in the loin, or kidney area, caused by obstruction of the ureters by a stone.

Causes

  • Urinary stones
  • Rarely, blood clot
  • Rarely, tumour

Clinical features

  • Acute severe colicky loin pain
  • Pain may radiate to the iliac fossa, testes, or labia on the same side
  • Dysuria may occur
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting

Differential diagnosis

  • Lower urinary tract infection
  • Acute upper urinary tract infection
  • Other causes of acute abdominal pain

Investigations

  • Urinalysis for blood
  • Plain abdominal X-ray for radio-opaque stones
  • Ultrasound

Management

Treatment LOC Give oral or IV fluids to maintain hydration. HC4 Give antiemetics if necessary, such as metoclopramide 10 mg IM or IV. HC4 Give diclofenac 75 mg IM as a single dose. HC4 Give pethidine 50 to 100 mg IM as a single dose, if required. HC4 Refer if episodes are repeated or unresolved. HC4

Prevention

  • Ensure oral fluid intake of 3 to 4 L/day.
  • Reduce salt intake.
  • Reduce animal protein intake.

docs.title: 7.2.5 Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N40

Benign prostatic hyperplasia is enlargement of the prostate causing urinary symptoms. It is common in men above 50 years.

Cause

  • Benign age-related growth of the prostate

Clinical features

Obstructive symptoms include:

  • Weak urine stream
  • Straining during micturition
  • Hesitancy
  • Intermittency
  • Sensation of incomplete bladder emptying

Irritative symptoms include:

  • Frequent micturition, especially at night
  • Urgency
  • Urge incontinence

Complications include:

  • Acute urinary retention
  • Frequent infections, which may precipitate symptoms

Investigations

  • Urine analysis for blood and leucocytes
  • Renal function tests
  • Abdominal ultrasound

Management

Treatment LOC Treat with antibiotics if infection is present. See prostatitis or acute cystitis in sections 7.2.3 and 7.2.1. HC2 Refer for surgical management if symptoms are severe. RR

docs.title: 7.2.6 Bladder Outlet Obstruction
docs.text:
Bladder outlet obstruction is obstruction of the urinary tract anywhere below the bladder, causing distension and incomplete emptying of the bladder. It may be acute, presenting as acute urinary retention, or chronic.

Causes

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia
  • Prostate cancer
  • Bladder tumours
  • Bladder stones
  • Pelvic masses
  • Rarely, pregnancy
  • Rarely, neurological causes
  • Infection, which can precipitate acute retention

Chronic obstruction can cause hydronephrosis and chronic kidney damage.

Clinical features

Acute obstruction may present with:

  • Painful and tender pelvic mass
  • Difficulty passing urine

Chronic obstruction may present with:

  • Obstructive and irritative urinary symptoms, as described under benign prostatic hyperplasia
  • Painless pelvic mass

Investigations

  • Urine analysis
  • Urine culture and sensitivity
  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Renal function tests
  • Specialised investigations, such as cystourethrogram

Management

Treatment LOC Insert a urethral catheter to relieve obstruction, usually size 18 F. HC4 Insert a suprapubic catheter if urethral catheterisation fails. RR Treat infection if present. HC4 Refer to a specialist for assessment and care. RR

docs.title: 7.2.7 Urinary Incontinence
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: N39.3–N39.4

Urinary incontinence is involuntary urine leakage.

Causes and clinical features

  • Pelvic floor muscle dysfunction, such as following pregnancy, causing stress incontinence during straining, coughing, or sneezing
  • Overactive bladder causing urge incontinence, with a sudden compelling need to urinate that is difficult to defer
  • Anatomical problems causing continuous incontinence, such as vesicovaginal fistula or ectopic ureter
  • Chronic bladder outlet obstruction causing overflow incontinence

Investigations

  • Careful history and examination
  • Urine analysis
  • Abdominal ultrasound

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Stress incontinence Advise pelvic floor exercises. HC2 Other causes of urinary incontinence Manage according to the specific cause. H

docs.text:
ICD10 CODE: N30

An infection/inflammation involving the bladder, a part of the lower urinary tract. It is a common manifestation of uncomplicated UTI (Urinary Tract Infection) in non- pregnant women.

Cause

Bacterial infection, usually gram negative (from intestinal flora) e.g. Escherichia coli

Clinical features Dysuria (pain and difficulty in passing urine)

Urgency of passing urine, frequent passing of small amounts of urine

Suprapubic pain and tenderness

Pyuria/haematuria (pus/blood in the urine makingit cloudy)

Foul smelling urine

There may be retention of urine in severe infection

Investigations  Midstream urine: urine analysis for protein, blood, leucocytes,

nitrates, sediment  Culture and sensitivity (if resistant/repeated infections) Diagnostic criteria

Symptoms ± leucocytes and/ or nitrates at urine analysis

CHAPTER 7: Renal and Urinary Diseases

Uncomplicated cystitis is less common in men and needs to be differentiated from prostatitis and urethritis (sexually transmitted).

Differential diagnosis

Women: vaginitis

Men: urethritis (in young sexually active patients), prostatitis (fever, chills, malaise, perineal pain, confusion, in older men)

Note: Asymptomatic bacteriuria or pyuria (leucocytes in urine) does not need treatment except in risk groups such as pregnant women, patients undergoing urological interventions and post kidney transplant patients

Management TREATMENT

LOC

Uncomplicated UTI (cystitis) in non-pregnant women

HC2



Ensure high fluid intake

First line agents:



Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6 hourly for 5-7 days[advise patient to take after meals]



Ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12 hourly for 7 days (adults)

Refer for investigation of culture and sensitivity and further management

Malformations of urinary tract

Pregnancy

Vomiting

docs.text:
This chapter covers renal and urological conditions including acute renal failure, chronic kidney disease, safe use of medicines in renal failure, glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, cystitis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, renal colic, benign prostatic hyperplasia, bladder outlet obstruction, and urinary incontinence.

Use this chapter to support recognition, safe prescribing, treatment initiation, monitoring, and referral for kidney and urinary tract disease.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Addison’s Disease
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: E27.1–E27.4

Addison’s disease is a condition where the adrenal gland produces insufficient glucocorticoid hormones. This is also called adrenal insufficiency.

Causes

  • Abrupt cessation of steroid treatment after long-term use, which is the most common cause
  • Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal gland
  • Tuberculosis of the adrenal glands
  • HIV/AIDS
  • Surgical removal of the adrenal glands
  • Cancer affecting the adrenal glands
  • Bleeding into the adrenal glands
  • Necrosis of the adrenal glands

Clinical features

Acute adrenal insufficiency may present with:

  • Weakness and easy fatigability
  • Shock
  • Very low blood pressure
  • Hypoglycaemic attacks
  • Mental changes, such as irritability and restlessness, progressing to coma
  • Fever
  • Hyponatraemia, or low sodium
  • Hyperkalaemia, or high potassium
  • Acidosis

Chronic adrenal insufficiency may present with the above features plus:

  • Weight loss
  • Hair loss
  • Darkening of the skin and mouth
  • Menstrual disturbance
  • Infertility

Symptoms are worse during stress, such as infections.

Differential diagnosis

  • HIV/AIDS
  • Tuberculosis
  • Cancer
  • Depression
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hypothyroidism

Investigations

  • Drug history
  • Refer to a higher level for hormone tests if there is no clear history of abrupt withdrawal of steroid treatment

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute crisis Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 hours until stable, then switch to oral treatment. H Acute crisis in children aged 0 to 3 years Give hydrocortisone 25 mg. H Acute crisis in children aged 3 to 12 years Give hydrocortisone 50 mg. H Acute crisis Give IV fluids and dextrose to maintain normal volume and blood sugar. H Acute crisis Treat complications and concomitant illnesses, such as infections. H Chronic case Give hydrocortisone tablets 10 mg. H Abrupt steroid cessation Restart prednisolone treatment, then slowly decrease the dose by 2.5 to 5 mg per week. H Replacement treatment Give prednisolone 5 to 7.5 mg/day. H Replacement treatment in children Give prednisolone 1 to 5 mg/day. H Stress situations, such as surgery, disease, or labour Use doses as in acute regimens. H

Prevention

  • Avoid self-medication with steroids, such as prednisolone and dexamethasone.
  • Decrease steroids gradually if used for treatment durations longer than 2 weeks.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Cushing’s Syndrome
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: E24

Cushing’s syndrome is a constellation of signs and symptoms caused by chronic glucocorticoid, or steroid, excess. It may result from excessive secretion, but is more commonly caused by chronic glucocorticoid therapy.

Causes

  • Iatrogenic causes, especially steroid treatment
  • Cushing’s disease
  • Adrenal adenoma
  • Adrenal carcinoma

Clinical features

  • Central or truncal obesity
  • Moon face
  • Buffalo hump
  • Thinning of the skin
  • Striae
  • Poor wound healing
  • Muscle weakness and atrophy
  • Hirsutism and acne in females
  • Hypertension
  • Hyperglycaemia

Differential diagnosis

  • Ordinary obesity
  • Alcoholism, including alcohol-induced pseudo-Cushing’s syndrome

Investigations

  • Drug history
  • Refer to a higher level for hormonal tests, such as dexamethasone suppression test, if there is no history of steroid overuse

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome Slowly decrease the steroid dose by 2.5 to 5 mg every 1 to 2 weeks. H Non-iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome Refer to a higher level of care. RR Iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome with complications Refer to a higher level of care. RR

docs.title: 8.1.3 Diabetes Mellitus
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: E08–E13

Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disease resulting from insulin insufficiency or ineffectiveness. This may be due to decreased insulin secretion, peripheral resistance to the action of insulin, or a combination of both.

Types of diabetes mellitus

  • Type 1 diabetes: decreased insulin production due to autoimmune destruction of the pancreas. It usually starts at a young age.
  • Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance, usually combined with insufficient insulin production as the disease progresses. It usually starts in adulthood.
  • Gestational diabetes: any degree of glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.
  • Secondary diabetes: diabetes due to other identifiable causes, such as Cushing’s syndrome or chronic pancreatitis.

Causes and risk factors

Type 1 diabetes risk factors include:

  • Genetic factors
  • Environmental factors, such as some viral infections

Type 2 diabetes risk factors include:

Non-modifiable risk factors

  • Age above 40 years
  • Family history in first-degree relatives
  • History of gestational diabetes mellitus
  • Delivery of a big baby weighing more than 4 kg

Modifiable risk factors

  • Unhealthy diet
  • Physical inactivity
  • Tobacco use
  • Harmful use of alcohol
  • Hypertension
  • Stress
  • Obesity
  • High cholesterol levels
  • Impaired glucose tolerance

Clinical features

Classical symptoms include:

  • Polyuria, meaning frequent urination or waking at night to urinate
  • Polydipsia, meaning frequent thirst or drinking a lot of water
  • Polyphagia, meaning increased appetite, feeling hungry all the time, or frequent eating
  • Polyneuropathy, including burning pains, pins and needles, or numbness

Other symptoms include:

  • Weight loss despite high appetite
  • Frequent skin infections, such as boils
  • Itchy genitalia, such as candidiasis
  • Slow-healing wounds
  • Fatigue or feeling tired all the time
  • Children not wanting to play
  • Bed-wetting in children
  • Poor vision
  • Presentation with complications

Type 2 diabetes often presents with minor non-specific symptoms. It may be diagnosed through screening or when the patient presents with complications.

Complications

Acute complications include:

  • Coma due to diabetic ketoacidosis
  • Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia
  • Hypoglycaemia

See section 8.1.4 and section 1.1.6.

Chronic complications include:

  • Microvascular complications affecting small blood vessels, including:
    • Retinopathy
    • Nephropathy
    • Neuropathy
  • Macrovascular complications affecting large blood vessels, including:
    • Stroke
    • Ischaemic heart disease
    • Peripheral artery disease
    • Heart attack
  • Kidney failure
  • Blindness
  • Impotence
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Diabetic foot, which may lead to amputation

Differential diagnosis

  • Diabetes insipidus
  • HIV/AIDS
  • Tuberculosis

Investigations

  • Blood glucose:
    • Fasting blood glucose
    • Random blood glucose
    • Two-hour blood glucose after 75 g glucose
  • Urine testing for glucose
  • Urine testing for ketones, especially in type 1 diabetes
  • HbA1c, or glycated haemoglobin A1c
  • Renal function tests
  • Lipid profile
  • ECG
  • Urine protein or microalbuminuria

Diagnostic criteria

Diabetes mellitus may be diagnosed using any of the following:

  • Fasting blood sugar above 7.0 mmol/L, or 126 mg/dL
  • Two-hour blood sugar after 75 g glucose above 11.1 mmol/L, or 200 mg/dL
  • HbA1c above 6.5%
  • In a patient with classical symptoms of hyperglycaemia, random blood sugar above 11.1 mmol/L, or 200 mg/dL

Caution

In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia, meaning very high blood sugar levels, criteria 1 to 3 should be confirmed by repeated testing.

One single slightly elevated blood sugar in the absence of symptoms is not diagnostic for diabetes.

General management

The goals of treatment are:

  • Treatment of hyperglycaemia
  • Treatment of associated risk factors
  • Prevention and treatment of acute and chronic complications
Management area Treatment LOC Lifestyle modification Advise a diabetic diet. See section 19.1.3. HC2 Lifestyle modification Advise weight loss if overweight. HC2 Lifestyle modification Encourage regular physical exercise. HC2 Lifestyle modification Advise moderate alcohol intake or no alcohol intake. HC2 Lifestyle modification Support smoking cessation. HC2 Risk factor management Assess for other risk factors, such as hypertension, obesity, and smoking, and manage accordingly. HC2 Hypertension Target blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg. First-line medicines are ACE inhibitors because of renal protection, such as enalapril. See section 4.1.6. HC4 Dyslipidaemia Consider statin treatment, such as atorvastatin 20 to 40 mg once daily or simvastatin 20 to 40 mg once daily in the evening. H Dyslipidaemia Statin treatment is especially indicated if ischaemic heart disease or cerebrovascular disease is already present, or if the patient is above 40 years. H

Caution

Do not use beta blockers, such as atenolol, in diabetes.

Management of complications

Complication area Treatment LOC Screening and assessment Assess for complications, including renal disease, eye problems, diabetic foot, peripheral neuropathy, heart problems, and stroke. Refer or treat accordingly. HC3 Ischaemic heart disease or stroke Give aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily. HC3 Peripheral neuropathy Give amitriptyline 10 to 25 mg at night, up to a maximum of 100 mg in divided doses. H Ischaemic heart disease or stroke Give atorvastatin 20 to 40 mg once daily. H

Treatment targets

  • Fasting blood sugar below 7 mmol/L
  • Postprandial blood sugar below 10 mmol/L
  • HbA1c below 7%
  • HbA1c below 7.5% in elderly patients

Elderly people are at higher risk of hypoglycaemia. Monitor carefully and do not aim for very strict blood sugar control.

Management of type 1 diabetes

Treatment LOC Give insulin subcutaneously at 0.6 to 1.5 IU/kg/day. HC4 Children below 5 years: start with insulin 0.5 IU/kg/day and refer to a paediatrician. HC4

Common insulin preparations

Type of insulin Usual protocol Onset Peak Duration Short-acting regular soluble insulin, such as Actrapid Three times daily, 30 minutes before meals 30 minutes 2 to 5 hours 5 to 8 hours Rapid-acting insulin analogue, such as insulin aspart Three times daily, 10 to 15 minutes before meals 10 to 20 minutes 45 minutes 3 to 5 hours Intermediate-acting insulin, NPH, such as Insulatard Once or twice daily, evening with or without morning dose 1 to 3 hours 6 to 12 hours 16 to 24 hours Biphasic insulin, mixture of regular and NPH, such as Mixtard 30/70 Once or twice daily 30 minutes 2 to 12 hours 16 to 24 hours

Preferably, a combination of intermediate-acting and short-acting insulin should be used.

Examples of regimens include:

  • Pre-meal short-acting insulin, such as Actrapid, or rapid-acting insulin analogue, such as insulin aspart, plus evening intermediate-acting insulin, such as Insulatard, or long-acting insulin analogue, such as glargine.
  • The evening dose should be 40 to 50% of the daily dose. This is basal-bolus therapy.

Alternatively:

  • Give twice-daily premixed insulin, such as Mixtard.
  • Usually give two-thirds of the total dose in the morning and one-third in the evening, 30 minutes before meals.
  • For biphasic insulin aspart, give two-thirds of the total dose in the morning and one-third in the evening, 10 to 15 minutes before meals.

Note

Patients on insulin should measure their blood glucose at least twice daily, before breakfast and before dinner, and insulin doses should be adjusted accordingly.

docs.title: 8.1.4 Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: E10.1 / E11.0

Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state are acute metabolic complications of diabetes mellitus.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is characterised by:

  • Ketosis
  • Acidosis
  • Hyperglycaemia

It is more common in type 1 diabetes.

Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is characterised by:

  • Hyperglycaemia
  • Severe dehydration
  • Hypovolaemia
  • No ketosis
  • No acidosis

It is more common in type 2 diabetes.

Causes and precipitating factors

  • Newly diagnosed diabetes
  • Poor control of diabetes mellitus
  • Treatment interruptions
  • Infections
  • Trauma

Clinical features

Diabetic ketoacidosis may present with:

  • Acute onset, usually within 24 hours or less
  • Excessive thirst
  • Excessive fluid intake
  • Frequent urination
  • Weight loss
  • Tiredness
  • Abdominal pain
  • Vomiting
  • Altered consciousness
  • Coma
  • Deep acidotic breathing
  • Sweet acetone smell on the breath due to ketosis
  • Cardiovascular collapse with hypotension

Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state may present with:

  • Slower onset
  • More severe dehydration and fluid deficit
  • No ketosis or acidosis
  • No or few ketones in urine

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of ketoacidosis or hyperglycaemia
  • Other causes of acute abdominal pain
  • Other causes of coma

Investigations

  • Blood sugar
  • Urine analysis for ketones
  • Full blood count
  • Renal function tests
  • Electrolytes, especially sodium and potassium

Management

Management area Treatment LOC General measures Monitor blood pressure, urine output, and blood sugar hourly. HC4 General measures Insert urinary catheter if unconscious. HC4 General measures Treat infections if present because they may be a precipitating factor. HC4 Prevention of thromboembolism Give enoxaparin 4,000 IU SC until the patient is able to move. H Fluid replacement Give normal saline, NaCl 0.9%. HC4 Fluid replacement Give 15 to 20 mL/kg in the first hour, usually 500 to 1,000 mL. HC4 Fluid replacement in children Give 10 to 20 mL/kg. HC4 Ongoing fluid replacement Continue with 5 to 15 mL/kg/hour according to vital signs, urine output, and clinical condition. HC4 Dextrose switch If blood sugar is below 14 mmol/L, switch to dextrose 5% if ketones are still present and/or the clinical condition is not yet normal, such as when the patient is unable to eat. HC4 Insulin Give soluble insulin 4 to 6 IU IM every hour until the condition stabilises. HC4 Insulin in children above 5 years Give soluble insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hour. HC4 Insulin in children below 5 years Give soluble insulin 0.05 IU/kg/hour. HC4 Insulin continuation Continue insulin until ketosis resolves and the patient is able to eat. HC4 Transition to SC insulin Once the clinical condition normalises, including normal blood pressure, consciousness, urine output, and ability to eat, start the SC insulin regimen. See section 8.1.3. Start SC insulin 1 to 2 hours before stopping IM insulin. HC4

Potassium replacement

If potassium level is not available:

Situation Treatment LOC Potassium level not available Add potassium chloride 1 ampoule to every 1 litre of infusion as soon as the patient has started passing urine. HC4

If potassium levels are available:

Potassium level Treatment LOC K⁺ below 3.5 mmol/L Add 40 mmol potassium chloride, equivalent to 2 ampoules, per 1 litre of fluid. HC4 K⁺ 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L Add 20 mmol potassium chloride, equivalent to 1 ampoule, per 1 litre of infusion. HC4 K⁺ above 5.5 mmol/L Do not add potassium. HC4

Prevention

  • Early detection of diabetes
  • Good control of diabetes
  • Prompt treatment of infections
  • General patient education

Hypoglycaemia

For hypoglycaemia in patients on antidiabetic medicines, manage as described in section 1.1.6.

For severe hypoglycaemia in diabetes patients treated with insulin who are unconscious or cannot take sugar by mouth:

Treatment LOC Give glucagon 1 mg, equivalent to 1 unit, IM or SC. HC4 Repeat every 15 minutes once or twice according to response. HC4

docs.title: 8.1.5 Goitre
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: E04

Goitre is visible enlargement of the thyroid gland. It may or may not be associated with abnormal thyroid function, such as hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.

Causes

  • Iodine deficiency
  • Graves’ disease
  • Thyroiditis
  • Multinodular goitre
  • Physiological causes, such as pregnancy or puberty

Clinical features

  • Visible neck swelling
  • Rarely, difficulty in swallowing

Investigations

  • Thyroid hormone tests
  • Neck ultrasound

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Goitre Refer for thyroid hormone testing and specialist management. RR Goitre associated with hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism Manage according to the relevant thyroid disorder section. RR Goitre causing obstruction Surgery is indicated. RR

docs.title: 8.1.6 Hyperthyroidism
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: E05

Hyperthyroidism is a condition resulting from excess thyroid hormones, usually due to excessive production.

Causes

  • Graves’ disease, which is autoimmune and common in females
  • Neonatal thyrotoxicosis
  • Thyroid gland tumours, such as adenomas
  • Multinodular toxic goitre
  • Thyroiditis
  • Iatrogenic causes, such as side effects of some medicines

Clinical features

  • Weight loss with increased appetite
  • Swelling in the neck, or goitre
  • Palpitations
  • Tachycardia
  • Irritability
  • Nervousness
  • Inability to rest or sleep
  • Irregular or scanty menstrual periods
  • Profuse sweating
  • Extreme discomfort in hot weather
  • High blood pressure
  • Protruding eyes, or exophthalmos, in some forms
  • Frequent defecation

Differential diagnosis

  • Anxiety states
  • Tumours of the adrenal gland, such as pheochromocytoma
  • Other causes of weight loss
  • Other causes of protruding eyes

Investigations

  • Blood levels of thyroid hormones, showing high T3 and T4 with low TSH
  • Thyroid ultrasound scan
  • Thyroid gland biopsy for cytology or histology

Management

The aim of treatment is to restore the euthyroid state.

Use pulse rate and thyroid hormone levels to monitor progress.

Treatment LOC Give carbimazole 15 to 40 mg daily, maximum 60 mg, in 2 to 3 divided doses for 1 to 2 months. H Children: give carbimazole 750 micrograms/kg/day in divided doses, maximum 30 mg/day. H Adjust the dose according to thyroid hormone levels, under specialist management only. H To control excessive sympathetic symptoms, such as palpitations, add propranolol 40 to 80 mg every 12 hours for at least 1 month. H Children: give propranolol 250 to 500 micrograms/kg 3 to 4 times daily. H Once the patient is euthyroid, stop propranolol and progressively reduce carbimazole to a daily maintenance dose of 5 to 15 mg. H Continue carbimazole for at least 18 months. H Surgery may be required in selected cases, such as obstruction, intolerance, or lack of response to medicine treatment. RR Radioactive iodine may be used, especially in toxic multinodular goitre. RR

Caution

Patients treated with carbimazole should be advised to report any sore throat immediately because of the rare complication of agranulocytosis, which is a low white blood cell count.

docs.title: 8.1.7 Hypothyroidism
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: E03

Hypothyroidism is a condition resulting from thyroid hormone deficiency. It is more common in females than in males.

Causes

  • Autoimmune disease
  • Post-therapeutic causes, especially after radiotherapy or surgical treatment for hyperthyroidism
  • Secondary causes due to congenital enzyme defects
  • Iodine deficiency
  • Iatrogenic causes, such as side effects of some medicines

Clinical features

  • Dull facial expression
  • Puffiness
  • Periorbital swelling
  • Hoarse voice
  • Slow speech
  • Weight gain
  • Drooping eyelids
  • Sparse, coarse, and dry hair
  • Dry, scaly, and thick skin
  • Forgetfulness
  • Other signs of mental impairment
  • Gradual personality change
  • Bradycardia
  • Constipation, often
  • Anaemia, often
  • Paraesthesia, or numbness, of hands and feet

Differential diagnosis

  • Myasthenia gravis
  • Depression

Investigations

  • Blood levels of thyroid hormones, showing low T3 and T4 with high TSH

Management

Treatment LOC Give levothyroxine. H Initial dose: levothyroxine 50 to 100 micrograms once daily before breakfast. H Elderly patients: start with levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily. H Gradually increase by 25 to 50 micrograms every 4 weeks to a maintenance dose of 100 to 200 micrograms daily, according to hormonal levels. H Once stable, check hormone levels every 6 to 12 months. H Children: refer for specialist management. H

Note

In most cases, treatment is for life.

Prevention

  • Educate patients on the use of iodised salt.

docs.title: 8.1.8 Central Precocious Puberty
docs.text:
Central precocious puberty is also referred to as gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty. It is an endocrine-related developmental disease characterised by the onset of pubertal changes, with development of secondary sexual characteristics and accelerated growth and bone maturation, before the normal age of puberty.

The normal age of puberty is 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys.

Causes

  • Premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis
  • Idiopathic causes
  • Secondary causes, including:
    • Brain tumours such as glioma and astrocytoma
    • CNS infections such as meningitis and encephalitis
    • Brain malformations such as hydrocephalus and arachnoid cysts
    • Trauma
    • Injuries

Clinical features

  • Accelerated growth and bone maturation
  • Premature breast development
  • Early menarche in girls
  • Testicular and penile enlargement in boys
  • Development of facial and sexual hair in boys

Genetic counselling

Most cases are sporadic. Familial cases show autosomal dominant mode of transmission with incomplete, gender-dependent penetrance.

Differential diagnosis

  • Gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty
  • McCune-Albright syndrome
  • Gonadal tumours
  • Benign premature thelarche

Investigations

  • Pelvic ultrasound
  • Screening of basal luteinizing hormone (LH) levels
  • Measurement of gonadotropin levels after stimulation tests using gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)

Management

Treatment LOC Treat progressive central precocious puberty using GnRH agonists, such as leuprolide acetate for depot suspension. NH Give leuprolide acetate for depot suspension 7.5 mg injection monthly. NH

Prognosis

The disease has minimal consequences during adulthood, although the association of variation of pubertal timing with adult disease or behaviour may be questioned.

Metabolic disease resulting from insulin insufficiency or ineffectiveness, due to decreased insulin secretion, or peripheral resistance to the action of insulin, or a combination of the two.

This chapter provides guidance on endocrine and metabolic conditions including Addison’s disease, Cushing’s syndrome, diabetes mellitus, diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, goitre, hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, and central precocious puberty.

Use this chapter to guide diagnosis, emergency recognition, long-term management, monitoring, counselling, and referral for endocrine and metabolic disorders.
