docs.title: Chapter 9: Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders
Chapter 9: Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders
9.1.1 Epilepsy
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: G40

Epilepsy is a chronic condition characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures. Seizures are caused by abnormal discharges in the brain and may present as convulsive or non-convulsive forms.

Convulsive epilepsy may present with sudden muscle contraction, causing the person to fall and become rigid, followed by alternating relaxation and rigidity of muscles, with or without loss of bowel or bladder control.

Non-convulsive epilepsy may present with changes in awareness, behaviour, emotions, or senses, such as taste, smell, vision, or hearing. These features may resemble mental health conditions and may therefore be confused with them.

Consider a diagnosis of epilepsy if a person has had at least two seizures in the last calendar year on two different days.

Seizures during an acute event, such as meningitis or acute traumatic brain injury, are not epilepsy.

Causes

  • Genetic causes
  • Congenital malformation
  • Birth asphyxia
  • Brain tumour
  • Brain infections
  • Cysticercosis
  • Trauma, either acute or in the past
  • Metabolic disorders
  • In some cases, no specific cause can be identified

Clinical features

Clinical features depend on the type of epilepsy.

Type of epilepsy Description Generalised epilepsy Seizure involves the whole brain. Consciousness is lost at onset. Tonic-clonic, grand mal, or convulsive epilepsy May commence with a warning sensation, such as sound, light, or abdominal pain, called an aura.There may be a sharp cry followed by loss of consciousness and falling.Tonic contraction, or rigidity, of muscles occurs, followed by jerking movements, called the clonic phase.There may be incontinence of urine or faeces, frothing, and tongue biting.A period of deep sleep follows. Absence seizures, or petit mal Mainly a disorder of children.The attack is characterised by a brief loss of consciousness, usually 5 to 10 seconds, during which posture is retained but other activities cease.The child has a vacant stare.Previous activities are resumed at the end of the attack.Several attacks may occur in a single day. Atonic or tonic seizures, or drop attacks Sudden loss of muscular tone of brief duration, usually about 15 seconds, with consciousness maintained.Alternatively, there may be sudden stiffening of muscles. Myoclonic epilepsy Abnormal jerking movements, usually occurring in the limbs, but may involve the whole body. Focal epilepsy Seizure activity starts in one area of the brain. Simple focal seizure The patient remains alert but has abnormal sensory, motor, psychic, or autonomic manifestations.Examples include jerking of a limb, déjà vu, nausea, strange taste or smell, sweating, flushing, gastric sensation, motor contraction, or sensory change in a particular part of the body. Complex focal seizure Altered awareness and behaviour, such as confusion or repetitive movements. Status epilepticus A convulsive state in which convulsions last more than 30 minutes, or several epileptic convulsions occur in succession without recovery of consciousness in between, or convulsions are not responsive to two doses of diazepam. It is a medical emergency.

Differential diagnosis

  • Syncope, or fainting
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Hypocalcaemia
  • Conversion disorder, previously known as hysteria
  • Hyperventilation
  • Panic attacks

Investigations

  • Complete medical and mental health assessment
  • Electroencephalogram (EEG)
    • Useful in petit mal and focal seizures
    • To be done at specialist level, regional referral or national referral level
  • Other investigations guided by suspected cause

General principles

  • All suspected cases of non-convulsive epilepsy should be confirmed and treated by a specialist.
  • Convulsive epilepsy can be diagnosed at hospital or HC3 level, but medicine refills should be available at lower levels.
  • One brief isolated seizure does not need further treatment, but review after 3 months and reassess.
  • Treat patients with repeated episodes according to the case definition.
  • Treatment can effectively control epilepsy in most cases.
  • Treatment should include psychological and social support.
  • Start with a single anti-epileptic medicine.
  • Start with low doses and increase gradually according to response.
  • If a patient has been seizure-free for 2 years, consider gradual stopping of medication.

Commonly used antiepileptic medicines include:

  • Generalised tonic-clonic seizures:
    • Children below 2 years: phenobarbital or carbamazepine
    • Children above 2 years: carbamazepine or valproate
  • Absence seizures:
    • Valproate or ethosuximide

Caution

Avoid phenobarbital and phenytoin in children with intellectual disability and/or behavioural problems.

Management

Situation Treatment LOC First aid for acute seizure Do not restrain the patient. HC2 First aid for acute seizure Do not put anything in the mouth. HC2 First aid for acute seizure Protect the person from injury by ensuring they are in a safe place, away from fire or other hazards. HC2 First aid for acute seizure Do not leave the patient alone. Seek help if possible. HC2 After the seizure Check airway, breathing, and circulation. While the patient is unconscious, put the person in the recovery position, on their side. HC2 Most seizures Most seizures resolve spontaneously. HC3

Status epilepticus

Treatment LOC Give dextrose 50%, 1 mL/kg in adults. HC4 In children, give dextrose 10%, 5 mL/kg. HC4 Give diazepam 10 mg IV or rectally. HC4 Child: diazepam 0.05 mg/kg rectally or 0.02 mg/kg IV. Repeat dose after 5 to 10 minutes if seizures persist. HC4 If not responsive, consider phenobarbital 10 to 15 mg/kg slowly IV. Dilute the solution with 10 times its volume of water for injection and give very slowly, at a rate of 0.1 mg/minute. HC4 Monitor blood pressure and respiration. Be ready to administer IV fluids if hypotension develops and ventilate with Ambu bag if respiratory depression occurs. HC4 Alternatively, give phenytoin 15 to 18 mg/kg over 1 hour. HC4 Phenytoin can cause severe tissue damage, so use a good IV line. HC4 If still not responsive, give another medicine if available, or add phenytoin 10 mg/kg over 30 minutes. HC4 Monitor for respiratory depression. HC4

Long-term management

Treatment LOC Start with a single anti-epileptic medicine. The effective dose must be reached progressively and the patient monitored for tolerance and side effects. Aim for the lowest dose able to control, or prevent, seizures. HC3 If treatment is ineffective, meaning less than 50% reduction in seizures, try another monotherapy. Slowly reduce the current antiepileptic medicine and introduce the new one. HC3 If high doses with side effects are required and seizures are infrequent, less than complete control may be the goal. HC3 Follow up monthly until stable, then every 3 months. HC3 Warn the patient that treatment interruptions can trigger seizures or even status epilepticus. HC3 If there has been no seizure for 2 years and there is no known cause such as head trauma or infection, consider stopping treatment gradually over 2 months. Discuss this with the patient. HC3 If two monotherapy trials fail, refer to a specialist. HC3

Common anti-epileptic medicines

Medicine Use and dosing LOC Carbamazepine Effective in generalised tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures.Given twice daily. Steady state is reached in 8 days.Adult: start with 100 to 200 mg daily and increase in 100 mg increments every 1 to 2 weeks to a maintenance dose of 400 to 1400 mg daily.Child: start with 5 mg/kg/day and use a maintenance dose of 10 to 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses.Side effects include skin rash, diplopia, blurred vision, ataxia, nausea. HC4 Phenobarbital Effective for tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures, but it is sedative in adults and may cause behavioural disturbances and hyperkinesia in children. It may be tried for atypical absences, atonic seizures, and tonic seizures.Given once daily in the evening to reduce drowsiness.Adult: start with 1 mg/kg, usually 60 mg daily, for 2 weeks. If not controlled, increase to 2 mg/kg, usually 120 mg, for 2 months. If still not controlled, increase to 3 mg/kg, usually 180 mg.Child: start with 2 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks. If not controlled, increase to 3 mg/kg for 2 months. If still not controlled, increase up to a maximum of 6 mg/kg/day.It takes 2 to 3 weeks for the medicine to achieve steady blood levels, so assess effect only after this period.Side effects include drowsiness, lethargy, hyperactivity and irritability in children, skin rash, confusion in elderly patients, and depression. HC3 Phenytoin Effective in all forms of epilepsy except absences.Adult: start with 150 to 200 mg daily as a single dose or in 2 divided doses. Maintenance dose is 200 to 400 mg daily.Child: start with 3 to 4 mg/kg. Maintenance dose is 3 to 8 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg daily.Increase slowly by 25 to 30 mg every 2 weeks.Side effects include drowsiness, ataxia, slurred speech, blurred vision, twitching, confusion, gum hyperplasia, blood abnormalities, rash, and hepatitis. HC4 Ethosuximide Effective in absence seizures.Child above 6 years: initially 500 mg daily in 2 divided doses. Increase if necessary by 250 mg every 5 to 7 days, up to a usual daily dose of 1 to 1.5 g in 2 divided doses.Child 1 month to 6 years: initially 250 mg as a single dose at night. Increase gradually every 5 to 7 days as required to the usual dose of 20 to 40 mg/kg daily in 2 divided doses.Side effects include gastrointestinal disorders, blood disorders, gum hyperplasia, and drowsiness. RR

Note

In children, look for associated intellectual disability or behavioural problems.

If intellectual disability or behavioural problems are present, consider carbamazepine or valproate. Avoid phenobarbital and phenytoin, and manage the associated intellectual disability or behavioural problem.

All pregnant women with epilepsy should be referred to a specialist for appropriate management.

Health education

  • Provide health and psycho-education to patients, carers, and the community.
  • Advise on management of seizures and safety precautions.
  • In children, look for and manage associated intellectual disability or behavioural problems.

Prevention

  • Promote good antenatal care and delivery.
  • Avoid causative factors.

docs.title: 9.1.2 Nodding Disease
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: G40.4

Nodding disease is an unexplained neurological condition characterised by episodes of repetitive dropping forward of the head, often accompanied by other seizure-like activity, such as convulsions or staring spells.

The condition predominantly affects children aged 5 to 15 years and has been reported in South Sudan, especially the states of Western and Central Equatoria, northern Uganda, and southern Tanzania.

Cause

The cause is not yet certain, but a consistent association with onchocerciasis has been found.

Other associated factors include:

  • Malnutrition
  • Pyridoxine deficiency

Clinical features

  • Starts at age 5 to 7 years in a previously normal child
  • Early symptoms include problems in concentration and thinking
  • “Nodding” starts, which is a type of seizure, also called atonic seizure, often triggered by eating or cold temperatures
  • Cognitive impairment appears
  • Neurological deterioration, delayed puberty, and growth retardation progress until the child becomes mentally and physically disabled

Investigations

  • No diagnostic investigations have been identified

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Chronic epilepsy Supportive care. HC4 Chronic epilepsy Give antiepileptic medicines as above, including valproate and phenobarbital. HC4

docs.title: 9.1.3 Headache
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: R51

Headache is a common complaint and cause of disability. Pain can be of varying intensity and may affect different areas of the head.

Causes

  • Facial and frontal headache: sinusitis, eye problems, oropharyngeal disorders
  • Temporal headache: severe hypertension, stress, ear disorders, subarachnoid haemorrhage
  • Top of the head: stress, tension
  • Unilateral, or one-sided headache: migraine
  • Whole head: malaria, meningitis, severe hypertension, dehydration
  • Back of the head, occiput and neck: meningitis, malaria, refractive eye problems, neck trauma or sprain, tension

Danger signs

Sign or symptom Possible cause Recent trauma to the head Intracranial bleeding Head injury Intracranial bleeding High fever Malaria, meningitis, or other infections Acute onset, severe headache Intracranial bleeding Chronic worsening headache Tumours, hypertension Altered consciousness and/or focal neurological symptoms and/or seizure Tumour, intracranial bleeding, intracranial infection

Management

Treatment LOC Investigate and treat the cause if found or possible. HC2 If there are any danger signs, refer to hospital for further assessment. HC2 Follow the pain ladder for control of symptoms. HC2

docs.title: 9.1.3.1 Migraine
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: G43

Migraine is a periodic severe headache, usually unilateral, which may occur with or without an aura, meaning neurological warning signs. It is commonly associated with nausea and/or vomiting.

Causes

The cause is unknown, but migraine is thought to be linked to:

  • Familial factors
  • Craniovascular disorders

Migraine may be precipitated by:

  • Stress
  • Anxiety
  • Menstruation
  • Flashing lights
  • Hunger
  • Lack of sleep
  • Oestrogens, including combined oral contraceptives
  • Perfumes
  • Tyramine-containing foods, such as red wine, cheese, and chocolate

Clinical features

  • Warning signs, or aura, such as visual or sensory symptoms, including flashing lights, preceding the start of the headache
  • Migraine with warning signs is called migraine with aura, although warning signs are not always present
  • Moderate to severe episodic unilateral headache
  • Throbbing or pulsating headache
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Sensitivity to light and sound

Differential diagnosis

  • Any cause of headache
  • Conversion disorder, previously known as hysteria

Investigations

No specific investigations are needed unless another cause is suspected.

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute episode Give paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours. HC2 Acute episode Or give ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 to 8 hours. HC2 Acute episode Or give acetylsalicylic acid 300 to 900 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 4 g daily. HC2 Severe migraine, or migraine not responding to the above treatment Give diclofenac 75 mg IM. HC4 Severe migraine, or migraine not responding to the above treatment Plus metoclopramide 10 mg IM or IV for nausea and vomiting. HC4 Severe migraine, or migraine not responding to the above treatment Or give ergotamine 2 mg sublingually, then 1 to 2 mg hourly to a maximum of 6 mg in 24 hours. RR Severe migraine, or migraine not responding to the above treatment Or give sumatriptan 50 mg, repeat after 2 hours if necessary, maximum 300 mg in 24 hours. RR Prophylaxis, if there are more than 3 attacks per month and/or functional impairment Give amitriptyline 10 to 75 mg at night. HC3 Prophylaxis, if there are more than 3 attacks per month and/or functional impairment Or give propranolol 40 to 80 mg every 12 hours. HC4

Prevention

  • Avoid precipitating factors.

docs.title: 9.1.4 Dementia
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: F01, F03

Dementia is a chronic, slowly progressive organic mental disorder characterised by progressive loss of memory and cognitive function, with difficulty carrying out everyday activities.

Causes

  • Primary degeneration of the brain
  • Vascular disorders
  • Infections, such as syphilis, TB, HIV/AIDS, and meningitis
  • Metabolic disorders, such as hypothyroidism
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Vitamin B1 deficiency
  • Brain trauma, including chronic subdural haematoma and hydrocephalus
  • Toxic agents, such as carbon monoxide and alcohol

Clinical features

  • Impairment of short-term and long-term memory
  • Impaired judgement
  • Poor abstract thinking
  • Language disturbances, such as aphasia
  • Personality changes
  • Apathy or withdrawal
  • Anxiety or depression associated with failing memory
  • Aggressive behaviour
  • Wandering in later stages
  • Incontinence in later stages

Differential diagnosis

  • Normal ageing
  • Delirium
  • Chronic psychosis
  • Depression

Investigations

Investigations should be guided by history and clinical picture to establish the cause.

Recommended assessment may include:

  • Thorough physical examination
  • Neurological examination
  • Mental state examination
  • Thyroid hormone tests
  • RPR
  • Vitamin B12 levels
  • Other tests as indicated

Management

Treatment LOC Where possible, identify and treat the cause. HC2 Provide psychosocial interventions. HC2 Provide psychoeducation to family members about the illness and the importance of following a regular routine programme. HC2 Provide regular orientation information. HC2 Create an environment that supports activities of daily living. HC2 Assess for and treat other co-occurring health problems, such as depression and HIV. HC2 Give donepezil 5 mg once daily initially. Increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if appropriate. Preferably give at bedtime. H Alternatively, give memantine 10 mg once daily initially. Increase to 20 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if appropriate. Preferably give at bedtime. H If the patient is restless and agitated, give haloperidol 0.5 to 1 mg every 8 hours, with a higher dose at night if required. HC4 Alternatively, give risperidone 0.5 to 1 mg once daily, preferably at night. HC4 Adjust antipsychotic dose according to response and review regularly. Monitor for extrapyramidal side effects and treat with benzhexol 2 mg every 12 hours if necessary. HC4

Note

Donepezil and memantine only slow progression of symptoms. They do not cure dementia.

Caution

Avoid diazepam. It can lead to falls and is often not effective.

Prevention

  • Avoid and treat preventable causes.

docs.title: 9.1.5 Parkinsonism
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: G20, G21

Parkinsonism is a syndrome characterised by tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, meaning slow movement, and postural disturbances. It is due to primary degeneration or damage to particular areas of the brain, especially the basal ganglia.

Causes

Primary parkinsonism:

  • Cause is unknown

Secondary parkinsonism may be caused by:

  • Infections, such as sleeping sickness and syphilis
  • Poisoning, such as manganese and carbon monoxide
  • Medicines, such as chlorpromazine and haloperidol
  • Vascular disorders
  • Intracranial tumour
  • Trauma

Clinical features

  • Non-intentional tremor
  • Muscle rigidity
  • Slowness of voluntary movement
  • Walking with short, quick steps, also called shuffling gait
  • Vacant facial expression, also called mask face
  • Excessive salivation
  • Urinary incontinence, which may sometimes occur
  • Variable cognitive impairment

Differential diagnosis

  • Essential tremor, meaning isolated intentional tremor, usually benign
  • Thyrotoxicosis
  • Dementia
  • Depression

Investigations

  • Good history and clinical examination

Management

Treatment LOC Give levodopa-carbidopa 10/100 mg. The dose can be increased to 25/100 mg. RR Start with 1 tablet every 8 hours. Specialist-only management. RR For drug-induced parkinsonism, give benzhexol 2 to 15 mg daily in 1 to 3 divided doses. HC2 Initially give benzhexol 1 mg daily, then increase by 2 mg increments at intervals of 3 to 5 days. HC2 Usual benzhexol dose is 6 to 10 mg daily in 3 to 4 divided doses. Doses of 12 to 15 mg daily may be required. HC2

Caution

Benzhexol side effects include dry mouth, constipation, palpitations, urine retention, confusion, and agitation, especially in elderly patients.

Do not give benzhexol routinely to patients on antipsychotic medicines in the absence of Parkinson-like symptoms.

docs.title: 9.1.6 Delirium
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: F05

Delirium, also called acute confusional state, is a clinical syndrome usually with acute onset. It involves abnormalities in thought and perception and a fluctuating level of consciousness. It is caused by impaired brain function resulting from diffuse physiological change.

Causes

  • Infections, such as malaria, trypanosomiasis, syphilis, meningitis, rabies, typhoid fever, and HIV/AIDS
  • Pneumonia and urinary tract infections in elderly patients
  • Intoxication with, or withdrawal from, alcohol or other substances of dependence
  • Some medicines, such as anticonvulsants and neuropsychiatric medicines
  • Cerebral pathology, such as head trauma and tumour
  • Severe anaemia
  • Dehydration
  • Electrolyte imbalances
  • Hyperglycaemia

Clinical features

  • Acute onset of mental confusion with associated disorientation, developing within hours or a few days
  • Attention, concentration, and memory for recent events are impaired
  • Reduced ability to think coherently
  • Reasoning and problem-solving are difficult or impossible
  • Illusions and hallucinations are common
  • Symptoms tend to fluctuate
  • Patients may feel better during the day and worse at night
  • Some patients may present with reduced activity and/or movement, also called hypoactive delirium

Differential diagnosis

  • Acute psychosis

Investigations

Investigations should be guided by history and physical examination, and should aim at identifying the cause.

Note

Drug history is very important.

Suggested investigations include:

  • Complete blood count
  • Blood glucose
  • Rapid diagnostic test, where malaria is suspected
  • Renal function tests
  • Electrolytes

Management

Due to the complexity of underlying conditions, patients with acute confusional state should be referred to hospital for appropriate management and investigation.

Treatment LOC Identify and treat the cause, such as substance and alcohol use disorders, diabetes, head injury, or infections such as malaria, UTI, and pneumonia in older people. H Provide supportive treatment. H Ensure hydration. H Control fever. H Provide a safe and quiet environment. H Apply constant monitoring. H Withdraw unnecessary medicines. H Keep medicines such as sedatives and antipsychotics to the minimum necessary. H If the patient is agitated and acutely disturbed, give haloperidol 5 mg IM. Repeat after 60 minutes if necessary. H Continue with haloperidol 1.25 to 5 mg every 8 to 12 hours if needed. H Or give chlorpromazine 25 to 50 mg every 8 to 12 hours, IM or oral. H Or give trifluoperazine 5 to 10 mg every 12 hours. H

Prevention

  • Early diagnosis and treatment of the underlying cause

docs.title: 9.2.1 Anxiety
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: F40–F48

Anxiety is a normal physiological response which enables a person to take steps to deal with a threat. When anxiety is prolonged or interferes with normal functioning, it constitutes the clinical condition of an anxiety disorder.

Causes

  • Not fully understood
  • External traumatic events may trigger anxiety in predisposed people
  • Association with other mental conditions, such as depression
  • Alcohol and substance abuse

Types and clinical features

Generalised anxiety:

  • Unrealistic and excessive worry about almost everything

Panic attacks:

  • Episodes of sudden onset of intense apprehension or fear
  • Anxiety symptoms usually peak within 10 to 15 minutes
  • Symptoms resolve within a few minutes to one hour

Phobia:

  • Excessive fear of a known stimulus, object, or situation
  • Examples include animals, water, and confined spaces
  • The person consciously avoids the object or situation

Each of the above clinical types may have one or more of the following features:

  • Sleep problems
  • Mood problems
  • Concentration problems
  • Palpitations
  • Dizziness
  • Shortness of breath
  • Shakiness or tremors
  • Excessive sweating
  • Easily frightened
  • Urinary frequency, hesitancy, or urgency
  • Diarrhoea

Differential diagnosis

  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Phaeochromocytoma

Management

Treatment LOC Provide psychosocial interventions, including counselling, individual psychotherapy, or group psychotherapy. HC2 For an acute episode or intense prolonged anxiety, give benzodiazepines, such as diazepam 5 mg once or twice daily. HC4 If necessary, increase diazepam to 15 to 30 mg daily in divided doses. HC4 In elderly patients, give alprazolam 0.25 to 0.5 mg twice daily initially. If necessary, increase to 3 to 6 mg daily in divided doses. HC4 If alprazolam is not available, give half the usual adult diazepam dose. HC4 Duration of benzodiazepine therapy should be 1 to 2 weeks, tapering off to zero within 6 weeks. HC4 If response is poor, refer to a specialist. HC4 For long-term management of anxiety disorder, give fluoxetine 20 mg once daily. HC4 Or give sertraline 50 mg once daily. HC4 Continue antidepressant treatment for 4 to 6 weeks, then evaluate response. HC4

Caution

Diazepam is addictive. Abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal symptoms. Use it for short periods and gradually reduce the dose. Avoid alcohol.

Note

Diazepam is not appropriate for treating depression, phobic or obsessional states, or chronic psychoses.

Antidepressants may be useful in managing panic disorders and other anxiety disorders that require long-term treatment.

Prevention

  • Good personality development
  • Good stress management

docs.title: 9.2.2.1 Postnatal Depression
docs.text: • 9.2.2.1 Postnatal Depression Refer to section 16.6.2

docs.title: 9.2.2.2 Suicidal Behaviour / Self Harm
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: T14.91, Z91.5

Suicidal behaviour is an emergency and requires immediate attention. It refers to a conscious act of self-destruction that the individual views as the best solution to their distress. It is usually associated with feelings of hopelessness, helplessness, and conflict between survival and death.

Self-harm is a broader term referring to intentional self-injury or poisoning, which may or may not involve intent to die.

Causes and risk factors

Physical illness may increase risk, including:

  • HIV/AIDS
  • Head injury
  • Malignancy
  • Body disfigurement
  • Chronic pain

Psychiatric disorders may increase risk, including:

  • Depression
  • Chronic psychosis
  • Dementia
  • Alcohol and substance use disorders
  • Personality disorders
  • Epilepsy

Risk is high in the following situations:

  • Age above 45 years
  • Alcohol and substance use
  • Previous suicide attempt
  • Family history of suicide
  • Recent loss or disappointment
  • Current mental illness, such as depression or psychosis
  • Evidence of violent behaviour
  • Previous psychiatric admission

Risk may be lower where the patient is:

  • Below 45 years of age
  • Married or in a stable interpersonal relationship
  • Employed
  • In good physical health

Clinical features

Patients may present in one of the following situations:

  • Current suicidal behaviour or act of self-harm
  • Imminent risk of suicidal behaviour or self-harm
  • No imminent risk, but recent thoughts, plans, or previous self-harm behaviour

A situation of imminent risk may include:

  • Current thoughts or plans of suicide or self-harm
  • History of thoughts or plans of suicide or self-harm in the last 1 month
  • Acts of self-harm or suicide attempt in the last 1 year
  • Agitation, violence, emotional distress, poor communication, social isolation, or hopelessness

A situation of no imminent risk may include:

  • Thoughts or plans of suicide or self-harm in the last 1 month
  • Acts of self-harm or suicide attempt in the last 1 year, but the person is not acutely distressed

Investigations

  • Take a complete medical, social, and family history.
  • Ask the patient about suicidal or self-harm thoughts, plans, acts, and reasons.
  • Asking about self-harm or suicide does not increase the risk. It may help the patient feel understood and considered.
  • First establish a good relationship with the patient before asking.
  • Always assess risk of suicide and self-harm in patients with:
    • Depression
    • Mania
    • Psychosis
    • Alcohol and substance abuse
    • Dementia
    • Behavioural or developmental disorders
    • Chronic pain
    • Severe emotional distress

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Admit the patient and treat any medical complications. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Keep the patient in a secure and supportive environment. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Do not leave the patient alone. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Remove means of self-harm. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Provide continuous monitoring. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Offer or activate psychosocial support. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Consult a mental health specialist. HC4 Acute suicidal behaviour, act of self-harm, or imminent risk Treat any medical or mental condition present. HC4 No imminent risk Offer or activate psychosocial support. HC4 No imminent risk Refer to a mental health specialist for further assessment. HC4 No imminent risk Establish regular follow-up. HC4

Note

Suicidal behaviour is less frequent in children and adolescents, but risk is increased where there is disturbed family background, such as death of parents or divorce, use of alcohol or other drugs, physical illness, or psychiatric disorder.

docs.title: 9.2.3 Bipolar Disorder (Mania)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODES: F30, F31

Bipolar disorder is a disorder of mood control characterised by episodes in which a person's mood and activity level are significantly disturbed.

In some occasions, there is elevation of mood and increased energy and activity, called mania. In other occasions, there is lowering of mood and decreased energy and activity, called depression.

Characteristically, recovery is complete between episodes.

Causes

  • Biological factors
  • Genetic factors
  • Environmental factors

Clinical features

The patient can present in:

  • An acute manic episode
  • A depressive episode
  • Between episodes

Mania

Clinical features of mania may include:

  • Elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
  • Increased activity or subjective experience of increased energy
  • Increased talkativeness
  • Flight of ideas
  • Increased self-image, self-esteem, or grandiosity
  • Decreased need for sleep
  • Distractibility
  • Impulsive or reckless behaviour, extravagance, partying, and increased spending
  • Increased sexual drive, sociability, and goal-directed behaviour
  • Increased appetite, but weight loss may occur due to overactivity
  • Auditory and visual hallucinations may be present

Depression

Features may be as described under depression, but with a history of manic episode.

A high index of suspicion for bipolar disorder is needed in early-onset depression with a family history of bipolar illness.

Differential diagnosis

  • Organic mental state, such as drug or alcohol intoxication
  • Delirium
  • Chronic psychosis

Investigations

  • Take a good medical, social, and personal history.
  • Assess for acute state of mania.
  • If depressive symptoms are present, investigate for previous manic episodes.
  • Assess for other medical or mental conditions, including alcohol or substance abuse, dementia, suicide, and self-harm.

Patients with suspected bipolar disorder should be referred for specialist assessment.

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Manic episode Multiple symptoms as above for more than 1 week, severe enough to interfere with work, social activities, or requiring hospitalisation. HC3 / HC4 / H Manic episode Assess risk to self and others. HC3 Manic episode Discontinue antidepressant if the patient is taking any. HC3 Manic episode Provide counselling and education. HC3 Manic episode Give chlorpromazine initially 100 to 200 mg every 8 hours, then adjust according to response. HC4 Manic episode Daily doses of chlorpromazine up to 300 mg may be given as a single dose at night. HC4 Manic episode Gradually reduce chlorpromazine when symptoms of mania resolve and maintain on doses as indicated in section 9.2.4 on chronic psychosis. HC4 Manic episode Or give haloperidol initially 5 to 10 mg every 12 hours, then adjust according to response. H Manic episode Up to 30 to 40 mg daily may be required in severe or resistant cases. H Manic episode Or give olanzapine 10 to 15 mg daily initially. May adjust to 20 mg according to response. H Manic episode Or give risperidone 2 to 3 mg initially. May increase to 6 mg in one week according to response. H Specialist supervision Initiate a mood stabiliser if under specialist supervision. H Specialist supervision Carbamazepine initial dose 200 mg at night. Increase slowly to 600 to 1000 mg per day in divided doses. RR Specialist supervision Or valproate initial dose 500 mg daily. Usual maintenance dose 1000 to 2000 mg. RR Specialist supervision Or lithium 900 to 1800 mg per day in two divided doses. RR

Note

Serum lithium should be monitored 12 hours after dose, twice weekly until serum concentration and clinical condition stabilise, and every 3 months thereafter.

Increase dose as tolerated to target serum lithium concentrations of 0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L.

Monitor weight, blood pressure, pulse, lipid profile, and liver function tests. For lithium, do renal function tests, TSH, and calcium levels.

Situation Treatment LOC Agitation or restlessness Add a benzodiazepine for a short period until symptoms improve. HC2 Agitation or restlessness Diazepam 5 to 10 mg every 12 hours. HC2 Agitation or restlessness Zuclopenthixol acetate 50 to 100 mg, given 48 to 72 hours apart, if available. HC2

Note

If extrapyramidal side effects occur, such as muscle rigidity, dripping saliva, tongue protrusion, tremors, and speech difficulty, add an anticholinergic.

Benzhexol may be given initially at 2 mg every 12 hours, then reduced gradually to once daily, and eventually given 2 mg only when required.

Caution

Do not initiate lithium and valproate at lower centre level except as continuation.

Refer if there is poor response, poor adherence, pregnancy, side effects, underlying physical or mental comorbidity, or bipolar depression.

Bipolar depression

Depressive symptoms with history of manic episode, diagnosis of bipolar disorder, or high suspicion of bipolar disorder.

Treatment LOC Provide psychological support for mild depression. Otherwise refer for specialist care. RR If on olanzapine, add fluoxetine or give quetiapine alone. RR If not available, begin treatment with a mood stabiliser, such as carbamazepine or valproate. RR Provide psychoeducation and psychotherapy if available. RR In moderate or severe depression, consider treatment with an antidepressant in addition to a mood stabiliser, but under specialist supervision because of the risk of triggering a manic episode. RR

Between episodes

Indication for use of mood stabilisers to prevent both manic and depressive episodes:

  • Two or more episodes, including at least two manic episodes or one manic and one depressive episode
  • One severe manic episode involving significant risk and consequences
Treatment LOC Use valproate or carbamazepine as above, or lithium at higher levels. RR Provide psychoeducation and support. RR

Caution

Avoid mood stabilisers in pregnant women.

Use low-dose haloperidol if necessary.

Use lower doses in elderly patients.

Refer adolescents for specialist management.

Prevention

  • Information and support
  • Self-management techniques
  • Adherence to care
  • Good psychosocial support

docs.title: 9.2.4 Psychosis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: F20–F29

Psychosis is a mental condition characterised by distortions of thinking and perception, as well as inappropriate or narrowed range of emotions.

Causes

The cause is not fully known, but psychosis is associated with biological, genetic, and environmental factors.

Clinical features

Any one or more of the following may be diagnostic:

  • Delusions, meaning abnormal, fixed, false beliefs
  • Excessive and unwarranted suspicions, which may be multiple, fragmented, or bizarre
  • Disconnected ideas with vague or incoherent speech
  • Speech that is inadequate in content
  • Hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that are not witnessed by others
  • Severe behavioural abnormalities, such as agitation, disorganised behaviour, excitement, inactivity, or overactivity
  • Disturbance of emotions, such as marked apathy
  • Disconnection between reported emotions and observed affect
  • Inappropriate mood
  • Difficulty forming and sustaining relationships
  • Social withdrawal
  • Neglect of usual responsibilities

Chronic psychosis or schizophrenia is suggested by:

  • Symptoms of psychosis lasting 3 or more months
  • Deterioration in social, general, and occupational functioning

Differential diagnosis

  • Alcohol intoxication or withdrawal
  • Drug intoxication or withdrawal
  • Organic delirium
  • Dementia
  • Mood disorders

Investigations

  • Take a good social, personal, and family history.
  • Investigate for infectious diseases, such as HIV, where clinically indicated.
  • Other investigations should be guided by history and clinical findings.

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute psychosis Provide counselling and psychoeducation to the patient and carers. HC2 Acute psychosis Use antipsychotic medicines. HC4 Acute psychosis Chlorpromazine: start with 75 to 150 mg daily. Maintenance dose is 75 to 300 mg daily. Up to 1000 mg daily in divided doses may be required for severe disturbance. HC4 Acute psychosis Or haloperidol: start with 5 to 10 mg daily. Use lower doses in elderly patients. Maintenance dose is 5 to 20 mg daily in divided doses. H Acute psychosis Or olanzapine 5 to 10 mg daily. Maintenance dose is 10 to 20 mg daily. H Acute psychosis Or risperidone 2 mg initially. May increase to 8 mg daily in divided doses. NR Acute psychosis Or quetiapine 150 to 750 mg daily in two divided doses. NR Treatment-resistant schizophrenia Clozapine 25 to 50 mg daily initially. If well tolerated, titrate to 450 mg per day over 2 weeks depending on response. NR Agitation Administer antipsychotic medicine orally or IM as appropriate. HC4 General principle Use only one antipsychotic at a time. HC4 General principle Gradually adjust doses depending on response. HC4 General principle Monitor for side effects, including extrapyramidal side effects. HC4 General principle Use a therapeutic dose for 4 to 6 weeks to assess effect. HC4 General principle Provide psychological interventions, such as family therapy or social skills therapy, if available. RR General principle Ensure follow-up. RR Acute psychosis Continue treatment for at least 12 months. Discuss discontinuation with the patient, caregivers, and specialist. RR

If extrapyramidal side effects occur

Treatment LOC Add an anticholinergic medicine. Give benzhexol initially 2 mg every 12 hours, then reduce gradually to once daily, and eventually give 2 mg only when required. HC2 If there is no response, refer to a specialist. HC2

Chronic psychosis

Treat as above. If adherence is a problem, or if the patient prefers, use depot antipsychotic treatment.

Treatment LOC Fluphenazine decanoate 12.5 to 50 mg every 2 to 5 weeks by deep IM injection into the gluteal muscle. HC4 Or haloperidol oily injection 50 to 200 mg, up to 300 mg, by deep IM injection into the gluteal muscle every 3 to 4 weeks. RR Or zuclopenthixol decanoate 200 to 500 mg every 4 weeks depending on response. RR Provide psychosocial support for long-term care. RR

docs.title: 9.2.4.1 Postnatal Psychosis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: F53, Postpartum

Postnatal psychosis is a psychiatric emergency occurring after delivery.

Risk factors

  • First child
  • Previous episode of postnatal psychosis
  • Previous major psychiatric history
  • Family history of mental illness
  • Inadequate psychosocial support during pregnancy
  • Infections in the early puerperium

Clinical features

  • Symptoms usually develop within the first 2 postpartum weeks
  • Symptoms may develop as early as 48 to 72 hours after delivery
  • The condition may resemble a rapidly evolving manic or mixed episode
  • Restlessness
  • Insomnia
  • Irritability
  • Rapidly shifting depressed or elated mood
  • Disorganised behaviour
  • Delusional beliefs relating to the infant
  • Auditory hallucinations
  • High risk of harm to the mother or infant

Differential diagnosis

  • Depression with psychotic features
  • Mania
  • Chronic psychosis

Investigations

  • Good history
  • Physical assessment
  • Psychiatric assessment

Management

Treatment LOC Treat as a psychiatric emergency. Admit to hospital. H Treat any identifiable cause or precipitant, such as infection. H Give haloperidol 10 mg or chlorpromazine 200 mg by intramuscular injection or orally every 8 to 12 hours. H Monitor response to medication and adjust dosage accordingly. H If restless and agitated, add diazepam 5 to 10 mg by slow IV infusion or rectally. Repeat after 10 minutes if still agitated. H Continue diazepam tablets 5 mg every 12 hours until calm. H Refer to a specialist. H

Note

Postnatal psychoses are no different from other similar psychoses. Give concurrent psychosocial interventions and drug therapy.

Prevention

  • Proper antenatal screening
  • Good psychosocial support
  • Early detection and treatment
  • Adherence to treatment for current mental illness, such as depression, bipolar disorder, or chronic psychosis

docs.title: 9.2.5 Alcohol Use Disorders
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: F10

Alcohol use disorders are conditions resulting from different patterns of alcohol consumption, including acute alcohol intoxication, harmful alcohol use, alcohol dependence syndrome, and alcohol withdrawal state.

Causes

  • No single cause is usually identified.
  • A combination of factors usually leads to alcohol use disorders.

Risk / predisposing factors

  • Genetic factors
  • Social and environmental factors, including availability
  • Stress and peer pressure
  • Personality disorders

Clinical features

Acute intoxication

Acute intoxication is a transient condition following intake of alcohol, resulting in disturbances of:

  • Consciousness
  • Cognition
  • Perception
  • Affect
  • Behaviour

Harmful alcohol use

Harmful alcohol use is a pattern of alcohol consumption that is causing damage to health, either physical, such as liver disease, or mental, such as depressive disorder.

It may also cause problems in the person's social, occupational, or other important areas of life.

Criteria include:

  • More than five drinks on any given occasion in the last 12 months
  • More than two drinks per day
  • Drinking every day
  • The patient consumes more alcohol than recommended but does not yet meet criteria for alcohol dependence

Caution

Alcohol consumption during pregnancy is extremely harmful to the baby. It can cause foetal harm.

Alcohol dependence

Alcohol dependence is a disorder characterised by the need to take large daily amounts of alcohol for adequate functioning. Alcohol use becomes a much higher priority for the individual than other behaviours that once had greater value.

Complications may include:

  • Malnutrition
  • Thiamine deficiency, causing Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Liver disease
  • Chronic pancreatitis
  • Peptic ulcer
  • Cardiomyopathy
  • Neuropathy
  • Head trauma

Alcohol withdrawal

Alcohol withdrawal symptoms occur after stopping alcohol following prolonged daily use. Symptoms may occur from 6 hours to 6 days after stopping alcohol.

Symptoms include:

  • Tremor in hands
  • Sweating
  • Vomiting
  • Tachycardia
  • Hypertension
  • Agitation
  • Anxiety
  • Headache
  • Seizure
  • Confusion in severe cases

Diagnostic criteria for alcohol dependence

If three or more of the following features are present, alcohol dependence is likely:

  • A strong desire to take alcohol
  • Difficulty controlling alcohol use in terms of onset, termination, or levels of use
  • A physiological withdrawal state when alcohol use has ceased or reduced
  • Evidence of tolerance, where increased doses of alcohol are required to achieve effects originally produced by lower doses
  • Progressive neglect of alternative pleasures or interests because of alcohol use
  • Alcohol use persists despite clear evidence of harmful consequences, such as liver damage, depression, cognitive impairment, loss of job, friends, or relationships

Differential diagnosis

  • Abuse of other psychoactive substances
  • Depression
  • Chronic psychosis, often co-existing

Investigations

  • Complete blood count
  • Liver enzymes
  • Social investigations

Blood tests may show:

  • Elevated mean cell volume (MCV)
  • Elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute intoxication, withdrawal, and Wernicke encephalopathy See section 1.3.12. Harmful alcohol consumption Provide counselling and advice. HC3 Harmful alcohol consumption Investigate and treat concurrent medical or psychiatric illness, such as dementia, depression, anxiety, psychosis, or seizures. HC3 Harmful alcohol consumption Follow up and refer if the patient does not improve. HC3 Alcohol dependence Provide counselling and education to the patient. HC4 Alcohol dependence Assess and manage concurrent medical and mental conditions. HC4 Alcohol dependence Advise thiamine 100 mg daily for at least 2 weeks. HC4 Alcohol dependence If the patient is willing to stop, facilitate alcohol cessation. RR Alcohol dependence Determine the appropriate setting, refer for detoxification, and treat withdrawal symptoms with diazepam. RR Detoxification Detoxification should only be undertaken within inpatient settings. HC4 Detoxification Consider referral to self-help groups, such as AA groups. RR Detoxification Counsel the family and provide psychosocial interventions if available. RR

Prevention

  • Provide health education on the dangers of alcohol abuse.
  • Reduce accessibility to alcohol.

docs.text:

Periodic severe headache, usually unilateral, which may occur with or without an aura (neurological warning signs) and associated with nausea and/or vomiting

Causes The cause is unknown but thought to be linked to:

  • Familial factors

  • Craniovascular disorders, which can be precipitated by: stress, anxiety, menstruation, flashing lights, hunger, lack of sleep, oestrogens (in COC), perfumes, tyramine- containing foods e.g. red wine, cheese, chocolate

  • Clinical features

  • Warning signs (aura): visual or sensory sympotms (flashing

lights) preceeding the start of the headache

  • Migraine with warning signs is called migraine with aura. They are not always present

  • Moderate to severe episodic unilateral headache throbbing

(pulsating)

  • Nausea and vomiting, sensitivity to light and sound Differential diagnosis

  • Any cause of headache

  • Conversion disorder (hysteria)

Investigations  No specific investigations needed except if another cause is

suspected

A chronic slowly progressive organic mental disorder characterised by progressive loss of memory and cognitive function, with difficulty in carrying out everyday activities.

Causes

  • Vascular disorders

  • Brain trauma (chronic subdural haematoma, hydrocepha-

lus)

  • Impairment of short and long-term memory

  • Language disturbances (aphasia)

may have associated anxiety or depression because of failing memory, may become aggressive

9.1.3 Childhood Behavioural Disorders ICD10 CODE: F90-F98
docs.text:
A general term including more specific disorders such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and other behavioural disorders. Only children and adolescents with moderate to severe degree of psychological, social, educational or occupational impairment should be

diagnosed as having behavioural disorders. In some children the problem persists into adulthood.

Investigate if the child’s behavior is a reaction to trauma and/or fear (child is bullied or harmed at home or outside home). In this case, it is NOT a behavioral disorder; The bullying, and or Abuse must STOP’!

Causes

  • Genetic

  • Depression

  • Medical conditions, alcohol or drug use

  • Reaction to fear or trauma Clinical features

  • Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

  • Impaired attention (breaking off from tasks and leaving ac-

tivities unfinished) so severe as to affect normal functioning and learning

  • Excessive restlessness, overactivity especially in situations

requiring calm, talkativeness, fidgeting

  • Of early onset (<6 years) and lasting >6 months

  • Other behavioural disorders

  • Unusually frequent and severe tantrums, persistent severe

disobedience

  • Repetitive and persistent pattern of dissocial, aggressive or defiant conduct (bullying, cruelty to animals, destructiveness, fire setting etc.), more severe than ordinary mischief, not only in response to severe family or social stressors, and lasting >six months

Differential diagnosis

 Depression, psychosis  Epilepsy, developmental disorders  Medical conditions e.g. .hyperthyroidism

Management

TREATMENT LOC Family psychoeducation and counsellingParent skill trainingContact teachers, advise and plan for special needs educationPsychosocial interventions if available HC4 Support to familyRefer to specialist for further management For ADHD not improving with above interventionsConsider methylphenidate under specialist supervision RR

Parkinsonism

ICD10 CODE: G20, G21

A broad spectrum of disorders with childhood onset, characterized by impairment or delay in functions related to central nervous system maturation, and with a steady course rather than remissions and relapses as in other mental illnesses. They include intellectual disability/mental retardation as well as pervasive developmental disorders such as autism.

Causes

  • May not be known

  • Nutritional deficiencies e.g. iodine deficiencies

  • Medical conditions

  • Alcohol use during pregnancy

  • Risk factors: maternal depression, infections in pregnancy Clinical features

9.1 NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS
docs.text:
9.1.1

Epilepsy

ICD10 CODE: G40

  • A chronic condition characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures. Seizures are caused by abnormal discharges in the brain and present in two different forms: convulsive and non-convulsive forms.

  • Convulsive epilepsy has features such as sudden muscle contraction, causing the person to fall and lie rigidly, followed by the muscles alternating between relaxation and rigidity with or without loss of bowel or bladder control

  • Non-convulsive epilepsy has features such as change in awareness, behaviour, emotions or senses (such as taste, smell, vision or hearing) similar to mental health conditions, so may be confused with them

  • Consider a diagnosis of epilepsy if a person has had at least 2 seizures in the last calendar year on two different days.

  • Seizures during an acute event (e.g. meningitis, acute traumatic brain injury) are not epilepsy.

Causes

  • Genetic, congenital malformation, birth asphyxia, brain

tumour

  • Brain infections, cysticercosis, trauma (acute or in the past)

  • Metabolic disorders

  • In some cases, no specific causes can be identified.

Clinical features

  • Depending on the type of epilepsy:
TYPE OF EPILEPSY DESCRIPTION Generalized epilepsy Seizure involves whole brain, consciousness is lost at the onset Tonic Clonic (grandmal) or convulsive epilepsy May commence with a warning sensation in the form of sound, light or abdominal pain (aura) There may be a sharp cry followed by loss of consciousness and fallingTonic contraction (rigidity) of muscles occurs followed by jerking movements (clonic phase) There may be incontinence of urine or faeces, frothing, and tongue bitingA period of deep sleep follows Absence seizures (petit mal) Mainly a disorder of childrenThe attack is characterized by a brief loss of consciousness (5-10 seconds) in which posture is retained but other activities ceaseThe child has a vacant starePrevious activities are resumed at the end of the attackSeveral attacks may occur in a single day Atonic or tonic seizures (drop attacks) Sudden loss of muscular tone, of brief duration (15 seconds), with consciousness maintained orSudden stiffening of muscle Myoclonus epilepsy Abnormal jerking movements occurring usually in the limbs but may involve the whole body TYPE OF EPILEPSY DESCRIPTION Focal Epilepsy Seizure activity starts in one area of the brain Simple Patient remains alert but has abnormal sensory, motor, psychic or autonomic manifestation e.g. jerking of a limb, déjà vu, nausea, strange taste or smell, signs of autonomic nerve dysfunctioni.e. sweating, flushing, and gastric sensation, motor contraction or sensory change in a particular point of the body) Complex Altered awareness and behaviour e.g. confusion, repetitive movements Status epilepticus A convulsive state in which the convulsions last >30 minutes or several epileptic convulsions occur in succession without recovery of consciousness in between or convulsions not responsive to 2 doses of diazepam. It is a medical emergency.

Differential diagnosis

 Syncope (fainting),  Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar)  Hypocalcaemia (low blood calcium levels)  Conversion disorder (previously known as hysteria)  Hyperventilation (fast breathing) and Panic attacks Investigations

 A complete medical and mental health assessment  Electroencephalogram (EEG)

    • Useful in petit mal and focal seizures
    • To be done at specialist level (RR and NR)

 Other investigations are guided by suspected cause

General principles

  • All suspected cases of non-convulsive epilepsy should be

confirmed and treated by a specialist

  • Convulsive epilepsy can be diagnosed at hospital/HC3

  • level but drug refills should be available at lower levels

  • One brief isolated seizure does not need further treatment

but review at 3 months and re-assessment. Treat patients with repeated episodes as per definition

  • Treatment can effectively control epilepsy in most cases

  • Treatment should include psychological and social support

  • Start with a single anti-epileptic medicine

  • Start with low doses and increase gradually according to

response

  • If a patient has been seizure free for 2 years, consider grad-

ual stopping of medication Commonly used antiepileptics include:

  • Generalized tonic-clonic seizures

  • •Children <2 years: phenobarbital or carbamazepine

  • •Children >2 years: carbamazepine or valproate

  • Absence seizures: Valproate or ethosuximide

  • Caution: Avoid phenobarbital and phenytoin in children

with intellectual disability and/or behavioural problems Management

TREATMENT LOC First aid for acute seizureDO NOT RESTRAIN or put anything in the mouthProtect person from injury: make sure they are in a safe place away from fire or other things that might injure them HC2 TREATMENT LOC DO NOT leave patient alone. Seek help if possibleAfter the crisis, check airway, breathing and circulation and, while unconscious, put the person in recovery position (on their side) HC2 Most seizures resolve spontaneously. HC3 Status epilepticusDextrose 50% 1 mL/kg adults and Dextrose 10%Give diazepam 10 mg IV or rectal 5 mL/kg children- Child: 0.05 mg/kg rectally, 0.02 mg/kg IV repeat dose after 5-10 min if seizures persist If not responsive, considerPhenobarbital 10-15 mg/kg slowly IV. Dilute the solution with 10 times its volume of water forinjections and give VERY SLOWLY (at a rate 0.1 mg/minute)- Monitor BP and respiration, be ready to administer IV fluids if hypotension develops and ventilate with Ambu bag in case of respiratory depressionOr phenytoin 15-18 mg/kg over 1 hourPhenytoin can cause severe tissue damage so use a good IV line If not responsiveGive another drug (if available) or add phenytoin 10 mg/kg in 30 minutes- Monitor for respiratory depression TREATMENT LOC General principlesStart with a single anti-epileptic medicine. The effective dose must be reached progressively and patient monitored for tolerance and side effects. Aim at the lowest dose able to control (prevent) the seizuresIf treatment is ineffective (less than 50% reduction in crisis) try another monotherapy (slowly reduce the current antiepileptic and introduce the new one)If high doses with side effects are required and seizures are anyway infrequent, less than complete control can be the goalFollow up monthly until stable, then every 3 monthsWarn patient that treatment interruptions can trigger seizures or even status epilepticusIf no seizure for 2 years and no known cause like head trauma or infection, consider possibility of stopping treatment (over 2 months). Discuss with the patientIf 2 monotherapy trials fail, refer to specialist HC3 Carbamazepine Effective in all generalized tonic-clonic seizures, focal seizures- Given twice daily, steady state reached in 8 days- Adult: starting dose of 100-200 mg daily and increased in 100 mg increments every 1-2 weeks to a maintenance dose of 400 to 1400 mg daily- Child: starting dose of 5 mg/kg/day and maintenance dose of 10-20 mg/kg/day in divided dosesSide effects: skin rash, diplopia, blurred vision, ataxia (staggering gait), nausea HC4 TREATMENT LOC PhenobarbitalEffective for tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures but is sedative in adults and cause behavioural disturbances and hyperkinesia in children. It may be tried for atypical absences, atonic and tonic seizures- Given once a day in the evening to reduce drowsiness- Adult: starting dose of 1 mg/kg (60 mg) daily for 2- weeks, if not controlled increase to 2 mg/kg (120 mg) for 2 months, if not controlled increase to 3 mg/kg (180 mg)- Child: starting dose of 2 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks,if- not controlled increase to 3 mg/kg for 2 months, if not controlled increase until maximum of 6 mg/ kg/day- It takes 2-3 weeks for the drug to achieve steady blood levels so assess effect only after this periodSide effects: drowsiness, lethargy, hyperactivity and irritability in children, skin rash, confusion in elderly, depression HC3 Phenytoin Effective in all forms of epilepsy except absences.- Adult: starting dose of 150-200 mg daily as single dose or 2 divided doses and maintenance dose of 200-400 mg daily- Child: starting dose of 3-4 mg/kg and- maintenance dose of 3-8 mg/kg/day (max 300 mg daily)- Increase slowly by 25-30 mg every 2 weeksSide effects: drowsiness, ataxia, slurred speech, blurred vision, twitching, confusion, gum hyperplasia, blood abnormalities, rash, hepatitis TREATMENT LOC Ethosuximide Effective in absence seizures.- Child >6 years: initially 500 mg daily in 2 divided doses, increase if necessary by 250 mg every 5-7 days up to a usual daily dose of 1-1.5 g in 2 divided doses- Child 1 month to 6 years: Initially 250 mg single- dose at night increased gradually every 5-7 days as required to usual dose of 20 to 40 mg/kg daily in 2 divided dosesSide effects: gastrointestinal disorders, blood disorders, gum hyperplasia, drowsiness RR Note In children, look for presence of associated intellectual disability or behavioural problems. If present, consider carbamazepine or valproate. (avoid phenobarbital and phenytoin) and manage associated intellectual disability or behavioural problem All pregnant women with epilepsy should be referred to specialist for appropriate management (most Note In children, look for presence of associated intellectual disability or behavioural problems. If present, consider carbamazepine or valproate. (avoid phenobarbital and phenytoin) and manage associated intellectual disability or behavioural problem All pregnant women with epilepsy should be referred to specialist for appropriate management (most

Health education

  • Health/psycho-education to patients, carers and commu-

nity

  • Advice on management of seizures and safety precautions

  • In children, look for and manage presence of associated

intellectual disability or behavioural problems Prevention

  • Good antenatal care and delivery

  • Avoid causative factors

9.2.2.2 Suicidal Behaviour/Self Harm ICD10 CODES: T14.91, Z91.5
docs.text:
Causes/risk factors Physical illness e.g. HIV/AIDS, head injury, malignancies, body disfigurement, chronic pain

Psychiatric disorders e.g. depression, chronic psychosis, dementia, alcohol and substance use disorders, personality disorders, epilepsy

Risk is high in the following cases:

Patient >45 years old

Alcohol and substance use

History of suicide attempts

Family history of suicide

History of recent loss or disappointment

Current mental illness e.g. depression, psychosis

Evidence of violent behaviour or previous psychiatric admi sion

Risk may be low if patient is

<45 years old

Married or in stable interpersonal relationships

Employed

In good physical health

CHAPTER 9: Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders

Clinical features

Patients can present in one of the following situations:

A current suicide attempt or self harm

A situation of imminent risk of suicidal attempt or self harm:

  • Current thoughts or plans of suicide/self harm or history of

thoughts or plans of suicide/self harm in the last 1 month, or acts of self harm/suicide attempts in the last 1 years plus

  • Person is agitated, violent, emotionally distressed or uncommunicative and socially isolated, hopeless

A situation of no imminent risk but

  • Thoughts or plans of suicide/self harm in the last 1 month CHAPTER 9: Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders

or acts of self/harm/suicide attempt in the last one year in person not acutely distressed

Investigations  Complete medical, social and family history  Ask the patient about suicidal or self harm thoughts/plans/ acts

and reasons for it  Asking about self harm or suicide does not increase the risk of

those acts. On the contrary, it may help the patient to feel understood and considered. First try to establish a good relationship with the patient before asking  Always assess risk of suicide and self-harm in patient  With any other mental illness (depression, mania, psychosis, alcohol and substance abuse, dementia, behavioural or development disorders)  Chronic pain, severe emotional distress

TREATMENT

LOC

If acute suicidal behaviour/act of self harm or imminent risk Admit the patient and treat any medical complications (bleeding, poisoning etc.) Keep in a secure and supportive environment – Do not leave patient alone – Remove any means of self-harm Continuous monitoring Offer/activate psychosocial support Consult mental health specialist Treat any medical and mental condition present

HC4

Note

 Suicide is less frequent in children and adolescents, but there is increased risk if there is disturbed family background (e.g. death of parents, divorce), use of alcohol and other drugs of abuse, physical illness, psychiatric disorder

9.2.3

Bipolar Disorder (Mania)

ICD10 CODE: F30, F31

Suicidal behaviour is an emergency and requires immediate attention. It is an attempted conscious act of self-destruction, which the individual concerned views as the best solution. It is usually associated with feelings of hopelessness, helplessness and conflicts between survival and death.

Self-harm is a broader term referring to intentional poisoning or self-inflicted harm, which may or may not have an intent of fatal outcome.

Causes/risk factors

  • Physical illness e.g. HIV/AIDS, head injury, malignancies,

body disfigurement, chronic pain

  • Psychiatric disorders e.g. depression, chronic psychosis, dementia, alcohol and substance use disorders, personality disorders, epilepsy

Risk is high in the following cases:

  • Patient >45 years old

  • Alcohol and substance use

  • History of suicide attempts

  • Family history of suicide

  • History of recent loss or disappointment

  • Current mental illness e.g. depression, psychosis

  • Evidence of violent behaviour or previous psychiatric admi

sion Risk may be low if patient is

  • <45 years old

  • Married or in stable interpersonal relationships

  • Employed

  • In good physical health

Clinical features Patients can present in one of the following situations:

  • A current suicide attempt or self harm

  • A situation of imminent risk of suicidal attempt or self harm:

    • Current thoughts or plans of suicide/self harm or history of thoughts or plans of suicide/self harm in the last 1 month, or acts of self harm/suicide attempts in the last 1 years plus
    • Person is agitated, violent, emotionally distressed or uncommunicative and socially isolated, hopeless

  • A situation of no imminent risk but

  • Thoughts or plans of suicide/self harm in the last 1 month or acts of self/harm/suicide attempt in the last one year in person not acutely distressed

Investigations

 Complete medical, social and family history  Ask the patient about suicidal or self harm thoughts/plans/ acts

and reasons for it

 Asking about self harm or suicide does not increase the risk of those acts. On the contrary, it may help the patient to feel understood and considered. First try to establish a good relationship with the patient before asking

 Always assess risk of suicide and self-harm in patient  With any other mental illness (depression, mania, psychosis,

alcohol and substance abuse, dementia, behavioural or development disorders)

 Chronic pain, severe emotional distress

Management

TREATMENT LOC If acute suicidal behaviour/act of self harm or imminent riskAdmit the patient and treat any medical complications (bleeding, poisoning etc.)Keep in a secure and supportive environment– Do not leave patient alone– Remove any means of self-harmContinuous monitoringOffer/activate psychosocial supportConsult mental health specialistTreat any medical and mental condition present HC4 If no imminent riskOffer/activate psychosocial supportRefer to mental health specialist for further assessmentEstablish regular follow up Note Suicide is less frequent in children and adolescents, but there is increased risk if there is disturbed family background (e.g. death of parents, divorce), use of alcohol and other drugs of abuse, physical illness, psychiatric disorder Note Suicide is less frequent in children and adolescents, but there is increased risk if there is disturbed family background (e.g. death of parents, divorce), use of alcohol and other drugs of abuse, physical illness, psychiatric disorder

9.2.4.1 Postnatal Psychosis
docs.text:
RR

ICD10 CODE: F53 Postpartum

  • First child

  • Previous episode of post-natal psychosis

  • Previous major psychiatric history

  • Family history of mental illness

  • Inadequate psychosocial support during pregnancy

  • Infections in early puerperium Clinical features

  • Symptoms develop within the first 2 postpartum weeks

(sometimes as early as 48-72 hours after delivery)

  • The condition resembles a rapidly evolving manic or mixed episode with symptoms such as restlessness and insomnia, irritability, rapidly shifting depressed or elated mood and disorganized behavior

  • The mother may have delusional beliefs that relate to the infant (e.g. the baby is defective or dying, the infant is

  • Satan or God) or she may have auditory hallucinations

that instruct her to harm herself or her infant

  • The risk for infanticide and suicide is high Differential diagnosis

  • Depression with psychotic features

  • Mania, chronic psychosis Investigations

Good history, physical and psychiatric assessment

Management

TREATMENT LOC It is a psychiatric emergency: admit to hospitalTreat any identifiable cause/precipitant e.g. infectionHaloperidol 10 mg or Chlorpromazine 200 mg [Intramuscular Injection or tablets} every 8 or 12 hours. Monitor response to medication and adjust dosage accordinglyIf restless and agitated, add rectal or I.V H TREATMENT LOC Diazepam 5-10 mg slow infusion; repeat after 10 minutes if still agitated- Continue with diazepam tablet 5 mg every 12 hours until calmRefer to specialist H

Notes

 Post-natal psychoses are no different from other similar psychoses, give concurrent psychosocial interventions and drug therapy

Prevention

  • Proper antenatal screening, good psychosocial support

  • Early detection and treatment

  • Adherence to treatment for a current mental illness e.g de-

pression, bipolar, chronic psychosis

9.2.4 Psychosis ICD10 CODE: F20-F29
docs.text:
A mental condition characterized by distortions of thinking and perception, as well as inappropriate or narrowed range of emotions.

Causes

  • Not known, but there are associated biological, genetic and

environmental factors

Clinical features Any one or more of these may be diagnostic:

  • Delusions (abnormal, fixed, false beliefs) or excessive and

unwarranted suspicions (may be multiple, fragmented or bizarre)

  • Disconnected ideas with vague or incoherent speech and inadequate in content

  • Hallucinations: hearing voices or seeing things that are not witnessed by others

  • Severe behaviour abnormalities: agitation or disorganised behaviour, excitement, inactivity or overactivity

  • Disturbance of emotions such as marked apathy or discon-

nection between reported emotions and observed effect

  • Mood is usually inappropriate

  • Difficulty in forming and sustaining relationships

  • Social withdrawal and neglect of usual responsibilities Chronic psychosis or schizophrenia

  • Symptoms of psychosis lasting for 3 or more months

  • Accompanied by deterioration in social, general and occu-

pational functioning Differential diagnosis

  • Alcohol and drug intoxication or withdrawal

  • Organic delirium, dementia, mood disorders Investigations

 Good social, personal and family history  Laboratory investigations for infectious diseases e.g. HIV,

Management Management TREATMENT LOC - Acute psychosisCounselling/psychoeducation of patient and carers- Antipsychotic drugsChlorpromazine: starting dose 75-150 mg daily and maintenance dose of 75-300 mg daily. Up to 1000 mg daily in divided does may be required for those with severe disturbanceOr Haloperidol: starting dose 5-10 mg daily- (Lower in elderly) and maintenance dose of 5-20 mg daily in divided doses- Or Olanzapine 5-10 mg daily, maintenance dose is 10-20mg/day- Or Risperidone 2 mg initially, may increase to 8 mg/day in divided.- Or Quetiapine 150-750mg/day twice daily- Or For treatment resistant schizophrenia, Clozapine 25-50mg/day initially, if well tolerated titrate to 450mg per day in two weeks depending on response HC2HC4HHNRNR Administer orally or IM for those with agitationOnly use one antipsychotic at a timeGradually adjust doses depending on responseMonitor for side effects e.g. extrapyramidal side effectsUse therapeutic dose for 4-6 weeks to assess effectPsychological interventions (family therapy or social skills therapy) if availableEnsure follow upFor acute psychosis, continue treatment for at least 12 months. Discuss discontinuation with patient, carergivers and specialist RR TREATMENT LOC If extrapyramidal side-effectsAdd an anticholinergic: Benzhexol initially 2 mg every 12 hours then reduce gradually to once daily and eventually give 2 mg only when required If no responseRefer to specialist HC2 Chronic psychosis Treat as above, but if adherence is a problem or the patient prefers, use:Fluphenazine decanoate 12.5-50 mg every 2-5 weeks deep IM into gluteal muscleOr Haloperidol injection (oily) 50-200 mg (300 mg) deep IM into gluteal muscle every 3-4 weeks OR Zuclopenthixol decanoate 200-500mg every 4 weeks depending on response Psychosocial support for long term care HC4RR

9.2 PSYCHIATRIC AND SUBSTANCE USE DISORDERS
docs.text:
9.2.1

Anxiety

ICD10 CODE: F40-F48

Anxiety is a normal physiological response, which enables a person to take steps to deal with a threat. When anxiety is prolonged or interferes with normal functions of the

individual, it constitutes the clinical condition of an anxiety disorder. Causes

  • Not fully understood: possibly external traumatic events

may trigger anxiety in predisposed people

  • Association with other mental conditions e.g. depression, alcohol and substance abuse

Types and clinical features

  • Generalized anxiety: Unrealistic and excessive worry

about almost everything

  • Panic attacks: Episodes of sudden onset of intense apprehension or fear; anxiety symptoms usually peak within 10-15 minutes and resolve in a few minutes to one hour

  • Phobia: An excessive fear of a known stimulus (object or

  • situation) e.g. animals, water, confined space) causing the

person to consciously avoid the object or situation

Each of the above clinical types will have one or more of the following manifestations:

  • Sleep, mood and concentration problems

  • Palpitations, dizziness, shortness of breath

  • Shakiness or tremors, excessive sweatiness

  • Easily frightened

  • Other symptoms: urinary frequency, hesitancy, or urgen-

cy, diarrhoea

Differential diagnosis

  • Consider organic conditions e.g. hyperthyroidism, hypo-

glycaemia, phaeochromocytoma

Management

TREATMENT LOC Psychosocial interventions: counselling, psychotherapy (individual and group psychotherapy) For an acute episode or intense prolonged anxietyBenzodiazepines e.g. diazepam 5 mg 1-2 times daily- Increase if necessary to 15-30 mg daily individed doses Elderly: Alprazolam 0.25mg -0.5mg twice daily initially, Increase if necessary to 3-6 mg daily in divided doses. If alprazolam is not available, Give half the above dose of diazepam HC2HC4 TREATMENT LOC - Duration of therapy 1-2 weeks, tapering off to zero within 6 weeksIf poor response: refer to specialistFluoxetine 20 mg once a day for long term management of the anxiety disorder Or Sertraline 50mg once daily- Continue antidepressant for 4 to 6 weeks then evaluate the response HC2HC4 CautionDiazepam is addictive and abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal symptoms. Use for short periods and gradually reduce the dose. Avoid alcohol CautionDiazepam is addictive and abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal symptoms. Use for short periods and gradually reduce the dose. Avoid alcohol Notes Diazepam is NOT appropriate for treating depression, phobic or obsessional states, or chronic psychoses (see relevant sections for more information) Antidepressants: May be useful in managing panic disorders and other anxiety disorders which require long term treatment Notes Diazepam is NOT appropriate for treating depression, phobic or obsessional states, or chronic psychoses (see relevant sections for more information) Antidepressants: May be useful in managing panic disorders and other anxiety disorders which require long term treatment

Prevention

  • Good personality development

  • Good stress management
