Chapter 9: Mental, Neurological and Substance Use Disorders
docs.text:
This chapter covers neurological disorders, psychiatric conditions, and substance use disorders. It includes epilepsy, nodding disease, headache, migraine, dementia, parkinsonism, delirium, anxiety, depression, postnatal depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, alcohol use disorders, substance abuse, childhood behavioural disorders, and childhood developmental disorders.

Use this chapter to support recognition, initial management, counselling, follow-up, and referral for mental, neurological, and substance use conditions.

Digital navigation note

This chapter landing page was added to improve navigation in the digital version of the Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023. It provides orientation only and does not replace the detailed clinical guidance in the chapter sections.

docs.title: 10.1.1 Pyogenic Arthritis (Septic Arthritis)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: M00

Pyogenic arthritis, also called septic arthritis, is an acute infection of a single joint, usually a large joint, and commonly affects children.

Causes

  • Usually haematogenous spread from a primary focus following bacteraemia, such as:
    • Septic skin lesions
    • Sinus infections
    • Throat infections
    • Abrasions
    • Wounds
    • Pressure sores
    • Osteomyelitis
  • Common organisms in acute arthritis include:
    • Staphylococcus aureus
    • Gram-negative bacilli, such as Salmonella species
    • Streptococcus species
    • Gonococcus
  • Chronic septic arthritis may be caused by:
    • Brucella
    • Tuberculosis

Clinical features

  • Swollen and warm joint
  • Severe pain
  • Reduced or abolished movement
  • Temporary loss of limb function, also called pseudoparalysis
  • Localised heat and tenderness
  • Systemic symptoms, including fever and general malaise
  • Neonates may not show fever but may refuse to feed
  • Irreversible joint damage may occur if immediate treatment is not established

Differential diagnosis

  • Inflammatory joint disease
  • Intra-articular haemorrhage, such as haemophilia and other bleeding disorders
  • Trauma
  • Osteomyelitis of neighbouring bone

Investigations

  • Full blood count
  • Blood culture and sensitivity
  • ESR, usually elevated
  • Joint fluid aspiration for culture and sensitivity
  • Joint fluid Gram stain
  • If aspiration fails to obtain pus, use arthrotomy in theatre

Management

Treatment LOC Provide pain relief, such as paracetamol or ibuprofen. HC2 Immobilise the involved limb and try splinting. HC2 Refer urgently to HC4 or hospital. HC2 Aspirate articular fluid for Gram stain and culture and sensitivity, if available. Use local skin and subcutaneous anaesthesia if indicated. HC4 Repeat aspiration daily until no further pus is obtained. HC4 Use diazepam 2.5 mg rectally for sedation in children, if required. HC4 Alternatively, perform open drainage in theatre. RR Continue pain relief with paracetamol or ibuprofen. HC4 Alternatively, give diclofenac 50 mg every 8 hours. HC4 Child: diclofenac 0.32 mg/kg rectally every 6 to 8 hours, maximum 150 mg. HC4 Alternatively, give indomethacin 25 to 50 mg every 8 hours. HC4 Child: indomethacin 0.5 to 1 mg/kg every 12 hours. HC4

Antibiotic treatment

If possible, antibiotic treatment should be guided by Gram stain and culture and sensitivity results.

Situation Treatment LOC Gram-positive organisms on Gram stain, or negative Gram stain in an immunocompetent adult patient Give cloxacillin 500 mg to 1 g IV every 6 hours. HC4 Gram-positive organisms on Gram stain, or negative Gram stain in an immunocompetent adult patient Child: cloxacillin 50 mg/kg IV every 6 hours. HC4 Gram-positive organisms on Gram stain, or negative Gram stain in an immunocompetent adult patient Give IV treatment for 2 weeks, then if improving, switch to oral treatment to complete 4 weeks. HC4 Alternative or second-line treatment Give chloramphenicol 500 mg IV every 6 hours for at least 2 weeks. HC4 Alternative or second-line treatment Child: chloramphenicol 12.5 mg/kg every 6 hours. HC4 Gram-negative organisms on Gram stain Give ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for 2 to 4 weeks. HC4 Alternative for Gram-negative infection Give ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 weeks. HC4 Negative Gram stain in adults with underlying conditions, such as suspected Salmonella in sickle cell disease, all children with negative Gram stain, or patients with underlying conditions Give cloxacillin plus ceftriaxone. HC4 Suspected gonococcal infection, such as in sexually active adolescents Give ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for 1 week. HC4

docs.title: 10.1.2 Osteomyelitis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: M86

Osteomyelitis is infection of bone by pus-forming bacteria. It mainly affects older children and adults.

Causes

  • Any type of bacterium, but most commonly Staphylococcus aureus
  • Infection may follow infection elsewhere in the body
  • Sickle cell disease is a risk factor
  • In sickle cell disease, the causative agent is mostly Staphylococcus aureus, although Salmonella is also common

Clinical features

Acute osteomyelitis

  • Onset is usually over several days
  • Fever, usually high, but may be absent, especially in neonates
  • Severe pain
  • Tenderness and increased heat at the site of infection
  • Swelling of the surrounding tissues and joint
  • Reduced or complete loss of use of the affected limb
  • The patient is usually a child aged 4 years or above with reduced immunity, but adults may also be affected
  • A history of injury may be given and may be misleading, especially if there is no fever

Chronic osteomyelitis

  • May present with pain, erythema, or swelling
  • May be associated with a draining sinus tract
  • Deep or extensive ulcers that fail to heal after several weeks of appropriate ulcer care should raise suspicion of chronic osteomyelitis
  • Non-healing fractures should also raise suspicion of chronic osteomyelitis

Differential diagnosis

  • Infection of joints
  • Limb trauma or fracture, especially in children
  • Bone cancer, such as osteosarcoma around the knee
  • Pyomyositis
  • Cellulitis
  • Sickle-cell disease thrombotic crisis

Investigations

X-ray may show:

  • No abnormality in the first 1 to 2 weeks
  • Loss of bone density, or rarefaction, at about 2 weeks
  • A thin white line on the surface of the infected part of the bone, suggesting periosteal reaction
  • Later, a piece of dead bone, or sequestrum

Other investigations:

  • Complete blood count
  • ESR
  • Blood culture and sensitivity
  • ZN stain, GeneXpert, and culture if the lesion is suspicious
  • Calcofluor stain for fungus

Management

Patients with suspected osteomyelitis need to be referred to hospital for appropriate management.

Treatment LOC Immobilise and splint the limb. HC3 Provide pain and fever relief with paracetamol or ibuprofen. HC3 Refer urgently to hospital. HC3 Admit and elevate the affected limb. H Give cloxacillin 500 mg IV every 6 hours for 2 weeks. Continue orally for at least 4 weeks, and up to 3 months if required. H Child: cloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours. H See pyogenic arthritis for other antibiotic treatments. H For osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease, see section 11.1.3. H Surgical intervention may be indicated. RR

Surgical intervention may include:

  • Drainage of subperiosteal and soft tissue abscesses
  • Drainage of intramedullary purulence
  • Debridement of contiguous foci of infection, with antimicrobial therapy
  • Excision of sequestra, meaning devitalised bone
  • Surgery where there is failure to improve after 48 to 72 hours of antimicrobial therapy
  • Surgery and antibiotics for chronic osteomyelitis

docs.title: 10.1.3 Pyomyositis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: M60.0

Pyomyositis is a bacterial infection of muscle, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Causes

  • Bacterial infection, commonly Staphylococcus aureus

Clinical features

  • Usually localised in one muscle
  • Commonly affects large striated muscles
  • Fever
  • Painful swelling of the involved muscle
  • Affected area is hot, swollen, and tender
  • Fluctuation when pus forms

Differential diagnosis

  • Cellulitis
  • Boil
  • Osteomyelitis
  • Peritonitis, especially in pyomyositis of abdominal muscles

Investigations

  • Full blood count
  • Pus for culture and sensitivity
  • Consider HIV infection

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC General management Elevate and immobilise the affected limb. HC3 Antibiotic treatment Give cloxacillin 500 mg IV or orally every 6 hours for 5 to 10 days. HC3 / HC4 Antibiotic treatment in children Give cloxacillin 12.5 to 25 mg/kg per dose. HC3 / HC4 Early stage, when the muscle is indurated, hot, and swollen Antibiotic treatment may be sufficient to resolve the infection. HC3 / HC4 When abscess has formed Surgical drainage is the only effective treatment. HC4 After surgical drainage Leave the wound open, pack, and clean daily. HC4

docs.title: 10.1.4 Tuberculosis of the Spine (Pott's Disease)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: A18.01

Tuberculous spondylitis, also called Pott's disease, is the most common form of skeletal TB. It usually affects the lower thoracic and upper lumbar region.

Infection begins with inflammation of the intervertebral joints and can spread to involve the adjacent vertebral body. Once two adjacent vertebrae are involved, infection can involve the adjoining intervertebral disc space, leading to vertebral collapse. Subsequent kyphosis can lead to cord compression and paraplegia.

Causes

  • Chronic infection caused by mycobacteria

Clinical features

  • Most common in young adults
  • Local pain that increases in severity over weeks to months
  • Pain may be associated with muscle spasm and rigidity
  • Constitutional symptoms, such as fever and weight loss, are present in less than 40% of cases
  • With progression and spread of disease, anterior collapse of affected vertebrae may lead to visible deformity, such as angular kyphosis or gibbus
  • Risk of cord compression
  • Weakness of the legs, also called Pott's paraplegia
  • Visceral dysfunction

Differential diagnosis

  • Staphylococcal spondylitis
  • Brucellosis
  • Metastatic lesion

Investigations

  • Adequate history
  • Careful clinical examination
  • Spine X-ray, which may show:
    • Disc space narrowing
    • Paravertebral shadow
    • Single or multiple vertebral involvement
    • Destructive lesions of two or more vertebrae without new bone formation
    • Destruction of vertebral end-plates
  • ESR, usually raised
  • White blood cell count, usually within normal limits

Management

Treatment LOC Rest the spine. HC4 Fit a spinal corset or plaster jacket for pain relief. HC4 Give TB treatment as per guidelines. See section 5.3 for more details. HC4 Surgical intervention may be warranted in selected patients. RR

Surgical intervention is warranted in patients with:

  • Spinal disease and advanced neurological deficits
  • Spinal disease and worsening neurological deficits progressing while on appropriate therapy
  • Spinal disease and kyphosis greater than 40 degrees at presentation
  • Chest wall cold abscess

docs.title: 10.2.1 Rheumatoid Arthritis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: M05

Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of chronic inflammatory joint disease. It mainly affects women. Attacks tend to be bilateral with symmetrical involvement and may cause joint destruction.

Causes

  • Unknown origin
  • Probably autoimmune

Clinical features

  • Stiffness and pain in the joints
  • Usually more than 3 joints are affected
  • Joint involvement is usually symmetrical
  • Symptoms are worse in the morning
  • Joints are swollen, warm, inflamed, and sensitive to touch
  • Fingers are most affected, especially the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints
  • All small and medium-sized joints can be affected
  • Hips and spine are rarely affected
  • Extra-articular manifestations may include:
    • Mild fever
    • Weakness
    • Lethargy
    • Anorexia
    • Weight loss
    • Rheumatoid nodules, commonly on extensor surfaces such as the forearm below the joint
  • The disease is chronic, with flare-ups, remission, and exacerbations
  • In advanced cases, joint deformities may occur

Differential diagnosis

  • Osteoarthritis
  • Gout arthritis, especially in males
  • Reactive arthritis

Investigations

  • Full blood count
  • ESR
  • Rheumatoid factor
  • Antinuclear factor
  • X-ray of affected joints

Management

Goals of treatment are:

  • Relief of symptoms
  • Preservation of joint function
  • Suppression of active disease
  • Slowing progression of disease
  • Prevention of structural damage and deformity
  • Maintenance of the patient’s normal lifestyle

Symptomatic treatment can be started at lower level, but appropriate management requires referral for specialist care.

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Pain and inflammation in acute flare Rest the affected joints. HC2 Pain and inflammation in acute flare Give an NSAID such as ibuprofen 400 mg every 8 hours. HC2 Pain and inflammation in acute flare Or give diclofenac 50 mg every 8 hours. HC2 Pain and inflammation in acute flare Or give indomethacin 50 mg every 8 hours. HC2 NSAID use Long-term treatment is not advised because of toxicity and because NSAIDs do not modify disease progression. HC2 NSAID use Consider gastroprotection with omeprazole 20 mg once daily. HC3 Severe acute inflammation Give prednisolone 5 to 10 mg once daily in the morning. RR Corticosteroids Corticosteroids slow disease progression but should not be used for long periods because of side effects. RR Corticosteroids Use for treating acute symptoms and while waiting to start specific medicines. RR Disease-modifying treatment Refer to a specialist for disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs. RR Disease-modifying treatment Specialist options include methotrexate and chloroquine. RR Supportive care Provide counselling and health education. HC2 / HC3 Supportive care Advise weight loss and appropriate exercise or physiotherapy. HC2 / HC3

docs.title: 10.2.2 Gout Arthritis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: M10

Gout arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis caused by altered urate metabolism with deposition of urate salts in joints and, in advanced cases, other tissues.

Causes

  • Altered urate metabolism
  • Deposition of urate salts in joints
  • Deposition of urate salts in other tissues in advanced cases

Clinical features

Acute gout

  • Affected joint is hot, red, and swollen
  • Mostly affects the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint, called podagra
  • May occasionally start in other joints
  • Sudden severe pain, often at night

Chronic gout

  • Repeated acute attacks
  • Progressive cartilage and bone erosion
  • Deposition of tophi in soft tissue, such as:
    • Ear cartilage
    • Bursae
    • Tendon sheaths

Differential diagnosis

  • Joint infection
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Injury
  • Pseudogout
  • Osteoarthritis

Investigations

  • Joint aspiration for uric acid crystals viewed by polarising microscope
  • X-ray of the affected joint or joints
  • Serum uric acid, usually elevated

Management

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Acute attack Rest and immobilise the affected joint. HC2 Acute attack Start an NSAID such as ibuprofen 400 mg every 8 hours. HC2 Acute attack Or give indomethacin 50 mg every 8 hours. HC2 Acute attack Or give diclofenac 50 mg every 8 hours. HC2 Acute attack Continue NSAID treatment for the duration of the attack. HC2 If NSAIDs are contraindicated Give prednisolone 40 mg once daily for 5 days. HC4 If NSAIDs are contraindicated Or give colchicine 0.5 to 1 mg initially, followed by 0.5 mg every 2 to 3 hours until pain relief occurs or vomiting and diarrhoea occur. Maximum dose is 6 mg. Do not repeat the course within 3 days. HC3 / H Chronic gout Advise weight reduction. H Chronic gout Advise dietary control, including a healthy diet and limited alcohol consumption. Coffee may be beneficial. H Chronic gout Avoid medicines that may increase uric acid, such as thiazide diuretics. H More than 2 attacks per year and/or complications such as renal stones or chronic tophaceous gout Give allopurinol, starting at 100 mg. Increase monthly by 100 mg. Average maintenance dose is 300 mg. Maximum dose is 900 mg. Titrate to keep uric acid below 0.35 mmol/L. H Allopurinol use Do not start allopurinol during an acute attack, but continue it if already started. H Prevention of acute attacks after starting allopurinol Give prophylactic colchicine 0.5 mg every 12 hours for the first 3 months. H

Note

Do not use allopurinol to treat asymptomatic hyperuricaemia.

docs.title: 10.2.3 Osteoarthritis
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: M15–M19

Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease with damage to articular cartilage. It is the commonest form of joint disease. The pathological changes in osteoarthritis are irreversible.

Causes and risk factors

  • Previous injury
  • Overweight
  • Age

Clinical features

  • May involve any joint
  • Most commonly affects the hip, spine, and knees
  • Usually not symmetrical
  • Restriction of movement
  • Pain on moving the joint
  • Pain tends to be absent at rest
  • Limp if lower limbs are affected
  • Deformity
  • Moderate tenderness
  • Improvement with rest
  • Deterioration with physical activity
  • Deterioration with cold and wet weather conditions
  • Joints are usually not swollen or warm
  • There may be some accumulation of clear articular fluid

Differential diagnosis

  • Gout
  • Gouty arthritis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis

Investigations

  • Full blood count, usually normal
  • ESR, usually normal
  • X-ray of affected joint or joints

Management

Goals of treatment are:

  • Pain relief
  • Optimisation of function
  • Minimisation of progression
Clinical situation Treatment LOC General measures Advise weight reduction. HC2 General measures Encourage activity and regular exercise. HC2 General measures Advise use of appropriate footwear and walking aids. HC2 Pain relief Give paracetamol 1 g every 8 hours. HC2 Acute exacerbation or severe pain Give an NSAID, such as ibuprofen or diclofenac. Limit use to brief periods. HC4 Local pain relief Give diclofenac 1% gel if available. HC4 Specialist treatment Intra-articular steroids such as triamcinolone may be used by a specialist only, maximum 4 times per year. RR

docs.title: Chapter 10: Musculoskeletal andJoint Diseases
docs.text:
Causes

Usually haematologenous spread from a primary focus following bacteraemia (e.g. septic skin lesions, sinus infections, throat infections, abrasions, wounds, pressure sores, and osteomyelitis)

Commonly involved in acute arthritis: Staphylococcus aureus and Gram negative bacilli, e.g., Salmonella spp, Streptococcus spp, Gonococcus

docs.text:
A18.01

A18.01

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott’s disease) is the most common form of skeletal TB; it usually affects the lower thoracic and upper lumbar region. Infection begins with inflammation

of the intervertebral joints and can spread to involve the adjacent vertebral body. Once two adjacent vertebrae are involved, infection can involve the adjoining intervertebral disc space, leading to vertebral collapse. Subsequent kyphosis can lead to cord compression and paraplegia.

Causes

  • A chronic infection caused by Mycobacteria

Clinical features

  • Most common in young adults

  • Local pain, which increases in severity over weeks to

months, sometimes in association with muscle spasm and rigidity

  • Constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss are present in < 40% of cases

  • With the progression and spreading of the disease, anterior collapse of affected vertebrae leads to visible deformity (angular kyphosis or gibbus), and risk of cord compression:

  • Weakness of legs (Pott’s paraplegia)

  • Visceral dysfunction

  • Differential diagnosis

  • Staphylococcal spondylitis

  • Brucellosis

  • Metastatic lesion

Investigations

 Adequate history and careful examination  X-ray spine: disc space narrowing, paravertebral shadow, single/ multiple vertebral involvement, destruction lesions of 2 or more vertebrae without new bone formation, destruction of vertebral end-plates

 Blood: raised ESR, WBC (within normal limits) Management

TREATMENT LOC  Rest the spine  Fit a spinal corset or plaster jacket for pain relief  TB treatment as per guidelines (see section 5.3 formore details)  Surgical intervention is warranted for patients in the following circumstances: HC4RR TREATMENT LOC - Patients with spinal disease and advanced- neurological deficits- Patients with spinal disease and worsening neurological deficits, progressing while on appropriate therapy- Patients with spinal disease and kyphosis >40- degrees at the time of presentation- Patients with chest wall cold abscess HC4RR

docs.title: 10.2.1 Rheumatoid Arthritis
docs.text:
CHAPTER 10: Musculoskeletal andJoint Diseases

ICD10 CODE: M05

Most common form of chronic inflammatory joint disease affecting mainly women. Attacks tend to be bilateral with symmetrical involvement that cause joint destruction. Causes

Unknown origin, probably autoimmune

Clinical features

Stiffness and pain in the joints (usually >3, symmetrical, worse in the morning)

Joints are swollen, warm, inflamed, and sensitive to touch

Fingers are most affected (metacarpophalangeal, or proximal interpahalangeal), but all small and medium size joints can be affected (rarely hips and spine)

Extra articular manifestations: mild fever, weakness, lethargy, anorexia, weight loss, rheumatoid nodules (20%) at extensor surface like forearm below joint

It is a CHRONIC disease with flare-up, remission, and exacerbations

In advanced cases, joint deformities may occur

Osteoarthritis, gout arthritis (in males)

Reactive arthritis

Investigations  Blood: Full blood count, ESR, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear factor  X-ray of affected joints

Differential diagnosis

Management Goals of treatment Relief of symptoms

Preservation of joint function

Suppression of active disease, and slowing progression of disease (prevention of structure damage and deformity)

Maintenance of patient’s normal lifestyle

Symptomatic treatment can be started at lower level but appropriate management requires referral for specialist care. TREATMENT

LOC

  • For pain and inflammation in acute flare

  • Joints are swollen, warm, inflamed, and sensitive to touch

  • Fingers are most affected (metacarpophalangeal, or proxi-

mal interpahalangeal), but all small and medium size joints can be affected (rarely hips and spine)

  • Extra articular manifestations: mild fever, weakness, lethargy, anorexia, weight loss, rheumatoid nodules (20%) at extensor surface like forearm below joint

  • It is a CHRONIC disease with flare-up, remission, and exacerbations

  • In advanced cases, joint deformities may occur

  • Osteoarthritis, gout arthritis (in males)

  • Reactive arthritis Investigations

 Blood: Full blood count, ESR, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear factor  X-ray of affected joints Management

Goals of treatment

  • Relief of symptoms

  • Preservation of joint function

  • Suppression of active disease, and slowing progression of

disease (prevention of structure damage and deformity)

  • Maintenance of patient’s normal lifestyle

Symptomatic treatment can be started at lower level but appropriate management requires referral for specialist care.

TREATMENT LOC - For pain and inflammation in acute flare  Rest the affected joints  Any NSAIDS e.g. ibuprofen 400 mg every 8hours  Or diclofenac 50 mg every 8 hours  Or indomethacin 50 mg every 8 hours- Long term treatment is not advised because of toxicity, and because NSAIDS do not modify the progression of disease- Consider adding gastroprotection with omeprazole 20 mg once daily- For severe acute inflammation Prednisolone 5–10 mg once daily in the morning HC2HC3RR TREATMENT LOC - They slow disease progression, but should not be used for long periods due to side effects- Used for treating acute symptoms, and while- waiting to start specific medicines- Refer to specialist for Disease Modifying Anti-- Rheumatic Drugs Methotrexate  Chloroquine HC2 HC3 RR - Counselling and health education Weight loss and appropriate exercise/ physiotherapy

docs.title: Chapter 10: Musculoskeletal and Joint Diseases
docs.text:
This chapter provides guidance on infections and inflammatory or degenerative conditions affecting bones, joints, and muscles. It covers pyogenic arthritis, osteomyelitis, pyomyositis, tuberculosis of the spine, rheumatoid arthritis, gout arthritis, and osteoarthritis.

Use this chapter to guide assessment, pain control, infection management, functional support, treatment, and referral for musculoskeletal and joint conditions.

Digital navigation note

This chapter landing page was added to improve navigation in the digital version of the Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023. It provides orientation only and does not replace the detailed clinical guidance in the chapter sections.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Blood Diseases and Blood Transfusion Guidelines
Chapter 11: Blood Diseases and Blood Transfusion Guidelines
11.1.1 Anaemia
docs.text:
Anaemia is a reduction in haemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age, sex, and pregnancy status. It is not a final diagnosis. Careful history, physical examination, and laboratory tests are essential to determine the cause.

Normal haemoglobin levels by age

Category Normal value Mild anaemia Moderate anaemia Severe anaemia Men >15 years >13 g/dL 11–12.9 g/dL 8–10.9 g/dL <8 g/dL Women >12 g/dL 11–11.9 g/dL 8–10.9 g/dL <8 g/dL Pregnant women >11 g/dL 10–10.9 g/dL 7–9.9 g/dL <7 g/dL Child 12–14 years >12 g/dL 11–11.9 g/dL 8–10.9 g/dL <8 g/dL Child 5–11 years >11.5 g/dL 11–11.5 g/dL 8–10.9 g/dL <8 g/dL Child 6 months–5 years >11 g/dL 10–10.9 g/dL 7–9.9 g/dL <7 g/dL

Source: WHO/NMH/NHD/MNM/11.1.

Reference range in newborns and infants

Age Normal range Birth >13.5 g/dL 2 weeks >12.5 g/dL 1–6 months >9.5 g/dL

Adapted from Medscape, September 2016, haemoglobin concentration.

Causes

Anaemia may result from decreased red blood cell production, increased red blood cell destruction, or loss of red blood cells.

Decreased production of red blood cells

  • Nutritional iron deficiency
  • Folic acid deficiency
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Depressed bone marrow function, such as leukaemia or aplasia
  • Infections, such as HIV, TB, and visceral leishmaniasis
  • Aplastic anaemia

Increased destruction of red blood cells, or haemolysis

  • Malaria
  • Medicine side effects, such as dapsone, cotrimoxazole, and AZT
  • Congenital disorders, such as sickle cell anaemia and G6PD deficiency

Loss of red blood cells

  • Acute or chronic blood loss, including:
    • Haemorrhage after trauma
    • Hookworm infestation
    • Pregnancy-related bleeding
    • Abortion
    • Heavy menstrual loss
    • Schistosomiasis
    • Massive or chronic gastrointestinal bleeding

Clinical features

Common clinical features include:

  • Pallor of conjunctivae, mucous membranes, palms, and soles
  • Fatigue
  • Dizziness
  • Palpitations
  • Headache
  • Anorexia
  • Sometimes weight loss
  • Low exercise tolerance

Features of severe anaemia may include signs of heart failure:

  • Lower limb oedema
  • Dyspnoea
  • Tachycardia
  • Heart murmurs

If anaemia is due to acute blood loss, features may include:

  • Postural hypotension
  • Decreased cardiac output
  • Tachycardia
  • Sweating
  • Restlessness
  • Thirst

Look for signs of specific pathology, such as:

  • Splenomegaly
  • Malaria
  • Nutritional deficiency
  • Haemolytic jaundice

Investigations

Initial investigations should include:

  • Complete blood count with differentials
  • Mean corpuscular volume
  • Platelets
  • Peripheral blood smear
  • Reticulocyte count

Evaluate haemoglobin levels according to the patient’s age.

Classify anaemia according to mean corpuscular volume.

Microcytic anaemia

Microcytic anaemia means small red blood cells. Consider:

  • Serum ferritin to evaluate iron deficiency
  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis for thalassaemias
  • Sideroblastic anaemia, which may be caused by medicines such as isoniazid and chloramphenicol
  • Evaluation for chronic blood loss, especially gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Stool analysis for parasites and occult blood

Macrocytic anaemia

Consider:

  • Vitamin B12 levels
  • Fasting serum folate levels
  • TSH to evaluate thyroid disease
  • Chronic alcohol abuse
  • Medicine causes, such as zidovudine, methotrexate, hydroxyurea, and antifolate medicines

Normocytic anaemia

Consider:

  • Acute blood loss
  • Chronic disease
  • Renal failure
  • Haemolysis

Investigations for haemolysis may include:

  • Peripheral blood film for schistocytes, suggesting microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
  • Haemoglobin studies where indicated

Do bone marrow aspirate and biopsy if bone marrow failure or haematological malignancy is suspected, such as:

  • Aplastic anaemia
  • Leukaemia
  • Lymphoma
  • Myeloma

Note

Anaemia is not a final diagnosis. Careful history, physical examination, and laboratory tests are essential to determine the cause.

General principles of management

  • Determine and treat the cause.
  • For example, antithymocyte globulin is used in aplastic anaemia and should be managed by a specialist.
  • Consider the need for blood transfusion according to:
    • Haemoglobin level
    • Clinical condition
    • Haemodynamic status
    • Presence of heart failure
    • Ongoing blood loss

docs.title: 11.1.1.1 Iron Deficiency Anaemia
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: D50

Iron deficiency anaemia is anaemia caused by inadequate iron availability, commonly due to poor intake, increased requirements, or chronic blood loss.

Causes

  • Poor nutritional intake with iron-poor foods
  • Chronic blood loss, including:
    • Hookworm infestation
    • Prolonged or excessive menstrual bleeding
    • Chronic gastrointestinal bleeding
    • Chronic use of NSAIDs
    • Large bowel tumours
    • Oesophageal varices

Clinical features

Iron deficiency anaemia usually develops slowly.

Features include general anaemia symptoms plus:

  • Sore tongue
  • Atrophy of lingual papillae
  • Erosions at the corners of the mouth
  • Brittle or fragile fingernails

Differential diagnosis

  • Other conditions that cause microcytic red cells

Investigations

  • Complete blood count
  • Haemoglobin level
  • Haematocrit, although haematocrit is rarely below 28% unless iron deficiency is present
  • Low mean corpuscular volume
  • Low mean corpuscular haemoglobin
  • Hypochromia, which may not be obvious in patients who have already been transfused
  • Hypochromic microcytic red cells
  • Investigate the cause of iron deficiency

Management

Treatment LOC Identify and treat the cause of iron deficiency. HC2 Adjust diet if poor diet is one of the underlying causes. HC2 Adult: give oral ferrous sulphate 200 mg every 8 hours. HC2 Alternatively, give ferrous sulphate / folic acid 200 mg / 0.4 mg every 8 hours. This is equivalent to 180 mg elemental iron per day. HC2 Child: give oral ferrous sulphate 5 mg/kg every 8 hours, maximum 200 mg per dose. This is equivalent to about 5 mg/kg elemental iron per day. HC2 Haemoglobin usually rises in 2 to 3 weeks and returns to normal after about 2 months. HC2 Continue treatment for 6 months to 1 year to replenish iron stores. HC2 Give an antihelminthic. Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose may be used. HC2

Refer to hospital in case of:

  • Severe symptoms requiring blood transfusion
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Malabsorption
  • Intolerance to oral therapy
  • Unclear cause
  • Failure to improve

Note

Side effects of oral iron include diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort, constipation, and black stools. Warn the patient not to worry about black stools.

Parenteral iron is rarely necessary and can cause anaphylaxis. It should only be used by specialists.

docs.title: 11.1.1.2 Megaloblastic Anaemia
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: D51–D52

Megaloblastic anaemia is anaemia characterised by large red blood cells. It is usually due to folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, or both.

Some medicines, such as hydroxyurea, zidovudine, and stavudine, can cause macrocytic anaemia without folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.

Causes

  • Low dietary intake of folate
  • Increased folate requirements, such as in children and pregnancy
  • Low dietary intake of vitamin B12, especially in exclusively vegetarian diets without animal proteins
  • Malabsorption of folate and vitamin B12, such as in severe gastritis, giardia infection, or severe intestinal disease
  • Medicines, including:
    • Metformin
    • Zidovudine
    • Hydroxyurea
    • Stavudine
    • Phenytoin
  • Other causes of macrocytosis, including:
    • Myelodysplasia
    • Hypothyroidism
    • Chronic alcohol use
    • Multiple myeloma

Clinical features

  • General features of anaemia
  • Features of vitamin B12 deficiency, including:
    • Neuropsychiatric abnormalities
    • Hyperpigmented palms and feet
    • Smooth beefy tongue
    • Peripheral neuropathy
    • Impaired vibration and position sense
    • Abnormal gait
    • Weakness
    • Decreased muscle strength
    • Spastic movements
    • Memory loss
    • Disorientation
    • Depression
    • Acute confusional state

Investigations

  • Blood smear showing macrocytosis
  • Elevated mean corpuscular haemoglobin
  • Elevated mean corpuscular volume
  • Pancytopenia in severe cases
  • Full blood count showing oval macrocytes
  • Hypersegmentation of neutrophils
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Decreased serum vitamin B12
  • Decreased fasting red cell folate

Management

Treatment LOC Identify and treat the underlying cause of anaemia. HC2 / RR Oral vitamin B12 may be given at a dose of 1 mg, equivalent to 1000 micrograms, daily in patients who cannot tolerate parenteral therapy. HC2 / RR A nasal formulation of vitamin B12 may be given on alternate days where available. HC2 / RR Advise dietary modification to ensure adequate intake of folate and vitamin B12. Encourage green leafy vegetables and foods of animal origin. HC2 / RR Give folic acid 5 mg daily until haemoglobin levels return to normal. HC2 / RR Give vitamin B12 1 mg IM daily for 5 days, then weekly for a further 3 doses. HC2 / RR In patients with pernicious anaemia, follow with vitamin B12 1 mg every second month for life. HC2 / RR

Caution

If vitamin B12 deficiency is suspected, such as with low leucocytes and platelets, neuropsychiatric symptoms, or vegan diet, do not give folic acid alone. Refer for further testing and treatment.

Giving folic acid alone in patients with vitamin B12 deficiency may precipitate permanent neurological deficit.

Note

Anaemia normally corrects within 1 to 2 months. White cell count and thrombocytopenia usually normalise within 7 to 10 days.

Do not use ferrous-folate combination tablets to treat folate deficiency because the quantity of folic acid is too low.

docs.title: 11.1.1.3 Normocytic Anaemia
docs.text:
Normocytic anaemia is anaemia in which the red blood cells are of normal size, but the haemoglobin level is reduced.

Causes

  • Haemolysis, meaning destruction of red blood cells, including:
    • Autoimmune disorders
    • Hypersplenism
    • Haemoglobin abnormalities, such as sickle cell disease and thalassaemia
    • Medicine-related haemolysis, such as sulphonamides, dapsone, and primaquine
  • Decreased reticulocytosis, meaning reduced formation of new red blood cells, including:
    • Chronic kidney disease
    • Chronic diseases

Clinical features

  • General features of anaemia

Investigations

  • Evidence of haemolysis
  • Full blood count
  • Peripheral blood smear, including assessment for spherocytes
  • HIV serology

Management

Treatment LOC Identify and treat the cause of anaemia. HC4 Do not treat with iron, folic acid, or vitamin B12 unless there is clear documented deficiency. HC4 Treat all patients with haemolytic anaemia with folic acid 5 mg daily. HC4 Refer to hospital for further management. HC4

Prevention and health education for anaemia

Educate the public about:

  • The lifelong effects of anaemia on health and cognitive development
  • Dietary measures, including exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months
  • Use of locally available iron-containing weaning foods, such as red meat, beans, peas, and dark leafy vegetables
  • Hygiene measures, including avoiding walking barefoot to prevent hookworm infestation
  • Use of pit latrines for faecal disposal
  • Good handwashing practices
  • Periodic screening for children and pregnant women
  • Presumptive iron therapy for children and pregnant women in cases of anaemia, as guided by IMCI and pregnancy guidelines in chapters 16 and 17
  • Routine iron supplementation for all pregnant women
  • Early treatment of malaria, helminthic infections, and related causes

docs.title: 11.1.2 Bleeding Disorders
docs.text:
A bleeding disorder is suspected if a patient has unexplained bruising and bleeding, especially where there is no history of trauma. Prolonged bleeding or oozing may also occur after injury or surgery, such as tooth extraction or a small cut.

Causes

Bleeding disorders may result from blood vessel defects, platelet defects, or coagulation defects.

Blood vessel defects

  • Acquired causes, including age and medicine side effects, such as steroids and NSAIDs
  • Genetic causes, such as hereditary telangiectasia

Platelet defects

  • Decreased platelet number or function, such as in:
    • Blood cancer
    • Viral infections
    • Aplastic anaemia
  • Increased platelet destruction, such as in:
    • Hypersplenism
    • Autoimmune disease
    • Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
    • Massive blood transfusion

Coagulation defects

  • Hereditary causes, such as haemophilia A, haemophilia B, and von Willebrand disease
  • Acquired causes, such as:
    • Warfarin or heparin use
    • Liver disease
    • Alcoholism
    • Acquired factor inhibitors, for example in malignancies, autoimmune diseases, and pregnancy
  • Infections such as meningococcal sepsis and haemorrhagic fevers, which may cause widespread endothelial damage and disseminated intravascular coagulation

Clinical features

Features suggesting platelet disorders include:

  • Mucosal bleeding, such as gum bleeding or nose bleeds
  • Superficial ecchymoses
  • Excessive bleeding after minor injury
  • Petechiae
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding

Features suggesting coagulation disorders include:

  • Large deep haematomas
  • Haemarthrosis

Investigations

  • Complete blood count
  • Platelet count, which may be estimated using a peripheral smear if an auto-analyser is not available
  • Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy if haematological malignancy is suspected as the cause of bleeding
  • Bleeding time
  • Coagulation tests

Bleeding time is normal with coagulation factor deficiencies, except von Willebrand disease. It is abnormal in thrombocytopenia and qualitative platelet defects.

Coagulation tests include:

  • Prothrombin time, which is prolonged in factor VII, X, V, and II deficiencies, liver disease, and warfarin treatment
  • International normalised ratio, used to monitor anticoagulation with warfarin
  • Partial thromboplastin time, which is prolonged in factor VIII, XII, XI, IX, X, V, and I deficiencies

Note

INR is not useful for monitoring heparin or direct-acting anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban.

If the bleeding disorder is acute, consider haemorrhagic fevers as a possible cause.

Management

Patients with acute bleeding disorders should be referred to hospital for appropriate investigations and treatment.

Patients with chronic bleeding disorders should be referred to a specialist.

Clinical situation Treatment LOC General management Identify and treat the root cause of the bleeding disorder. HC2 / HC4 Newborn requiring vitamin K Give phytomenadione, or vitamin K, injection. Full-term newborn: 1 mg IM or IV. Preterm newborn: 500 micrograms IM or IV. Repeat every 8 hours if necessary. HC2 / HC4 Patient on warfarin with acute bleeding Give vitamin K 5 mg slow IV to reverse warfarin effect. HC4 Severe or active bleeding in a patient on warfarin Give fresh frozen plasma. HC4 Medicines interfering with coagulation or platelet function Discontinue medicines that interfere with coagulation or platelet function, such as cephalosporins, dipyridazole, thiazides, alcohol, chlorpromazine, sulfonamides, rifampicin, methyldopa, phenytoin, barbiturates, quinidine, and isoniazid. HC4 Immune thrombocytopenic purpura First-line treatment is oral prednisolone 0.5 to 2 mg/kg/day. H Immune thrombocytopenic purpura requiring second-line treatment Rituximab and intravenous immunoglobulin are second-line treatments and should be given by a specialist. H Platelet transfusion Transfuse platelets if the patient is bleeding, or prophylactically when platelet count is less than 10,000/µL in patients at high risk of bleeding, such as cancer patients. H Clotting factor-related bleeding Transfuse fresh frozen plasma if bleeding is thought to be due to clotting factor disorders. H If above options are not viable Refer to a higher level of care. RR

Referral criteria

Refer the patient to hospital if any of the following are present:

  • Cause cannot be determined locally
  • Spontaneous bleeding
  • Bleeding into muscles or joints
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Central nervous system bleeding
  • Bleeding in patients on warfarin
  • Postpartum bleeding
  • Family history of bleeding

Health education

Advise patients with chronic bleeding disorders to:

  • Prevent injury
  • Avoid injections and unnecessary surgery
  • Visit the clinic immediately if symptoms occur
  • Continue all medicines as prescribed

All haemophiliacs should receive prophylactic treatment before traumatic procedures, such as tooth extraction or surgery.

docs.title: 11.1.3 Sickle Cell Disease
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: D57

Sickle cell disease is an inherited disorder in which red blood cells that carry oxygen around the body change shape from a smooth doughnut shape into a crescent or half-moon shape. It is sometimes called sickle cell anaemia.

Cause

Sickle cell disease is caused by a defect in the beta chains of haemoglobin where valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the chain. This change creates abnormal haemoglobin called HbS.

Clinical features

Symptoms usually appear from 3 to 6 months of age and may include:

  • Anaemia
  • Dactylitis, or swelling of fingers
  • Lobar pneumonia
  • Recurrent severe bacterial infections

These features result from reduction of foetal haemoglobin, HbF, and increase in HbS in the blood.

Chronic anaemia

Chronic anaemia is common, usually with haemoglobin of 6 to 9 g/dL. Episodes of acute worsening may occur due to:

  • Aplastic crisis, which is sudden transient arrest of blood cell production in the bone marrow, with low haemoglobin and low reticulocytes, often due to parvovirus B19 infection
  • Splenic sequestration, which is pooling of large amounts of red blood cells in the spleen, with painful rapidly enlarging spleen, decreasing haemoglobin, and high reticulocyte count

Acute vaso-occlusive phenomena

Vaso-occlusion may cause:

  • Painful crisis, with acute intense pain in the back, chest, limbs, or abdomen
  • Pain and swelling of hands and feet in children below 2 years
  • Stroke, with hemiplegia, altered consciousness, or seizures
  • Acute chest syndrome, with fever, chest pain, difficulty in breathing, low oxygen level, cough, or wheezing
  • Acute abdomen or mesenteric crisis, with abdominal pain and distension, reduced or absent bowel sounds, pallor, and fever
  • Renal infarction
  • Bone infarction and necrosis, especially at the head of the femur
  • Priapism

In acute abdomen or mesenteric crisis, abdominal X-ray may show dilated bowel loops. Anaemia, high reticulocyte count, and high CRP may be present.

Chronic organ damage

Chronic organ damage may result from anaemia and vaso-occlusive phenomena. It may include:

  • Hyposplenia or autosplenectomy due to multiple splenic infarcts
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Asthma
  • Chronic renal disease
  • Chronic hepatic disease
  • Gallbladder stones
  • Nephropathy
  • Acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia and hypoperfusion
  • Osteoporosis
  • Retinopathy
  • Chronic leg ulcers

Transcranial Doppler velocity above 200 cm/second predicts high risk of stroke. This is less predictive in adults.

Patients with asplenia or hyposplenism are at increased risk of infections such as:

  • Pneumococcal infections
  • Osteomyelitis
  • Pneumonia
  • Septicaemia

Investigations

  • Family history of sickle cell disease
  • Full blood count
  • Peripheral film comment
  • Screening tests for sickling, although these are not fully reliable
  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis to confirm diagnosis
  • Chest radiography for acute chest syndrome
  • Abdominal ultrasound
  • Urinalysis
  • Liver function tests
  • Renal function tests

Chronic management

Treatment LOC Provide regular follow-up and education of patients and families. HC2 Provide family support. HC2 Advise patients to remain well hydrated. HC2 Give folic acid 5 mg daily for life. HC2 Promptly assess and treat any fever with antibiotics until the source of fever is identified. HC2 Ensure complete immunisation using the UNEPI programme, including pneumococcal vaccine for all infants. HC2 If available, give immunisation against meningococcus in regions within the meningococcal belt, and influenza. HC2 Give prophylactic penicillin V up to 5 years of age. HC2 Child 3 months to 3 years: penicillin V 125 mg every 12 hours. HC2 Child 3 to 5 years: penicillin V 250 mg every 12 hours. HC2 Give malaria prophylaxis with monthly sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine. HC2 Child 2 to 5 years: sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine half tablet monthly. HC2 Child 5 to 10 years: sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine 1 tablet monthly. HC2 Child 10 to 15 years: sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine 2 tablets monthly. HC2 Child above 15 years: sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine 3 tablets monthly. HC2 For patients with sulphur allergy, consider erythromycin 250 mg every 12 hours. HC2 Refer to a specialised treatment centre for specialised management, especially if symptoms are uncontrolled. RR

Hydroxyurea

Hydroxyurea may be used under specialist management.

Starting dose:

  • Hydroxyurea 20 mg/kg

Children aged 9 months and above should be initiated on hydroxyurea when indicated.

Indications for hydroxyurea include:

  • Frequent crises, meaning more than 3 crises in a year
  • Pain interfering with activities of daily living
  • Abnormal transcranial Doppler ultrasonography velocity above 200 cm/second
  • Recurrent or severe acute chest syndrome
  • Stroke

Note

The decision to give hydroxyurea should be made by a senior health worker after full laboratory investigation, including complete blood count, renal function tests, and liver function tests.

Management of acute complications

Clinical situation Treatment LOC Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Oral hydration. HC2 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Warm compresses, not cold compresses. HC2 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Give paracetamol 1 g every 8 hours. HC2 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Child: paracetamol 10 to 15 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours. HC2 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Give ibuprofen 400 to 600 mg every 6 to 8 hours if needed. HC4 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Child: ibuprofen 5 to 10 mg/kg every 8 hours. HC4 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Give oral diclofenac 50 mg every 8 hours if needed. HC4 Painful crisis, home management for mild to moderate pain Children above 9 years and above 35 kg: diclofenac 2 mg/kg in 3 divided doses. HC4 If pain is not controlled Add codeine 30 to 60 mg every 6 hours, only in patients above 12 years. RR If pain is not controlled Or give oral tramadol 50 to 100 mg every 6 to 8 hours, only in patients above 12 years. RR If pain is not controlled Or give oral morphine 0.2 to 0.4 mg/kg every 4 hours and reassess pain level. See section 13.1.2 for the WHO analgesic ladder. RR If pain is still not controlled Refer to hospital. RR

Painful crisis: hospital management for severe pain

Treatment LOC Give IV fluids for rehydration. HC4 Give oxygen and keep oxygen saturation above 95%. HC4 Assess for malaria and other infections. HC3 Give injectable diclofenac. HC4 Child: diclofenac 1 mg/kg IM every 8 hours. HC4 Adult: diclofenac 50 to 75 mg IM every 8 hours. HC4 Give oral morphine. See section 13.1.2. H Child and adult: morphine 0.3 to 0.6 mg/kg per dose and reassess. H Or give IV morphine. H Child: morphine 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg per dose. H Adult: morphine 5 to 10 mg per dose and reassess. H

Note

Use a laxative, such as bisacodyl 2.5 mg to 5 mg orally, to prevent constipation due to morphine.

Acute anaemia

Acute anaemia may occur due to acute splenic sequestration or aplastic crisis.

Treatment LOC Transfuse. See section 11.1.1. HC4 Give IV fluids if necessary. HC4 Investigate and treat malaria and infections. HC4 Avoid splenectomy in acute sequestration because mortality is high. HC4

Acute chest syndrome

Treatment LOC Restrict IV fluid use and always use calculated required amounts of IV fluids. Limit IV fluids in cases of pulmonary oedema. HC4 Give oxygen therapy. HC4 Manage pain as above. HC4 Give salbutamol inhaler 2 to 4 puffs as needed, or salbutamol nebulisation 5 mg. HC4 For children below 5 years, give salbutamol nebulisation 2.5 mg. HC4 Give ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once daily for 7 to 10 days. HC4 Child: ceftriaxone 80 to 100 mg/kg once daily. HC4 Plus erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours for 7 to 10 days. HC4 Child: erythromycin 5 to 10 mg/kg every 6 hours. HC4 Transfuse if there is no improvement and/or haemoglobin falls below 9 g/dL. HC4 Start incentive spirometry early, or use balloon blowing where incentive spirometry is not available. HC4

Stroke

Treatment LOC Give oxygen to maintain SpO₂ above 94%. RR Transfuse if haemoglobin is below 9 g/dL. RR Give IV fluids. RR Refer for neuroimaging and advanced management. RR

Acute abdomen / mesenteric crisis

Treatment LOC Give IV fluids. H Keep nil by mouth. H Insert NGT on free drainage. H Give antibiotics. H Give ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once daily for 7 to 10 days. H Child: ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg once daily. H Plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours for 7 to 10 days. H Child: metronidazole 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. H Give red cell transfusion. H Do plain abdominal X-ray to rule out obstruction or stool impaction. H Request surgical review. H

Infections

Treatment LOC Promptly assess and treat the cause, such as osteomyelitis, pneumonia, chronic leg ulcers, or cellulitis. H Treat according to the cause. H If there are no localising focal symptoms and no malaria, give ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g once daily for 7 to 10 days. H Child: ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg once daily. H If osteomyelitis or septic arthritis is suspected, give cloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours IV or orally. H Child: cloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for at least 21 days. H Or give ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for at least 21 days. H In children, give ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV once daily for at least 21 days. H

Indications for blood transfusion

Indication Examples LOC Acute exacerbation of baseline anaemia, defined as a drop in haemoglobin of at least 2 g/dL Hyperhaemolysis, hepatic sequestration, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis HC4 Severe vaso-occlusive events Stroke, acute chest syndrome, multi-organ failure HC4 Preparation for procedures Surgery, radiography with ionic contrast, general anaesthesia HC4

Prevention and health education

  • Provide patient, family, and community education.
  • Ensure timely initiation of hydroxyurea where indicated.
  • Conduct periodic comprehensive evaluations and other disease-specific health maintenance services.
  • Periodically evaluate for sickle cell complications, such as:
    • Urinalysis and renal function tests for sickle cell nephropathy
    • Echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension
    • Transcranial Doppler in children for early detection of stroke risk
  • Refer patients with complications to a specialist.
  • Ensure timely and appropriate treatment of painful crises and acute illness.
  • Provide genetic counselling for couples planning to have children.
  • Conduct antenatal screening.
  • Support early recognition and screening of children with low haemoglobin.
  • Ensure vaccination, including pneumococcal vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae vaccine, and hepatitis B vaccine.
  • Provide antibiotic prophylaxis, such as oral penicillin twice daily in eligible children.
  • Provide antimalarial chemoprophylaxis where indicated.

docs.title: 11.2 Blood and Blood Products
docs.text:
The Uganda Blood Transfusion Service collects blood and produces all blood products.

Whole blood is unseparated blood collected in an approved container and containing a preservative or anticoagulant solution.

In this guideline, “blood” refers to any blood component in which the main constituent is red blood cells, such as:

  • Whole blood

  • Red cell concentrate

  • Red cell suspension

Unless otherwise specified, other components are referred to as blood components or products. Blood components are prepared from whole blood and contain negligible quantities of red cells, such as:

  • Platelet concentrate

  • Fresh frozen plasma

  • Cryoprecipitate

Note

Refer to the National Blood Transfusion Guidelines for the appropriate use of blood.

The Uganda Blood Transfusion Service ensures that all blood and blood products are produced in a way that protects the health and safety of both patients and donors and minimises the risk of transmitting infection through blood.

docs.title: 11.2.1 General Principles of Good Clinical Practice in Transfusion Medicine
docs.text:
Blood is a scarce and expensive resource. Blood transfusion carries risks of adverse reactions and transfusion-transmitted infections.

Use blood appropriately, meaning only to treat conditions that can lead to significant morbidity or mortality and cannot be prevented or effectively managed by other means.

Minimise the need for transfusion by:

  • Early diagnosis and treatment of anaemia, particularly iron deficiency anaemia
  • Stopping blood loss through good surgical and anaesthetic management
  • Appropriate and timely management of coagulation disorders
  • Use of simple alternatives to transfusion when appropriate, such as IV fluids as first-line treatment for hypovolaemic shock

Prescribe transfusion according to the patient’s individual needs, using clinical signs and symptoms and the expected outcome. Do not prescribe transfusion based only on haemoglobin level.

Do not use blood transfusion to:

  • Expand blood volume, unless there has been blood loss of more than 30% of total blood volume
  • Enhance wound healing
  • “Top up” haemoglobin before surgery
  • Improve general well-being of the patient
  • Replace ongoing fluid losses, such as surgical blood loss, without clear clinical indication

Blood should not be transfused unless it has been:

  • Obtained from appropriately selected donors, preferably voluntary non-remunerated donors
  • Screened for transfusion-transmissible infections, namely:
    • HIV
    • Hepatitis B
    • Hepatitis C
    • Syphilis
  • Tested for compatibility between the donor’s red cells and the antibodies in the patient’s plasma, in accordance with national guidelines

The mandate to collect blood from donors and screen it for transfusion-transmissible infections is reserved for the Uganda Blood Transfusion Service.

Guidelines and procedures for requesting, administering, and recording blood transfusion should be clearly spelled out and strictly followed to avoid catastrophic mistakes.

Ensure that the transfused patient is closely monitored during and after transfusion, and that there is immediate response if any adverse reaction occurs.

docs.title: 11.2.2 Blood and Blood Products: Characteristics and Indications
docs.text: The following section presents only whole blood and red cell concentrate. Availability and use of other blood components is reserved for referral hospitals and is beyond the scope of this guideline.

docs.title: 11.2.2.1 Whole Blood
docs.text:
Whole blood provides:

  • Red blood cells
  • Plasma volume
  • Stable coagulation factors, including factors VII and XI
  • Other blood components

Whole blood may not have enough functional platelets and labile coagulation factors, including factors V and VIII.

Whole blood is also used as raw material from which other blood components are prepared.

One unit of whole blood is about 450 mL of donor blood obtained from a single donation, plus 63 mL of anticoagulant or preservative solution. It is available from HC4 level.

The haematocrit is approximately 35%.

Each unit of blood will raise haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL.

Indications

  • Red blood cell replacement in acute blood loss with significant hypovolaemia, such as:
    • Trauma
    • Surgery
    • Invasive procedures
    • Gastrointestinal haemorrhage
  • Patients who need red blood cell transfusion where red cell concentrates or suspensions are not available
  • Exchange transfusion in neonates, using blood units less than 5 days old, for specialist use only

Consider adding furosemide where there is risk of fluid overload.

Dose

  • Adults: 1 unit at a time
  • Children: 20 mL/kg

Caution

Transfusion must be started within 30 minutes of removal from the refrigerator and completed within 4 hours of starting.

Whole blood should be stored at 2–6°C in an approved blood bank refrigerator with temperature charts and alarm.

Whole blood is contraindicated in severe chronic anaemia and incipient cardiac failure because of the risk of volume overload.

Blood should not be warmed using improvised warming methods commonly used in health facilities. This is not necessary.

Routine use of diuretics such as furosemide before transfusion is not necessary in most patients. Pre-transfusion diuretics are indicated in known cardiac and renal patients to prevent circulatory overload.

docs.title: 11.2.2.2 Red Cell Concentrates / Packed Red Cells
docs.text:
Red cell concentrates, also called packed red cells, contain 80 to 150 mL per unit and are obtained from a single donation.

The haematocrit is approximately 55%.

Red cell concentrates are available from HC4 level.

Indications

  • Red blood cell replacement in anaemic patients
  • Acute blood loss, together with crystalloid solution if whole blood is not available

Caution

Transfusion must be started within 30 minutes of removal from the refrigerator and completed within 4 hours of starting.

Red cell concentrates should be stored at 2–6°C in an approved blood bank refrigerator with temperature charts and alarm.

docs.title: 11.2.2.3 Clinical Indications for Blood Transfusion
docs.text:
The indication for blood transfusion, using whole blood or red cell concentrates, depends on:

  • Degree of anaemia, estimated by haemoglobin level
  • Clinical condition, including high risk or presence of signs and symptoms of tissue hypoxia
  • Impaired tissue oxygenation resulting from anaemia or blood loss
  • Presence of ongoing blood loss, such as internal or external haemorrhage

Severe acute anaemia in children and infants

Transfuse if:

  • Haemoglobin is ≤4 g/dL, or haematocrit is ≤12%, regardless of clinical condition
  • Haemoglobin is 4–6 g/dL, or haematocrit is 13–18%, with life-threatening complications such as:
    • Clinical features of hypoxia
    • Cardiac decompensation
    • Acidosis, usually causing respiratory distress
    • Impaired consciousness or coma
    • Hyperparasitaemia above 20%
    • Cerebral malaria
    • Septicaemia
    • Meningitis

Dose

  • Packed red cells: 10–15 mL/kg
  • Whole blood: 20 mL/kg

Note

In children with chronic anaemia caused by iron deficiency, it may be possible to correct the anaemia with iron therapy alone.

Severe anaemia in adults

Consider blood transfusion only where the severity of anaemia is likely to cause, or has already caused, clinical signs of hypoxia or impaired tissue oxygenation.

Signs may include:

  • Tachycardia
  • Shock
  • Respiratory distress
  • Weakness
  • Dizziness
  • Unconsciousness

Transfusion may be indicated in:

  • Symptomatic anaemia in adults with haemoglobin below 7 g/dL
  • Haemoglobin below 8 g/dL in patients with cardiac disease or central nervous system symptoms

Give the minimum number of transfusions necessary to relieve hypoxia:

  • Transfuse 1 unit at a time, then reassess
  • If symptoms persist, give another unit
  • Transfuse over 2 to 4 hours

Severe anaemia in pregnancy

Screen for iron deficiency anaemia early in pregnancy and treat with iron where necessary.

Pregnancy below 36 weeks

Transfuse if:

  • Haemoglobin is 5 g/dL, irrespective of clinical condition
  • Haemoglobin is 5–7 g/dL with established or incipient heart failure, impaired tissue oxygenation, pneumonia, other serious infection, malaria, or pre-existing heart disease

Pregnancy above 36 weeks

Transfuse if:

  • Haemoglobin is ≤6 g/dL
  • Haemoglobin is 6–8 g/dL with established or incipient heart failure, impaired tissue oxygenation, pneumonia, other serious infection, malaria, or pre-existing heart disease

Elective caesarean section

If there is a history of antepartum haemorrhage, postpartum haemorrhage, or previous caesarean section:

  • If haemoglobin is 8–10 g/dL, establish or confirm blood group and save freshly taken serum for cross-matching
  • If haemoglobin is below 8 g/dL, have 2 units of blood cross-matched and made available

Pre-operative anaemia

Pre-operative anaemia should be investigated and promptly managed before surgery.

Prompt management may include iron supplementation, either oral or intravenous.

Where possible, surgery should be delayed or postponed until anaemia is corrected, because pre-operative anaemia is associated with poor surgical outcomes and increased need for blood transfusion.

Blood transfusion may be considered at haemoglobin ≤8 g/dL in case of:

  • Inadequate compensation for anaemia, meaning symptomatic anaemia
  • Significant co-existing cardiorespiratory disease
  • Major surgery or expected significant blood loss
  • Failure to correct anaemia before surgery

Management of acute haemorrhage / hypovolaemia

IV fluids, especially crystalloids such as normal saline, are first-line treatment for hypovolaemia during acute haemorrhage.

Whole blood, or red blood cells if whole blood is unavailable, are indicated when blood loss is more than 20–30% of blood volume, equivalent to more than 15–20 mL/kg.

The need for blood must be determined by:

  • Amount and speed of blood loss
  • Patient’s critical signs
  • Initial response to IV fluid resuscitation

Note

Haemoglobin level is not a reliable indicator of blood need in acute haemorrhage.

Sickle cell anaemia

Blood transfusion is not necessary for an asymptomatic sickle cell patient with steady haemoglobin of 6–8 g/dL, or for an uncomplicated painful episode.

In addition to general indications, blood transfusion is indicated if:

  • Acute severe anaemia occurs, with haemoglobin below 5 g/dL or 2 g/dL lower than the patient’s usual level, such as in aplastic crisis or acute sequestration crisis
  • Haemoglobin is below 6 g/dL in uncomplicated pregnancy
  • Haemoglobin is below 8 g/dL if caesarean section is planned
  • Haemoglobin is below 9 g/dL in acute chest syndrome or stroke

For pregnancy, caesarean section, acute chest syndrome, and stroke, the target haemoglobin is 11 g/dL and not higher.

Use packed cells if available rather than whole blood.

Neonatal conditions

Transfusion may be indicated in severe anaemia of any cause, including prematurity and sepsis.

Transfusion in neonates should be managed at specialist level.

docs.title: 11.2.3 Adverse Reactions Following Transfusion
docs.text:
Adverse reactions following transfusion may be acute or delayed.

Acute transfusion reactions may include:

  • Minor allergic reaction, such as urticaria
  • Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction
  • Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction, commonly caused by ABO incompatibility, which is severe and life-threatening
  • Bacterial contamination
  • Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
  • Transfusion-related acute lung injury
  • Severe allergic reaction, including anaphylaxis, which is relatively rare

Delayed transfusion reactions may include:

  • Transfusion-transmitted infections, such as HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C
  • Delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions

General principles

  • Acute transfusion reactions may occur in 1 to 2% of transfused patients.
  • Rapid recognition and management of transfusion reactions may save the patient’s life.
  • Accurate patient identification at the bedside is critical during:
    • Blood sample collection
    • Administration of blood
  • Monitoring transfusion is the only way to identify acute transfusion reactions.
  • Monitoring is performed by taking vital signs:
    • Before transfusion
    • 15 minutes after starting transfusion
    • Whenever a reaction is suspected
    • At the end of transfusion
  • Vital signs should always be taken at minimum:
    • Immediately before beginning the transfusion
    • 15 minutes after starting the transfusion
    • At the end of the transfusion
  • A nurse or physician should observe the patient during the first 15 minutes after a new blood unit is started, and vital signs should be recorded.
  • Errors and failure to follow correct procedures are the most common causes of life-threatening acute haemolytic reactions.

Common errors include:

  • Misidentification of patients
  • Administering the wrong blood unit to the wrong patient
  • Failure to repeat blood grouping of blood units received at the hospital
  • Failure to cross-match
  • Errors in labelling blood samples for pre-transfusion grouping and cross-match

These errors must be avoided.

Always store blood used for compatibility testing for 7 days at 2 to 8°C for possible investigation of transfusion reactions.

In a conscious patient with a severe acute haemolytic transfusion reaction, signs and symptoms may appear within minutes after infusion of only 5 to 10 mL of blood.

In an unconscious or anaesthetised patient, hypotension, hypoxia, and uncontrolled bleeding may be the only signs of a transfusion problem. Regular monitoring of vital signs is therefore important.

Vital signs to monitor

  • Temperature
  • Blood pressure
  • Respiratory rate
  • Pulse rate

Any unexpected change in vital signs should be treated as a possible acute transfusion reaction until proved otherwise.

If a transfusion reaction is suspected

  • Stop the transfusion and remove the giving set.
  • Before disconnecting, close the blood unit to avoid reflux of patient blood into the donor blood.
  • Check the blood pack labels and the patient’s identity.
  • If there is any discrepancy, consult the blood bank.
  • Evaluate the patient, take vital signs, and manage accordingly.
  • Maintain intravenous access.
  • Obtain a post-transfusion blood sample.
  • Return the implicated blood unit to the hospital blood bank.
  • Re-grouping and testing should be done on both patient and transfused samples.
  • Immediately report all suspected acute transfusion reactions to the hospital blood bank laboratory working with the clinician.
  • For severe reactions, record the following in the patient’s notes:
    • Type of reaction
    • Time the reaction occurred from the start of transfusion
    • Volume transfused
    • Type of blood product transfused
    • Pack numbers of blood products transfused
  • Diagnose the type of reaction and start a quick, clear investigation in the hospital blood bank laboratory.

docs.title: 11.2.3.1 Acute Transfusion Reactions
docs.text:
Acute transfusion reactions occur within 24 hours of transfusion.

Category 1: Mild reactions

Feature Details Possible causes Minor allergic reactions due to hypersensitivity.Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction due to inflammatory response. Signs and symptoms Localised cutaneous reactions, such as urticaria, hives, rash, or itching.No respiratory or other systemic symptoms.Mild fever below 38.9°C without any other symptoms or signs. Anaemia characterised by large red blood cells. Usually due to folate and/or vitamin B12 deficiency. Some medicines (hydroxyurea, zidovudine, stavudine can cause macrocytic anaemia without folate and/or vitamin B12 deficiency).

Cause

  • Low dietary intake of folate/increased need (e.g., children,

pregnancy)

  • Low dietary intake of vitamin B12 (in exclusively vegetarian diets, without any animal proteins)

  • Malabsorption of folate and vitamin B12 (severe gastritis, giardia infection, severe intestinal diseases)

  • Medicines e.g., metformin, zidovudine, hydroxyurea, stavudine, phenytoin

  • Other causes of macrocytosis: myelodysplasia, hypothy-

roidism, chronic alcohol use, multiple myeloma Clinical features

  • General anaemia signs

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency: neuropsychiatric abnormalities e.g., hyperpigmented palms and feet, smooth beefy tongue, peripheral neuropathy, impaired vibration and position sense, abnormal gait, weakness, decreased muscle strength, spastic motions, memory loss, disorientation, depression, and acute confusional state

  • Blood smear: macrocytosis

  • Elevated MCH/MCV

neutrophils, thrombocytopenia

Giving folic acid alone in patients with B12 deficiency may precipitate permanent neurological deficit.

 Anaemia normally corrects within 1-2 months. White cell count and thrombocytopenia normalise within 7-10 days  DO NOT use ferrous-folate combination tablets to treat folic deficiency because the quantity of folic acid is too low

11.1.2 Bleeding Disorders
docs.text:
A bleeding disorder is suspected if a patient has unexplained bruising and bleeding (i.e. no history of trauma). Prolonged bleeding or oozing can also occur after injury or surgery (e.g., tooth extraction, small cut).

Causes

  • Blood vessel defect

 Acquired: age, side effects of steroids, NSAIDS (e.g. easy bruising)  Genetic e.g. hereditary telangiectasia

  • Platelet defect  Decreased platelet number/function e.g., blood cancer, viruses,

aplastic anaemia  Increased destruction e.g., in hypersplenism, autoimmune disease,

immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) massive blood transfusion

  • Coagulation defect  Hereditary e.g., haemophilia A or B, von Willebrand disease  Acquired e.g., warfarin or heparin, liver disease, alcoholism, ac-

quired factor inhibitors for example in malignancies, autoimmune diseases and pregnancy.

 Infections: meningococcal sepsis, haemorrhagic fevers (causing widespread endothelial damage and disseminated intravascular coagulation)

Clinical features

  • Platelet disorder: mucosal bleeding (gingivitis, nose bleeds),

superficial ecchymoses, excessive bleeding after minor injury, petechiae, heavy menstrual bleeding

  • Coagulation disorder: large, deep haematomas or haemathrosis

Investigations

 Complete blood count, and platelet count (can be estimated using a peripheral smear if an auto-analyser is not available)

 A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy is indicated if a haematological malignancy is suspected to be the cause of the bleeding

 Bleeding time (time required for bleeding to stop). It is normal with coagulation factor deficiencies (except Von Willebrand disease), and abnormal in thrombocytopenia and qualitative platelet defects

 Coagulation tests

 Prothrombin time (PT): prolonged in factor VII, X, V, II deficiencies, liver disease, warfarin treatment

 International normalised ratio (INR) to monitor anticoagulation with warfarin (not useful for heparin and direct acting anticoagulants like rivaroxaban)

 Partial thromboplastin time (aPTT): prolonged in factor VIII,

(hemophilia A) XII, XI, IX, (hemophilia B) X, V and I deficiencies  If acute, consider if haemorrhagic fevers are the cause Management

Patients with acute bleeding disorders should be referred to hospital for appropriate investigations and treatment.

Patients with chronic bleeding disorders should be referred to a specialist.

TREATMENT LOC  Identify and treat root cause of bleeding disorder  Give phytomenadione (vitamin K) injection to: Newborn: 1mg for full-term baby; 500 mcg for a pre-term baby IM or IV. Repeat every 8 hours if necessary In patients on warfarin with acute bleeding, give vitamin K 5 mg slow IV to reverse warfarin effect. docs.text:
CHAPTER 11: Blood Diseases and Blood Transfusion Guidelines

ICD10: D57

red blood cells which carry oxygen around the body change shape from a smooth doughnut shape into a crescent or half-moon shape. It is sometimes called Sickle Cell Anaemia (SCA).

Cause

  • It is caused by a defect in beta chains where a given amino acid is replaced by another (Substitution of valine for glutamic acid) at position 6 of the chain. This change creates abnormal haemoglobin called HbS.

Clinical features

  • Symptoms usually appear from age of 3 to 6 months: anaemia, dactylitis (swelling of fingers), lobar pneumonia, recurrent severe bacterial infections. This results from the reduction of the foetal haemoglobin F (HbF), and increase in HbS in the blood

  • Chronic anaemia: Hb 6–9 g/dl with episodes of acute worsening, which can be due to

 Aplastic crisis: sudden transient arrest of blood cells production in the bone marrow (low Hb and low reticulocyes), often due to ParvoB19 virus infection)

 Splenic sequestration: pooling of large amounts of red blood cells in the spleen with painful and rapidly enlarging spleen, decreasing haemoglobin with high reticulocyte count

  • Acute vaso-occlusive phenomenon (occlusion of blood vessels) causing:

 Painful crisis (acute, intense) at the back, chest, limbs, abdomen.

In children <2 years, pain and swelling of hands and feet.  Stroke: hemiplegia, altered consciousness, seizures.  Acute chest syndrome: fever, chest pain, difficulty in breathing,

low oxygen level, cough, wheezing

 Acute abdomen or mesenteric crisis (“intestinal crisis”): abdominal pain and distension, reduced or absent bowel sounds, pallor, fever, Abdominal X-ray may show dilated bowel loops. Anaemia, high reticulocyte count, high CRP will be present.

 Renal infarction, bone infarction and necrosis, especially at the head of femur, priapism

  • Chronic organ damage due to anaemia and vasocclusive phenomenon:

 Hyposplenia (spleen undergoes autosplenectomy due to multiple infarcts and is not functional anymore or has to be removed because of splenic sequestration)

 Pulmonary hypertension, asthma  Chronic renal and hepatic disease, gallbladder stones  Nephropathy and acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia and

hypoperfuson  Trans-cranial doppler velocity of >200cm/sec predicts high risk

of having a stroke. This is less predictive in adults  Osteoporosis, retinopathy  Chronic leg ulcers

  • Infections associated with asplenia and hyposplenism like pneumococcal infections

 Osteomyelitis, pneumonia, septicaemia Investigations

  • Family history of sickle cell disease

  • Full blood count & peripeharl film comment

  • Screening tests for sickling (not fully reliable)

  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis (confirms diagnosis)

  • Chest radiography (for Acute Chest Syndrome)

  • Abdominal ultrasound

  • Urinalysis

  • Liver and renal function tests

Management Chronic Management

Anaemia characterised by large red blood cells. Usually due to folate and/or vitamin B12 deficiency. Some medicines (hydroxyurea, zidovudine, stavudine can cause macrocytic anaemia without folate and/or vitamin B12 deficiency).

Cause

  • Low dietary intake of folate/increased need (e.g., children,

pregnancy)

  • Low dietary intake of vitamin B12 (in exclusively vegetarian diets, without any animal proteins)

  • Malabsorption of folate and vitamin B12 (severe gastritis, giardia infection, severe intestinal diseases)

  • Medicines e.g., metformin, zidovudine, hydroxyurea, stavudine, phenytoin

  • Other causes of macrocytosis: myelodysplasia, hypothy-

roidism, chronic alcohol use, multiple myeloma Clinical features

  • General anaemia signs

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency: neuropsychiatric abnormalities e.g., hyperpigmented palms and feet, smooth beefy tongue, peripheral neuropathy, impaired vibration and position sense, abnormal gait, weakness, decreased muscle strength, spastic motions, memory loss, disorientation, depression, and acute confusional state

Investigations

  • Blood smear: macrocytosis

  • Elevated MCH/MCV

  • Pancytopenia in severe cases

  • Full blood count: oval macrocytes, hypersegmentation of

neutrophils, thrombocytopenia

  • Decreased serum Vitamin B12 or fasting red cell folate Management

Giving folic acid alone in patients with B12 deficiency may precipitate permanent neurological deficit.

 Anaemia normally corrects within 1-2 months. White cell count and thrombocytopenia normalise within 7-10 days  DO NOT use ferrous-folate combination tablets to treat folic deficiency because the quantity of folic acid is too low
