docs.text:
Goals

  • Exclude anaemia.
  • Check for pregnancy-induced hypertension.
  • Update birth and emergency plan.
  • Determine foetal growth.

History taking

  • Ask if there is or was any vaginal bleeding or discharge.
  • Ask for any social problems and illnesses.

Examination

  • Check foetal heartbeat.
  • Perform abdominal examination.
  • Measure symphysio-fundal height.
  • Check for pallor.
  • Measure blood pressure.

Laboratory investigations

  • If RDT or blood slide is positive, follow guidelines.
  • If mother has fever, temperature above 37.5°C, do RDT or blood slide.
  • Check haemoglobin.
  • If blood pressure is above 140/90 mmHg, check urine for protein.

Health promotion

  • Emphasise hygiene, nutrition, and adherence to treatment.
  • Discuss the danger of sexual and gender-based violence in pregnancy.
  • Teach care of the newborn, including:
  • Early exclusive breastfeeding
  • Thermal care
  • Cord care
  • Danger signs
  • Teach about postpartum care.
  • Counsel on ITN use.
  • If HIV-positive, counsel on eMTCT.
  • Discuss family planning.
  • Discuss and update birth and emergency plan.
  • Discuss labour.
  • Teach danger signs in pregnancy and labour.
  • Address any observed or volunteered problems and illnesses.

Actions

  • Health educate on LLIN use, care, and maintenance.
  • Counsel woman.
  • Counsel to use dual protection for family planning and HIV prevention.
  • If HIV-positive, continue eMTCT.
  • Treat any problems.
  • Give IPTp-SP if 1 month has passed since previous dose.
  • Refill iron and folic acid.

docs.title: Fourth Visit: After 36 Weeks
docs.text:
Goals

  • Determine foetal growth.
  • Exclude anaemia.
  • Check for pregnancy-induced hypertension.
  • Check for pre-eclampsia.
  • Exclude cephalopelvic disproportion.
  • Exclude abnormal presentation or lie.
  • Explain symptoms of labour.
  • Update birth and emergency plan.

History taking

  • Ask if there is any vaginal bleeding.
  • Ask for problems.

Examination

  • Check presentation.
  • Check lie.
  • Perform abdominal examination.
  • Count foetal heart rate.
  • Measure symphysio-fundal height.
  • Measure blood pressure.

Laboratory investigations

  • If RDT or blood slide is positive, follow guidelines.
  • If mother has fever, temperature above 37.5°C, do RDT or blood slide.
  • Check haemoglobin.
  • If blood pressure is above 140/90 mmHg, check urine for protein.

Health promotion

  • Emphasise hygiene, nutrition, and adherence to treatment.
  • Discuss the danger of sexual and gender-based violence in pregnancy.
  • Teach care of the newborn, including:
  • Danger signs in the newborn
  • Early and exclusive breastfeeding
  • Thermal care
  • Cord care
  • Teach about postpartum care.
  • Re-discuss family planning and HIV prevention.
  • Counsel on ITN use.
  • Teach eMTCT in labour, birth, and postpartum.
  • Update birth and emergency plan.
  • Discuss labour.
  • Address any observed or volunteered problems and illnesses.

Actions

  • Health educate on LLIN use, care, and maintenance.
  • Counsel woman.
  • Counsel to use dual protection for family planning and HIV prevention.
  • If HIV-positive, continue eMTCT.
  • Treat any problems.
  • Give IPTp-SP if 1 month has passed since previous dose.
  • Refill iron and folic acid.

docs.title: 16.1.2 Management of Common Complaints during Pregnancy
docs.text: Complaint Action Remarks Low backache and frequent urination Exclude urinary tract infection and local lesion. If none, reassure. Avoid unnecessary medication. Morning sickness, nausea and vomiting Reassure; usually lasts only up to 3 months.Give general advice: frequent small dry meals, avoid spicy and fatty foods, take ginger and lemon.If severe with dehydration, admit for observation and rehydration using IV Ringer’s lactate or normal saline.Give vitamin B6, pyridoxine 25 mg, 2 to 3 times daily. Avoid anti-emetics in the first trimester.Anti-emetics may be necessary only in severe forms. See section 16.3.1. Swelling of the feet Check for anaemia, blood pressure, and urine protein, and manage appropriately. Advise mother to elevate feet if findings are normal. Indigestion, flatulence and constipation Advise high-roughage diet and increased fluid intake.If severe, treat as constipation. Avoid strong laxatives and enemas. Excessive salivation, ptyalism Reassure.Advise mother to use ginger. Avoid anticholinergic drugs. Food craving, pica Ensure balanced diet. Discourage harmful materials, for example soil.Soil craving is a sign of iron deficiency anaemia. Give ferrous sulphate and folic acid. Generalised pruritus Reassure.If severe, treat as skin allergy or urticaria. Avoid steroids. Vulval pruritus with whitish non-foul-smelling discharge, or burning sensation on passing urine Treat as abnormal vaginal discharge, most likely candida.Use clotrimazole cream or pessaries.In severe cases, use fluconazole 150 mg stat.Avoid repeat doses or prolonged use. Avoid douching with antiseptics. Cramps Give calcium lactate 600 mg 8 hourly for 5 days. Avoid giving NSAIDs. Fatigue Reassure and advise bed rest. Avoid drugs.

docs.title: 16.1.3 High Risk Pregnancy (HRP)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O09

High-risk pregnancy is a pregnancy with a higher than average risk of an adverse outcome for the mother or baby, for example abortion, intrauterine death, stillbirth, prematurity, other morbidity, or mortality.

High-risk criteria

A pregnancy is high risk if the woman has a history of or current:

  • Extremes of reproductive age: below 18 years or above 35 years
  • Primigravida, especially if too young, below 18 years, short, below 150 cm, or older than 35 years
  • High parity, 5 or more, or short birth-to-pregnancy interval below 2 years
  • Maternal obesity, BMI above 30
  • History of large infants, 4 kg and above
  • History of prematurity or low birth weight below 2.5 kg
  • History of obstructed or difficult labour
  • History of instrumental delivery
  • Poor obstetric history, for example stillbirths, neonatal deaths, abortions, or caesarean section
  • History of reproductive tract surgery, for example VVF repair, repaired ruptured uterus, surgery on the cervix, or myomectomy
  • Genetic or familial diseases, such as sickle cell disease
  • Medical conditions, including diabetes, HIV, cardiac disease, renal disease, hypertension, rhesus problems, or disability
  • Obstetric conditions, for example multiple pregnancy, malpresentation, antepartum haemorrhage, postpartum haemorrhage, DVT, intrauterine growth restriction or foetal growth restriction, IVF pregnancy, PROM, post-dates, cephalopelvic disproportion, or surrogate pregnancy

Management principles

Treatment LOC Early identification of high-risk pregnant women and referral as appropriate.Provide preconception care and folic acid supplementation.Provide prophylaxis and antenatal counselling to prevent some high-risk pregnancies.Ensure early start of antenatal care.Provide close medical supervision during pregnancy.Conduct special investigations to evaluate foetal development and maternal well-being.Prepare a birth preparedness plan.Ensure timely intervention for therapy and delivery.Ensure skilled birth attendance.Refer early to higher level as appropriate. HC3/HC4

Note

Skilled attendance at birth remains the most important component of comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care.

docs.title: 16.2 Management of Selected Conditions in Pregnancy
16.2.1 Anaemia in Pregnancy
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O99.019

Anaemia is the most frequent and major complication of pregnancy. It may be defined as haemoglobin level below normal, that is below 11 g/dL for pregnant women. In the second trimester, the cut-off is 10.5 g/dL.

Causes

Causes include:

  • Nutritional causes, including iron deficiency and folic acid deficiency
  • Infections and infestations, including hookworm infestation, malaria, UTI, and HIV/AIDS
  • Haemorrhagic causes, including bleeding in pregnancy and trauma
  • Haemoglobinopathies, for example sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemias
  • Malignancies
  • Medicines used for HIV or cancer treatment
  • Other causes

Clinical features

The mother may give a history of:

  • Gradual onset of exhaustion or weakness
  • Swelling of the legs
  • Dyspnoea
  • Dizziness
  • Palpitations

On examination, findings may include:

  • Pallor of conjunctiva, tongue, palm, vagina, or other sites, varying with severity of anaemia
  • Glossitis
  • Stomatitis
  • Oedema of the legs
  • In very severe cases, evidence of heart failure, such as engorged neck veins, dyspnoea, hepatomegaly, ascites, gallop rhythm, and oedema

Complications

Untreated anaemia may increase the risk of:

  • Premature labour
  • Poor intrauterine foetal growth
  • Weak uterine contractions
  • Foetal hypoxia
  • Postpartum haemorrhage
  • Poor lactation
  • Postpartum sepsis

Investigations

Investigations include:

  • Blood tests:
  • Haemoglobin level; below 11 g/dL is considered abnormal
  • Peripheral smear to determine the type of anaemia and presence of malaria parasites
  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis
  • Stool examination for ova and cysts of hookworm infestation

Management

Treatment LOC ProphylaxisAll pregnant women should receive ferrous sulphate and folic acid daily from 12 weeks.Continue supplementation until 6 months after delivery. HC2 Severe anaemia or heart failureIf haemoglobin is ≤7 g/dL or the patient has heart failure, refer to a well-equipped facility for further management. HC4 Haemoglobin above 7 g/dLGive combination of ferrous sulphate and folic acid once daily, Fe 200 mg plus folic acid 400 micrograms.Review the mother every 2 weeks. Haemoglobin should rise by 0.7 to 1 g/dL per week. HC2 Emphasise a realistic balanced diet rich in proteins, iron, and vitamins, for example beans, peas, millet, sorghum, peanuts, red meat, liver, dark green vegetables, fortified foods, and bananas.Treat malaria presumptively with SP and follow up.Deworm the patient with mebendazole 500 mg single dose in the second and third trimesters.Treat any other cause found from investigations.Advise child spacing with an interval of at least 2 years.If not improving, refer to hospital. HC2 Anaemia at 36 weeks or at deliveryIf the mother is still anaemic at 36 weeks gestation or at the time of delivery, refer to a well-equipped facility for further management, including blood transfusion. HC4 Sickle cell diseaseIf the patient has sickle cell disease, refer to a higher level for antenatal care and delivery. HC4

Prevention, health education, and mother self-care

  • Explain the possible causes of anaemia.
  • Advise on nutrition and diet. The mother should increase consumption of foods rich in iron and vitamins.
  • Instruct the patient to use medicines as prescribed and explain the dangers of non-compliance.
  • Advise on side effects of iron medicines, for example darkened stools.
  • Instruct the patient to come every 2 weeks for follow-up.

docs.title: 16.2.2 Pregnancy and HIV Infection
docs.text:
All HIV services for pregnant mothers are offered in the MCH clinic.

After delivery, mother and baby will remain in the MCH postnatal clinic until the HIV status of the child is confirmed. They will then be transferred to the general ART clinic.

All pregnant mothers and partners should receive routine counselling and testing for HIV.

If the mother tests negative:

  • Counsel on HIV prevention.
  • Repeat HIV test in the third trimester or during labour and delivery.

If the mother tests positive or is already known positive but not yet on ART:

  • Enrol on HIV care for eMTCT.

If the mother is already HIV-positive and already on ART:

  • Continue the existing regimen.
  • She may not need to be switched to Option B+ regimens.
  • Perform viral load at first contact.

docs.title: 16.2.2.1 Care for HIV-Positive Women (eMTCT)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O98.719

All HIV services for pregnant mothers are offered in the MCH clinic. After delivery, mother and baby will remain in the MCH postnatal clinic until the HIV status of the child is confirmed. They will then be transferred to the general ART clinic.

Note

All pregnant mothers and partners should receive routine counselling and testing for HIV.

If the mother tests negative:

  • Counsel on HIV prevention.
  • Repeat HIV test in the third trimester or during labour and delivery.

If the mother tests positive or is already known positive but not yet on ART:

  • Enrol on HIV care for eMTCT.

If the mother is already HIV-positive and already on ART:

  • Continue the existing regimen.
  • She may not need to be switched to Option B+ regimens.
  • Perform viral load at first contact.

For more information on HIV, including clinical diagnosis, management, and psychosocial support, refer to the specific HIV/AIDS guidelines. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: 16.2.2.2 Counselling for HIV-Positive Mothers
docs.text:
Provide counselling and psychosocial support to HIV-positive mothers.

Psychosocial support and nutrition

  • Give psychosocial support.
  • Encourage mothers to enrol in Family Support Groups for peer support.
  • Advise on the importance of good nutrition.
  • Talk to family members to encourage the woman to eat enough and help her avoid hard physical work.
  • Provide micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy and breastfeeding, including iron, folic acid, and multivitamins.
  • Advise her that she is more liable to infections and should seek medical help as soon as possible.

Birth plan

Review the birth plan and advise her:

  • To continue attending antenatal care.
  • To deliver in a health facility where appropriate care can be provided for her and the baby.
  • To go to the health facility as soon as labour starts or membranes rupture.

Lochia and blood-stained sanitary pads

Advise on the infectiousness of lochia and blood-stained sanitary pads, and how to dispose of them safely according to local facilities.

Family planning

If not breastfeeding exclusively, advise her to use a family planning method immediately to prevent unwanted pregnancy.

Ongoing care

Ensure linkage of the mother-baby pair and her family for ongoing care beyond puerperium.

Breast care if not breastfeeding

If not breastfeeding, advise that:

  • The breasts may be uncomfortable for a while.
  • She should avoid expressing breast milk to remove milk, because the more milk is removed, the more it forms.
  • She should support her breasts with a firm, well-fitting bra or cloth.
  • She may use paracetamol for painful breasts.
  • She should seek care if breasts become painful, swollen, or red, or if she feels ill or has fever.

Counselling on infant feeding choice

Begin infant feeding counselling before birth when the pregnant mother has been identified to be HIV-positive.

The decision on how she will feed the baby should be made before delivery. The mother should then be supported to implement the feeding option she has chosen.

All mothers are encouraged to breastfeed their babies exclusively for 6 months and then introduce complementary feeding until 1 year.

The mother should continue ARVs throughout breastfeeding.

The child should continue cotrimoxazole prophylaxis until HIV status is confirmed negative with a PCR test at 6 weeks after stopping breastfeeding.

During the postpartum period, if a mother chooses replacement feeding from the beginning, the choice of replacement feeds should fulfil the AFASS criteria:

  • Affordable
  • Feasible
  • Available
  • Sustainable
  • Safe

docs.title: 16.2.3 Chronic Hypertension in Pregnancy
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O10, O13

Chronic hypertension in pregnancy is blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg that is present before pregnancy or starts before 20 weeks gestation.

Pregnant women with chronic hypertension should continue lifestyle modifications for controlling hypertension, including:

  • No alcohol.
  • Regular moderate exercise, such as brisk walking for 30 minutes at least 3 times a week.
  • Smoking cessation.

The health worker should:

  • Ask the mother about foetal movements at each visit.
  • Aim for blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg.
  • Consider labour if blood pressure is persistently ≥160/90 mmHg, pregnancy is ≥37 weeks gestation, or there is maternal or foetal compromise, for example poor symphysio-fundal height growth.

Management

Treatment LOC Switch chronic antihypertensive medication to, or start, methyldopa 250 mg 8 hourly. Increase as necessary, up to a maximum of 500 mg 6 hourly.And/or give nifedipine 20–40 mg every 12 hours.If blood pressure is not controlled or there is any sign of pre-eclampsia, refer to hospital. HC3 CautionACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.Avoid beta blockers and diuretics. HC3

docs.title: 16.2.4 Malaria in Pregnancy
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: B54

Malaria can contribute to pregnancy complications such as:

  • Abortion
  • Poor foetal mental development
  • Premature labour
  • Intrauterine growth retardation
  • Foetal death
  • Severe maternal anaemia due to haemolysis
  • Maternal death

Complications are more common in:

  • Mothers of low gravidity, especially primigravidae and secundigravidae
  • HIV-positive mothers
  • Adolescents
  • Women with sickle-cell disease
  • Women from areas of low malaria endemicity, for example Kisoro and Kabale

See section 2.5.2 for more information on features and diagnosis of malaria.

Management of malaria in pregnancy

Approach Management LOC Prophylaxis for all pregnant mothers, except those with HIV on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis Give intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulphadoxine/pyrimethamine once a month starting at 13 weeks until delivery. HC2 Treatment of uncomplicated malaria in first trimester Give quinine oral 600 mg 8 hourly for 7 days.If quinine is not available, ACT may be used. HC2 Treatment of uncomplicated malaria in second and third trimesters First line: artemether/lumefantrine 80/480 mg 12 hourly for 3 days.First-line alternative: dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine 3 tablets, 1080 mg, once daily for 3 days.If no response, give quinine oral 600 mg 8 hourly for 7 days. HC2/HC3/HC4 Severe malaria in all trimesters and during lactation Give IM or IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then once daily until mother can tolerate oral medication. Complete treatment with 3 days of oral ACT.First-line alternative: IM artemether 3.2 mg/kg loading dose, then 1.6 mg/kg once daily until mother can tolerate oral medication. Complete treatment with 3 days of oral ACT.If artesunate or artemether is not available, use quinine 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours in dextrose 5%. HC3 Caution Quinine is associated with an increased risk of hypoglycaemia in late pregnancy. HC3

Prevention and control of malaria in pregnancy

  • Use insecticide-treated mosquito nets before, during, and after pregnancy.
  • Give all pregnant women intermittent preventive treatment with sulphadoxine/pyrimethamine, except where there is allergy to sulphonamides.
  • Ensure prompt diagnosis and effective treatment of malaria in pregnancy.

Education messages to mothers and the community

  • Malaria is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • Pregnant women and children are at particular risk of malaria.
  • If untreated, malaria can cause severe anaemia and death in pregnant women.
  • Malaria can lead to anaemia, miscarriage, stillbirth, foetal mental impairment, or low birth weight babies, who are more prone to infant and childhood mortality than normal weight babies.
  • It is better and cheaper to prevent malaria than to treat it.
  • The individual, family, and community can control malaria by taking appropriate actions.
  • Sleeping under an insecticide-treated mosquito net is the best way to prevent malaria.
  • It is important to complete the course of treatment in order to achieve cure.
  • Severe complicated malaria needs special management; refer.

docs.title: 16.2.5 Diabetes in Pregnancy
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O24

Risk factors and indications for screening

Screen for diabetes in pregnancy where there is:

  • BMI above 35 kg/m²
  • Age above 40 years
  • Gestational diabetes mellitus in a previous pregnancy
  • Family history of diabetes in a first-degree relative
  • Previous unexplained third trimester death
  • Previous macrosomic baby, weight above 4 kg
  • Polyhydramnios
  • Glycosuria
  • Foetus large for gestational age

Diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes

Diagnostic criteria include:

  • Fasting blood sugar above 5.6 mmol/L
  • Plasma glucose above 7.8 mmol/L 2 hours after 75 g glucose tolerance test

Therapeutic targets

  • Pre-prandial blood glucose below 5.3 mmol/L
  • 1-hour postprandial glucose below 7.8 mmol/L
  • 2-hour postprandial glucose below 6.4 mmol/L

Management

Treatment LOC Advise smoking cessation, moderate exercise, and dietary modification. See section 19.1.3.If obese and diabetes is mild, consider metformin 500 mg. Start with one tablet daily and increase by 500 mg per week up to a maximum of 2 g per day in divided doses. HC3 If not controlled, use insulin. See section 8.1.3. HC4 !!! noteMothers with diabetes should be advised to deliver in hospital. HC4

docs.title: 16.3.1 Hyperemesis Gravidarum
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O21

The cause is not known, but hyperemesis gravidarum may be more common in multiple pregnancy and molar pregnancy.

Clinical features

  • May occur from the 4th week of pregnancy and can continue beyond the 12th week.
  • Defining symptoms are nausea and vomiting so severe that oral intake is compromised.
  • The patient may develop complications of excessive vomiting, such as vomiting blood and dehydration.

Differential diagnosis

  • Intestinal obstruction
  • Other causes of vomiting
  • Molar pregnancy

Investigations

  • Blood:
  • Complete blood count
  • RDT for malaria parasites
  • Urinalysis to exclude urinary tract infection
  • Ultrasound scan to detect molar or multiple pregnancy

Management

Treatment LOC Give IV fluids to correct dehydration and ketosis. See section 1.1.3.Use Ringer’s lactate or normal saline and 5% glucose.Give promethazine 25 mg IM or orally every 8 hours when required.Give vitamin B6, pyridoxine, 1 tablet every 12 hours for 7 days.Or give metoclopramide 10 mg IM, IV, or orally every 6 to 8 hours when required.If not responding to the above, give chlorpromazine 25 mg IM or orally every 6 hours when required and refer. HC3/HC4

docs.title: 16.3.2 Vaginal Bleeding in Early Pregnancy / Abortion
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O20

Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy is almost always abnormal, and patients may need admission or referral.

The most common causes of bleeding in the first 6 months, before 26 weeks gestation, are abortion and ectopic pregnancy.

Abortion, or miscarriage, occurs when the foetus is lost before 28 weeks of pregnancy.

Causes

  • Not known in the majority of patients
  • May be intentional, induced abortion
  • May be spontaneous, often as a result of fever
  • If the mother has more than 2 miscarriages, refer for assessment

Differential diagnosis

  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Other causes of vaginal bleeding, for example cancer
  • Other causes of lower abdominal pain, for example PID

Investigations

  • Urine pregnancy test
  • Ultrasound scan
  • Complete blood count

Clinical features, terminology, and management

Clinical features and management depend on the stage of abortion.

Features Management LOC Threatened abortionLittle vaginal bleeding.No or moderate lower abdominal pain.Uterus is of expected size by date.Cervix is closed.Pregnancy may still continue. Medical treatment is usually not necessary. Hormones and tocolytics will not prevent miscarriage.Observe for 4 to 6 hours.Give paracetamol 1 g every 6 to 8 hours when required for 5 days.If bleeding stops, advise the patient to avoid strenuous activity and abstain from sex for at least 14 days.Follow up in 2 days in ANC clinic.If bleeding persists, refer to HC3. HC2 Inevitable abortionProcess is irreversible.Products of conception not yet expelled.Painful contractions, similar to labour pains, and bleeding.Cervix opens. Bed rest.If there are signs of infection, give antibiotics.Observe for continued bleeding.If patient is in shock, resuscitate with IV normal saline.If anaemic, refer to HC4 for replacement of blood lost.Establish IV access before referral.Give stat dose of antibiotics before referral. HC3/HC4 Incomplete abortionUterine contents not completely passed out.Bleeding, sometimes severe and with clots, from the vagina.Severe lower abdominal cramps.Cervix open.Products of conception may be felt in the cervical canal. If evacuation of uterus is not immediately possible, give oral misoprostol 600 micrograms sublingual stat. Repeat once after 4 hours if necessary.If at HC2, refer to HC3 after misoprostol.Use fingers to remove products of conception protruding through the cervix.Evacuate the uterus by manual vacuum aspiration if pregnancy is below 16 weeks, or by dilation and curettage.Ensure follow-up.Give stat dose of antibiotics before referral.Treat anaemia. HC2/HC3/HC4 Incomplete abortion with signs of infectionFever or foul-smelling blood. Give stat dose of IV ceftriaxone 2 g and IV metronidazole 500 mg.Then give amoxicillin 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days plus metronidazole 400 mg orally every 8 hours for 7 days. HC2/HC3/HC4 Complete abortionAll uterine contents have been passed out.Bleeding is decreasing.Cervix is closed.Uterus is empty and reduced in size. Examine to make sure all products have been passed.Follow up for continued bleeding. Bleeding should stop in a few days. HC3 Septic abortionIncomplete abortion with infection, which may follow induced abortion.Fever.Offensive vaginal discharge.Lower abdominal pain.Tenderness on palpating the abdomen. Give 7-day course of antibiotics as in incomplete abortion above.Evacuate the uterus. HC4 Post-abortal sepsisSigns and symptoms of sepsis following abortion, but no products of conception in the uterus. Give IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 8 hourly for 48 hours until fever has disappeared.Then switch to oral treatment as for septic abortion. HC4 Missed abortionFoetus died.Contents of uterus not expelled.May have dark blood drops or spotting from the vagina.Uterus smaller than expected by dates or not growing. Refer to hospital for evacuation. H Molar abortionAbnormal placenta with no foetus.Vaginal bleeding and passing of red material like ripe coffee berries or white translucent grape-like material.Uterus much bigger than expected.Mother feels no foetal movements even after 5 months. Resuscitate and refer the patient.Do not attempt to evacuate the uterus unless there are facilities for blood transfusion and oxytocin.Refer to hospital for further management. H

docs.title: 16.3.3 Ectopic Pregnancy
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O00

Ectopic pregnancy may result from partial blockage of the fallopian tube.

Causes and predisposing factors

  • Previous infection causing partial blockage of the tube
  • Congenital malformation of the fallopian tubes
  • Excessively long tubes

Risk factors

  • History of prior ectopic pregnancy
  • Prior abdominal or tubal surgery
  • History of PID
  • Endometriosis
  • History of infertility
  • Cigarette smoking
  • Multiple sexual partners

Clinical features

  • Period of amenorrhoea, as in normal pregnancy
  • Lower abdominal pain, often acute and followed by slight vaginal bleeding
  • If the tube ruptures, the patient may suddenly become anaemic and go into shock
  • Abdomen may be very tender, with rebound tenderness and guarding on palpation
  • Abdomen may not move with normal breathing
  • Cervical motion tenderness during vaginal examination
  • Features of free fluid in the abdomen may be present

Differential diagnosis

  • Other causes of acute abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, for example twisted ovarian cyst
  • Appendicitis
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Incomplete abortion

Investigations

Ectopic pregnancy is usually diagnosed clinically.

If the tube ruptures, there may be little time for investigations, but ultrasound can be useful if the patient is not in shock.

Investigations include:

  • Pregnancy test to exclude other causes
  • Complete blood count
  • Blood grouping and cross-matching

Management

Treatment LOC Set up IV drip with normal saline and run very slowly, just to maintain IV access.Refer to hospital for surgery. HC3/H

Warning

Do not run a lot of fluids before surgery. This raises blood pressure, which may worsen bleeding and worsen the state of shock.

docs.title: 16.3.4 Premature Rupture of Membranes (PROM and PPROM)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O42

PROM is rupture of membranes before the start of labour. It can occur either:

  • At or after 37 weeks when the foetus is mature or term. This is PROM.
  • Between 24 and 37 weeks when the foetus is immature or preterm. This is preterm PROM, or PPROM.

In all cases of PPROM, prematurity and its attendant problems are the principal concerns for the foetus, while infection morbidity and its complications are the primary concerns for the mother.

Risk factors associated with PPROM

  • Low socioeconomic status
  • Tobacco use
  • Low body mass index
  • Prior history of vaginal bleeding during pregnancy
  • History of preterm labour
  • Urinary tract infection
  • Chorioamnionitis
  • Cervical cerclage
  • Amniocentesis

Clinical features associated with PROM

  • Leakage of fluid or vaginal discharge
  • May be with or without vaginal bleeding
  • Pelvic pressure but no contractions
  • If rupture of membranes has been prolonged, the patient may present with fever, abdominal pain, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge

Investigations

  • Typical odour of amniotic fluid is diagnostic.
  • Place a vaginal pad over the vulva; examine visually and by smell after 1 hour.
  • Use a high-level disinfected or sterile speculum for vaginal examination; fluid may be seen coming from the cervix or forming a pool in the posterior fornix.
  • Ask the patient to cough; this may cause a gush of fluid.
  • If membrane rupture is not recent or leakage is gradual, confirming diagnosis may be difficult.
  • Abdominal ultrasound scan may show absence of, or very low, amniotic fluid.
  • If available, do nitrazine test and ferning test.

Warning

Do not do digital vaginal examination. It does not help diagnosis and may cause infection.

Management of PROM after 37 weeks

Key points:

  • Over 90% of patients with PROM go into spontaneous labour within 24 hours.
  • Expectant management carries a risk of infection.
  • Induction of labour decreases the risk of infection without increasing caesarean section delivery rate.
  • Expectant management also carries neonatal risks, including infection, abruptio placentae, foetal distress, foetal restriction deformities, and death.
Management LOC Refer all patients to hospital and keep in hospital until delivery. HC4 If membranes have been ruptured for more than 18 hours and there are no signs of infection, give prophylactic antibiotics until delivery to help reduce neonatal group B streptococcus infection:- Ampicillin 2 g IV every 6 hoursOr:- Benzylpenicillin 2 million units IV every 6 hoursAssess the cervix.Refer to HC4 or above, with facilities for emergency obstetric management, for induction with oxytocin. See section 16.4.2. HC4

Management of PPROM before 37 weeks

Key points:

  • The primary determinant of neonatal morbidity and mortality is gestational age at delivery; therefore conservative management is needed whenever possible.
  • All patients with PPROM should receive antenatal steroids for foetal lung maturity.
  • All patients with PPROM should receive prophylactic antibiotics because of the high risk of infection.
  • Administration of tocolytics for 48 hours may allow administration of steroids to accelerate lung maturity.
  • In general, prognosis is good after 34 weeks gestation.
  • All patients with PPROM should be cared for in a facility where a neonatal intensive care unit is available.
Treatment LOC Refer all patients to hospital and keep in hospital until delivery. H If there are no signs of infection and pregnancy is 24 to 34 weeks, with accurate gestational age, give dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for a total of 4 doses.Or give betamethasone 12 mg IM, 2 doses 24 hours apart. H Give routine antibiotics:- Erythromycin 250 mg every 8 hours- Plus amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hoursStop them after delivery if there are no signs of infection.Deliver at 34 weeks. H If palpable contractions and blood-stained mucus are present, suspect preterm labour.Hydrate with IV fluids before administering nifedipine.Consider administration of tocolytics:- Nifedipine 10 mg sublingual tablet every 15 minutes if necessary, up to a maximum of 40 mg in the first hour.- Then 60 to 160 mg daily in 3 to 4 divided doses, adjusted to uterine activity, for maximum 48 hours. H If vaginal bleeding with abdominal pain, intermittent or constant, is present, suspect and treat as abruptio placentae. See section 16.3.6. H If signs of infection are present, such as fever or foul-smelling vaginal discharge, give antibiotics as for chorioamnionitis. See section 16.3.5.Deliver immediately. H

Warning

Do not use steroids in the presence of infection.

docs.title: 16.3.5 Chorioamnionitis
docs.text:
Risk factors

  • Prolonged rupture of membranes
  • Prolonged labour
  • Untreated STI

Clinical features

  • History of vaginal draining of liquor
  • Fever above 37.8°C
  • Maternal tachycardia
  • Foetal tachycardia
  • Uterine tenderness
  • Foul-smelling or purulent vaginal discharge
  • Acute complications, including postpartum haemorrhage, puerperal sepsis, and renal failure
  • Chronic complications, including infertility due to salpingitis and/or uterine synechiae

Investigations

  • RDT or blood slide to rule out malaria
  • Urinalysis to rule out UTI
  • Vaginal discharge swab for Gram stain

Management

Care for mother and neonate includes early delivery and antibiotic administration. The risk of neonatal sepsis is increased.

Treatment LOC Start antibiotics and refer to hospital.Give ampicillin 2 g IV every 6 hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV every 24 hours.For penicillin-allergic patients, give clindamycin 300 to 600 mg IV 12 hourly. H If the patient delivers vaginally, continue parenteral antibiotics until the woman is afebrile for 48 hours and there is no foul-smelling discharge.If the mother returns with complications, refer for further care. H If the woman has a caesarean section, continue the above antibiotics and add metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours.Continue until 48 hours after fever has gone. H NewbornExamine the neonate for suspected sepsis before discharge.If newborn sepsis is suspected, manage as in section 2.1.7.1.Advise the mother on how to recognise danger signs. See section 17.1.1. H

docs.title: 16.4.2 Induction of Labour
docs.text:
Induction of labour may be indicated for medical reasons, such as:

  • Pre-eclampsia
  • Diabetes
  • Post-term pregnancy

Possible risks of induction include:

  • Failed induction
  • Hyperstimulation syndrome requiring emergency caesarean section

Induction is contraindicated in para 5 and above and in patients with a previous scar. In these cases, caesarean section is indicated.

Management

Treatment LOC Favourable cervix in HIV- and hepatitis B-negative mothersArtificially rupture the membranes using an amniotic hook or Kocher clamp.After 2 hours, give oxytocin IV 2.5 IU in 500 mL normal saline.Start with 10 drops per minute.Increase infusion rate by 10 drops every 30 minutes, up to 60 drops per minute, until a good contraction pattern is established, that is 3 to 5 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting more than 40 seconds. Maintain until delivery is complete.If there is no good contraction pattern at 60 drops per minute, increase oxytocin concentration to 5 IU in 500 mL dextrose or normal saline at 30 drops per minute. Increase by 10 drops every 30 minutes to a maximum of 60 drops per minute.Only in primigravida, if no good contraction pattern is established, increase oxytocin concentration to 10 IU in 500 mL and repeat as above, from 30 to 60 drops per minute.Do not use 10 IU in 500 mL in multigravida or women with previous caesarean section.Refer other cases or primigravida not responding to the higher concentration for surgical management.Never leave the woman alone. H If there are more than 4 contractions in 10 minutes, contraction longer than 60 seconds, or foetal distress:- Stop the infusion.- Give salbutamol 5 mg in Ringer’s lactate or normal saline 500 mL IV infusion at 10 drops per minute.- Monitor foetal heart rate. H Unfavourable cervixRipen cervix using one of the following:- Misoprostol 25 micrograms inserted vaginally every 6 hours for 2 doses. If no response, increase to 50 micrograms every 6 hours, maximum 200 micrograms in 24 hours. Stop when in established labour.Or:- Misoprostol 20 micrograms orally. Dissolve one 200 microgram tablet in 200 mL water and give 20 mL every 2 hours until labour starts, or up to maximum 24 hours.Or:- Foley catheter: insert Foley catheter through internal cervical os under sterile technique, inflate bulb with 50 mL water, and tape catheter under light traction. Leave until contractions begin or up to 12 hours.If cervical ripening fails, proceed to caesarean section.If cervix ripens but labour does not start, start oxytocin induction. H CautionDo not start oxytocin within 8 hours of using misoprostol.Carefully control oxytocin infusion; do not give rapidly.Monitor uterine contractions and foetal heart rate closely.If foetal distress occurs, do emergency caesarean section. H

docs.title: 16.4.3 Obstructed Labour
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O64-O66

Causes

  • Cephalopelvic disproportion
  • Large baby
  • Foetal abnormalities, such as hydrocephalus or conjoined twins
  • Small or deformed pelvis
  • Malpresentation, where the presenting part of the foetus is not the head, for example breech, shoulder, or face presentation
  • Malposition, an abnormal position of the foetal head when the head is the presenting part, for example occipito-posterior
  • Any barrier that prevents the baby’s descent down the birth canal

Clinical features

  • Strong contractions but no evidence of descent of the presenting part
  • Malposition or malpresentation may be felt on abdominal examination
  • In a first delivery, pains may stop spontaneously
  • Foetal distress with meconium-stained liquor
  • Fever and dehydration with maternal exhaustion
  • In late stages, regular colicky strong pains may stop when the uterus ruptures and may be replaced by dull continuous pain
  • Signs of shock if the uterus has ruptured
  • Physical examination may reveal signs of shock, tender uterus, formation of Bandl’s ring, and oedematous vulva or vagina

docs.title: 16.4.4 Ruptured Uterus
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O71.1

Ruptured uterus is partial or complete tearing of the uterus. It is common in:

  • Multiparous women, meaning women who have had more than one live baby
  • Women with previous caesarean section

Causes and predisposing factors

  • Assisted deliveries or obstetric procedures
  • Neglected obstructed labour
  • Tearing of a poorly healed uterine scar during labour
  • Short interpregnancy interval of less than 18 months after caesarean section
  • Previous uterine surgery, for example myomectomy
  • Damage to the uterus due to a blow, for example kick or accident
  • Use of oxytocic herbs

Clinical features

  • Cessation of regular uterine contractions or labour pains
  • Continuous abdominal pain
  • Vaginal bleeding
  • Anxiety
  • Anaemia
  • Shock
  • Abdomen irregular in shape
  • Foetal parts easily felt under the skin if the foetus is outside the uterus
  • Foetal heart not heard

Differential diagnosis

  • Abruptio placentae
  • Placenta praevia
  • Other causes of acute abdomen in late pregnancy
  • Ruptured spleen
  • Bowel obstruction

Investigations

  • Complete blood count
  • Blood grouping and cross-matching

Management

Mothers with suspected ruptured uterus should be referred immediately to hospital for blood transfusion and surgical management.

Treatment LOC Set up IV normal saline infusion.Give IV ceftriaxone 2 g and IV metronidazole 500 mg stat.Refer to hospital immediately for surgical management, caesarean section with or without hysterectomy. HC3/H

Prevention

  • Good antenatal care and education on early arrival to the facility for labour and delivery
  • Skilled birth attendance at all deliveries
  • Careful monitoring of labour using a partogram
  • Minimise use of oxytocin in multiparous women
  • Do not attempt fundal pressure during labour
  • Do not use misoprostol for induction of labour

docs.title: 16.4.5 Retained Placenta
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O73

Causes

  • Poor management of the third stage of labour
  • Failure of the uterus to contract
  • Failure of the placenta to separate, for example if it is stuck in uterine muscle, as in placenta accreta
  • Closure of the cervix before the placenta is expelled

Clinical features

  • Umbilical cord protrudes from the vagina
  • Bleeding may be present, especially in partial separation
  • Uterus may be poorly contracted and high in the abdomen
  • Signs of infection may be present if the placenta is retained for long, for example fever or unpleasant bloody discharge

Differential diagnosis

  • Retained second twin
  • Ruptured uterus

Investigations

  • Haemoglobin
  • Blood grouping
  • Cross-matching

Management

Treatment LOC If the woman is bleeding, manage as postpartum haemorrhage. See section 16.4.6. HC3 If the woman is not bleeding:- Set up IV normal saline infusion.- Empty the bladder voluntarily or by catheterisation.- Encourage breastfeeding.- Repeat controlled cord traction.If the placenta is not delivered in another 30 minutes:- Perform manual removal of placenta. Use diazepam 10 mg IM or IV.- Repeat oxytocin 10 IU IM or slow IV injection after manual removal.- If there are no signs of infection and no obstructed labour, give ceftriaxone 2 g IV stat.- If there are signs of infection, give antibiotics as for amnionitis.- If obstructed labour is present, give antibiotic prophylaxis as indicated in section 16.4.3. HC3 If unable to remove placenta manually:- Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV stat.- Give oxytocin 20 IU in 500 mL normal saline at 30 drops per minute during transfer.- Refer to HC4 or hospital. HC4/H

docs.title: 16.4.6 Postpartum Haemorrhage (PPH)
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O72

Postpartum haemorrhage is vaginal bleeding of more than 500 mL after vaginal delivery or more than 1,000 mL after caesarean section.

  • Primary PPH occurs in the first 24 hours after delivery.
  • Secondary PPH occurs between 24 hours and 6 weeks after delivery.

PPH is an emergency. It can occur in any woman and needs prompt recognition and treatment.

Causes

The main causes are:

  • Tone: failure of the uterus to contract, including after precipitated labour
  • Tissue: retained placenta, part of placenta, or membranes, which may lead to uterine atony and infection
  • Trauma: tears or rupture involving the perineum, vagina, cervix, or uterus
  • Thrombin: thrombotic or clotting disorders, which may occur with DIC following abruptio placentae or severe antepartum haemorrhage

High-risk patients

  • History of previous PPH
  • Multiple previous caesarean sections
  • Multiple pregnancy
  • Placenta praevia
  • Abruptio placentae
  • Precipitated labour
  • Prolonged labour
  • Large baby
  • Hypertensive disorders

Clinical features

  • Bleeding from the genital tract, which may be a gush of blood or a small but persistent trickle, for example more than 1 pad soaked in 5 minutes
  • Uterus may still be large, soft, and not contracted, especially in primary PPH
  • If the uterus is well contracted, look for tears on the perineum, vagina, cervix, or uterus
  • Signs of shock may be present, including tachycardia, low blood pressure, cold clammy skin
  • In secondary PPH, there may be signs of infection, such as fever or abdominal tenderness

Investigations

  • Haemoglobin and blood group should already have been done and recorded during antenatal care. If not, do them urgently.
  • Women at high risk of PPH should have blood cross-matched and at least 2 units booked.
  • If time allows, for example in secondary PPH, check haemoglobin and clotting.

Management principles

Management has two major components:

  1. Resuscitation and management of obstetric haemorrhage and possible hypovolaemic shock.
  2. Identification and management of the underlying cause.
Treatment LOC First aidCheck whether the uterus is contracted.Massage the uterus to expel clots.Give oxytocin 10 IU IM or slow IV.Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV slowly over 10 minutes, within 3 hours after delivery of the baby.Empty the bladder.Start IV fluids using normal saline through 2 large-bore cannulae. Run 2 L as fast as possible, then give 40 drops per minute according to the patient’s blood pressure. HC3 If oxytocin is not available, give misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually, or ergometrine 0.2 mg IM if the mother is not hypertensive.Check whether the placenta has been expelled and is complete.If placenta is complete, expel any clots in the birth canal.If placenta is not expelled or is incomplete, perform manual removal or refer.Give prophylactic antibiotics: ampicillin 2 g IV stat plus metronidazole 500 mg IV.If signs of infection are present, give antibiotics as for puerperal fever. HC3 If the uterus is contracted and placenta has been expelled, check for local causes if bleeding continues.Inspect carefully the lower genital tract for perineal lacerations, haematomas, vaginal tears, and cervical tears. HC3 If bleeding is not responding:- Repeat oxytocin 10 IU in 0.5 L normal saline at 60 drops per minute.- Give misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or ergometrine 0.2 mg IM if not given before and if not contraindicated.- Repeat tranexamic acid 1 g after 30 minutes from the first dose.- If bleeding persists, insert uterine balloon tamponade and apply non-pneumatic anti-shock garment.- Restore blood volume with IV fluids.- Refer to higher level for further management with uterine balloon tamponade and non-pneumatic anti-shock garment in situ.- Check for coagulation problems. HC3

Warning

Do not give heat-stable carbetocin for treatment of PPH. It is used for prevention of PPH.

Warning

Do not give ergometrine to hypertensive mothers.

Prevention

  • Ensure active management of the third stage of labour for all women in labour, with delivery by skilled staff.
  • Give heat-stable carbetocin 100 micrograms IV or IM as a single dose, or oxytocin 10 IU IM, or misoprostol 600 micrograms orally, within 1 minute of delivery after ruling out presence of another baby.
  • Clamp and cut the cord 3 to 5 minutes after birth or when the cord stops pulsating.
  • Use controlled cord traction during a contraction with counter-traction to deliver the placenta.
  • Massage the uterus immediately after delivery of the placenta to ensure the uterus is contracted.
  • Identify mothers at risk and manage accordingly.
  • Give 5 days of prophylactic antibiotics in prolonged or obstructed labour, or where other risk factors are present, such as rupture of membranes, birth before arrival at a health facility, or instrument delivery.

Note

Carbetocin should be given as a single dose.

docs.title: 16.4.8 Care of Mother and Baby Immediately After Delivery
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: Z39

Provide the following care for the first 2 hours after complete delivery of the placenta.

General measures

  • Give constant attention. Never leave mother and baby alone.
  • Request the mother or attendant to report any unusual changes in the mother or baby to the health worker.
  • Record findings, treatment, and procedures in the postpartum record.

For additional information on care of the HIV-positive mother, refer to section 16.2.2.

docs.title: 16.4.8.1 Care of Mother Immediately After Delivery
docs.text: Treatment LOC Take blood pressure.Rapidly assess for danger signs, such as excessive vaginal bleeding, difficulty breathing, or severe headache.Feel whether the uterus is hard and round. HC3 Monitoring of motherCheck every 15 minutes for 2 hours, then at 3 and 4 hours, then every 4 hours until discharge. HC3 Assess, classify, and treat raised diastolic blood pressureIf diastolic blood pressure is above 110 mmHg with proteinuria 3+ and signs or symptoms of eclampsia, manage as severe eclampsia. See section 16.3.8.If diastolic blood pressure is 90 to 110 mmHg with proteinuria, manage as pre-eclampsia. See section 16.3.7.If diastolic blood pressure is above 90 mmHg with no proteinuria and no symptoms of eclampsia, monitor and treat as hypertension. See section 16.6.1.2. HC3 Assess feverIf fever occurs with chills, uterine tenderness, or foul-smelling discharge, treat as puerperal fever. See section 16.4.7.If there is isolated raised temperature, monitor, hydrate, and observe for 12 hours. Treat for puerperal fever if it persists. HC3 If there is bleeding from a perineal tear, suture if trained or refer for further management. HC3 If bleeding occurs, for example pad soaked in less than 5 minutes or constant trickle of blood, and the uterus is not hard and round, treat as PPH. See section 16.4.6. HC3 For anaemia, monitor for bleeding, look for conjunctival or palmar pallor, check haemoglobin if indicated, and manage appropriately. HC3 Care of motherEncourage mother to pass urine, eat, and drink.Ask the companion to stay with her. HC3

docs.title: 16.4.8.2 Care of Baby Immediately After Delivery
docs.text:
Treatment LOC Monitoring of babyCheck every 15 minutes for breathing, warmth, pulse, and SpO₂.Ensure the umbilical cord stump is well ligatured. HC3 Care of babyEnsure the room is warm.Wipe off blood or meconium with a wet cloth.Do not remove vernix or bathe the baby within the first 24 hours.Apply an eye antimicrobial, for example tetracycline eye ointment. Leave in place and do not wash it away.Apply chlorhexidine digluconate gel to the cord stump daily after every bath until the cord falls off. Provide the gel to the mother and teach her how to use it at home.Give vitamin K 1 mg IM.Keep baby warm with skin-to-skin contact.If feet are cold or mother and baby are separated, cover baby with a blanket and cover the baby’s toes, fingers, and head with warm clothing.Reassess after 1 hour. HC3 If there is breathing difficulty, examine the baby according to first newborn examination requirements, classify the condition, and treat accordingly. See sections 16.5 and 17.1. HC3

Breastfeeding

Ensure the mother starts breastfeeding as soon as possible, preferably within the first hour.

  • Offer the mother help to position and attach the baby correctly to the breast to avoid cracked nipples.
  • Counsel and reassure the mother.

If unable to start breastfeeding:

  • Plan for an alternative feeding method.
  • Ensure that the alternative method is affordable, feasible, acceptable, sustainable, and safe.
  • Do not give artificial feeds, sugar water, or local feeds before the baby has attempted to initiate natural breastfeeding.
  • Consider referral to a higher level.

Baby dead or stillborn

If the baby dies or is stillborn:

  • Give supportive care to the mother.
  • Respect local customs.
  • Find out whether the mother or family would like to look at or hold the stillborn baby.
  • Check identity and give the wrapped body to the family for disposal or burial according to local customs.
  • Provide death certificate and complete required reporting formalities.
Treatment LOC Advise on postpartum care and hygiene.Advise mother on breast care: wear a firm bra and do not express the breasts.Give paracetamol if breasts are painful.You may give lactation suppression medicine such as bromocriptine 2.5 mg once daily for 2 weeks.Counsel on appropriate family planning. HC3

docs.title: 16.5.1 Newborn Resuscitation
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: P22

Start resuscitation within 1 minute of birth if the baby is not breathing or is gasping for breath.

General principles

  • Observe universal hygiene precautions to prevent infection.
  • Prepare for resuscitation at each delivery, even where there are no signs of foetal distress, in case the baby requires it.

Minimum preparation for every birth

Ensure that the following equipment is available and in good working order:

  • Two warm cotton cloths and a small one to position the head
  • Heat source to keep the baby warm
  • Mucus extractor, such as a penguin sucker or bulb syringe
  • Ambu bag and newborn masks of varying sizes, size 0 and size 1
  • Pulse oximeter
  • Clock or watch
  • Birth attendant skilled in newborn resuscitation

Management

Management LOC Keep the baby warm by drying the baby using the first cotton cloth, then change to the second dry cotton cloth.Rub the back 2 to 3 times.Clamp and cut the cord if necessary.Transfer the baby to a dry, clean, warm surface.Tell the mother that the baby is having difficulty starting to breathe and that you will help the baby. HC3 Open the airway:- Position the head so that it is slightly extended.- Place a folded towel less than 2 cm thick under the baby’s shoulders.- Suction only if there are secretions in the mouth or nose, or if the baby was born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid.- Suction 5 cm in the mouth and 3 cm in the nose while withdrawing, for a maximum of 10 seconds in total.- Do not suction too deep into the throat, because this may cause the heart to slow down or breathing to stop. HC3 If still not breathing, select an appropriate mask size to cover the chin, mouth, and nose, then ventilate:- Form a seal with the mask covering the chin, mouth, and nose.- Squeeze the bag 5 times.- Observe the chest.If the chest is not rising:- Reposition the head.- Check the mask seal.- Squeeze the bag harder.Once there is a good seal and the chest is rising, ventilate for 1 minute at 40 squeezes per minute, then stop and look for breathing. HC3 If breathing is more than 30 breaths per minute and there is no severe chest in-drawing:- Stop ventilating.- Put the baby skin-to-skin on the mother’s chest.- Observe every 15 minutes for breathing and warmth.- Take temperature.- Count breaths.- Observe for chest in-drawing or grunting respiration.- Monitor SpO₂.- Encourage the mother to breastfeed within 1 hour.- Do not leave the baby alone. HC3 If breathing is less than 30 breaths per minute or there is severe chest in-drawing:- Continue ventilating.- Arrange immediate referral.- Give oxygen if available.- Reassess every 1 to 2 minutes.- Continue ventilation during referral.If the baby is not gasping or breathing at all after 20 minutes of ventilation, stop ventilation. The baby is dead. HC3

Notes

  • Room air is sufficient in the absence of oxygen.
  • Cardiac massage is rarely required and is dangerous when done incorrectly.
  • A slow heart rate almost always responds to good breathing assistance only.
  • Usually, drugs are not needed if prompt and sufficient ventilation is provided.

Harmful and ineffective resuscitation practices

Avoid:

  • Routine suction of the newborn’s mouth and nose as soon as the head is born
  • Stimulation of the newborn by slapping or flicking the soles of the feet
  • Postural drainage, such as putting the baby upside down, and slapping the back
  • Squeezing the back to remove secretions from the airway
  • Routine giving of sodium bicarbonate to newborns who are not breathing
  • Intubation by an unskilled person

docs.title: 16.5.2 General Care of Newborn After Delivery
docs.text:
Provide the following care up to the time of discharge.

Type of care and monitoring Notes Keep baby with mother in the same bed or within easy reach, under a mosquito net. If baby is in a cot, ensure baby is dressed or well wrapped, covered with a blanket, head covered, and feet and hands covered with socks. Ensure the room is warm, above 25°C, and has no cold breeze or draughts. Do not put the baby in direct sun, on any cold surface, or directly in the line of a cold breeze. Advise and teach the mother how to keep the baby warm, give cord care, and ensure hygiene. If the mother is unable to care for the baby, provide the required care or teach her next of kin.Wash hands before and after handling the baby.Do not bathe the baby for the first 24 hours. Support exclusive breastfeeding on demand, day and night, whenever the baby wants. If breastfeeding is difficult, help the mother to position and attach the baby.If breastfeeding is not possible, advise on safe replacement feeding using AFASS principles. Ask the mother and companion to watch the baby and report breastfeeding or breathing problems, cold feet, bleeding from the cord, or any other bleeding. Check every baby at 4 and 8 hours, then daily for warm feet, normal pink colour, feeding, and breathing problems. If feet are cold, treat as a sign of hypothermia. Teach the mother how to rewarm the baby.Apply one to two layers of clothes more than adults and use hats or caps.Reassess in 1 hour. If no improvement, take temperature and manage accordingly. If there is a breathing problem, assess and manage accordingly. Refer urgently if breathing problem worsens or persists for more than 8 hours. If cord tie is loose or cord is bleeding, retie the cord. If bleeding persists, refer urgently. Check any baby with warning signs at 2, 4, 8, and 12 hours. Listen for grunting.Look for chest in-drawing.Count breaths per minute.Measure temperature.Observe breastfeeding. Give prescribed treatments according to dosage schedule. If referring the baby, write treatments given, when they were given, and why. Assess breastfeeding in every baby before planning discharge. Do not discharge if the baby is not feeding well. Do not discharge a baby who is less than 24 hours old. Do not plan early discharge if the baby is small, low birth weight, preterm, or not feeding well. Advise mother when to seek care and when to return if danger signs appear. Danger signs include refusal to feed, excessive crying, bleeding from the cord stump, fever, bulging fontanelle, abdominal distension, and grunting respiration. Give BCG and polio 0 before discharge. Counsel mother on the next routine check in 3 to 7 days and next immunisation at 6 weeks.

docs.title: 16.5.1.2 Postpartum Examination of the Mother Up to 6 Weeks
docs.text:
Use this section to examine the mother at any postpartum visit up to 6 weeks after delivery.

Ask and check record

Ask:

  • When and where did you deliver?
  • How are you feeling?
  • Have you had any pain, fever, or bleeding since delivery?
  • Do you have any problem passing urine?
  • Have you started having sex with your partner?
  • Have you decided on any contraception?
  • How do your breasts feel?
  • Do you have any other concerns?
  • Do you use tobacco, alcohol, or drugs?
  • Are you exposed to second-hand smoke?

Check records for:

  • Complications during delivery
  • Treatments she is receiving
  • HIV status

Look, listen, and feel

  • Measure blood pressure and temperature.
  • Feel the uterus. Check whether it is hard and round.
  • Look at vulva and perineum for tear, swelling, or pus.
  • Look at pad for bleeding and lochia.
  • Check whether lochia smells offensive or bleeding is profuse.
  • Look for pallor.

docs.title: Check for Hypertension
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Check blood pressure. Diastolic BP below 90 mmHg on 2 readings. Normal blood pressure No additional treatment. Review in 1 week if clinically indicated. Check blood pressure. Diastolic BP 90–110 mmHg. Moderate hypertension Assess for pre-eclampsia.If not pre-eclampsia, give or continue appropriate antihypertensive treatment as in non-pregnant women. See section 4.1.6. Check blood pressure. Diastolic BP 110 mmHg or more, or signs of eclampsia/pre-eclampsia. Severe hypertension, eclampsia, or pre-eclampsia Assess and treat for pre-eclampsia. See section 16.3.7.Refer to hospital.

docs.title: Check for Anaemia
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Check record for bleeding in pregnancy, during delivery, or after delivery.Ask whether there has been heavy bleeding since delivery.Ask whether she tires easily or becomes breathless during routine housework.Look for conjunctival and palmar pallor.Measure haemoglobin where indicated. No pallor and Hb above 11 g/dL. No anaemia Continue treatment with ferrous sulphate 200 mg, or Fefol, once daily to complete 3 months of treatment. Same assessment. Hb 7–11 g/dL or palmar/conjunctival pallor. Moderate anaemia Give double dose of ferrous sulphate 200 mg, or Fefol, 1 tablet twice daily for 3 months.Reassess in 4 weeks.If anaemia persists, refer to hospital. Same assessment. Hb below 7 g/dL and/or severe palmar or conjunctival pallor.Any pallor with any of the following: respiratory rate above 30 breaths per minute, tires easily, or breathlessness at rest. Severe anaemia Refer urgently to hospital.Give double dose of ferrous sulphate 200 mg, or Fefol, 1 tablet 2 to 3 times daily for 3 months while arranging referral.Follow up in 2 weeks to check clinical progress and compliance with treatment.

docs.title: Check for Vaginal Bleeding and Uterine, Urinary Tract, or Febrile Infection
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Ask about heavy vaginal bleeding since delivery.Look at pad for bleeding and lochia.Feel whether uterus is well contracted.Measure temperature.Ask about fever, foul-smelling lochia, burning on urination, or heavy bleeding.Feel lower abdomen and flanks for tenderness.Count breaths per minute. More than 1 pad soaked in 5 minutes.Still bleeding 6 weeks after delivery.Heavy vaginal bleeding.Heavy or light vaginal bleeding after 6 weeks. Postpartum bleeding See PPH section 16.4.6.Refer urgently to hospital.Give oxytocin 10 IU IM where indicated.Give appropriate IM/IV antibiotics where infection is suspected. Same assessment. Mother feeling well.Did not bleed more than 250 mL.Uterus well contracted and hard.No perineal swelling.Blood pressure, pulse, and temperature normal.No pallor.No breast problem.No fever, pain, or concern.No problem with urination. Normal postpartum Ensure woman and family know what to watch for and when to seek care.Advise on postpartum care, hygiene, and nutrition.Reinforce counselling on safer sexual practices.Counsel on birth spacing and family planning.Dispense 3 months of iron supply and counsel on compliance.Give any treatment or prophylaxis due, for example TT.Promote use of an insecticide-treated bed net for mother and baby.Advise when to return to the health facility for the next visit.Advise avoidance of tobacco, alcohol, drugs, and exposure to second-hand smoke. Same assessment. Temperature above 38°C and any of the following:- History of heavy vaginal bleeding- Lower abdominal pain- Uterus not well contracted- Profuse lochia- Foul-smelling lochia- Abdominal tenderness- Very weak- Stiff neck or lethargy Uterine infection / puerperal fever or very severe febrile disease Refer urgently to hospital. See puerperal fever section 16.4.7.Give appropriate IM/IV antibiotics.Insert IV line and give fluids rapidly. Same assessment. Burning on urination. Lower urinary tract infection Give appropriate oral antibiotic. See UTI in pregnancy section 16.2.6.Encourage her to drink more fluids.Follow up in 2 days. Same assessment. Burning on urination and flank pain. Upper urinary tract infection Refer urgently to hospital. See UTI in pregnancy section 16.2.6.Give appropriate IM/IV antibiotics.Insert IV line and give fluids rapidly plus glucose where indicated. Same assessment plus malaria test. Fever above 38°C and RDT or blood slide positive for malaria parasites. Malaria Give oral antimalarial. See section 16.2.4.Follow up in 2 days.Refer if not better in 2 days.

docs.title: Check for Perineal Trauma or Infection
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Ask whether there is pus or perineal pain.Inspect vulva and perineum. Excessive swelling of vulva or perineum.Pus in perineum.Pain in perineum. Perineal trauma, perineal infection, or pain Remove sutures if present.Clean wound.Counsel on care and hygiene.Give paracetamol for pain.Follow up in 2 days.If no improvement, refer to hospital.

docs.title: Check for Dribbling of Urine
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Ask if there is dribbling or leaking of urine. Continuous leaking of urine and/or faeces. Suspect obstetric fistula Refer for proper assessment and management. See section 16.6.4. Same assessment. Non-continuous dribbling or leaking urine, such as urge or stress incontinence. Urinary incontinence Check perineal trauma.Assess for urinary tract infection and treat if appropriate.Recommend pelvic floor exercises.Refer if not improving.

docs.title: Check for Vaginal Discharge 4 Weeks After Delivery
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise If vaginal discharge occurs 4 weeks after delivery, ask about abnormal vaginal discharge.Ask whether partner has urethral discharge or burning on passing urine.If partner is present, ask whether he has urethral discharge, pus, or burning on passing urine.If partner cannot be approached, explain the importance of partner assessment and treatment to avoid reinfection.Separate the labia and look for abnormal vaginal discharge: amount, colour, odour, and smell.If no discharge is seen, examine with a gloved finger and look at discharge on the glove. Abnormal vaginal discharge and partner has urethral discharge or burning on passing urine. Possible gonorrhoea and/or chlamydia infection Give appropriate oral antibiotics to the woman.Treat partner with appropriate oral antibiotics.Counsel on safer sex, including use of condoms.If no improvement, refer. Same assessment. Intense vulval itching and/or curd-like vaginal discharge. Possible candida infection Give clotrimazole pessaries, 1 each evening for 6 days.Counsel on safer sex, including use of condoms. Same assessment. Abnormal vaginal discharge without features above. Possible bacterial or trichomonas infection Give metronidazole 2 g single dose to woman.Counsel on safer sex, including use of condoms.

docs.title: Check for Breast Problems
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Ask how breasts feel.Observe a breastfeed if not yet done.Measure temperature.Feel gently for painful part of the breast.Look at breasts for swelling, shininess, and redness.Look at nipple for fissure. Baby not well attached. Breastfeeding attachment problem Teach correct positioning and attachment.Encourage mother to continue breastfeeding. Same assessment. Nipple sore or fissured. Nipple soreness or fissure Teach correct positioning and attachment.Encourage mother to continue breastfeeding. Same assessment. Temperature below 38°C and one or both breasts swollen, shiny, and patchy red.Baby not well attached or not yet breastfeeding. Breast engorgement Advise mother to feed more frequently.Teach correct positioning and attachment.Encourage continued breastfeeding.Reassess after 2 feeds or 1 day.If not better, teach mother how to express enough breast milk before the feed to relieve discomfort.If needed, teach her how to express milk from the affected breast, feed baby by cup, and continue breastfeeding on the healthy side. Same assessment. Painful breast, swollen and red.Temperature above 38°C.Feels ill. Mastitis See section 16.6.3.

docs.title: Check for Psychosocial Problems
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Ask about current or previous smoking, alcohol use, drug abuse, and previous or current history of violence. Current or previous smoking, alcohol use, drug abuse, or violence. Possible psychosocial problem Provide counselling and refer for specialist management where needed. Ask if she is feeling unhappy or crying easily, has low energy, sleep problems, lack of concentration, inability to do usual work or care for the baby, negative feelings towards the baby or herself, or generalised body pains not otherwise explained. Any of the described signs and symptoms during the first week after delivery. Possible baby blues Counsel, reassure, and review in 2 weeks.If persisting, see section 16.6.2. Same assessment. Two or more of the described signs or symptoms for more than 2 weeks. Possible postnatal depression See section 16.6.2. Refer for appropriate care.

docs.title: Check for HIV Infection
docs.text: Assessment Signs Classify as Treat and advise Check HIV status. HIV-positive. HIV-positive Manage mother and baby as per eMTCT guidelines. See section 16.2.2.Encourage partner testing. Same assessment. HIV-negative. HIV-negative Do counselling and testing if never tested before.Counsel on safe sex and staying negative.See Chapter 3.

docs.title: 16.5.3 Extra Care of Small Babies or Twins in the First Days of Life
docs.text:
Provide the following care for small babies, including:

  • Preterm babies up to 1 month early
  • Low birth weight babies below 2,500 g

Refer very small babies for specialised attention, including:

  • Very preterm babies more than 1 month early
  • Very low birth weight babies below 1,500 g
Type of care and monitoring Notes Ensure the room is warm. Teach the mother how to keep the baby warm. Provide an extra blanket for mother and baby if needed. Teach the mother how to ensure hygiene for the baby. Do not bathe the baby. Clean when necessary using swabs or cloth. Give special support for breastfeeding and assess daily. If not breastfeeding well, teach the mother alternative feeding methods. Assess the small baby daily. Measure temperature.Assess feeding progress and weight.Assess breathing.Check for jaundice. See sections 17.1.2 and 17.2.2. If there is a breathing problem, breastfeeding problem, or hypothermia, examine and manage accordingly. If there is maternal concern, examine and manage the baby accordingly. If breastfeeding problem persists for more than 3 days, or weight loss is more than 10% of birth weight and there are no other problems, refer for breastfeeding counselling and management. Keep mother and baby, or twins, longer before discharge. Plan discharge when the baby is breastfeeding well and gaining weight on 3 consecutive days. Also ensure body temperature is normal for 3 consecutive days and mother is confident in caring for the baby. If mother and baby are not able to stay, ensure daily home visits or send to hospital.

docs.title: 16.5.4 Newborn Hygiene at Home
docs.text:
Category Care Eye care Explain to the mother to seek care if the eyes drain pus.Advise her not to apply anything into the eyes. Cord care Wash hands before and after cord care.Apply chlorhexidine gel daily for 7 days. If chlorhexidine is not available, put nothing on the cord stump.Keep the stump loosely covered with clean clothes.Fold the nappy below the stump.If the stump is soiled, wash with clean water and soap, then dry completely with a clean cloth.Do not bandage the stump or abdomen.Do not apply anything else to the stump.Avoid touching the stump unnecessarily.If the umbilicus is red or draining pus or blood, examine the baby and manage accordingly. General baby care hygiene Wash the face, neck, and underarms daily.Wash the buttocks when soiled and dry completely.Use cloth on the baby’s bottom to collect stool.Dispose of stool as for sanitary towels or pads, and wash hands.Bathe when necessary using warm water.Ensure the room is warm with no cold breezes.Dry the baby completely, then dress and cover the baby.

Note

Small babies need especially careful attention. Wash hands before and after baby care.

docs.title: 16.6.1 Postpartum Care
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: Z39

The postpartum period, also known as the puerperium, begins with delivery of the baby and placenta and continues up to 6 weeks after delivery.

Health care providers should be aware of the medical and psychological needs of the postpartum mother and should be sensitive to cultural practices surrounding childbirth, including foods eaten and activity restrictions.

Postpartum care services

The mother and baby should be seen:

  • At 6 hours after birth
  • Again before discharge if delivery occurred in a health facility
  • Any time the mother reports concern about herself or the baby
  • Approximately 6 hours after home delivery

Routine follow-up visits are at:

  • 6 days
  • 6 weeks

These visits include:

  • Counselling
  • Assessment and management of observed or reported problems
  • Checking for:
  • Hypertension
  • Anaemia
  • Vaginal bleeding and discharge
  • Uterine infection
  • Puerperal fever
  • Malaria
  • UTI
  • Urine dribbling
  • Pus or perineal pain
  • Postpartum depression
  • Breast problems
  • HIV
  • Any other complaint

docs.title: 16.6.1.1 Postpartum Counselling
docs.text:
General counselling

Counsel on:

  • Breastfeeding and breast care
  • Nutrition
  • Ferrous sulphate and folic acid supplements
  • Avoiding alcohol and tobacco

Complications and danger signs for the mother

Counsel on:

  • Danger signs
  • Readiness plan in case of an emergency
  • Having someone nearby for at least 24 hours after delivery to respond to any change in condition
  • Emergency planning with partner or family, including:
  • Where to go if danger signs appear
  • How to get there
  • Costs involved
  • Family or community support
  • Seeking help from the community if needed
  • Bringing any home-based maternal record to the health facility, even for emergency visits

Self-care and health practices

Counsel on:

  • Personal hygiene
  • Handwashing
  • Genital hygiene, including care of episiotomy or repaired tears
  • Pelvic floor exercises
  • Sleeping under mosquito nets
  • Postpartum checks at 6 days and 6 weeks

Bonding and shared newborn care

  • Encourage the mother to hold, touch, and explore her baby.
  • Encourage rooming-in.
  • Discuss with the couple the need for shared care of the newborn.
  • Build the mother’s confidence by reassuring her that she is capable of caring for the newborn.

Counselling on baby care

Counsel on:

  • Hygiene and care of the baby
  • Danger signs for the baby
  • Immunisation schedule
  • Letting the baby sleep on the back or side
  • Keeping the baby warm without overcovering
  • Applying chlorhexidine digluconate gel to the cord stump daily after every bath until the cord falls off
  • Keeping the baby away from smoke and smokers
  • Keeping the baby, especially if small, away from anyone who is ill
  • Not sharing supplies, such as clothing or feeding utensils, with other babies

Danger signs requiring immediate care

Type of danger sign Action to take Vaginal bleeding, for example more than 2 pads soaked in 30 minutes after delivery, or bleeding that increases instead of decreasing after delivery Go to health facility immediately. Fever or convulsions Go to health facility immediately. Fast or difficult breathing Go to health facility immediately. Too weak to get out of bed Go to health facility immediately. Severe abdominal pain Go to health facility immediately. Severe headache or blurred vision Go to health facility immediately. Pain in the calf or ankle muscles Go to health facility immediately.

Danger signs requiring care as soon as possible

Type of danger sign Action to take Fever Go to health facility as soon as possible. Abdominal pain Go to health facility as soon as possible. Feeling ill Go to health facility as soon as possible. Breasts red, tender, or swollen Go to health facility as soon as possible. Sore nipple Go to health facility as soon as possible. Urine dribbling or pain on urination Go to health facility as soon as possible. Perineal pain or draining pus Go to health facility as soon as possible. Foul-smelling lochia Go to health facility as soon as possible.

docs.title: 16.6.3 Mastitis / Breast Abscess
docs.text:
ICD-10 CODE: O91

Mastitis or breast abscess may occur when organisms enter through a cracked nipple into an engorged breast. Less commonly, streptococci may be involved.

Clinical features

  • Pain in the breast
  • Swollen, often shiny, tender breast with enlarged veins
  • Often occurs in the second postpartum week
  • Fever
  • May progress to breast abscess, a collection of pus within the breast tissue
  • Localised erythema, shiny red skin
  • Firm lump, which may later become fluctuant
  • May drain pus spontaneously

Complications

  • Recurrent infection
  • Scarring
  • Loss of breast size
  • Noticeable breast asymmetry
  • Mammary duct fistula formation due to recurrence

Differential diagnosis

  • Breast engorgement, for mastitis
  • Breast lump or cancer, for abscess

Investigations

  • Breast milk for culture and sensitivity
  • Ultrasound scan to rule out breast abscess in patients with recurrent mastitis

Management

Treatment LOC Stop breastfeeding on the affected breast, but express and discard milk to avoid breast engorgement.Give analgesics such as paracetamol 1 g every 8 hours for 3 days.Apply warm compresses to relieve pain in the affected breast.Continue breastfeeding on the normal breast.Give cloxacillin 500 mg 6 hourly for 10 days.If cloxacillin is not available, give amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours for 10 days. HC2/HC3/H If penicillin allergy is present, give erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours for 10 days.Or give cephalexin 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 10 days. HC2/HC3/H If not improving, refer to hospital for ultrasound scan and further management.If clinical or ultrasound features of breast abscess are present, incise and drain. H

Prevention

  • Ensure proper attachment of baby on the breast.
  • Encourage frequent emptying of the breast.
  • Ensure the baby sucks on the areola and not the nipple.
  • Manage breast engorgement if not breastfeeding or after loss of baby. Refer to the section on care of mother and baby immediately after delivery.

docs.title: 16.7 Intrauterine Fetal Demise (IUFD) or Fetal Death in Utero (FDIU)
docs.text:
Fetal demise (fetal death) refers to situations in which the fetus is no longer alive, but the uterus has not yet started to expel its contents and the cervical os remains closed. Intrauterine fetal demise or death refers to babies with no signs of life in utero. “Early IUFD” refers to fetal demise before 20 weeks’ gestation and IUFD for demise of a fetus at 20 weeks gestation through to term.

Causes

  • Birth defects (congenital abnormalities of the fetus)
  • Blood transfer from baby to mother (feto-maternal haemorrhage)
  • Maternal or fetal infection
  • Genetic abnormality of the fetus
  • Placenta separated from the inner uterine wall (placental abruption)
  • Umbilical cord issues
  • Uterine rupture

Prevention

This should be done during antenatal and intrapartum to reduce fetal death.

  • Detection and treatment of syphilis / malaria
  • Detection and management of hypertensive disease of pregnancy
  • Management of sickle cell disease
  • Detection and management of diabetes
  • Monitoring during labour

Diagnosis

  • Vaginal bleeding
  • Absence or cessation of fetal movements — the usual reason for consultation
  • A uterus that is significantly smaller than the expected size i.e., fundal height too small for gestational age or decrease in fundal height from a prior visit
  • Absence of fetal heart sounds on electronic auscultation
  • Sometimes, breast engorgement, indicating the end of the pregnancy
  • The above signs suggest fetal death but are not sufficiently sensitive to justify a hasty, rash decision. Errors are common. Repeat the exam, do not rush.
