docs.title: 1.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Ministry of Health (MoH) has the responsibility to develop and implement national health policies, standards and guidelines required to operationalise Government health interventions.

These guidelines are meant to outline the process of engaging clients as key stakeholders in the management of health services and to get feedback on the quality of health services provided in health facilities so that gaps are identified and addressed to improve the quality of services in the national health system. The routine client satisfaction feedback tool included in this guide contains key aspects of healthcare service delivery to ensure that emerging issues are addressed and services are responsive to their expectations/needs.

docs.title: 1.2 Who should use this guide?
docs.text: The guide applies to different levels of stakeholders from the national to community level including, MoH departments, health facility managers (public and private), health care workers, District Health Teams (DHTs), community actors, and implementing partners.

docs.title: 1.3 General objective
docs.text: To provide guidance on how to implement the routine client feedback initiative using standardized tools across the national health system

docs.title: 1.3.1 Specific objectives of the guide
docs.text:
• • To describe the organizational arrangements and actors that will be involved in the implementation of routine client feedback
  • • To systematically guide health workers on how to collect, analyze and use routine client feedback information to improve services
  • • To provide elaborate and harmonized routine client feedback mechanism across the health service delivery system
  • • To describe the appropriate tools to use in the routine client feedback initiative

docs.title: 2.1 Implementation approach
docs.text: The implementation of the initiative involves the various levels at national, regional, district, health facility and community.

docs.title: 2.1.1 At national level
docs.text:
• • The MoH will be responsible for implementing this initiative through the Directorate of Governance and Regulation that will report directly to the Director General of Health Services and the Permanent Secretary.
  • • The MoH will develop, update and distribute the relevant tools for implementing the routine client feedback initiative at all levels.
  • • The MoH will mobilize resources and coordinate the implementation of the routine client feedback initiative.

Routine Client Feedback Satisfaction Implementation Guidelines 1

docs.title: 2.1.2 At sub-national level
docs.text: The Regional Referral Hospital (RRH)-Public Health Department (PHD) will take lead in planning and implementing the routine client feedback initiative in the RRHs and districts/urban authorities within their catchment areas.

docs.title: 2.1.3 At district level
docs.text: The District Health Officer (DHO)/City Health Officers will coordinate the routine client feedback initiative for all health facilities in their respective districts/cities.

docs.title: 2.1.4 At health facility level
docs.text: This is the primary implementing unit that includes: National Referral Hospitals (NRH), Regional Referral Hospitals (RRH), General Hospitals (GH), Health Centers IV, III and II. The health facility head will be responsible for implementing the routine client feedback initiative including taking immediate actions to improve quality of services.

docs.title: 2.1.5 Community level
docs.text: The health facility in-charge will be responsible for implementing the routine client feedback initiative within the designated catchment area.

docs.title: 2.2 Orientation
docs.text:
The various stakeholders shall be oriented and guided on the process of implementing the routine client feedback initiative using virtual platforms and where applicable hybrid, as follows:

  • 2.2.1 National level

MoH will orient the central team, National referrals, RRH leadership, Public Health Department (PHD) and implementing partners including the private sector etc.

  • 2.2.2 Regional level

The RRH through the PHD, in collaboration with regional health partners, will plan, coordinate and orient key actors in the RRH, districts and urban authorities including the private sector.

  • 2.2.3 District level

The districts in collaboration with health partners will orient district/urban/health facility teams.

2.3.4 Health facility level

The head of the health facility leadership shall designate a person to orient the facility teams and coordinate implementation of the routine client feedback initiative at the facility level.

docs.title: 3.1 Procedure for obtaining routine client feedback
docs.text:
This section describes the intervals for obtaining client feedback; who should collect client feedback, the procedure for obtaining client feedback, the timing and place of interview, the

number of clients to be interviewed and how they should be distributed per level of health facility; client rights and exclusion criteria.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Introducing the routine client feedback initiative to the clients during routine care
docs.text:
The routine client feedback initiative shall be implemented routinely in all health facilities. The standard tool shall be administered; data collected and analysed; and a report generated. The key emerging issues from the routine client feedback initiative shall be discussed by the respective management to improve the quality of health services in the national health system.

Clients should be informed and sensitized about the initiative by health workers during health education talks at all levels of interface with clients and through mass media and community engagement channels. At this point, clients should be informed that the time taken for the feedback is less than 10 minutes.

docs.title: 3.1.2 How the routine client satisfaction feedback tool shall be implemented?
docs.text:
1. The MoH standard routine client satisfaction feedback tool shall be used to collect feedback from clients about the quality of services provided in the health facility and community.
    1. The health facility management shall plan to routinely collect client feedback information on selected days of the month and analyze it monthly.
    1. A Quick Response (QR) code will be permanently displayed in all the departments for clients with smart phones to access and give feedback at anytime, and the findings will be included in the monthly report.
    1. The health facility management shall guide on the days to be considered for data collection, designate responsible persons and select the departments to be involved in the routine client feedback initiative.
    1. There should be a focal person appointed by the health facility management and all in charges of the sub units in the facility shall actively participate in the initiative and addressing the gaps identified from the routine client feedback.
    1. The data from routine client feedback should be discussed in the monthly health facility management meetings and actions taken to address client needs.
    1. Feedback should be given to staff during quarterly staff meetings by the health facility leadership.
    1. The health facility will identify and utilize different avenues to establish a feedback loop, including but not limited to the following:

  • • Established governance structures (HUMCs and Hospital Management Boards)

  • • Health talks
  • • Community dialogue meetings
  • • Community resource persons and platforms e.g., religious leaders, political leaders, community leaders and other opinion leaders
  • • Media (local radio, TV, print media, social media)
  • • Community outreaches, etc

docs.title: 3.1.3 What do you need to inform the client of before obtaining their feedback?
docs.text:
• • Explain their role as key stakeholders in improving the quality of health services in the health facility and community. They have a right to demand for better quality of services provided to them by the health facility.
  • • Assure the client that participation is voluntary; feedback is confidential; feedback will be analysed in aggregate; there are no reprisals from giving their opinions whatsoever and that client personal identifiers shall not be captured anywhere on the tool.

docs.title: 3.1.4 How to administer the routine client satisfaction feedback tool:
docs.text:
1. Clients can provide feedback by scanning a QR code displayed at a readily accessible location (e.g., notice board)
    1. Self-administered approach where the clients are provided with the routine client satisfaction tool to fill by themselves
    1. Interviewer administered tool where a designated person will interview the client

Where the QR code is used, clients can submit feedback anytime while at the health facility or after leaving the facility.

docs.title: 3.1.5 Who should be interviewed?
docs.text:
• • Patients/clients or caretakers who have accessed services in the health facility. Effort should be made to cover different service units in the health facility.
  • • The tool shall be administered individually, in privacy and clients shall not be discriminated for services on the account of their views.

docs.title: 3.1.6 Who should be excluded from giving feedback?
docs.text: Patients in critical condition, or unable to engage in conversation, and those who decline to share their experience of services.

docs.title: 3.1.7 How many clients should be interviewed monthly for feedback?
docs.text:
The following minimum number of clients/caretakers are recommended to be interviewed monthly per level of health facility. The number of clients interviewed should be fairly/randomly distributed across the days of the month.

National & Regional Referral Hospitals General Hospitals Health Center IVs Health Centers IIIs Health Centre II Community eg outreach 60 40 40 30 10 5

NB. The minimum number of clients doesn’t include feedback collected via the QR code

docs.title: 4.1 Data storage and access
docs.text: Routine client feedback data and reports will be uploaded into the Open Data Kit (ODK)Central, housed at the MoH-Division of Health Information (DHI). The different levels of stakeholders will be granted access rights by the responsible officer at the MoH-DHI.

docs.title: 5.1.1 National stakeholder utilization of data
docs.text:
1. The MoH-SCAPP department will generate the overall client feedback from all regions. The data shall be discussed quarterly by the department, technical working group (Governance Standards and Policy Regulation), Senior Management Committee, and finally Health Policy Advisory Committee.
    1. The data will be used to guide MoH actions to address gaps during supportive supervision and other deliberate interventions to improve quality of care, e.g., Maternal Newborn Child Health Quality of Care, Local Maternity and Neonatal System, Maternal Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response, quality improvement (QI) platforms.
    1. Additionally, briefs will be included in the quarterly performance review meetings and reports from the Directorate of Governance and Regulation.

docs.title: 5.1.2 Regional stakeholder utilization of data
docs.text:
1. The RRH will consolidate routine client feedback from the RRH, the districts and urban authorities within the catchment area of the RRH.

The regional routine client feedback data shall be disseminated to all key stakeholders and discussed routinely (monthly/quarterly) using regional platforms including but not limited to the following:

  • • Regional performance review meetings
  • • Regional QI Committee meeting (RECO)
  • • Regional Reproductive Health, Maternal and Child Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH-N)
  • • Local Maternity and Neonatal Systems (LMNS)

  • • Regional health assemblies

    1. The regional QI officer, biostatistician and facility QI focal person shall be the focal points for dashboard and actions taken for the previous client feedback initiatives.
    1. In addition, the regional QI officer and biostastician shall generate and distribute analytics inform of dashboards on client feedback parameters to the region.

docs.title: 5.1.3 District level utilization of data
docs.text:
The district will consolidate routine client feedback from the health facilities (including private) within their catchment area. The data from routine client feedback shall be discussed during the district quarterly meetings including:

  • • District performance review meeting
  • • District QI Committee meeting (DICO)
  • • Partner coordination meeting
  • • District support supervision of facilities

The district biostatistician and district QI focal person shall generate analytics in form of dashboards and graphs on routine client satisfaction parameters.

docs.title: 5.1.4 Health facility
docs.text:
1. The health facility head shall consolidate routine client feedback from the sub units, develop action plans and give feedback to clients. The client feedback data shall be discussed during the routine monthly management and general staff meetings.
    1. Monthly analytics in the form of dashboards and charts/graphs shall be developed and shared within the facility teams.
    1. A brief update on the routine client feedback shall be shared with the governance structures (Health Unit Management Committees)/Hospital Management Boards.

docs.title: 5.1.5 Community
docs.text: Community resource persons (village health teams, community health extension workers, etc) will collect client feedback information during community-based service delivery interventions such as outreaches. The data shall be submitted to the nearby facility for inclusion in the analysis. The findings shall be relayed back to the community teams for dissemination.

docs.title: 5.1.6 Acting on the feedback at facility level
docs.text:
• Step 1: Review the feedback using graphs, charts, trends and dashboard to identify common issues or patterns that need attention.
  • Step 2: Prioritise action items: Rank the identified issues based on their impact on the overall customer experience. Focus on the areas of client feedback that will have the most significant positive impact when improved.
  • Step 3: Conduct a root cause analysis using QI tools such as 5 ‘Whys’ to get to the bottom of the problem.
  • Step 4: The identified problem areas require focused interventions. The QI team, inclusive of relative stakeholders in the facility, recommend solutions.
  • Step 5: Develop a clear plan of action to address the identified issues. Assign responsibilities and set deadlines to ensure accountability using the template below. As much as possible, low-cost and context-based interventions should be used for short-term improvements.
Gaps Interventions to address the gaps Timelines Responsible person
  • Step 6: Monitor implementation of intervention to help you assess the effectiveness of your actions and make any necessary adjustments.

docs.title: 6.1 Data analysis, visualization
docs.text:
• 6.1.1 Data analysis

The routine client satisfaction feedback tool has been integrated in digital platforms to analyse routine client feedback in real-time and automatically convert it into graphs, charts, and trends that are easy to understand using MoH digital systems. The visualizations are designed to mirror strengths and gaps from the routine client feedback and inform on the areas for quality improvement efforts within healthcare facilities.

  • 6.1.2 Visualisation for client feedback will display

  • • Automated graphs, charts, and dashboards for each client feedback parameter and overall satisfaction rate layered from national, regional, district, facility and facility type.

  • • The thresholds of routine client satisfaction are as follows; Excellent and good are considered as satisfied while fair and poor are considered as unsatisfied.
  • • Pareto charts showing the dominant gaps that contribute to 80% of client dissatisfaction.

Users will visualize the data in diverse formats by selecting dropdown options. These options enable the display of different scenarios, including routine client satisfaction parameters categorized by variables such as sex, age, service point, facility type, facility level, district, region, or national level or period. Users can also compare single variables against any selection option.

docs.title: 7.1 Supportive supervision
docs.text: All supervision should prioritize and aim to address issues emerging from the routine client feedback.

docs.title: Appendix 3: Operational definition
docs.text:
Overall cleanliness of the facility: Refers to the physical state of cleanliness and tidiness observed throughout the healthcare facility, including waiting areas, compound, restrooms, corridors, and other public spaces. It encompasses the absence of dirt, dust, clutter, and unpleasant odors. (Client’s feedback may be based on their visual observations and impressions).

Overall timeliness of services: Refers to the client experience and observation of the time taken from arrival to delivery of services and encompasses the duration of waiting times for consultations, tests, treatment, and other healthcare interventions.

Privacy: Refers to client perception of the extent to which their personal information, discussions, examinations, and treatments are kept confidential and protected from unauthorized access or disclosure within the facility. It encompasses physical privacy, such

  • as the availability of private consultation rooms and partitions to shield clients from view during examinations or discussions with healthcare providers. It also includes measures to keep confidential records, verbal communications, and any other sensitive information exchanged between clients and healthcare staff.

Respect: Refers to the manner in which clients are treated with dignity, consideration, and courtesy by healthcare providers and staff throughout their interactions within the facility. It encompasses behavior and communication that demonstrate recognition of clients' autonomy, cultural beliefs, values, and preferences, as well as sensitivity to individual needs and concerns. Respectful conduct includes active listening, empathy, non-judgmental attitudes, and provision of understandable information about diagnoses, treatments, and care plans.

Medicines were available during this visit: Refers to the accessibility and availability of prescribed medications or necessary pharmaceutical products within the healthcare facility

  • at the time of the client's visit. It encompasses medical supplies required for treatment or management of the client’s health conditions.

Received all the services you needed during this visit: Refers to whether clients' healthcare needs were fully addressed and met during their visit to the healthcare facility. It encompasses the extent to which clients received all the necessary medical examinations, treatments, diagnostic tests, consultations, and other healthcare services required to address their health concerns or conditions. The assessment considers whether clients felt that their healthcare needs were comprehensively evaluated, understood, and attended to by healthcare providers and staff during the visit.

Health workers were available to provide the services you needed during this visit: Refers to the availability and accessibility of healthcare professionals within the facility to deliver the required services to clients during their visit. It encompasses the presence of qualified and skilled healthcare providers, including doctors, nurses, specialists, and other allied health professionals, who are capable of addressing clients' healthcare needs effectively. The assessment considers whether clients encountered any difficulties or delays in accessing healthcare services due to the availability or absence of healthcare workers during their visit.

Accessed health/medical information about your condition and what needs to be done: Refers to whether clients were provided with comprehensive information regarding their health condition and the necessary steps to be taken for treatment or management during their visit to the healthcare facility. It encompasses the extent to which clients received clear explanations, instructions, and educational materials from healthcare providers regarding their diagnosis, prognosis, treatment options, medication regimen,

lifestyle modifications, and follow-up care. The assessment considers whether clients felt adequately informed and empowered to make informed decisions about their health and healthcare interventions based on the information provided during the visit.

Able to access health services of your interest in your local community evaluates the ease and availability of healthcare services within the local community that align with clients' preferences and needs. It encompasses the extent to which clients can readily locate and access a variety of healthcare services, including primary care, preventive services, and additional services, such as immunization, health education, diagnostic tests and community outreach services within their locality.

Cost of services (where services are formally paid for): Evaluates the financial implications associated with accessing healthcare services. It encompasses the expenses incurred by clients for receiving healthcare services, including consultation fees, treatment costs, diagnostic tests, medications, medical procedures, and any other out-of-pocket expenses or co-payments required for accessing services. The assessment considers the affordability and transparency of service costs, as well as any financial assistance or insurance coverage available to mitigate the financial burden on clients. It also includes clients' perceptions of the value received in relation to the cost paid for healthcare services.

For the services you received, were you educated on them and your permission requested? Assesses the extent to which clients received information about the healthcare services provided to them and whether their consent was sought before proceeding with the services. It encompasses the provision of clear explanations, instructions, and educational materials by healthcare providers regarding the nature, purpose, risks, benefits, and alternatives of the services offered. Additionally, it evaluates whether clients were given the opportunity to ask questions, express concerns, and make informed decisions about their healthcare based on the information provided. The assessment considers whether healthcare providers obtained clients' consent before initiating any procedures, treatments, or interventions, respecting clients' autonomy and rights to make decisions about their own care.

Did you pay any charges that were not receipted in the form of a bribe? Assesses whether clients made any unofficial payments or financial transactions not documented through receipts, often referred to as bribes, in exchange for healthcare services or preferential treatment within the health facility. It encompasses any monetary exchanges or gifts offered by clients to healthcare providers or staff outside of official billing procedures and documented financial transactions. The assessment aims to identify instances of corruption, unethical conduct, or abuse of power within the healthcare system, where clients may feel compelled to pay additional fees or gratuities to expedite or ensure access to healthcare services.

Overall, were you satisfied with the services you received? Overall, were you satisfied with the services you received? evaluates clients' overall satisfaction with the healthcare services they received during their visit to the facility. It encompasses overall clients' perceptions, feelings, and judgments regarding the healthcare services provided, as well as their overall experience and outcomes of care. The assessment considers various factors that contribute to clients' satisfaction, including the accessibility, responsiveness, competence, empathy, and respectfulness of healthcare providers and staff, timeliness, as well as the availability and effectiveness of healthcare facilities and treatments.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text: Health Information System (HIS) is the processes and mechanisms through which health‐related data is produced and made accessible to users, through networking within and outside the Health Sector. HIS has several sub‐systems, each with specialized roles and responsibilities based on their comparative advantage. HIS sub‐systems in Uganda comprise of Health Management Information system (HMIS), Integrated Disease Surveillance (IDSR), Vital Registration (VR) for births and deaths, National Health Accounts (NHA), Human Resource Information System (HRIS), Logistics Management Information System, Population‐Based Information Systems, Community‐Based Health Information System, Research‐generated health information, administrative records.

docs.title: 1.1 Definition of Standard Operating Procedures
docs.text: By definition, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) within the context of HIS, is a written description of steps for all significant activities relating to the practice of management of HIS that has been approved by a program/ persons in charge of an HIS sub‐system. SOPs should accurately reflect good information management practices, be sufficiently practical and be usable in the HIS sub‐system. The good HIS management practices relate to general aspects of HIS management functions including data collection, compilation, analysis, storage, data processing, record storage, handling of urgent data requests/ needs, management of the devices/ tools/ appliances used to manage the data .

docs.title: 1.2 Justification for Standard Operating Procedures
docs.text:
There are several challenges the existing HIS is facing these include the following among others;

  • • Mushrooming of donor‐driven parallel information systems which have affected the efficiency of data management in various sub‐systems as it overloads the already existing government systems and affects quality of data produced
  • • Poor and incomplete recording of health data,
  • • Use of non‐standardized forms at service delivery points, has been happening owing to lack of or failure to use existing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for setting up information management systems and on management of HIS.
  • • Lack of guidance on how to access health data from the producers
  • • Lack of guidance on how to share data produced e.g. that generated through research and program implementation.

The following are the anticipated benefits of having generic SOPs for HIS;

    1. Harmonization of HIS data management procedures of HIS sub‐systems to ensure efficiency and effective coordination in the use of scare resources
    1. Complete and good quality health data
    1. To provide guidance on how to access health data from the producers
    1. To provide guidance on how to share the health data produced

docs.title: 2.1 Standard Operating Procedures for the Documentation Centre
docs.text: The Ministry of Health (MoH) Documentation Centre has the mandate of book‐keeping including keeping samples of various tools for training, data management (HMIS tools) among others. The Documentation Centre also stores records of regularly produced reports by the Ministry of Health (e.g. Weekly Epidemiological newsletter, quarterly health bulletin, Ministry of Health Statistical Abstract, Annual Health Sector Performance Reports, etc). Other records stored are in the category of research‐generated information including publications and non‐ published research findings. In addition to this, the Documentation Centre disseminates of health information materials (hard copies), a system that has of now been facilitated through establishment of electronic Documentation Centre (e‐Documentation Centre).

docs.title: 2.1.1 Storing Health Records
docs.text:
• Step 1: Write officially to the Librarian expressing the need to send information to the Documentation Centre for storage from both within and outside the health sector.

  • Step 2: The written request should include the following:

  • i. The institution or individual sending the request.

  • ii. Producer/originator of the health information, or Author in case it is a publication or the source of information (e.g. a survey, assessment, etc)
  • iii. Year of publication or compilation or collection.
  • iv. Who published and/or compiled the information.

  • v. If it is a publication published in series, identify the Volume and the Number.

  • Step 3: The Librarian classifies where the information material falls based on the subject, e.g. Malaria, Reproductive Health, Statistics, WHO reports, etc. The librarian receives the health information, after which he/she identifies the appropriate section to store the information material.

  • Step 4: Storage is done according to Classification, the Subject and Number of series.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Accessing/Handling Health Information Material
docs.text:
• Step 1: To access a publication or information material, the user contacts the Librarian and states what he/ she is seeking to access from the Documentation Centre.
  • Step 2: He/ She records his/ her particulars in the Documentation Centre computer, namely:
  • i. Title/ designation
  • ii. Name
  • iii. Organization
  • iv. Purpose for accessing the Documentation Centre
  • v. In case of research, record topic of research being sought.
  • vi. Date of request

  • vii. Telephone/email contact

  • Step 3: User should contact the Librarian for directions on how to access the information material.

  • Step 4: The material should only be read while in the Documentation Centre (NOT TO BE CARRIED OUT), but can be photocopied.

docs.title: 2.2 Standard Operating Procedure for the Knowledge Management Portal
2.2.1 Accessing Knowledge Management Portal
docs.text:
• Step 1: To access the KMP, the user contacts the Librarian and states what he/ she is seeking to access from the e‐Documentation Centre.

  • Step 2: The Librarian provides the web‐site to be accessed. This web‐site is http://library.health.go.ug. There is free access to all documents in the e‐KMP.

  • Step 3: This web‐site allows users access to the electronic publications and health information materials.

  • Step 4: The user can download or print or save the health information material or publication on a flush disk. Most of the materials are in pdf format to prevent modification by users.

docs.title: 2.2.2 Loading Health Information Materials onto the Knowledge Management Portal
docs.text:
• Step 1: Head of the office responsible for management of information in the institution (e.g. Ministry of Health) informs program managers/ Heads of departments about the presence and services provided by the KMP.
  • Step 2: Head of the office responsible for management of information writes officially by email requesting the programs/ departments, to submit all health information materials that they wish to disseminate to users.
  • Step 3: Program manager/ Division Head submits the health information material through the Head of department to the librarian of the institution either by sending through e‐mail of the Librarian (in the case of Ministry of Health, it is librarian.moh@health.go.ug) electronic copies of the publications or health information materials, preferably in pdf format (but can be in any format), or by taking the electronic file physically to the KMP ready for loading.
  • Step 4: Librarian then uploads the health information material onto the KMP
  • Step 5: The submitted document is now ready to be accessed.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Security for Health Information Materials on the Knowledge Management Portal
docs.text:
• Step 1: The producers of health information materials/ publications should endeavor to convert word documents into formats that are not easily edited, for example pdf formats, before they are submitted to the office responsible for management of information in the institution.

  • Step 2: The converted material is then submitted to the Librarian using the following steps:

  • a) Program manager/ Division Head sends an official written request to the Head of the section responsible for the Documentation Centre.

  • b) The request should include:

  • i) Name of sender of information

  • ii) Title/ designation of the sender
  • iii) Organization
  • iv) Topic of the health information to be sent
  • v) In case of research, record topic the research covered.
  • vi) The geographical area and time period of coverage (in case of data).

  • vii) Telephone/email contact

  • c) Once the Documentation Centre has given a go‐ahead to send the health information, the sender can now send, through e‐mail of the Librarian (in the case of Ministry of Health, it is librarian.moh@health.go.ug), electronic copies of the publications or health information, preferably in pdf format (but can be in any format), or by taking the electronic file physically to the Documentation Centre ready for loading.

  • d) Librarian then uploads the health information onto the KMP according to Classification, the Subject and Number of series for the health information.

  • Step 3: The submitted document is now ready to be accessed.

docs.title: 2.3 Standard Operating Procedure for Resource Centre/ HMIS
docs.text:
Health Management Information System (HMIS) is a routine integrated system of collection, collation, analysis, presentation, dissemination and utilization of relevant health‐related information. It is designed for use at the community, health facility, health sub‐district, district health office, and Ministry of Health headquarters for planning, resource allocation, managing and evaluating the health care delivery system. It covers other HIS sub‐systems like Administrative records, Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response.

HMIS procedure manuals including HMIS Data Management Curriculum developed by the Ministry of Health should be used for capacity building at all levels at all times.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Collecting HMIS Data
docs.text:
All health data should be collected using the standard HMIS tools developed and produced by the Ministry of Health as reflected in the HMIS procedure manuals.

Not all health data can be collected through the routine HMIS. In such scenarios other HIS sub‐ systems e.g. UDHS, HIV‐Sero Surveys can be utilized to supplement the routine HMIS. It is important however, to note that such results from such surveys/studies be shared with the Resource Centre, so as to enrich the databases and indicators.

Projects carrying out activities utilising the existing health units should report through these health units using the HMIS tools, so that the Ministry of Health is able to capture the information from their services/activities.

No other person/project/partner is allowed to up‐date, add or edit the HMIS tools without approval from Director General of Health Services through the Assistant Commissioner of Health Services in‐charge of the Resource Centre

No other person/project/partner is allowed to introduce parallel data collection and reporting tools without approval from Director General of Health Services through the Assistant Commissioner of Health Services in‐charge of the Resource Centre.

Steps involved in HMIS data collection include;

  • Step 1: Health data is captured from the clients/patients at the health facility or during out‐reaches and recorded on various medical forms.
  • Step 2: Data recorded on the medical forms is immediately entered into the individual registers. Both steps 1 and 2 above are done by the health workers who are providing the health services. This is done by the incharge while being assisted by the Records Assistant, to ensure that forms are available since he/she (Incharge) has the power to make resource allocation decisions, and also has the role of ensuing that the right HMIS tools are available and utilized by the health workers in collecting health data in steps 1 and 2

  • Step3: The Records Assistant should obtain the different registers and respective tally sheets to tally the recorded health data and generate daily summaries.

  • Step 4: For any unclear information the Records Assistant should consult the health worker before the end of the day to verify the information recorded in the registers.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Reporting HMIS Data
docs.text:
All health data should be reported using the standard HMIS tools developed and produced by the Ministry of Health. This should be done in the stipulated time to ensure timely decision making. Please refer to the HMIS procedure manuals for the deadlines for the different datasets for reporting.

Steps involved in HMIS reporting include;

  • Step 1: Using the daily summary tables compile the weekly and monthly reports.
  • Step 2: Using the monthly summary tables compile the quarterly and annual reports
  • Step 3: The health unit in‐charge should cross check the HMIS reports for errors before submission to the next level
  • Step 4: Submit the respective HMIS form to the next level e.g. HMIS 105 from the health unit to the Health Sub‐District (HSD)
  • Step 5: The summary tables should be retained and regularly up‐dated in the health facility/HSD/District databases.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Providing Feedback to Stakeholders
docs.text:
All health data collected should be analyzed at all levels to generate outputs that will be provided as feedback to improve health service delivery. This should be done regularly on a quarterly basis but can also be done more frequently.

  • Step1: Clean the database before and during data analysis
  • Step2: Analyse the cleaned data to generate the HSSIP and program specific health indicators
  • Step3: Share the findings from your analysis with the stakeholders using any available method e.g. Bulletin, electronic media, meetings etc

docs.title: 2.4 Standard Operating Procedure for Storing and Accessing HMIS Data
docs.text:
Every health unit/HSD/District/National level should have a secure place for storing all HMIS data, preferably metallic cabinets. The person in‐charge of records should be responsible for storing all filled HMIS data in the records store.

Health data should be stored by year and department to ease retrieval. The most current health files (not more than 5years back) should be kept within the records office while other old files (greater than 5years) should be archived.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Accessing Health Facility HMIS Data
docs.text:
• Step 1: The person seeking health data from the health facility begins by expressing his request, in writing, to the District Health Officer copied to the HSD In‐charge and Health Unit in‐charge.

The letter (hardcopy or scanned softcopy) should include: The person/ institution requesting the data The reason why the data is being requested (e.g. research purpose, production of report, monitoring, etc) Data variables required and the period of coverage for the data, indicating:

  • • specific area like maternal deaths, number of live births, number of DPT3
  • • disaggregation by year and or month (Jan, Feb, March, etc), or by sex, or by
  • • geographical coverage (can be the entire country or it may be for list of districts).

This applies to only health facility aggregated data as individual data is confidential. For individual data the individual/institution requesting for data MUST present a letter from the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST).

  • Step 2: After being granted permission from the District Health Officer (through an authority note/letter granting him/her permission to access data), the person requesting presents the authority letter to the health unit in‐charge.
  • Step 3: The person responsible for giving out data, records the details of this person in a register/form, and then the data request is processed.
  • Step 4: After the data has been processed, the data requested is given to the person/institution.

Data accessed through the HMIS MUST be acknowledged and the period. The period for which the data was accessed and the date accessed should be quoted.

The letter (hardcopy or scanned softcopy) should include: The person/ institution requesting the data The reason why the data is being requested (e.g. research purpose, production of report, monitoring, etc) Data variables required and the period of coverage for the data, indicating:

docs.title: 2.4.4 Accessing the National Health Databank
docs.text:
Note that: There is a link between the HIS web‐page and the Ministry of Health web‐site (www.health .go.ug). SOPs will be posted to the HIS web‐page,

This is provided in the steps narrated below:

  • Step 1: The person seeking data from the National Health Data‐bank begins by expressing his request, in writing, to the Assistant commissioner Resource centre copied to Principal Biostatistician, and to the Director General The letter (hardcopy or scanned softcopy) should include:

The person/ institution requesting for data The reason why data is being requested (e.g. research purpose, production of report, monitoring, etc) Data variables required and the period of coverage for the data, indicating:

  • Step 3: The person responsible for giving out data, records the details of this person in a register/form, and then the data request is processed.
  • Step 4: After data has been processed, the data requested is sent to the Principal Biostatistician, who then sends it to the recipient through the person’s/ institution’s email.

docs.title: 2.5 Standard Operating Procedure on ICT for HIS
Software platform:
docs.text:
• • Choice of software to be used for data management will be determined by the data management unit of the Ministry of Health in consultation with other users of health information in the institution like the programs.
  • • Relevant operating systems, applications, programs, and modules that are to be used for management of health information will be tried out by the MoH or designated institution. This will be done to ensure that operating systems, applications, programs, and modules for use at the various levels of health care (health facility, HSD, district and national levels) can withstand the bulk of the database.
  • • The final software selected will be determined based on the technical soundness of the software, usability, inter‐operability and preferably in the public domain.

docs.title: Equipment maintenance:
docs.text:
• • Coordination for maintenance of equipment used for data management will be a responsibility of the data management unit of the Ministry of Health or any other designated institution.
  • • User department/ program/ division/ section should have their data management equipment maintained at least once every 6 months.
  • • Actual maintenance will be carried out by a company identified by the MoH.

docs.title: Technical support on ICT including Data security for transmission and storage sites, provision of system back‐up and data recovery procedures
docs.text:
When a user department/ program/ division/ section is in need of technical services, including anti‐virus security update, these are the steps to follow:

  • Step 1: User department/ program/ division/ section writes a request to the Head of the data management unit of the Ministry of Health, expressing nature of technical support being sought.
  • Step 2: Data management unit Head assigns a person to touch base with the user department/ program/ division/ section and provides the needed technical support, anti‐virus security updates, firewalls, or carry out data back‐up or recovery for computers that have crushed.
  • Step 3: In case of total equipment failure, the Data management unit Head will communicate to the relevant user so that steps can be taken to replace the equipment.
  • Step 4: Thereafter, the user department/ program/ division/ section should log onto the internet at least twice a week, in order to update the anti‐virus security.

The Systems Administrator (SA) will maintain security standards for the use of computing infrastructure in the sector. The SA will also provide support in establishment of Local Area Networks/ Wide Area Networks (LAN/WAN), internet and intranet connectivity, data encryption and decryption methodologies.

  • • This will detail data storage, backup, restore, and disaster‐recovery mechanisms and approaches.
  • • The ICT technical staff will continuously provide direction on relevant systems security to ensure zero level fault tolerance.

docs.title: 2.6 Standard Operating Procedure for Web‐based Health Information System
2.6.1 Accessing Data from the National Health Information System Web‐Page
docs.text:
Health information materials handled by the webpage through linkages with the respective web‐pages or web‐sites include:

  • • Ministry of Health web‐site: National documents/reports produced by Ministry of Health, e.g. like National strategies, National policies, emerging epidemics, current events, weekly epidemiologic newsletters, reports, any reports on health issues that require urgent dissemination. Also handles information on medicines, financing, equipment and health supplies
  • • UNHRO web‐page: For research related publications.
  • • UBOS web‐site, which is www.ubos.org : For population‐based survey results and relevant statistics
  • • Births and Deaths web‐page: For births and deaths statistics.

When a “user” of health data/ information wishes to access health information from the HIS web‐page, these are the steps that should be followed:

  • Step 1: The person seeking health data from the HIS web‐page should first log into internet, ensure that he is on internet. Then type www.health.go.ug in the browser window to access the Ministry of Health web‐site on the internet.

  • Step 2: Click the “Health Information System” link to access the HIS web‐page. There is a linkage to the UBOS, UNRHO web‐sites.

  • Step 3: Once on the HIS web‐page, click onto the category of health data that you wish to access.
  • Step 4: Data is now displayed and is ready to be either printed or saved onto a flush disk or CD.

When a “producer” of health data/ information wishes to have any health information posted onto the HIS web‐page, for the purpose of dissemination to users, these are the steps that should be followed:
